note: Misconceptions our practice items' wrong options represent, by skill, snapshot for the course tree's 'mistakes' text. From the exam-prep bank's generation (prompt v7/v8); every item is still gated before it ships.

access.anchorages.why_wrong: The rule specifically says the decision is made without an engineering analysis, and the person is a competent person. A qualified person's determination is the load-line rule.

access.anchorages.misconception: Duty assigned to the operator's inspection
access.anchorages.why_wrong: The rule does not require a part to be listed as an anchor point in any inspection. The test is whether it looks substantial, checked by a competent person's visual inspection.

access.anchorages.misconception: Field myth that only labeled points are allowed
access.anchorages.why_wrong: The rule allows any apparently substantial part of the equipment and does not require manufacturer markings. Only a competent person's visual conclusion rules a part out.

access.anchorages.misconception: Applies the fall arrest standard to restraint
access.anchorages.why_wrong: Restraint has its own criterion of twice the maximum load the employee may impose. The fall arrest anchorage criteria apply to personal fall arrest systems.
The factor is two, not three, and it is based on the maximum load the employee may impose, not simply body weight plus tools.
Hook and load-line capacity come into play only when a fall arrest system is anchored to the load line. Restraint anchorages are judged by the twice-the-maximum-load test.

access.anchorages.misconception: Borrows the person from the equipment-anchorage rule
access.anchorages.why_wrong: A competent person's visual check governs apparently substantial parts of the equipment. Anchoring to the load line needs a qualified person's determination.
The operator must be at the work site and informed of the use, but the operator is not the one assigned to make the capacity determination.
The assembly/disassembly director supervises assembly and disassembly. The load-line tie-off rule assigns the determination to a qualified person.
The rule specifically says the competent person's judgment is made without an engineering analysis. Requiring one would cancel the allowance.

access.anchorages.misconception: Field myth about designated points only
access.anchorages.why_wrong: The allowance covers any apparently substantial part of the equipment, not only points the manufacturer has designated.
A qualified person's determination is required for tie-off to the hook or load line, not for an apparently substantial part of the crane's structure.

access.anchorages.misconception: Extends the visual allowance to portable devices
access.anchorages.why_wrong: A visual check of the boom does not prove the portable device is strong enough. The device must meet the anchorage criteria on its own.

access.anchorages.misconception: Applies the restraint criterion to fall arrest
access.anchorages.why_wrong: Twice the maximum load is the fall restraint criterion. A device used for personal fall arrest must meet the fall arrest anchorage criteria.
The qualified person's determination is only one of three required conditions. The operator's presence and the empty hook are also required.

access.anchorages.misconception: Substitutes lockout for the operator condition
access.anchorages.why_wrong: Shutting the crane down is not one of the conditions. The rule still requires the operator to be at the site and informed.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: Four feet is a general-industry walking-working surface number. The construction crane rule for non-assembly work uses more than 6 feet.
No 10-foot trigger appears in this rule. The general trigger is more than 6 feet, and 15 feet applies only to walking on horizontal lattice booms.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Special-case number used as the general rule
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: The 15-foot figure applies only to moving point-to-point on a horizontal lattice boom. It is not the general trigger.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: General trigger applied to the horizontal lattice exception
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: More than 6 feet is the general trigger. It applies to walking on non-lattice booms and on lattice booms that are not horizontal, not on horizontal lattice booms.
Twenty feet is too high. Protection is required starting at a 15-foot fall distance.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Harness-only habit assumed to be the crane rule
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: Many crews assume belts are banned everywhere. For crane fall arrest and fall restraint, the rule allows either a belt or a harness.
The rule does not split body wear by system type. Either a belt or a harness may be used in both arrest and restraint systems.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Specific gear combination mistaken for the rule
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: The rule does not specify a harness plus a particular lanyard. It permits belts or harnesses, and components must meet § 1926.502(d), except (d)(15).

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Lattice-boom exception applied to a telescopic boom
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: The 15-ft exception applies only to horizontal lattice booms. A telescopic boom is non-lattice, so the 6-ft trigger applies.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Belief that walking on a lowered boom is exempt
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: Walking point-to-point is not exempt. It is specifically covered on non-lattice booms, on lattice booms that are not horizontal, and on horizontal lattice booms at 15 ft or more.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Work-station rule thought to be the only trigger
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: Work stations are covered, but so is walking on a non-lattice boom above 6 ft. Protection is needed during the walk itself.
Only lattice booms that are not horizontal are covered at the 6-ft trigger. Horizontal lattice booms are covered only at a 15-ft fall or more.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Invented split between restraint and arrest
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: The rule does not split restraint and arrest by height. Below 15 ft on a horizontal lattice boom, walking does not trigger the requirement at all.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Walking allowance applied to a work station
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: The 15-ft condition applies to moving point-to-point on a horizontal lattice boom, not to working at a station on it.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Deck exception stretched to cover the boom
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: The deck exception covers the deck only. The rule names the boom, of any type, as a covered work-station location.

access.fall-protection-thresholds.misconception: Draw-works condition applied to the boom
access.fall-protection-thresholds.why_wrong: Running equipment matters only for the draw-works exception. A boom work station is covered whether or not the engine runs.

access.maintenance.misconception: Applying the general threshold to horizontal lattice travel
access.maintenance.why_wrong: The general exposure threshold is more than 6 feet, but point-to-point travel on a horizontal lattice boom has the specific threshold of 15 feet or more.
The requirement includes a fall distance of exactly 15 feet; it does not begin only above that height.
The specified threshold for this travel is 15 feet or more, not 20 feet.
This crane maintenance provision specifies more than 6 feet, not a 4-foot threshold.
The work-station trigger is more than 6 feet above a lower level.

access.maintenance.misconception: Treating an exclusive threshold as inclusive
access.maintenance.why_wrong: The wording is more than 6 feet, so exactly 6 feet does not trigger this provision.

access.maintenance.misconception: Assigning employer duties to the operator
access.maintenance.why_wrong: Assigning an operator to the crane does not transfer the employer's training duty to that operator.

access.maintenance.misconception: Assigning all site safety duties to the controlling entity
access.maintenance.why_wrong: This provision assigns the duty to the exposed employee's employer, not to the controlling entity merely because it controls the project.

access.maintenance.misconception: Confusing equipment ownership with employment responsibility
access.maintenance.why_wrong: Ownership alone does not establish this duty; the requirement is directed to the employee's employer.

access.maintenance.misconception: Inventing one threshold for all horizontal booms
access.maintenance.why_wrong: Eight feet is not a special horizontal-boom travel threshold. Boom construction matters: horizontal lattice travel has a 15-foot threshold.

access.maintenance.misconception: Classifying all inspection activity as stationary work
access.maintenance.why_wrong: Moving between inspection locations is point-to-point travel, not automatically work at a station. Non-lattice boom travel is covered directly.

access.maintenance.misconception: Removing the height threshold for telescopic cranes
access.maintenance.why_wrong: This provision retains the more-than-6-foot exposure threshold; it does not require protection at every height.
Travel on an inclined lattice boom is itself covered when the unprotected exposure exceeds 6 feet.

access.maintenance.misconception: Applying the horizontal-lattice threshold to an inclined boom
access.maintenance.why_wrong: The 15-foot travel threshold applies to horizontal lattice booms, not inclined lattice booms.

access.maintenance.misconception: Making tool carrying the fall-protection trigger
access.maintenance.why_wrong: Carrying tools does not determine whether this travel requirement applies; boom orientation and fall exposure do.
The general more-than-6-foot condition does not eliminate the specific 15-foot threshold for horizontal lattice travel.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Ladder rung width carried over to walkways
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: 16 inches is a figure people remember from ladder rung clear width, not boom walkways. The boom walkway minimum is 12 inches.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: General walking-surface figure applied to booms
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: 18 inches is a common guess borrowed from general walking-surface figures. The crane rule sets 12 inches for boom walkways.
24 inches is much wider than a lattice boom section usually allows. The rule requires only 12 inches.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Construction guardrail height applied to booms
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: 42 inches is the nominal top-rail height in general construction guardrail rules. Boom walkway railings are capped at 45 inches.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Treating a maximum as a minimum
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: This treats the rule as a minimum height. Boom walkway railings have only a 45-inch maximum, and they are not required at all.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Guardrail tolerance band applied to booms
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: 39 inches is the low end of the general 42 ± 3 inch guardrail tolerance. The boom walkway rule sets only a 45-inch maximum.
A 4-foot profile does not trigger the rule. Walkways are required at 6 feet or more.
8 feet is a neighboring guess. The trigger is 6 feet, so a 7-foot boom built after the cutoff needs a walkway.
10 feet would leave out many large booms that the rule covers. The trigger is 6 feet.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Optional height limit read as a requirement
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: 45 inches is the most a railing may be where one is allowed, but no railing is required. On a pendant boom, a rail that could snag the pendants is prohibited.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Construction guardrail rule applied to cranes
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: That is the general construction guardrail design, and it does not apply to crane equipment. Boom walkway railings are not required.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Prohibited railing type proposed as a fix
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: Removable railings, the kind installed and removed at each assembly or disassembly, are prohibited on boom walkways.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Height limit treated as the only test
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: Meeting the height limit does not matter here. Railings designed to be installed and removed at each assembly are prohibited no matter how tall they are.

access.walkways-steps.misconception: Applying only one of two prohibitions
access.walkways-steps.why_wrong: Snagging is one ground for prohibition. The removable-type ban is a separate ground that applies on its own.
No sign-off makes a removable railing acceptable. The removable type is prohibited outright.
The November 8, 2011 date controls what new equipment must have. Steps, handholds and grabrails a crane was originally equipped with must be kept in good condition no matter its age.

assembly.boom-dismantling.why_wrong: Clearing a bearing surface is partial removal. The prohibition applies before that point, while the pendant remains in tension.
There is no halfway allowance. Any partial removal is prohibited while the pendant is in tension.
Leaving the tapered end engaged does not satisfy the restriction. The pin must not be partly removed under pendant tension.
The restriction includes bottom pins as well as top pins. It does not distinguish between the two rows in this portion of the boom.
Top pins are also prohibited from removal. The restriction covers both rows while the pendants are in tension.
The restriction is not limited to the boom foot. It covers section pins throughout the stated region between the pendant attachments and the crane body.
The restriction also applies when the uppermost section rests on another support. Bare ground is not the only triggering surface.
Raised cribbing can trigger the restriction, but so can the ground. The rule covers either support condition.

assembly.boom-dismantling.misconception: Confusing pendant support with resting support
assembly.boom-dismantling.why_wrong: This restriction concerns the uppermost section resting on the ground or another support. Pendant tension creates separate pin-removal restrictions.
Controlling sideways movement does not remove pendant tension. Partial pin withdrawal remains prohibited while that tension exists.
Remaining engaged in one plate does not authorize partial removal. The pendant must no longer be in tension before withdrawal starts.
Reducing tension by half leaves the pendant in tension. The rule provides no reduced-tension allowance.
The top pin is also prohibited from removal under this condition. Changing which row goes first does not resolve pendant tension.
Another stack alone does not establish that pendant tension has been relieved. The pin remains prohibited from removal while that tension continues.
Retaining the opposite pin does not create an exception. No top or bottom section pin in this region may be withdrawn while the pendants are tensioned.
A sling becoming taut does not by itself establish full support. The entire cantilevered section being removed must be fully supported first.

assembly.capacity-limits.why_wrong: An assist crane does not determine when the limits apply. Rated capacity limits apply during every phase of assembly and disassembly.
The limits also apply before connections are secured. Partially assembled components must remain within their applicable ratings.
Contact with a support does not suspend capacity limits. Limits apply to the loads imposed during supported and suspended phases.

assembly.capacity-limits.misconception: Proof load treated as working capacity
assembly.capacity-limits.why_wrong: A proof-test load is not the permitted assembly load. The applicable rated capacity governs.

assembly.capacity-limits.misconception: Stability treated as the only limit
assembly.capacity-limits.why_wrong: Tipping is not the only possible limit. A component's rated capacity can be reached before the crane approaches tipping.
Breaking strength is not an allowable working load. Assembly loads must remain within rated capacity.
Using multiple attachments does not eliminate an individual lug's limit. Each lug must remain within its applicable rating.
Unused crane capacity cannot offset an overloaded lug. The separate capacity limits must all be respected.
Blocking can change the load imposed on a lug, but it does not permit that load to exceed the lug's rating.
An 8,000 lb section would exceed the lug's 6,000 lb rating. The sling's higher rating does not remove that restriction.

assembly.capacity-limits.misconception: Crane capacity governs the entire system
assembly.capacity-limits.why_wrong: That load would exceed both the sling and lug ratings. All applicable capacity limits must be satisfied.
Components in the same load path do not contribute additive capacity. Each must carry the load without exceeding its own rating.
The pickup load is below the attachment's 9,000 lb rating. The support-transfer load is the listed overload.
The alignment load is within the attachment's rating. A separate, later phase exceeds that rating.
The pinned-position load is within the rating. An acceptable final load does not excuse the earlier overload.
Removing the blocking would overload the 8,000 lb attachment. The support transfer must not impose that load.

assembly.components.misconception: Duty assigned to the A/D director
assembly.components.why_wrong: The A/D director supervises the assembly but cannot set the cantilever limit. Without manufacturer data, a registered professional engineer must set it.

assembly.components.misconception: Qualified person substituted for an RPE
assembly.components.why_wrong: Calling someone a qualified person does not meet this requirement. The rule calls for a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment type.

assembly.components.misconception: Competent person substituted for an RPE
assembly.components.why_wrong: Inspecting the sections does not set a structural limit. Only the manufacturer, or a registered professional engineer when manufacturer data is unavailable, can set it.

assembly.components.misconception: Specific marking method assumed to be required
assembly.components.why_wrong: Marking the component is one way to make the weight available, but the rule only requires that it be readily available. It does not require a specific marking method.
The requirement covers each component, not only those lifted by an assist crane. Weights also matter for blocking, cantilevering and the crane's own stability.

assembly.components.misconception: Duty assigned to the controlling entity
assembly.components.why_wrong: The rule does not require a controlling-entity lift plan for component weights. It requires the weights to be readily available.
The rule covers reusable shipping hardware and requires it to be stowed or stored, not thrown away. It will be needed again for transport.

assembly.components.misconception: Keeps hardware with the section but creates a drop hazard
assembly.components.why_wrong: Loose hardware lying on a boom walkway is exactly the falling object hazard the rule is meant to prevent once the boom is raised.

assembly.components.misconception: Storage tied to the wrong event
assembly.components.why_wrong: The rule does not link storage of the hardware to the post-assembly inspection. It only requires storage that creates no falling object hazard.
A physical fit check does not show the insert meets this crane's structural design. The A/D director cannot replace the manufacturer's specifications.
Weight is only one factor. Chord size, lacing and design loads differ between models, and the rule ties component selection to manufacturer specifications.

assembly.components.misconception: Inspection or testing treated as approval
assembly.components.why_wrong: The post-assembly inspection confirms compliance with the selection rule. It cannot make an unapproved component compliant, and a test lift does not either.
The assembly rule requires an inspection for configuration compliance. It does not require a proof load test after every assembly.
A shift inspection does not replace the post-assembly inspection, which specifically checks that the assembled configuration is compliant.
Changing the boom length does not trigger an annual inspection. The required check is the post-assembly inspection for configuration compliance.
Removing them from the jib meets only half of the rule. Once removed, they must also be stored where they cannot fall.

assembly.director.misconception: Operator experience substitutes for competent-person criteria
assembly.director.why_wrong: An experienced operator's presence does not establish the required competent-person role. The director must meet both criteria or be a competent person assisted by qualified persons.

assembly.director.misconception: Crew experience substitutes for qualified assistance
assembly.director.why_wrong: Experience with similar work does not by itself establish that the assistants meet qualified-person criteria. Qualified assistance is required when the competent director does not also meet those criteria.

assembly.director.misconception: Two qualified persons replace a competent person
assembly.director.why_wrong: Two qualified persons do not establish that either meets competent-person criteria. The director must be a competent person as part of either permitted arrangement.

assembly.director.misconception: Shift-start review satisfies the timing requirement
assembly.director.why_wrong: A shift-start review is not the specified timing if assembly begins later. The required review occurs immediately before assembly or disassembly starts.

assembly.director.misconception: Planning review replaces the immediate review
assembly.director.why_wrong: An earlier planning meeting does not replace the required review immediately before the work begins when the exception does not apply.

assembly.director.misconception: First pin connection defines the review deadline
assembly.director.why_wrong: Assembly operations can begin before the first boom pin connection. The review must precede commencement of the operations, not just that connection.
Rated capacities do not replace instruction about hazardous positions or locations. The director must ensure understanding of all three required subjects.

assembly.director.misconception: Signals replace instruction about task hazards
assembly.director.why_wrong: Communication signals do not replace understanding of task hazards. Task hazards are a separate required subject.
Discussing qualifications does not establish that crew members understand their assigned tasks. Task understanding is expressly required.

assembly.director.misconception: Same crane type is enough for the exception
assembly.director.why_wrong: The exception requires prior application to the same type and configuration. Experience with the crane type alone is insufficient.

assembly.director.misconception: Crew review substitutes for director review
assembly.director.why_wrong: Crew review does not replace the director's required review. The director has not previously applied the procedures to this configuration.

assembly.director.misconception: Review can wait until the changed step
assembly.director.why_wrong: The review must occur immediately before assembly begins. Waiting until a later assembly step misses that deadline.

assembly.director.misconception: Documented procedure review replaces crew understanding
assembly.director.why_wrong: A recorded review of the complete procedure is not the stated requirement for each crew member. The director must ensure understanding of the three required subjects.
Pairing the replacement with an experienced rigger does not postpone the instruction requirement. The required understanding must be established when personnel are added.

assembly.director.misconception: Matching qualifications transfers the earlier briefing
assembly.director.why_wrong: Matching qualifications does not establish understanding of this assignment's hazards and locations to avoid. New personnel must receive the required instruction.

assembly.director.misconception: Instruction may follow the first supervised step
assembly.director.why_wrong: The requirements must be met before the crew member takes on the different task. The first positioning step is already part of that task.

assembly.fall-protection.misconception: General construction trigger applied to A/D
assembly.fall-protection.why_wrong: Many workers know 6 feet as the trigger for other construction work. The A/D rule sets a higher trigger: more than 15 feet.
10 feet is not the A/D trigger. Fall protection is required when the unprotected edge is more than 15 feet above a lower level.
20 feet is too high. The requirement starts once the surface is more than 15 feet above a lower level.

assembly.fall-protection.misconception: Fixed arrest-anchor rating applied to restraint
assembly.fall-protection.why_wrong: A fixed pound rating is not the restraint test for crane parts. The part must withstand twice the maximum load the employee may impose under reasonably anticipated use.
The restraint rule calls for no qualified-person analysis. The test is whether the part can withstand twice the maximum load the employee may impose.
Four times overstates the rule. The required factor for restraint anchorages on the equipment is two.
The boom is not a listed exception. Work on boom sections above 15 feet requires fall protection.
The gantry is not on the exception list. The exceptions are the draw-works when the equipment is running, the cab, and the deck.
Jib sections are not excepted. Above 15 feet at an unprotected edge, fall protection is required.
The A/D rule has a set height trigger, more than 15 feet. It does not require fall protection at every height.
The height alone would trigger the rule, but the deck is a listed exception, so the requirement does not apply there.

assembly.fall-protection.misconception: Exception assigned to the wrong person
assembly.fall-protection.why_wrong: The exception is tied to where the employee is, not to the job title. Any employee on the deck is covered by it.
The deck is not treated as the lower level. The worker is excepted because the deck is a listed location, not because the height is measured from it.
Neither a qualified person nor written approval is required. The only check is a competent person's visual judgment.
A portable anchor device is not required. The worker may tie off directly to an apparently substantial part of the equipment.

assembly.fall-protection.misconception: Direct tie-off rule applied to portable device
assembly.fall-protection.why_wrong: The apparently-substantial test applies when tying off directly to the equipment, not to portable anchor devices.

assembly.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: ASME B30.5 is a consensus practice standard. The federal rule ties component selection to the manufacturer's requirements, not to a general standard.
A lift plan covers how a lift is made. It cannot authorize a jib configuration the manufacturer does not allow.

assembly.jibs-extensions.misconception: Wrong person; borrowing another model's data
assembly.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: The A/D director supervises assembly but cannot replace manufacturer specifications. Charts for a different model never apply to this crane.
A qualified person handles many crane tasks, but this approval specifically requires a registered professional engineer.
The A/D director runs the assembly. When manufacturer instructions are missing, the director cannot approve the configuration.
The approval must be in writing and must come from a registered professional engineer. A competent person's verbal approval meets neither requirement.
Monthly inspections are a separate requirement. The configuration check is due as soon as assembly is complete, not weeks later.
Shift inspections are routine visual checks. The rule calls for a specific inspection once assembly is complete.
Waiting for the annual inspection would mean running an unverified configuration. The rule requires the inspection upon completion of assembly.

assembly.jibs-extensions.misconception: RPE path used when instructions exist
assembly.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: The standalone engineer approval in (m)(1)(i) applies only when manufacturer instructions are unavailable. Here they exist and prohibit the jib.
A load test does not authorize a configuration the manufacturer prohibits. The configuration must follow the manufacturer or an approved modification.

assembly.jibs-extensions.misconception: Physical fit equals approval; wrong person
assembly.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: A jib whose pins fit is still not approved. The A/D director has no authority to override a manufacturer prohibition.
The requirement covers any attached jib, whether fixed or luffing. The only exception is for derricks.
Pendants do not stop a jib from being pulled back over the boom if a load releases suddenly. Stops are required anyway.
The rule ties jib stops to the jib being attached, not to a particular offset angle.
Extending the boom pulls the tip away from the extension's lugs and stowage brackets, so the pins cannot be lined up as designed.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Assigning personal notification to the director
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: Supervising assembly does not transfer this notification duty to the director. The entering crew member must inform the operator.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Assigning all communication to the signal person
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: Directing movements does not make the signal person responsible for the entering crew member's notification duty.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Treating a work assignment as notification
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: Assigning work does not replace the entering crew member's obligation to inform the operator before entering.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Restricting only the component under repair
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: The restriction is not limited to the assembly receiving work. It covers any part of the equipment or load.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Allowing movement away from the worker
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: The restriction is not limited to movement toward the worker. Moving away also remains prohibited until the required communication.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Treating radius change as the trigger
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: A movement need not change radius to be prohibited. The restriction covers any equipment part or load.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Treating a radio method as mandatory
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: A dedicated radio channel may be part of the arrangement, but this rule does not require that particular method.
This rule requires communication through the pre-arranged system, not a mandatory written release from the director.
A face-to-face exchange is not universally required. The communication must follow the arrangement established in advance.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Reporting arrival instead of planned entry
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: Notification after entry is too late. The operator must be informed before the crew member goes to that location.
The notification duty is triggered by entry into the covered location, not by a later request to move.
Waiting until work begins could leave the entry itself unannounced. Notification must precede going into the hidden location.
Notifying the director instead of the operator does not fulfill the requirement to inform the operator.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Treating physical contact as the trigger
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: Contact with the counterweight is not the trigger. Entry into the hidden location where movement could injure the worker requires prior notification.

assembly.out-of-view.misconception: Replacing entry notification with movement warning
assembly.out-of-view.why_wrong: A warning just before swinging does not replace notification before the worker enters the covered location.
A horn warning does not replace the required safe-position communication. The empty hook remains part of the equipment.

assembly.outriggers.misconception: capacity margin substitutes for chart position
assembly.outriggers.why_wrong: No percentage of capacity allows partial extension. The beams must be fully extended or set in a position the manufacturer permits and the load chart covers.
No one on site can approve an extension the manufacturer does not provide for. Partial positions are allowed only through the manufacturer's procedures and the load chart.

assembly.outriggers.misconception: visibility rule confused with extension rule
assembly.outriggers.why_wrong: A cramped site does not create an exception, and a signal person watching only covers the visibility rule. The position still has to be one the load chart covers.
The float rule covers both: outrigger floats go on the outriggers, and stabilizer floats go on the stabilizers.
Each outrigger and each stabilizer must be visible to the operator or a signal person during extension and setting.
The blocking placement rule names both outriggers and stabilizers.
The operator does not have to see it personally. A signal person can watch an outrigger the operator cannot see.
The visibility rule names the operator or a signal person, not the A/D director.
A rigger is not one of the people the rule names. The watcher must be the operator or a signal person.
The rule has a separate sentence for stabilizers: stabilizer floats that are used must be attached to the stabilizers.
Centering a loose float does not meet the rule. The float must be attached, not just placed in the right spot.
Floats are not prohibited. If they are used, they must be attached, and blocking belongs under the float or pad.
Sound timber is required of all blocking, but it does not make this location acceptable. On a jacked outrigger, blocking goes only under the float or pad.

assembly.outriggers.misconception: visibility rule confused with blocking rule
assembly.outriggers.why_wrong: The visibility rule covers extending and setting the outriggers. It does not allow blocking at points other than the float or pad.

assembly.outriggers.misconception: jackless-design rule applied to jacked outrigger
assembly.outriggers.why_wrong: The outer bearing surface is the blocking point only for outriggers built without a jack. This crane has jacks, so blocking goes under the float or pad.
Cutting the full-extension rating by a rule-of-thumb factor is not a rating. The beams must be set as the load chart specifies, and that table's capacities apply.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Confuses competent person with qualified person
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: A competent person identifies hazards and has the authority to correct them, but this inspection must be done by a qualified person.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Assumes operator certification covers the inspection
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: Operator certification does not make someone a qualified person. The operator can do this inspection only if he separately meets the qualified-person standard.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Applies the no-criteria RPE path to every inspection
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: An engineer is not required for the standard inspection. An RPE comes in only when manufacturer criteria are unavailable and a qualified person decides one is needed to develop criteria.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Substitutes the lift plan for the equipment criteria
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: A lift plan describes a particular lift. It does not set the standard for how the crane has to be configured after assembly.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Confuses periodic inspection records with configuration criteria
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: The annual record documents the crane's earlier condition. The post-assembly check is against the manufacturer's configuration criteria.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Treats an in-house checklist as the governing criteria
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: A crew checklist can help, but the required standard is the manufacturer equipment criteria. Criteria are developed by others only when the manufacturer's are unavailable.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Assigns the duty to the site controller
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: The controlling entity coordinates the site, but the rule gives the RPE decision to the qualified person.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Confuses the employer's duty to ensure with the qualified person's duty to decide
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: The employer must make sure the criteria get developed by the right person, but the qualified person decides whether an RPE is needed.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Assigns an inspection decision to the operator by default
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: The operator has no assigned role in this decision unless he is also the qualified person.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Substitutes the shift inspection for the post-assembly inspection
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: A shift inspection does not replace the post-assembly inspection, and the rule bars any use before that inspection.
Holding the crane is right, but the release must come from a qualified person's inspection against the criteria, not a competent person's checklist.
The rule has no light-load exception. A pick on a misconfigured boom can fail even at a small load.

assembly.post-assembly.misconception: Assumes missing criteria always require an RPE
assembly.post-assembly.why_wrong: Missing criteria do not automatically require an RPE. The qualified person decides, and here decided one is not needed.
The rule assigns development to the qualified person (or to an RPE if one is needed), not to the operator.
Criteria must be developed first, and the crane is then inspected against them. Judgment alone is not enough.
The rule does not require an independent inspector. Being qualified is what counts.

assembly.procedures.why_wrong: Assignment as the operator does not establish qualification to develop procedures. A qualified person must develop them.
Assignment as the inspector does not establish qualification to develop procedures. The developer must be a qualified person.
Supervisory responsibility alone is insufficient. The person developing employer procedures must be qualified.
Wire-rope slings do not trigger this specific requirement. Synthetic slings do.
Alloy-chain slings do not trigger this specific requirement. The stated trigger is synthetic slings.
A spreader beam alone does not trigger this requirement. The use of synthetic slings does.
Manufacturer prohibitions apply under either procedure choice. Selecting employer procedures does not remove them.
Qualified-person involvement does not authorize an employer to override applicable manufacturer prohibitions.
Applicable manufacturer prohibitions remain mandatory when employer procedures are used.

assembly.procedures.misconception: Employer procedures are only a fallback
assembly.procedures.why_wrong: The employer-procedure option is not limited to cases with missing manufacturer instructions. It depends on meeting the specified requirements.
Manufacturer approval is not the stated condition for selecting employer procedures. The employer must demonstrate compliance with the employer-procedure requirements.
Inspector authorization is not the stated basis for selecting employer procedures. The required demonstration of compliance controls.
Calling the work routine setup does not exclude attachment assembly from the procedure-selection requirements.
Selecting and using slings does not replace the requirements governing assembly of the crane attachment.
Attachment assembly is covered without a condition that the main boom also be removed.
The support and stability requirement applies to all parts, including a detached boom section.

assembly.rigging.misconception: competent person confused with qualified rigger
assembly.rigging.why_wrong: A competent person is a different qualification from a qualified rigger. The A/D rigging rule names a qualified rigger for the rigging work.

assembly.rigging.misconception: duty assigned to the A/D director
assembly.rigging.why_wrong: The rule does not reserve rigging for the A/D director. It requires that whoever does the rigging is a qualified rigger.

assembly.rigging.misconception: operator certification assumed to cover rigging
assembly.rigging.why_wrong: Operator certification covers running the crane, not rigging. The rigging must be done by a qualified rigger.
Paragraph (r)(3) requires following the synthetic sling manufacturer's instructions. It says nothing about wire rope slings.

assembly.rigging.misconception: crane rope rules confused with sling rules
assembly.rigging.why_wrong: The A/D rigging paragraph does not send you to this section for sling protection. It points to 1926.251(c)(9).

assembly.rigging.misconception: qualified rigger paragraph mistaken for protection rule
assembly.rigging.why_wrong: Paragraph (r)(1) requires a qualified rigger. It does not cover how wire rope slings are protected.

assembly.rigging.misconception: crane manufacturer instead of sling manufacturer
assembly.rigging.why_wrong: The crane manufacturer's procedures govern the crane, but the rule names the sling manufacturer as the source for how the synthetic slings are used.
The qualified rigger does the rigging but cannot replace the sling manufacturer's limits with personal judgment. The rule requires following the sling manufacturer.

assembly.rigging.misconception: capacity margin substituted for edge protection
assembly.rigging.why_wrong: Extra rated capacity does not stop a sharp edge from cutting webbing under load. The rule requires protecting the sling from the edge.
Spreading the load does not keep the edges off the webbing. Every sling that touches a sharp edge still needs protection.
Synthetic slings are permitted in A/D. The rule sets protection and manufacturer requirements for them; it does not ban them.
The rule is about who does the rigging, not who watches it. The person rigging must be a qualified rigger.
The rigger requirement applies whenever rigging is used for assembly/disassembly, and that includes counterweight, not only boom sections.
A low load does not cancel a manufacturer limitation. A tight bend also concentrates stress on the sling, which is the reason the minimum exists.
The rigger cannot waive the sling manufacturer's limitations. The rule says they must be followed.
No rule bans basket hitches for synthetic slings in A/D. Here the problem is the pin size, not the hitch type.

assembly.specific-hazards.misconception: Shift-inspection interval applied to an event-based test
assembly.specific-hazards.why_wrong: No once-per-shift test satisfies the rule. The test is tied to each time the brake will be relied on, which can happen several times in one shift.

assembly.specific-hazards.misconception: One test covers the whole job
assembly.specific-hazards.why_wrong: One test at the start does not cover later steps. Each new reliance on the brake needs its own test first.

assembly.specific-hazards.misconception: Confusing the A/D brake test with periodic inspection
assembly.specific-hazards.why_wrong: Routine inspections are separate from this A/D requirement. The brake must be tested right before each reliance during assembly or disassembly.
The operator may run the crane during A/D, but the duty to address the listed A/D hazards belongs to the A/D director.

assembly.specific-hazards.misconception: Duty assigned to the controlling entity
assembly.specific-hazards.why_wrong: The controlling entity has site duties such as ground conditions. Addressing the A/D hazards belongs to the A/D director.
A rigger may carry out rigging tasks, but the rule makes the supervising A/D director responsible for the hazards.

assembly.specific-hazards.misconception: Trigger tied to assist crane use
assembly.specific-hazards.why_wrong: Which crane makes the lift does not trigger the requirement. What matters is whether the stability method needs the CG.
The rule does not require the CG of every component in every case. It applies when the stability method depends on it.

assembly.specific-hazards.misconception: Confusing weight with center of gravity
assembly.specific-hazards.why_wrong: A marked weight does not tell you the CG location, and the trigger is the stability method, not the markings.

assembly.specific-hazards.misconception: Thinking only hook loads cause tipping
assembly.specific-hazards.why_wrong: In this configuration the danger comes from the counterweight, not a hook load. An empty hook gives the least forward moment.
Backward stability applies before swinging, before travel and when attaching or removing components, not only to travel.
A brake test is required only when the crew will rely on the brake to hold the boom. It does not deal with tipping backward during the swing.

assembly.specific-hazards.misconception: Pin order as a substitute for support
assembly.specific-hazards.why_wrong: Pulling the pins at the same time does not make the sections stable. Stability has to come from rigging or support before any pin comes out.
Resting on the ground does not make a section stable. Once the pins are out, a poorly supported section can shift or fall off its blocking.
Having enough blocking capacity is a separate requirement. Even strong blocking can damage the lacing if it is in the wrong place.
Stacking method affects stability, but it does not fix blocking that loads the wrong members.

assembly.under-boom.why_wrong: The rule assigns this demonstration to the employer, not to the operator by virtue of operating the crane.
Inspecting the crane does not assign responsibility for demonstrating site constraints. That responsibility belongs to the employer.
Directing assist-crane movements does not make the signal person responsible for this demonstration. The employer must make it.
Being the operator does not assign this duty. The assembly/disassembly director must implement the procedures.

assembly.under-boom.misconception: Rigging supervision substitutes for A/D direction
assembly.under-boom.why_wrong: A rigging supervisor does not receive this duty merely through that title. The duty belongs to the A/D director.
The inspector's role does not replace the A/D director's responsibility to implement the exception procedures.
The restriction is not limited to the main boom or to devices called pins. It includes jibs, other components, and similar devices.

assembly.under-boom.misconception: Literal pins and named components only
assembly.under-boom.why_wrong: The rule also covers other components and devices similar to pins.
The restriction applies while pins or similar devices are being removed, not just when the final connection is removed.
A spotter does not establish the exception. Available side access means the proposed exposure is a convenience, not a demonstrated site necessity.
There is no one-minute allowance. Minimizing duration is required within the exception; it does not create the exception.
This rule does not require another crane for every pin-removal operation. For the stated access issue, the worker must remain out from underneath.
Support can reduce unintended movement, but it does not independently authorize exposure underneath. The exception's site-constraint requirement must also be met.
Blocking does not automatically waive the restriction. Support measures do not replace the requirement to demonstrate necessary exposure.
The restriction applies during pin removal, including removal of the first pin. It is not limited to the last connection.

assembly.under-boom.misconception: Only the last jib pin matters
assembly.under-boom.why_wrong: The restriction applies while pins are being removed, not only when the last pin is reached.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Applies the post-2011 lattice rule to an older crane
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: The automatic-only requirement applies to lattice cranes and derricks built after November 8, 2011. A 2005 lattice crane may use a warning device instead.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Treats temporary measures as permanent compliance
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Cable marking or a spotter is a temporary alternative measure, not a substitute for the device. A lattice crane built after Feb 28, 1992 must have a device.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Adds a spotter requirement the rule does not impose
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: A warning device alone is acceptable if it warns in time at every point where two-blocking could occur. The rule does not require a spotter with it.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Misses that concrete bucket work is excepted
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Concrete bucket work is on the exception list for lattice boom equipment, so the device requirement does not apply to it.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Misses that magnet work is excepted
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Magnet work is on the exception list for lattice boom equipment.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Misses that pile driving is excepted
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Pile driving work is on the exception list for lattice boom equipment.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Applies the lattice 'or' measure to a telescopic crane
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Marking or a spotter (either one) is the lattice boom measure. Telescopic cranes need both, with the spotter used during boom extension.
The telescopic measure requires the cable to be clearly marked. A spotter alone does not satisfy it.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Substitutes a field practice for the required spotter
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Slowing the hoist is not a listed measure. The rule pairs the cable mark with a spotter when extending the boom.
This is the requirement for lattice cranes built after Nov 8, 2011, but the drop ball exception overrides it for this work.
This is the requirement for lattice cranes built between 1992 and 2011. Neither date rule applies to excepted drop ball work.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Confuses the exception with temporary measures
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Cable marking and spotters are temporary measures for when a required device is not working. Drop ball work does not require a device at all.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Overlooks the personnel limit on the marine exception
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Marine operations are excepted only when they do not involve hoisting personnel. Hoisting workers removes the exception.
Prevent-or-warn applies to lattice cranes built from 1992 to 2011. A 2012 lattice crane needs automatic prevention.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Treats temporary measures as the requirement
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: Marking or a spotter is only a temporary measure for a device that is not working, and this work is not excepted.

devices.anti-two-block.misconception: Applies the lattice warning option to a telescopic crane
devices.anti-two-block.why_wrong: The prevent-or-warn option exists only for lattice cranes built between 1992 and 2011. Telescopic cranes have no warning-only option.

devices.boom-hoist-limiting.why_wrong: The cutoff is December 16, 1969. Moving it back one year incorrectly includes equipment covered by the older-equipment provision.
The cutoff is December 16, 1969, rather than the start of the following calendar year.
The rule uses December 16, 1969. Equipment manufactured earlier that year falls under the older-equipment provision.
The rule requires at least one listed method, not two.
The methods are alternatives. Using all three is not the minimum requirement.
The rule allows one or more methods. It does not prohibit combining them.

devices.boom-hoist-limiting.misconception: Boom cutoff applied to luffing jib
devices.boom-hoist-limiting.why_wrong: That date distinguishes boom hoist limiting requirements. It does not limit the luffing jib requirement.
The presence of a luffing jib triggers the requirement, regardless of whether the operator can see the load.
The requirement is not restricted to lifts at rated capacity. Equipment with a luffing jib must have the device.

devices.boom-hoist-limiting.misconception: Boom length confused with boom angle
devices.boom-hoist-limiting.why_wrong: The listed alternative is a boom angle indicator. Boom length indication is not the specified substitute.
The listed indicator alternative measures boom angle, not hoist load.

devices.boom-hoist-limiting.misconception: Crane level confused with boom angle
devices.boom-hoist-limiting.why_wrong: Crane level indication is not the listed substitute. The permitted indicator method uses boom angle.
A pre-movement check does not provide the operator the required view. The separate spotter method requires timely observation and signaling as the boom moves.
Slower movement does not satisfy the visibility requirement. The operator must be able to see the mark when relying on this method.

devices.boom-hoist-limiting.misconception: Separate alternative confused with method completion
devices.boom-hoist-limiting.why_wrong: A boom angle indicator is a separate listed alternative. Marking a gauge does not complete the operator-visible cable-mark method.

devices.boom-hoist-limiting.misconception: Signal point treated as stopping point
devices.boom-hoist-limiting.why_wrong: Signaling at the limit does not account for the operator's response and hoist stopping time. The mark must provide time for both.

devices.category-i.why_wrong: 14 days is twice the limit. Without a documented parts order, the deadline is 7 calendar days.
A monthly window does not apply to Category I aids. Their repair deadline is 7 calendar days.

devices.category-i.misconception: Counts working days from the report
devices.category-i.why_wrong: The rule counts calendar days from when the deficiency occurs, not working days from when someone reports it.

devices.category-i.misconception: Uses the boom hoist limiting device date
devices.category-i.why_wrong: December 16, 1969, is the cutoff date for the boom hoist limiting device, not for anti-two-block devices.
December 31, 1999, is the cutoff for articulating cranes that have a load hoist. Telescopic boom cranes use February 28, 1992.

devices.category-i.misconception: Uses the lattice boom automatic-device date
devices.category-i.why_wrong: November 8, 2011, is the date after which lattice boom cranes and derricks need automatic prevention. Telescopic boom cranes are covered from February 28, 1992.

devices.category-i.misconception: Ignores the personnel limit on the marine exemption
devices.category-i.why_wrong: Marine operations are exempt only when they do not involve hoisting personnel. A personnel lift from a barge is still covered.
Ordinary hook work with precast panels is not on the exempt list, so the device or a temporary measure is required.
Steel erection on the hook is not an exempt use. The anti-two-block requirement applies.

devices.category-i.misconception: Applies the lattice boom either/or rule
devices.category-i.why_wrong: The choice between a mark or a spotter is the lattice boom measure. Telescopic cranes need the mark and also a spotter when extending.

devices.category-i.misconception: Treats the spotter as a substitute for the mark
devices.category-i.why_wrong: A spotter alone is not enough on a telescopic crane. The cable must also be clearly marked for the operator.

devices.category-i.misconception: Uses the boom hoist limiting measure
devices.category-i.why_wrong: A boom angle indicator is a temporary measure for a failed boom hoist limiting device, not for anti-two-block. Lowering the block by habit does not replace the cable mark and spotter.
Using both a mark and a spotter is the telescopic crane requirement. Lattice boom cranes need only one of the two.

devices.category-i.misconception: Believes no temporary measure is allowed
devices.category-i.why_wrong: Temporary alternative measures exist so work can continue while the repair is done within the deadline. The mark is a valid measure.

devices.category-i.misconception: Mixes in the boom hoist limiting measure
devices.category-i.why_wrong: A boom angle indicator is an alternative for a failed boom hoist limiting device. It plays no part in the anti-two-block measure.

devices.category-i.misconception: Thinks the crane is grandfathered entirely
devices.category-i.why_wrong: Older equipment is exempt only from having the device. It must still use at least one of the alternative measures.

devices.category-ii.misconception: Parts-order window mistaken for repair deadline
devices.category-ii.why_wrong: Seven calendar days is the parts-order documentation window for the exception, not the normal repair period. The normal deadline is 30 calendar days.
The Category II repair period is 30 calendar days. A two-week deadline does not apply here.
The Category II repair period is 30 calendar days, not three weeks.
This device requirement uses a threshold over 6,000 pounds. A 2,000-pound threshold does not decide this requirement.
The threshold is over 6,000 pounds. A crane rated at exactly 6,000 pounds does not meet that threshold.
The threshold is over 6,000 pounds, so covered cranes between 6,000 and 10,000 pounds also meet it.

devices.category-ii.misconception: Load-device date applied to drum indicator
devices.category-ii.why_wrong: March 29, 2003 is the cutoff associated with load weighing and similar devices on certain equipment. The drum rotation indicator cutoff is November 8, 2011.
The manufacturing cutoff for this requirement is November 8, 2011, not 2010.
The applicable manufacturing cutoff is November 8, 2011. Using a 2014 cutoff would exclude equipment covered by the requirement.
A visual estimate does not satisfy the measuring-device requirement. Radius or boom angle must be measured.
A stored or remembered reading is not the required temporary measurement. Radius or boom angle must be determined with a measuring device.
Keeping another aid active does not perform the required measurement. The temporary measure specifically requires measuring radius or boom angle.

devices.category-ii.misconception: Drum turns substitute for jib measurement
devices.category-ii.why_wrong: Ascertaining main boom angle is required, but estimating jib angle from drum turns does not satisfy the required measurement of radius or jib angle.

devices.category-ii.misconception: Jib angle substitutes for main boom angle
devices.category-ii.why_wrong: Jib angle does not replace main boom angle. The sequence requires ascertaining main boom angle and then measuring radius or jib angle.

devices.category-ii.misconception: Level load eliminates main boom angle step
devices.category-ii.why_wrong: Keeping the load level does not remove the main boom angle step. Main boom angle must be ascertained before measuring radius or jib angle.

devices.category-ii.misconception: Extension speed treated as a length measurement
devices.category-ii.why_wrong: Extension time is not a listed alternative. The listed methods use measured marks, angle and radius measurements, or direct measurement.

devices.indicators.why_wrong: This date is one year too early. The requirement for these two devices starts with equipment manufactured after November 8, 2011.

devices.indicators.misconception: Confusing other rule dates with the device cutoff
devices.indicators.why_wrong: These devices are not tied to this date. The rule requires them on equipment manufactured after November 8, 2011.

devices.indicators.misconception: Confusing the operator-certification timeline with the device cutoff
devices.indicators.why_wrong: This date is too late. Cranes built between late 2011 and 2014 already need these devices, because the cutoff is November 8, 2011.
A boom angle indicator is a separate required aid and does not replace the length indicator. Angle alone does not tell you the boom length.
The rule has no exception for working at a fixed extension. The only exception is when rated capacity is independent of boom length.
Having an LMI does not remove the boom length indicator requirement. The LMI itself depends on correct length input.
An estimate by eye is not a measurement. The rule requires the radius or angle to be measured with a measuring device.

devices.indicators.misconception: Load chart used as a measuring tool
devices.indicators.why_wrong: A load chart gives capacities. It cannot tell you the actual angle of the boom. The angle or radius has to be measured.

devices.indicators.misconception: Self-imposed derate instead of the required measure
devices.indicators.why_wrong: The rule does not offer a capacity restriction as an alternative. It requires measuring the radius or boom angle.

devices.indicators.misconception: Indirect estimate treated as a measurement
devices.indicators.why_wrong: Extension speed varies with engine speed, oil temperature and load, so timing is not a listed method. Length must be marked, calculated from angle and radius, or measured.
A stored reading no longer matches the boom once it telescopes. The rule requires current marks, a calculation or a measurement.
Counting sections does not show how far each section is extended, and an estimate is not one of the listed methods.

devices.indicators.misconception: Duty assigned to the wrong person
devices.indicators.why_wrong: The timing and procedure are right, but the rule assigns the check to the operator, not the lift director.

devices.indicators.misconception: Full extension assumed to be required
devices.indicators.why_wrong: The rule does not require full extension. It requires the operator to verify that the actual positions are correct per manufacturer procedures.
This has the wrong person and the wrong timing. The operator must verify positions before operations begin, not after a lift.
The rule does not allow a spotter in place of a mark. The drum must be marked so the operator can see its rotation.

devices.lmi.misconception: Rigging tension replaces the pre-lift deadline
devices.lmi.why_wrong: The required timing is before the lift, not a particular stage of tensioning the rigging.

devices.lmi.misconception: A test pick may precede weight information
devices.lmi.why_wrong: The load has already been lifted when it clears the ground. The operator must receive its determined weight beforehand.

devices.lmi.misconception: The deadline applies to swinging rather than lifting
devices.lmi.why_wrong: Waiting until the swing allows hoisting without the required weight information. The deadline is before the lift.
A boom-angle aid is not one of the listed choices for this requirement. An angle reading alone does not provide the listed weighing, indicating, or limiting function.
A wind-speed aid is not among the devices listed for this requirement. It supplies weather information rather than the required load-related function.

devices.lmi.misconception: Hoisting-motion feedback qualifies as load feedback
devices.lmi.why_wrong: A drum-rotation aid is not one of the listed alternatives. Sensing drum movement does not satisfy the load weighing and similar devices requirement.
The threshold is over 6,000 pounds. A rated capacity of exactly 6,000 pounds does not cross it.
The stated threshold for this requirement is over 6,000 pounds, not over 2,000 pounds.
Neither this amount nor an inclusive threshold matches the requirement. The rated capacity must exceed 6,000 pounds.
A limiter is a permitted alternative, not a mandatory addition to a load weighing device.

devices.lmi.misconception: Weighing and moment indication must be paired
devices.lmi.why_wrong: The rule requires at least one listed device. It does not require an indicator in addition to a functioning load weighing device.

devices.lmi.misconception: Temporary alternatives always supplement working aids
devices.lmi.why_wrong: Determining and providing weight is the stated temporary alternative measure. This crane already has one of the listed devices.

devices.lmi.misconception: Applying the threshold to the lifted load
devices.lmi.why_wrong: The threshold applies to the equipment's rated capacity, not the weight of the pump.

devices.lmi.misconception: Using a chart cell as the equipment threshold
devices.lmi.why_wrong: Capacity at the planned radius matters to lift planning, but the device applicability language uses the equipment's rated capacity.

devices.lmi.misconception: Using the weakest configuration as the threshold
devices.lmi.why_wrong: The rule does not substitute the longest-boom configuration capacity for the equipment's rated capacity.

devices.lmi.misconception: Articulating cranes require automatic prevention exclusively
devices.lmi.why_wrong: Automatic overload prevention is one choice. A load weighing device, indicator, or limiter is also permitted.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Common supply protection replaces integral protection
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: A common supply-line valve does not satisfy the requirement for an integral holding device or check valve at the jacks.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Control manifold valve provides required protection
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: A manifold shutoff is not the required integral holding device or check valve.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Pressure relief and load holding are interchangeable
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: A pressure relief valve does not replace the required integral holding device or check valve.
A pump-mounted device does not meet the requirement for an integrally mounted boom holding device.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Hose installation is equivalent to integral mounting
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: An in-line hose device is not the required integrally mounted holding device.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Remote control valve satisfies integral mounting
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: The required boom holding device must be integrally mounted; locating it at the operator's manifold does not satisfy that requirement.
Outlet pressure depends on resistance to flow and pressure controls. Fixed displacement does not mean fixed pressure.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Fixed displacement means constant shaft torque
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: Required shaft torque rises as the pressure difference across the pump rises, even when displacement stays fixed.
Hydraulic power depends on both pressure and flow. Either can change without changing pump displacement.
Passing a static test does not replace the requirement for an integral holding device or check valve.
Hydraulic stabilizer jacks are expressly included in the integral-device requirement.
The rule requires an integral holding device or check valve, not two holding valves at each jack.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Recovery after failure satisfies holding requirement
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: Stopping after pressure returns does not satisfy the requirement to prevent retraction during hydraulic failure.
Integral mounting alone is insufficient. The device must also prevent retraction in the event of hydraulic failure.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Failure protection requires a compensating movement
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: The required response is to prevent retraction, not to extend the boom automatically.

devices.power-flow.misconception: Relief valve replaces lost supply flow
devices.power-flow.why_wrong: A relief valve limits pressure by opening a discharge path. Holding here results from blocking oil from leaving the supporting chamber.

devices.repair-deadlines.why_wrong: The deadline uses calendar days, so weekends and other nonworking days count.

devices.repair-deadlines.misconception: Category II deadline applied to Category I
devices.repair-deadlines.why_wrong: Thirty calendar days is the ordinary Category II deadline. Category I has a 7-calendar-day deadline.
Category I allows 7 calendar days, not 30 working days.

devices.repair-deadlines.misconception: Category I deadline applied to Category II
devices.repair-deadlines.why_wrong: Seven calendar days is the ordinary Category I deadline. Category II ordinarily allows 30 calendar days.
The rule counts calendar days, including days when the crane is not working.
Category II has a 30-calendar-day deadline, not a 7-working-day deadline.

devices.repair-deadlines.misconception: Repair period used as ordering period
devices.repair-deadlines.why_wrong: Thirty days is the ordinary repair period. The order must be placed within 7 calendar days to qualify for the exception.
The ordering period starts with the deficiency, not receipt of a repair estimate.
Neither the 30-day ordering period nor the estimate-based starting point qualifies. The requirement is ordering within 7 calendar days of the deficiency.
Inspection confirmation does not start a new period. The deadline runs from when the deficiency occurs.
Reporting the failure does not change its occurrence date. Monday's failure starts the repair period.
Diagnosis does not postpone the deadline. The repair period begins with the deficiency.

devices.repair-deadlines.misconception: Order date starts final repair period
devices.repair-deadlines.why_wrong: Under the exception, receipt of the parts starts the final repair period. The order date establishes eligibility for the exception.

devices.repair-deadlines.misconception: Category II period applied after receipt
devices.repair-deadlines.why_wrong: The exception allows 7 calendar days after receipt, not 30.

devices.repair-deadlines.misconception: Parts delay changes the aid category
devices.repair-deadlines.why_wrong: Category I does not acquire the ordinary Category II deadline. Its qualifying exception requires repair within 7 calendar days after parts receipt.

devices.repair-deadlines.misconception: Any delayed order earns an extension
devices.repair-deadlines.why_wrong: The order was placed after the 7-calendar-day qualifying period. Late delivery does not make that late order eligible for the exception.

devices.safety-device-failure.why_wrong: A signal person is an alternative measure, and the rule says alternative measures are not permitted for these devices.
No one, including the lift director, can approve a substitute. The rule bars alternative measures outright.

devices.safety-device-failure.misconception: Operational-aid repair period applied to safety devices
devices.safety-device-failure.why_wrong: Temporary measures with repair deadlines apply to some operational aids, not to safety devices. Safety devices get no grace period.

devices.safety-device-failure.misconception: Only devices needed for the planned lifts
devices.safety-device-failure.why_wrong: The rule covers all listed devices, not only the ones the operator expects to need that day.
Tagging and reporting a defect does not allow operation. The device has to be working before operations begin.
The rule does not rank the devices. Every listed device must work, not only a chosen few.
The lift director oversees the lift. The rule puts the duty to stop on the operator, who is at the controls when the device fails.
A signal person can give a stop signal, but the rule names the operator as the person who must safely stop operations.
The A/D director supervises assembly and disassembly, not the response to a device failure during operations.
Once the device fails, the operator must safely stop operations. Finishing the pick keeps the crane working with a failed device.

devices.safety-device-failure.misconception: Defer the decision to a supervisor
devices.safety-device-failure.why_wrong: No one may decide to keep operating. The operator must stop, and the crane stays out of service until the horn works.
A hand-held horn is an alternative measure, and alternative measures are not permitted.
How carefully the hand level is used does not matter. It is an alternative measure, and the rule prohibits those.
Writing down a temporary measure does not make it allowed. Alternative measures are barred for safety devices.
No one can approve a substitute. A qualified person's sign-off does not change the ban on alternative measures.
A barricade is an alternative measure. The rule does not allow alternative measures in place of a required device.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Assumes outriggers make a level indicator unnecessary
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: Rough-terrain cranes are not on the exemption list. A level indicator is required whether the crane is on outriggers or on rubber.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Thinks the terrain decides whether the device is required
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: A sloped site is exactly where a level indicator is needed. Truck cranes are not exempt.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Confuses ground support with an exemption
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: Mats spread the load but do not exempt the crane. Only portal cranes, derricks and floating or flotation-mounted equipment are exempt.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Mixes in the level indicator exemptions
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: These categories are exempt from the crane level indicator rule, not from the boom stop rule.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Confuses rail stops with boom stops
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: Derricks are exempt, but rail-mounted equipment is not. The rail rule covers clamps and stops on the rails, not boom stops.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Applies the flotation exemption to the wrong device
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: Being a portal crane or sitting on a barge removes the level indicator requirement. It does not remove the boom stop requirement.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Applies the built-in rule to a removable device
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: Tagging out is an option only for a built-in level indicator. A faulty removable indicator must be removed.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Treats tag-out as the universal fix
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: Tagging out alone is never enough for a removable indicator, because a tagged unit could still be carried around and read. It has to be removed.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Invents a repair deadline in place of the removal rule
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: The rule sets no repair deadline. It requires the faulty removable indicator to be removed.
The boom stop rule exempts hydraulic booms, so this crane needs only jib stops.
This gets it backward. The hydraulic boom is exempt from boom stops, and the attached jib does need jib stops.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Extends the hydraulic boom exception to the jib
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: The hydraulic exception covers only boom stops. The jib stop rule exempts only derricks.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Moves the outrigger jack device to the brakes
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: The integral holding device/check valve requirement applies to hydraulic outrigger and stabilizer jacks, not to brake pedals.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Assumes redundant controls are what the rule requires
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: No backup hand lever is required. For foot pedal brakes, the required device is a lock.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Confuses an indicator with a holding device
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: No warning light is required. The required device is a pedal lock that keeps the brake applied.

devices.safety-devices.misconception: Confuses beam extension pins with jack holding
devices.safety-devices.why_wrong: Beam pins hold the horizontal extension. They do not stop a vertical jack from retracting. The rule requires a holding device/check valve in the jack.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Articulating crane date applied to telescopic boom
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: December 31, 1999 is the cutoff for articulating cranes with a load hoist. Telescopic boom cranes use the earlier date, February 28, 1992.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Lattice boom date applied to telescopic boom
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: November 8, 2011 is the date after which lattice boom cranes and derricks need an automatic-prevention device. Telescopic cranes have been covered since after February 28, 1992.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Standard's effective date mistaken for equipment cutoff
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: Many people treat the effective date of the crane standard as the cutoff, but the equipment rule is tied to manufacture after February 28, 1992 for telescopic booms.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Post-2011 rule applied to an older lattice crane
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: Automatic prevention is mandatory only for lattice cranes and derricks manufactured after November 8, 2011. A crane built in 2005 may use a warning-type device instead.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: 2011 date read as start of coverage
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: Lattice cranes manufactured after February 28, 1992 are covered. The 2011 date only changes which type of device is required. It does not create an exemption.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Temporary measure confused with device requirement
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: A spotter is one of the temporary alternative measures used when the device is not working. A warning-type device that works complies by itself on a crane built in 2005.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Marine exception applied to personnel hoisting
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: Marine operations are exempt only when they do not involve hoisting personnel. Lifting workers from a barge is not exempt.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Lattice exception applied to telescopic crane
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: The magnet exception covers lattice boom equipment only. Telescopic boom cranes have no listed exemption for magnet work.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Assumes all lattice crawler work is exempt
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: Ordinary hook work with a load block is exactly what the lattice boom device requirement covers. It is not on the exception list.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Lattice 'or' rule applied to telescopic boom
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: "Mark or spotter" is the lattice boom temporary measure. On a telescopic boom, extending the boom can two-block the crane without the hoist moving, so both measures are required.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Spotter treated as substitute for cable mark
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: The telescopic rule does not let a spotter replace the cable mark. The mark is what tells the operator when to stop the hoist during hoisting.
The spotter is tied to extending the boom, not to personnel lifts. A telescopic crane needs a spotter for any boom extension while the device is out of service.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Telescopic 'and' rule applied to lattice boom
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: Requiring both measures is the telescopic boom rule. The lattice boom rule accepts either one.
