devices.two-blocking.misconception: Believes no temporary measures exist for lattice
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: Lattice boom cranes do have temporary alternative measures: a marked cable or a spotter.
A spotter alone is one of the two accepted options for lattice boom cranes. A cable mark is the other option, not a required one.

devices.two-blocking.misconception: Thinks block rides out with the boom
devices.two-blocking.why_wrong: Raising the block first removes the little clearance there is. Extension then pulls the block straight into the tip.

inspections.annual.why_wrong: Six months is more frequent than this requirement. The longest permitted interval is 12 months.
A quarterly inspection schedule exceeds the frequency required here. The annual/comprehensive interval is at most 12 months.
Nine months is not the specified maximum interval. This inspection is required at least every 12 months.

inspections.annual.misconception: Competent and qualified treated as interchangeable
inspections.annual.why_wrong: Designation as a competent person alone does not satisfy this requirement. The annual/comprehensive inspection requires a qualified person.

inspections.annual.misconception: Operator certification substitutes for inspection qualification
inspections.annual.why_wrong: Operator certification alone does not establish the qualification required to conduct this inspection. The person must be qualified for the inspection work.

inspections.annual.misconception: Jobsite authority substitutes for technical qualification
inspections.annual.why_wrong: Supervisory authority alone does not satisfy the inspection requirement. A supervisor conducting it must also be a qualified person.
Six months is shorter than the required retention period. Annual/comprehensive inspection documentation must be retained for at least 12 months.
Three years exceeds the minimum specified for these records. The required minimum is 12 months.
Ninety days does not meet the annual/comprehensive documentation requirement. The minimum retention period is 12 months.

inspections.annual.misconception: Functional operation substitutes for internal inspection
inspections.annual.why_wrong: Functional testing does not replace access needed to inspect the device. Necessary disassembly is part of completing the inspection.
A future overhaul does not complete the current inspection. Disassembly must occur when needed to inspect the required component.
The requirement is disassembly as necessary, not automatic teardown of every assembly. The extent depends on what is needed to complete the inspection.

inspections.annual.misconception: Simplified configuration substitutes for inspected configuration
inspections.annual.why_wrong: Testing with the jib removed would test a different configuration. The inspection must include functional testing of the configuration being inspected.

inspections.annual.misconception: Annual inspection requires testing every possible configuration
inspections.annual.why_wrong: This requirement addresses the configuration in the inspection. It does not require assembling and testing every approved combination.

inspections.annual.misconception: Functional testing is conditional on visible defects
inspections.annual.why_wrong: Functional testing is required even when visual and internal checks reveal no suspected malfunction.

inspections.annual.misconception: Annual finding waits for annual recheck
inspections.annual.why_wrong: Waiting for annual inspections does not meet the monitoring requirement. The deficiency must be checked in monthly inspections.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Confuses qualified person with competent person
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: A qualified person has engineering or technical standing, but this decision belongs to the competent person, and it must be made immediately, not just before the next lift.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Assigns the duty to the operator by default
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: The operator decides only if the operator has been designated the competent person. The duty belongs to the competent person role, not to whoever is in the seat.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Assigns the duty to the controlling entity
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: The controlling entity runs the site but does not make this determination. The competent person makes it, immediately.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Allows the decision to wait until end of shift
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: End of shift is too late. The crane could make many lifts with a hazard before then. The determination must be immediate.
There is no 24-hour window. The determination must be immediate.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Defers to a different inspection interval
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: The monthly inspection is a separate check. It does not postpone the immediate decision required when a shift inspection finds a deficiency.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Field myth of an annual overload test
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: No overload test is part of this inspection. What is required is functional testing to confirm the crane works properly.
NDT may be used when a problem is suspected, but it is not the required element here. Functional testing is.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Requires a configuration other than the one inspected
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: The test is of the crane as configured in the inspection. It does not have to be at maximum boom length.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Derating instead of removing from service
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: Reducing the load does not fix a hazard. The rule requires removal from service, not derating.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Wrong timing: one more lift first
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: Removal is required as soon as the hazard is determined. One more pick with a known hazard is not allowed.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Defers a hazard to a later inspection
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: A deficiency ruled a hazard cannot wait for a later inspection. The crane stays out of service until it is corrected.

inspections.deficiencies.misconception: Treats every deficiency as requiring removal
inspections.deficiencies.why_wrong: This treats every deficiency as a hazard. The rule ties removal to the competent person's finding of a safety hazard.
This rule has no derating requirement. Without a hazard, the crane is not restricted by this provision.
The competent person makes the determination. No qualified person sign-off is required.
Shift inspections do not replace the functional testing that the annual/comprehensive inspection itself must include.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Thinks each new monthly record replaces the last one
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: A new monthly inspection does not replace the old record. The minimum is three months, so the last few monthly records stay on file together.
Six months is not a federal retention period for crane inspections. Monthly records must be kept three months, and annual records 12 months.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Applies the annual retention period to monthly records
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: Twelve months is the minimum for the annual/comprehensive inspection record. The monthly record minimum is three months.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Applies the monthly retention period to the annual record
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: Three months is the minimum for monthly inspection records. The annual record must be kept at least 12 months.
No 36-month period applies to the annual inspection record. The federal minimum is 12 months.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Ties retention to the next inspection instead of a fixed period
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: The rule sets a fixed minimum of 12 months. It is not tied to when the next inspection happens, and an annual that runs late does not shorten or stretch that minimum.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Assigns the duty to the controlling entity
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: The controlling entity has other duties on the site, but the inspection record belongs to the employer that conducted the inspection.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Assigns the duty to the crane owner
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: Ownership does not decide this. The employer that conducts the inspection documents and maintains the record.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Assigns the duty to the operator's employer
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: The operator's employer keeps the record only if it is also the employer that conducted the inspection. The rule names the employer that conducts the inspection.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Assigns the signature to the operator
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: The rule requires the signature of the person who conducted the inspection. It does not require the operator to countersign.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Treats a common form field as a federal requirement
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: Many forms ask for hours, but the federal minimum contents are the items checked, the results, and the inspector's name, signature and date.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Thinks a supervisor must approve the record
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: No supervisor approval is required on the record. The required signature is the inspector's.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Assigns the duty to the owner or the party that paid
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: Owning the crane and paying for the inspection does not make A the employer that conducted it. The rule puts the duty on the employer that conducts the inspection.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Field myth that the operator keeps the records in the cab
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: No federal rule requires the operator to keep the annual record or store it in the cab. The employer that conducted the inspection keeps it.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Confuses the duty to retain with control over who may see records
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: The employer keeps the records, but it must also make them available to the people who conduct inspections while the retention period runs.

inspections.documentation.misconception: Thinks records must be available only to enforcement officials
inspections.documentation.why_wrong: The rule names all persons who conduct inspections as entitled to the documents, not only government inspectors.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Frequent inspections may extend to quarterly
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: Frequent inspections have a daily-to-monthly range, not a weekly-to-quarterly range.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Periodic interval used for frequent inspections
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: The 1- to 12-month range belongs to periodic inspections, subject to the manufacturer's specific recommendations.
Daily is the correct short end of the range, but the general frequent-inspection range ends at monthly.
The general range begins at one month, not three months. The manufacturer-recommendation provision does not change the stated general range.
Six months is not the beginning of the general periodic-inspection range; one month is.
The general range is 1–12 months, not 12–24 months.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Annual periodic interval applied to standby status
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: An annual inspection alone does not meet the standby requirement of at least semiannual inspection.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Monthly certification interval applied to standby status
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: The standby provision specifies at least semiannual inspection, not a blanket monthly requirement.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Extra caution mistaken for the required minimum
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: Quarterly inspection is more frequent than the stated minimum. Standby status alone does not require that interval.
A weekly maintenance visit does not satisfy the expressly stated daily inspection requirement.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: General range overrides a specific interval
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: The general daily-to-monthly range does not override the daily requirement for hydraulic deterioration or leakage.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Periodic inspection substitutes for daily checks
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: Including these checks in a periodic inspection does not satisfy their daily frequency.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Daily hydraulic check classified as an additional periodic item
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: Hydraulic deterioration or leakage is specifically listed under frequent inspection, with a daily interval.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Safety-device check classified as an additional periodic item
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: Safety-device malfunction is listed under frequent inspection. Periodic inspections include that scope, but it is not an additional periodic item.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Hook condition assigned only to periodic inspection
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: Hook deformation or cracks are listed under frequent inspection, which is also included in periodic inspections.

inspections.general-industry.misconception: Overhead-crane electrical classification transferred to mobile cranes
inspections.general-industry.why_wrong: These mobile-crane electrical conditions appear in the frequent-inspection list. Periodic inspections include them through their inclusion of frequent-inspection requirements.

inspections.hooks.why_wrong: The specified increase is more than 15 percent. Ten is the numerical limit associated with twist in degrees.
The criterion is more than 15 percent, so waiting for an increase above 20 percent misses hooks that already meet it.
Five percent is not the specified threshold. The throat-opening criterion uses more than 15 percent.

inspections.hooks.misconception: Applying the opening number to twist
inspections.hooks.why_wrong: The twist criterion is more than 10 degrees. Fifteen is the percentage used for throat-opening increase.
The criterion is more than 10 degrees, not more than 20 degrees.
Five degrees is not the specified threshold. The criterion requires twist greater than 10 degrees.
The bowl's inside width is not the specified throat measurement. Measure the opening at its narrowest point.

inspections.hooks.misconception: Using latch hardware as a reference
inspections.hooks.why_wrong: The latch pivot is not the specified reference. The rule identifies the narrowest point of the throat opening.
A measurement along the shank does not measure the throat opening. The opening is measured at its narrowest point.

inspections.hooks.misconception: Using an opening threshold below 15 percent
inspections.hooks.why_wrong: The opening criterion is an increase greater than 15 percent. An 8 percent increase does not meet that numerical criterion.

inspections.hooks.misconception: Using a twist threshold below 10 degrees
inspections.hooks.why_wrong: The twist criterion is greater than 10 degrees. Six degrees does not meet that numerical criterion.
A percentage and an angle cannot be added to evaluate these criteria. Opening and twist are assessed separately.

inspections.hooks.misconception: Confusing block rotation with hook deformation
inspections.hooks.why_wrong: Rotation of the complete block is not the specified hook-twist measurement. The reference is the plane of the unbent hook.
Subtracting block rotation does not determine hook twist. The measured displacement from the unbent plane is 12 degrees.
Adding block rotation does not determine hook twist. Only the displacement from the hook's unbent plane applies.

inspections.hooks.misconception: Treating the opening boundary as inclusive
inspections.hooks.why_wrong: Exactly 15 percent is not more than 15 percent. The opening criterion has not been exceeded.

inspections.idle.misconception: General industry threshold applied to construction
inspections.idle.why_wrong: One month is the general industry trigger in 1910.180(d)(5)(i). The construction rule in 1926.1412(h) uses 3 months or more.

inspections.idle.misconception: Confusing with the general industry complete-inspection trigger
inspections.idle.why_wrong: Six months is the general industry point where a complete inspection is required. Construction equipment needs its inspection at 3 months.

inspections.idle.misconception: Annual interval mistaken for idle threshold
inspections.idle.why_wrong: Twelve months matches the annual inspection interval, not the idle threshold. The construction idle threshold is 3 months or more.
A competent person can do the regular monthly inspection. The idle-equipment rule specifically calls for a qualified person.
The person is right, but the rule points to the paragraph (e) monthly criteria, not the annual/comprehensive inspection.

inspections.idle.misconception: General industry terms and wrong person
inspections.idle.why_wrong: "Frequent inspection" is general industry wording. The construction rule requires a monthly-level inspection by a qualified person.
Three months is the construction idle threshold. The standby crane minimum is semiannual.
Twelve months is the annual interval. Standby cranes need inspection at least twice as often.
Thirty days matches the 1-month idle trigger and the monthly inspection idea. The standby minimum is semiannual, with more frequent checks only advised in adverse environments.

inspections.idle.misconception: Grace period after return to service
inspections.idle.why_wrong: The person is right, but the rule allows no grace period. The inspection must happen before initial use.

inspections.idle.misconception: Folding it into the routine schedule
inspections.idle.why_wrong: Waiting for the next scheduled monthly inspection doesn't meet the rule. The idle inspection is required before initial use.
The timing is right, but an operator's shift inspection doesn't meet the rule. It calls for a qualified person and the monthly criteria.
One month is the general industry trigger in 1910.180(d)(5)(i). Construction uses 3 months.
The idle rule calls for an inspection, not a load test, and here it isn't triggered at all.

inspections.idle.misconception: Wrong threshold and wrong inspection level
inspections.idle.why_wrong: The answer is right but the reason is wrong. The construction trigger is 3 months, and it calls for a monthly-level inspection, not an annual.
Adding (d)(4) makes it the complete inspection, which is only required at six months. Leaving out (g)(2)(ii) skips the required rope inspection.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Competent person swapped for qualified person
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: A competent person handles shift and monthly inspections. A post-modification inspection must be done by a qualified person.
The operator may run the shift check, but the rule gives the post-modification inspection to a qualified person.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: RPE role from the repair rule misapplied
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: An RPE comes in only on the repair path, and only when the qualified person decides one is needed to develop criteria. The inspector is still a qualified person.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Repair standard applied to a modification
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: Manufacturer equipment criteria are what a repair or adjustment is checked against. A modification is checked against its § 1926.1434 approval.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Load test treated as the acceptance criterion
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: The rule calls for functional testing plus a check against the approval. It does not set a test lift at rated capacity as the standard.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Repair-path criteria applied to a modification
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: Criteria developed by the qualified person apply to repairs when no manufacturer criteria exist. A modification is measured against its approval.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Test scope limited to the replaced part
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: Testing only the repaired parts misses components the repair may affect, and the rule requires those to be tested too.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Full load test assumed to be required
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: The rule scopes testing to the repaired parts and affected components. It does not require a full rated-load test of every function.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Overload test percentage invented for repairs
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: The repair inspection rule sets no overload test percentage. It requires functional testing of the repaired and affected components.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Fallback criteria used when the primary source exists
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: A qualified person develops criteria only when manufacturer criteria are unavailable or do not apply. Here they exist.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: RPE assumed to be needed for every repair
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: An RPE develops criteria only when manufacturer criteria are lacking and the qualified person decides an RPE is needed.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Modification standard applied to a repair
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: The § 1926.1434 approval governs modifications. A like-for-like brake repair is checked against manufacturer criteria.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Shift inspection substituted for the required inspection
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: A shift inspection does not replace the post-modification inspection by a qualified person before initial use.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Inspection deferred to the scheduled interval
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: The inspection is triggered by completing the addition and must happen before initial use. It is not deferred to the monthly cycle.

inspections.modified-repaired.misconception: Installer check accepted in place of the inspection
inspections.modified-repaired.why_wrong: A power-up check by the installer is not an inspection by a qualified person that confirms the work matches the approval.
An RPE is not automatically required. The qualified person decides whether one is needed.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Keep the record only until the next monthly
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: One month is only the gap until the next monthly inspection. The record has to be kept for a minimum of three months.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Confusing monthly retention with an annual interval
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: Twelve months is longer than the rule requires. The minimum for the monthly record is three months.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Tying monthly records to the annual cycle
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: The monthly record is not tied to the annual inspection. It must be kept for a minimum of three months.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Recording only defects and machine hours
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: Hour meter readings are not required, and listing only deficiencies leaves out the items checked. A name without a signature and date is also incomplete.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Treating a repair log as the inspection record
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: The required content is the items checked, the results, and the inspector's name, signature and date. A repair list does not replace the items checked and the results.
The signature required is that of the person who conducted the inspection. A supervisor's approval is not part of the required content, and the items checked are missing.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Assigning the duty to the controlling entity
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: The controlling entity has other duties on a multi-employer site, but the monthly record belongs to the employer that conducts the inspection.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Assigning the duty to the owner
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: Owning the crane does not create this duty. The employer that conducts the inspection documents and maintains the record.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Assigning an employer duty to an individual
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: The operator may do the inspection as a worker, but the rule puts the documentation duty on the employer that conducts the inspection.
The annual inspection is a separate, more thorough inspection. The monthly inspection follows the shift-inspection scope.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Limiting the monthly to prior defects
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: The monthly inspection is a full shift-inspection scope, not a recheck of earlier problem items.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Adding a load test to routine inspections
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: The monthly inspection does not include a load test. It follows the shift-inspection items and must be documented.

inspections.monthly.misconception: Using a spotter instead of making the repair
inspections.monthly.why_wrong: A spotter does not correct the deficiency. The crane stays out of use until an inspection shows no corrective action is required.
Derating does not satisfy the rule. Use is barred until an inspection shows no corrective action is needed.
Writing the deficiency down does not permit use. It must be corrected and cleared before the crane works again.
A signature and date are required, but so are the items checked and their results. A general statement does not meet that.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Scaffold-style height confused with the crane rule
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: No 10-foot trigger applies to crane walking/working surfaces. The baseline is more than 6 feet above a lower level.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Horizontal lattice exception applied to all work
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: 15 feet applies only to moving point-to-point on a horizontal lattice boom. The general trigger is more than 6 feet.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: General-industry height used for construction cranes
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: 4 feet is the general-industry trigger for walking-working surfaces. The crane construction rule uses more than 6 feet.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Non-lattice or raised-boom rule applied to horizontal lattice
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: More than 6 feet is the trigger for non-lattice booms and for lattice booms that are not horizontal. A horizontal lattice boom uses 15 feet for point-to-point movement.
No 10-foot threshold exists in the crane fall protection rule. The horizontal lattice figure is 15 feet or more.
20 feet is too high. Protection is required starting at a 15-foot fall distance for horizontal lattice booms.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Function tag rule applied to whole equipment
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: A conspicuous position is the rule for a single function taken out of service. For the whole machine, the tag goes in the cab.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Tag at defect instead of at controls
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: Tagging the defect location does not meet the rule. The out-of-service tag for the equipment must be in the cab.
A ladder tag can be missed or removed and is not the required location. The rule puts the tag in the cab.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Horizontal lattice rule applied to telescopic boom
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: The 15-foot allowance applies only to horizontal lattice booms. A telescopic boom is non-lattice, so the 6-foot trigger applies.
Moving point-to-point is covered separately from work stations. Non-lattice booms require protection while moving.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Boom angle treated as the deciding factor
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: For non-lattice booms, the rule covers both horizontal and non-horizontal positions. Boom angle does not matter.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Baseline applied without the lattice exception
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: More than 6 feet is the baseline, but horizontal lattice booms have their own 15-foot figure for moving point-to-point.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Raised-lattice rule applied to horizontal boom
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: Only lattice booms that are not horizontal are covered at the baseline height. A horizontal lattice boom is covered while moving only at a 15-foot fall distance or more.
Inspections are non-assembly/disassembly work and are fully covered by this rule. The walk is not covered here only because of the 15-foot lattice figure.

inspections.personnel-safety.misconception: Moving allowance applied to work station
inspections.personnel-safety.why_wrong: The 15-foot figure applies only to moving point-to-point on a horizontal lattice boom. Work stations on any boom use the more-than-6-foot trigger.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Confuses routine-inspection person with severe-service inspector
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: A competent person handles routine inspections. The severe-service rule specifically requires a qualified person.
The operator may be the one who spots the overload, but the rule gives the structural inspection to a qualified person, not the operator.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Duty assigned to the person in charge of the lift
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: A supervisor directs the work but is not the person the rule names. The inspection must be done by a qualified person.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Derating as a substitute for stopping
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: The rule has no option to keep working at reduced capacity. Use stops until a qualified person inspects the crane.
Writing it on a routine record does not meet the rule. The employer must stop use and get a qualified person's inspection.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Rescheduling a routine inspection instead of stopping
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: Moving the annual inspection earlier still lets the crane run in the meantime. The rule requires stopping use now.
The rule says 'may have exceeded.' It does not wait for confirmation, which is often impossible after a shock load.
The threshold in the rule is rated capacity itself, not a percentage of it.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Counts events instead of applying the capacity test
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: The rule does not count events. One shock load that may have exceeded rated capacity is enough.
Overload damage such as cracked welds or bent members can be hidden. The rule requires a qualified person's inspection, not an operator walkaround.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Routine inspection substituted for severe-service inspection
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: A routine shift inspection does not meet the severe-service rule. The rule requires a qualified person's structural inspection.
Waiting for the annual inspection leaves a possibly damaged crane in service. The employer must stop use now.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Wrong person and wrong inspection type
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: A routine inspection by a competent person does not satisfy the severe-service rule. It requires a qualified person.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Passing routine inspections means no severe service
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: Shift inspections are visual checks that can miss hidden corrosion. Severe-service conditions require a separate inspection by a qualified person.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Wrong person and automatic full annual
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: The rule does not require the manufacturer. A qualified person inspects the structure and decides which annual-inspection items also need inspecting.

inspections.severe-service.misconception: Right timing, wrong person and inspection
inspections.severe-service.why_wrong: Stopping is correct, but moving up a routine inspection does not meet the rule. A qualified person must do the severe-service inspection.

inspections.shift.misconception: Confuses competent person with qualified person
inspections.shift.why_wrong: A qualified person is a different designation. The shift rule calls for a competent person, not a qualified person.

inspections.shift.misconception: Assumes operator certification is what the rule requires
inspections.shift.why_wrong: Operators often do the shift inspection, but only when they meet the competent-person requirement. Holding operator certification does not make someone the person the rule calls for.

inspections.shift.misconception: Duty assigned to the wrong person
inspections.shift.why_wrong: The rule does not give the shift inspection to whoever directs the lift. It names a competent person.

inspections.shift.misconception: Overly strict timing the rule does not require
inspections.shift.why_wrong: Finishing before the shift is allowed but not required. The rule lets the inspection be completed during the shift, and some checks, such as trial operation, happen with the crane running.
The rule sets no two-hour window, and the inspection must begin before the shift, not after it starts.

inspections.shift.misconception: Ties timing to the first lift instead of the shift start
inspections.shift.why_wrong: Starting partway into the shift does not meet the rule. The inspection must begin before the shift starts.

inspections.shift.misconception: Treats the shift inspection as a hands-on teardown
inspections.shift.why_wrong: The rule states that booming down is not required as part of the shift inspection unless the results call for it.
Boom length is not the trigger. The trigger is what the visual inspection or trial operation shows.
The shift inspection rule contains no weekly boom-down requirement. Booming down depends on findings, not on the calendar.

inspections.shift.misconception: Assumes every deficiency means automatic removal from service
inspections.shift.why_wrong: The rule does not remove the crane automatically. The competent person decides whether the deficiency is a safety hazard, for example whether the crack hampers the operator's view.

inspections.shift.misconception: Wrong person, and a workaround instead of correction
inspections.shift.why_wrong: The hazard determination belongs to the competent person, and a hazard means out of service until corrected. Adding a signal person does not fix it.

inspections.shift.misconception: Defers the shift finding to a later inspection
inspections.shift.why_wrong: The determination must be made immediately by the competent person, not deferred to a later inspection or to a different person.

inspections.shift.misconception: Assumes one check per shift is enough
inspections.shift.why_wrong: The morning check does not carry over to a new setup. The rule calls for a level check after each move and setup.

inspections.shift.misconception: Ties a required check to a load percentage
inspections.shift.why_wrong: The level check after a move does not depend on how heavy the load is. Every move and setup requires it.
The tolerance comes from the equipment manufacturer's recommendations, not from one fixed number for every crane.
Pressure rating is not the factor the rule names. It singles out lines that flex in normal operation.

inspections.testing.misconception: Operating rating mistaken for test ceiling
inspections.testing.why_wrong: The test-load ceiling is 110%, not 100%, of the rated load at the selected working radius.

inspections.testing.misconception: Overhead-crane limit applied to mobile crane
inspections.testing.why_wrong: The 125% figure belongs to the overhead-crane testing provision. The truck-crane provision limits the test load to 110%.
A 150% test load exceeds the truck-crane limit of 110% at the selected working radius.
For a new production crane supplied complete by one manufacturer, this testing duty belongs to the manufacturer.

inspections.testing.misconception: Operator checks substituted for production testing
inspections.testing.why_wrong: An operator's checks do not replace the manufacturer's required production operational testing.

inspections.testing.misconception: Site supervision confused with production responsibility
inspections.testing.why_wrong: The production operational testing requirement assigns this duty to the manufacturer, not the site's lift director.

inspections.testing.misconception: Owner authority substituted for rating approval
inspections.testing.why_wrong: Ownership or responsibility for a lift does not provide the approval required to increase original load ratings.

inspections.testing.misconception: Technical competence mistaken for approval authority
inspections.testing.why_wrong: An inspector's or engineer's approval alone does not meet this requirement. Approval must come from the manufacturer or final assembler.

inspections.testing.misconception: Field responsibility mistaken for rating authority
inspections.testing.why_wrong: Operating or directing assembly does not confer authority to approve ratings above the original ratings.

inspections.testing.misconception: Component tests substituted for assembled-crane tests
inspections.testing.why_wrong: Testing separate components before shipment does not meet the requirement to conduct these tests at final assembly.

inspections.testing.misconception: Production testing deferred to periodic inspection
inspections.testing.why_wrong: The required stage is final assembly, not a later annual inspection.

inspections.testing.misconception: Prototype approval substituted for production testing
inspections.testing.why_wrong: Prototype testing does not replace operational testing of the production crane at final assembly.

inspections.testing.misconception: Maintenance records substituted for test report
inspections.testing.why_wrong: Repair and parts records do not establish how testing was performed or confirm repair adequacy through the required report.

inspections.testing.misconception: Personnel credentials substituted for repair verification
inspections.testing.why_wrong: Listing weights and operator credentials does not provide the required test procedures and confirmation of repair adequacy.

inspections.testing.misconception: Periodic inspection records substituted for test documentation
inspections.testing.why_wrong: An inspection schedule and maintenance completion record do not meet the stated test-report content requirements.

inspections.testing.misconception: Batch sampling substituted for individual testing
inspections.testing.why_wrong: The requirement applies to each new production crane, not a sample selected from a production batch.

lift-planning.basics.why_wrong: Half capacity is a field rule of thumb, not the trigger. The rule sets the threshold at 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used.
85 percent is the stability margin often built into outrigger ratings on load charts. It is not the weight-verification trigger, which is 75 percent.
Many indicators give a warning near 90 percent, but the rule's trigger is 75 percent. A load between 75 and 90 percent must already be verified before the lift continues.
The pick radius is often the shortest and most generous one. The rule uses the longest radius that will be used during the lift, where capacity is lowest.
The set radius counts only if it happens to be the longest. If the load swings out farther in the middle of the lift, that longer radius governs.
Averaging radii has no basis in the rule. The comparison uses the single longest radius that will be used during the lift.
Mats and other supporting materials can help meet the manufacturer's specifications. They do not waive the drainage requirement.
Frozen ground has no exception, and it can lose strength as it thaws. Only marshes and wetlands are exempt from the drainage requirement.
Pavement has no exception. Water that collects under or beside a slab can still undermine support, so drainage still applies.
The hoisting method requires a load weighing device, indicator, or limiter. How the crane feels is not an accepted way to determine weight.
A visual guess is not an industry-recognized source or calculation. Writing it in the plan does not make it reliable.
Accepting responsibility does not establish the weight. The operator still needs the weight from a reliable source before the lift.

lift-planning.basics.misconception: reads depth as weight per foot
lift-planning.basics.why_wrong: This multiplies the 12 by the length. In a W12 x 50, the 12 is the nominal depth in inches; the 50 is the weight in pounds per foot.
This multiplies the two numbers in the designation (12 x 50) and never uses the measured length.
This multiplies 50 lb/ft by the length in inches (36 x 12 = 432 in), which mixes units. Weight per foot must be multiplied by length in feet.
The boom foot pin is usually set off from the centerline of rotation. Measuring from it gives a radius that is too short and overstates capacity.

lift-planning.critical.misconception: Operator certification substitutes for planning qualification
lift-planning.critical.why_wrong: Operator certification alone does not establish qualification to develop this plan. The developer must be a qualified person.
Designation as a competent person does not by itself meet the requirement for a qualified plan developer.

lift-planning.critical.misconception: Every multiple-crane plan requires an engineer
lift-planning.critical.why_wrong: The rule requires a qualified person, rather than a professional engineer for every multiple-crane plan.
A trial pick is part of the operation. Planning must precede the operation, including that pick.
Waiting until both cranes take weight places planning after the operation has begun.

lift-planning.critical.misconception: Planning is needed only for movement
lift-planning.critical.why_wrong: Holding radius constant does not permit an unplanned initial lift. Planning is required before beginning.
This provision does not establish a capacity percentage as its engineering trigger. It uses the qualified person's determination.

lift-planning.critical.misconception: Engineering begins with a third crane
lift-planning.critical.why_wrong: The provision does not reserve engineering assistance for three-crane lifts. The qualified planner may need it for two cranes.

lift-planning.critical.misconception: Project classification replaces the federal trigger
lift-planning.critical.why_wrong: A project classification may impose additional requirements, but this federal trigger is the qualified person's determination.
Capacity margin does not remove the consequences of losing an essential, irreplaceable item.
A single-crane lift can warrant critical planning because of potential damage consequences.
The stated basis is the consequence of damage, not a universal 25% threshold.

lift-planning.critical.misconception: Trial pick substitutes for advance planning
lift-planning.critical.why_wrong: A trial pick may verify planned behavior, but it cannot precede the planning required for the operation.
The rule does not use a 50% threshold. Joint support triggers planning regardless of this capacity margin.

lift-planning.critical.misconception: Planning applies only to traveling lifts
lift-planning.critical.why_wrong: Travel is not the trigger. A stationary operation with two cranes supporting one load requires advance planning.

lift-planning.critical.misconception: Controlling entity owns every planning duty
lift-planning.critical.why_wrong: Site coordination does not transfer this specific duty. The provision assigns it to the employer.

lift-planning.load-sharing.why_wrong: An engineer is required only when the qualified person decides engineering expertise is needed. Even then, the employer provides that expertise and the qualified person still develops the plan.
The controlling entity has other site duties, but the multi-crane rule gives the planning to a qualified person.
The lift director directs the lift and reviews the plan with the crew, but the rule does not say the director must write it.
This reverses the lever. The far crane has the longer arm, so it needs less force to balance the beam. The near crane carries more.
The load splits evenly only when the center of gravity is exactly midway between the pick points. Here it is not.
Load share comes from geometry, meaning where the center of gravity sits between the hooks. Crane capacity does not change how much weight each hook carries.
The operators and signal person must be there, but the rule covers everyone who will be involved, including riggers and tag line workers.
The rule requires the plan to be reviewed with the workers who will do the lift, not only with the person who wrote it.
Owners and the controlling entity are not the required audience. The rule names the workers who will be involved with the operation.
This multiplies by crane A's own distance to the center of gravity, which gives crane B's share. Each crane's share uses the distance from the center of gravity to the other crane.
An even split applies only when the center of gravity is midway between the pick points. Here it is 10 ft from A and 30 ft from B.
This divides by the far distance instead of the full 40 ft span between the pick points. The shares must add up to 20,000 lb.
This multiplies by crane A's own distance (12 ft), which gives crane B's share. Crane A's share uses the 8 ft from the center of gravity to crane B's lug.
This treats the center of gravity as if it were at the 10 ft midpoint. It is 8 ft from B, so the shares are not equal.
The share is right, but the hook block and slings under crane A are part of that crane's load and must be added.
This uses crane B's capacity. Each crane's load is checked against its own chart at its own radius.

lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.why_wrong: Being qualified alone is not enough. The director must also meet the competent-person criteria or be a competent person with qualified help. A rigging credential does not change that.
A competent person who is not also qualified must be assisted by one or more qualified persons. The rule makes no exception for matching crane models.

lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.misconception: Duty assigned by crane role rather than by competence
lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.why_wrong: No role comes with the lift director job automatically. Whoever directs must meet the competent and qualified criteria in one of the two allowed ways.

lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.misconception: Meeting limited to crane control personnel
lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.why_wrong: Riggers, tag-line handlers and others involved in the lift must also attend. The meeting is not limited to the people running the cranes and giving signals.

lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.misconception: Meeting treated as a management sign-off
lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.why_wrong: The rule names all workers involved in the operation, not a management group. The ground crew must hear the plan too.
Experience is no exemption. Each lift has its own plan, so everyone involved must go over that plan.

lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.misconception: Duty assigned to the controlling entity
lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.why_wrong: A safety manager may attend, but the plan review duty belongs to the lift director.
Operators attend the meeting as workers involved. They do not run it unless one of them is also the lift director.

lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.misconception: Duty assigned to the signal person
lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.why_wrong: The signal person is one of the workers who must attend the meeting. Running the plan review is the lift director's job.
Meeting both sets of criteria is only one of the two options. The rule also allows a competent person with qualified assistance.
A written plan does not replace a qualified person assisting during the lift. The superintendent still needs that help to direct.
This reverses the roles. The rule has the competent person direct with qualified help, not a qualified person direct with competent help.

lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.misconception: Duty assigned to the wrong person
lift-planning.multi-crane-implement.why_wrong: A foreman's task briefing does not meet the requirement. The plan review is the lift director's duty.
The rule calls for a review in a meeting with the lift director. Reading the plan and signing a sheet does not take its place.
A tag-line handler controls the load directly and is part of the operation. He is not exempt.
Plumb lines keep the loads vertical, but the split depends on where the CG is. It is half and half only when the CG is centered.

lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.why_wrong: Operating the larger crane does not automatically qualify someone to develop the plan. The plan developer must be a qualified person.
Responsibility for the schedule does not establish the qualifications needed to develop the lift plan.
Directing crane movements does not automatically qualify a signal person to develop the multiple-crane plan.
A trial lift is part of the operation. Planning must occur before the operation begins.

lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.misconception: Planning starts after balance is confirmed
lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.why_wrong: Checking balance with the cranes already supporting the vessel cannot precede the required planning.
The planning requirement is not postponed until the load leaves its original support. It applies before beginning the operation.
An unequal load split is not the stated trigger. The trigger is the qualified person's determination that engineering expertise is needed.
Using two cranes requires planning, but it does not by itself establish the stated condition requiring engineering expertise.
This provision does not establish a percentage threshold for engineering involvement. It assigns that determination to the qualified person.
During the handoff, more than one crane will support the pump. Its short duration does not remove the planning requirement.

lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.misconception: Trial handoff can establish the plan afterward
lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.why_wrong: The trial handoff would itself involve shared support. The operation must be planned before it begins.

lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.misconception: Receiving crane's plan covers the transfer
lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.why_wrong: Planning only one crane's lift does not address the operation involving both cranes supporting the load.

lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.misconception: Low individual utilization removes shared planning
lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.why_wrong: Separate plans that omit shared support do not address the multiple-crane operation. The site's threshold does not remove the planning requirement.
Adding utilization percentages from different cranes does not establish this planning requirement or the engineering trigger. Shared support requires planning.

lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.misconception: Briefing replaces planning below a site threshold
lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.why_wrong: A briefing cannot substitute for developing the required plan. Low utilization does not exempt a multiple-crane operation.

lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.misconception: Operator bears the employer's procurement duty
lift-planning.multi-crane-plan.why_wrong: The provision assigns the duty to ensure expertise is provided to the employer, not automatically to the operator.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Essential-task exception extended to under the load
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: Installing bracing can make an employee essential, but that only allows them into the fall zone. It never allows them directly under the load.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Guiding treated as permission to be under the load
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: Guiding the load is a listed essential task. It allows the employee into the fall zone, beside the load, and not under it.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Fall-zone exception confused with the under-load ban
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: An employee shown to be essential may enter the fall zone. The rule still keeps every employee out from directly under the load.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Any safety task treated as essential
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: Inspecting rigging is not one of the three listed tasks (guide, monitor and instruct, attach or detach). It can also be done with no load hanging.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Crane monitoring confused with load monitoring
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: Watching the crane's support does not guide the load, instruct its movement or attach or detach it. It also does not require being in the panel's fall zone.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Authority treated as an essential role
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: A job title does not make someone essential. Only the three listed tasks qualify, and only when they cannot be done from outside the fall zone.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Boom free fall trigger applied to the load line
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: The fall zone is the trigger for boom free fall. Load line free fall is banned when an employee is directly under the load.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Swing-radius hazard confused with free fall rule
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: The swing-radius barricade protects against being struck or crushed by the rotating superstructure. It is not what triggers the load line free fall ban.
The rule does not use this zone. Load line free fall is barred only when an employee is directly under the load.
This would be required if guiding from outside were feasible. Here the employer has shown it is not, so the laborers count as essential.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Essential status extended to under the load
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: Being essential opens the fall zone only. The rule keeps everyone out from directly under the load.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Added condition not in the rule
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: The rule does not require a signal person beside the guiders. Their own task, plus the shown infeasibility, is what allows them in the fall zone.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Under-load ban treated as the only limit
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: Staying out from under the load is the minimum for everyone. The fall zone itself is open only to essential employees.

lift-planning.tilt-up.misconception: Swing radius confused with fall zone
lift-planning.tilt-up.why_wrong: The swing radius has nothing to do with this. The panel can fall onto him anywhere in its fall zone.
Telling the operator does not make a worker essential. Only the listed tasks, shown infeasible from outside, allow entry.
The rule expects bracing to be installed while the crane holds the panel. It lets the ironworker into the fall zone because he cannot do the work from outside.

loadchart.arithmetic.why_wrong: A U.S. short ton contains 2,000 pounds. Dividing by 1,000 gives twice the correct number of short tons.
Multiplication by 2,000 converts short tons to pounds. Converting pounds to short tons requires division.

loadchart.arithmetic.misconception: Confuses short tons with long tons
loadchart.arithmetic.why_wrong: A 2,240-pound ton is a long ton. This chart uses 2,000-pound short tons.

loadchart.arithmetic.misconception: Treats inches as hundredths of a foot
loadchart.arithmetic.why_wrong: Writing inches as hundredths does not convert them to feet. Divide 9 by 12 to get 0.75 foot.
This places the decimal one position too far left. Nine inches is 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 foot.
A foot has 12 inches, not 10. Nine inches is 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 foot.

loadchart.arithmetic.misconception: Uses a linear conversion for area
loadchart.arithmetic.why_wrong: Three is the length conversion factor. For area, convert both dimensions: 3 × 3 = 9 square feet.
Adding the two 3-foot dimensions does not give area. Multiply them to get 9 square feet.
Twelve feet is the perimeter of a 3-foot square. Its area is 3 × 3 = 9 square feet.
This loses a factor of ten. Calculate 24 × 3 = 72, then restore both factors of ten to get 7,200 pounds.

loadchart.arithmetic.misconception: Divides total weight between pick points
loadchart.arithmetic.why_wrong: Two lifting points do not halve the member's total weight on the crane. Its weight is 30 × 240 = 7,200 pounds.
This adds an extra factor of ten. Thirty feet at 240 pounds per foot weighs 7,200 pounds.
Six short tons is 12,000 pounds, not 6,000. Subtracting the 2,000-pound deductions leaves 10,000 pounds.
This subtracts the 2,000-pound deductions twice. Deduct them once from 12,000 pounds to get 10,000 pounds.
The available payload is 5 short tons, but that equals 10,000 pounds. A ton result cannot be labeled as thousands of pounds.
One thousand pounds is more than three-fourths of 1,200 pounds. One-fourth is 300 pounds, so three-fourths is 900 pounds.

loadchart.boom-angle-limits.why_wrong: A previous setup does not establish the current angle. The temporary alternative requires a measurement.
An estimate does not satisfy the measuring-device requirement, regardless of who makes it.
A planned location alone does not establish measured working radius. Radius or boom angle must be measured.
Before the rigging becomes taut, the crane has not taken the load. That reading does not capture loaded boom deflection.
Landing the load removes its force from the boom. The resulting angle does not represent the loaded geometry.
Averaging loaded and unloaded readings produces an angle that may never represent the crane's actual loaded condition.
The hoist line is approximately vertical. Measuring from vertical gives the complementary angle, which would be 30° here.
Ground slope is not the reference for boom elevation. Using sloping ground would change the reading without changing the boom's actual elevation.

loadchart.boom-angle-limits.misconception: Rotation axis supplies the elevation reference
loadchart.boom-angle-limits.why_wrong: The rotation axis is vertical on a level crane. Measuring from that axis would give the angle from vertical, not boom elevation.
The 45° row would follow from the unloaded 47° reading. The loaded reading is 43°, requiring the 40° row.
The chart requires the lower listed angle, not an average of capacities. The 40° capacity applies.
Selecting a higher angle contradicts the chart note. The loaded 43° angle requires the 40° row.
The 20,000-lb capacity applies at a permitted angle. It does not authorize operation beyond the maximum angle.
A smaller radius does not extend the chart's permitted angle range. The proposed 78° angle exceeds 75°.
The chart gives no half-capacity adjustment. The problem is exceeding the angle limit, not a missing percentage reduction.
Although 48° is closer to 50°, the chart requires the lower listed angle. The 40° row applies.

loadchart.boom-between-columns.why_wrong: The 90-ft column is shorter than the actual boom. The chart note directs you to the 100-ft column.
Averaging 12,000 and 10,000 gives 11,000 lb, but the chart note does not authorize interpolation.
The 80-ft column offers a higher rating but does not apply to 95 ft of boom under this chart note.

loadchart.boom-between-columns.misconception: Round to the nearest boom length
loadchart.boom-between-columns.why_wrong: Although 81 ft is closer to 80 ft, the chart requires the next longer column, which is 90 ft.

loadchart.boom-between-columns.misconception: Use a shorter column for extra capacity
loadchart.boom-between-columns.why_wrong: The 70-ft column does not apply to this boom length. Use the 90-ft column and its 9,000-lb rating.
Averaging the adjacent ratings is not the chart's specified method. The next longer column gives 9,000 lb.
The longer-boom column has the higher capacity here. The note requires the lower adjacent capacity, not automatically the longer length.
The average is 9,500 lb, but this note requires the lower rating, which is 9,000 lb.
The note supplies no additional 1,000-lb reduction. The applicable gross capacity is 9,000 lb.
This uses the correct radius row but the shorter boom column. Use 90 ft of boom and a 40-ft radius.
This uses the correct boom column but the smaller radius row. The 35-ft radius requires the 40-ft row.
The four values average to 15,000 lb, but the chart requires selecting a specific row and column rather than averaging.

loadchart.boom-between-columns.misconception: Deduct correctly from the wrong column
loadchart.boom-between-columns.why_wrong: 14,000 minus 2,000 equals 12,000 lb, but that starts with the shorter, inapplicable column. The correct payload limit is 10,000 lb.
Averaging gives 13,000 lb, and deducting 2,000 gives 11,000 lb. The averaging step is not permitted by the chart note.
Adding 2,000 lb to the applicable 12,000-lb rating reverses the deduction. Suspended equipment reduces the available payload to 10,000 lb.

loadchart.boom-between-columns.misconception: Use the shorter column in the correct chart
loadchart.boom-between-columns.why_wrong: The outrigger configuration is correct, but 85 ft requires the 90-ft column. That rating is 9,000 lb.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: Setup and configuration changes are not the only times charts must be available. They must be readily available in the cab at all times.
Chart availability does not end when the load leaves the ground. The requirement applies at all times.
The requirement does not depend on how close a load is to rated capacity.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.misconception: Signal person can hold the required charts
loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: Radio consultation does not replace the required availability of the charts in the cab.
Availability in a site office does not satisfy the required location, even if the operator can review the charts there.
Charts kept at the access steps are outside the cab. The specified location is in the cab.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.misconception: Any chart-related network failure triggers shutdown
loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: An interrupted download is not the stated trigger if the applicable rated capacities remain accessible.
Loss of printing does not itself make electronically displayed capacities inaccessible. This provision does not require paper copies.
Failure to send files elsewhere does not trigger this requirement when capacities remain accessible in the cab.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.misconception: Changing chart format requires inspector approval
loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: This provision does not require an inspector's approval before using an applicable paper chart.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.misconception: Electronic restoration is the only remedy
loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: Electronic repair is not required by this provision when the applicable rated capacities are available in another form.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.misconception: Electronic troubleshooting must precede backup use
loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: The provision does not require a restart attempt before using accessible rated capacities in another form.
An earlier check does not create an exception for repeated lifts after the rated capacities become inaccessible.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.misconception: A lighter load substitutes for chart access
loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: Reducing the load does not restore access to rated capacities or satisfy the required response.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.misconception: Supervisor confirmation substitutes for available charts
loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: A supervisor's confirmation does not replace available rated capacities or authorize continued lifting under this provision.

loadchart.chart-in-cab.misconception: Continuous radio support replaces cab charts
loadchart.chart-in-cab.why_wrong: Continuous radio assistance does not meet the requirement to have applicable charts readily available in the cab.

loadchart.chart-notes.why_wrong: Charts kept in an office are not readily available while the operator is working. The rule requires them in the cab at all times.

loadchart.chart-notes.misconception: Duty assigned to the wrong person
loadchart.chart-notes.why_wrong: A lift director may review the chart, but that does not replace the requirement. The charts must be in the cab for the operator.

loadchart.chart-notes.misconception: Somewhere on the crane is enough
loadchart.chart-notes.why_wrong: A carrier compartment is not the cab, and the operator cannot read it from the controls. The rule says the cab, at all times.
These numbers are reversed. Outriggers give a firmer, more predictable base, so the outrigger rating gets the higher percentage (85%) and the tire rating gets 75%.
Both values are too high. The usual limits are 85% on outriggers and 75% on tires.
Both values are too low. The usual limits are 85% on outriggers and 75% on tires, and crawlers are also commonly rated at 75%.
Stability governs below the bold line, at the longer radii. Above the line, structural strength is the limit.

loadchart.chart-notes.misconception: Confuses bold line with line-pull limit
loadchart.chart-notes.why_wrong: Line pull is a separate limit, set by the parts of line reeved. It is not what the bold line divides.

loadchart.chart-notes.misconception: Confuses chart zones with support conditions
loadchart.chart-notes.why_wrong: The chart assumes firm, adequate support. Ground bearing capacity is not what the bold line marks.
30 ft is the nearer value, but it is shorter than the actual radius. Its capacity is higher than the crane has at 32 ft.
Interpolating gives 20,000 − (2/5 × 4,000) = 18,400 lb. The chart does not allow interpolation, and capacity does not have to change in a straight line between radii.
Averaging the two values is not a method the chart allows. The note requires the next longer radius, 16,000 lb.
12,000 − 400 − 100 = 11,500 lb leaves out the stowed jib. The jib adds weight to the boom even when stowed, and the note requires the 1,000 lb deduction.
12,000 − 1,000 = 11,000 lb leaves out the hook block and slings. Both are part of the load the crane carries and must be deducted.
12,000 − 400 = 11,600 lb counts only the block. Slings, shackles and the stowed jib must also be deducted.
A field derate is not a manufacturer rating. Stability changes sharply as outrigger spread shrinks, so a flat percentage cut has no basis.

loadchart.configuration.why_wrong: An operator-selected reduction does not authorize partial extension. Manufacturer procedures must permit the deployment specified in the load chart.
Lift-director approval cannot replace manufacturer permission and the chart's deployment requirements.
A successful test lift does not establish an authorized partial-extension configuration.

loadchart.configuration.misconception: Carrier weight may stay on tires
loadchart.configuration.why_wrong: The carrier is part of the equipment. Equipment weight must be removed from the wheels.
Merely reducing wheel loading does not meet the requirement to remove equipment weight from the wheels.
The requirement does not exempt the steering axle. Equipment weight must be removed from all wheels.
The operator does not have to see every outrigger personally; visibility to a signal person also satisfies the requirement.

loadchart.configuration.misconception: Supervisory title substitutes for signal role
loadchart.configuration.why_wrong: Those titles alone do not satisfy the specified role. Each outrigger must be visible to the operator or a signal person.
Assignment as the load's rigger alone does not meet the requirement; the person observing must be the operator or a signal person.

loadchart.configuration.misconception: Lower chart validates any wider setup
loadchart.configuration.why_wrong: Using the lower chart does not authorize a mixed deployment. The permitted mid-extension arrangement requires all four beams at the marks.
Averaging capacities creates an unsupported rating and does not correct the unlisted outrigger arrangement.
The marked mid-extension setup has its own chart. Half of the full-extension rating is not a substitute for that chart.

loadchart.configuration.misconception: Tire chart cures incomplete outrigger setup
loadchart.configuration.why_wrong: Selecting an on-rubber rating does not waive the wheel-unloading requirement when this truck crane uses outriggers.
An arbitrary capacity reduction does not satisfy the requirement to remove equipment weight from the wheels.
Sharing equipment weight between tires and outriggers is insufficient. The wheels must be unloaded.
15,000 − 1,000 = 14,000 lb uses the full-extension rating. The actual mid-extension rating is 10,000 lb gross.

loadchart.counterweight.why_wrong: The lift director's approval does not replace the manufacturer's counterweight specification.
A site calculation does not replace the manufacturer's specified counterweight configuration.
The operator must select a configuration consistent with the manufacturer's specifications, rather than independently establish the required counterweight.
A tipping calculation does not establish permission to exceed the manufacturer's maximum counterweight.
The mounting frame's apparent strength does not replace the maximum specified for the equipment.
An approved lift plan cannot authorize counterweight or ballast above the manufacturer's maximum.

loadchart.counterweight.misconception: Self-erecting tower treated as mobile equipment
loadchart.counterweight.why_wrong: This is a tower crane, which is excluded from the equipment scope of this provision.

loadchart.counterweight.misconception: Fixed-jib tower included in mobile provision
loadchart.counterweight.why_wrong: Tower cranes are excluded from this provision's scope, including hammerhead tower cranes.
A luffing-jib tower crane is still a tower crane and is excluded from this provision's scope.
A proportional chart reduction does not authorize operation without the specified counterweight.
Lift-director approval cannot substitute for the manufacturer's specified counterweight.

loadchart.counterweight.misconception: Short radius compensates for missing counterweight
loadchart.counterweight.why_wrong: A shorter radius does not cure the missing specified counterweight.

loadchart.counterweight.misconception: Secure attachment makes excess weight acceptable
loadchart.counterweight.why_wrong: Improved attachment does not authorize exceeding the manufacturer's maximum counterweight.
Reducing the lifted load does not permit counterweight above the specified maximum.
Restricting the operating sector does not remove the prohibition against exceeding the manufacturer's maximum.
A short working radius does not replace required carrier ballast.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Block rating mistaken for block weight
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: The block's rating is how much it can support, not how much it weighs. Subtract its 800 lb actual weight.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Unused component rating treated as a deduction
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: Subtracting block weight from block rating does not produce a chart deduction. The deduction is the block's 800 lb weight.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Installed block assumed included in net capacity
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: Being part of the crane does not make the block weight disappear from the suspended load. Deduct 800 lb from the gross capacity.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Rigging rating substituted for rigging weight
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: A working load limit describes lifting capability, not weight. The suspended assembly adds 200 lb.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Rigging capacity calculation used as crane deduction
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: Subtracting assembly weight from its working load limit does not calculate a crane capacity deduction. Deduct the actual 200 lb.
Certification does not remove suspended weight. The chart requires the assembly's 200 lb weight to be deducted.
The payload rating is the load the beam can carry, not the beam's own weight. The beam deduction is 1,000 lb.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Maximum payload included in device deduction
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: That total describes the beam carrying its maximum payload. The question asks for the beam alone, which weighs 1,000 lb.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Payload rating treated as gross device capacity
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: The marking already identifies 10,000 lb as payload capacity. Subtracting tare from that rating does not establish the beam's crane-chart deduction.
This omits the 200 lb rigging assembly. Both suspended weights must be subtracted, leaving 11,000 lb.
This omits the 800 lb hook block. The combined deduction is 1,000 lb.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Gross capacity treated as payload capacity
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: Gross capacity includes the suspended equipment. It leaves 11,000 lb for payload after the required deductions.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Stowed jib assumed to have no capacity effect
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: The stated chart also requires the 1,000 lb stowed-jib deduction. Total deductions are 2,000 lb.
This leaves out the 400 lb rigging weight. Subtracting it gives 13,000 lb.
This leaves out the 600 lb hook block. The correct payload capacity is 13,000 lb.

loadchart.deductions.misconception: Attachment weight substituted for chart deduction
loadchart.deductions.why_wrong: The chart specifies a 3,000 lb erected-jib deduction, not the jib's 2,000 lb physical weight. With suspended gear, deductions total 4,000 lb.

loadchart.jib.why_wrong: That is the jib's inclination above horizontal. Offset measures the jib's departure from the main boom axis.
That is the main boom angle. It does not identify the angle at the jib connection.

loadchart.jib.misconception: Vertical reference substituted for boom reference
loadchart.jib.why_wrong: That angle is the complement of the main boom angle. It does not measure jib offset.
The rigging also uses part of the gross capacity. Both specified weights must be deducted.
The hook block also uses part of the gross capacity. Both specified weights must be deducted.
Adding these weights would increase the apparent payload allowance. Their weight consumes capacity, so it must be subtracted.

loadchart.jib.misconception: Boom heel used as radius origin
loadchart.jib.why_wrong: The boom heel pin is not the radius reference. Its position can differ from the crane's axis of rotation.

loadchart.jib.misconception: Support point used as radius origin
loadchart.jib.why_wrong: That distance relates to the support geometry, but it is not the chart's load radius. Chart radius starts at the axis of rotation.

loadchart.jib.misconception: Jib reach mistaken for total radius
loadchart.jib.why_wrong: That measures only the jib's horizontal reach. It leaves out the main boom's contribution to the load radius.
8,000 − 500 = 7,500 lb uses the 0° column. The installed jib is at 30°.
6,000 − 500 = 5,500 lb uses the 15° column. The installed jib is at 30°.
4,000 lb is the correct gross rating. The 500-lb deduction leaves 3,500 lb for payload.

loadchart.jib.misconception: Jib inclination used as boom angle
loadchart.jib.why_wrong: This uses a 4,000-lb rating, such as the 45° boom-angle row at 15° offset. The main boom is at 60°; 45° is the jib's inclination.
6,000 lb is the selected gross rating. Subtracting the 500-lb lifting equipment leaves 5,500 lb.

loadchart.jib.misconception: Wrong angle row and offset column
loadchart.jib.why_wrong: 3,000 − 500 = 2,500 lb uses the 45° boom-angle row and 30° offset column. Neither matches the installed configuration.
6,000 − 500 = 5,500 lb uses the shorter 35-ft radius. The chart requires the next longer listed radius.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: steel unit weight applied to concrete
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: About 490 lb per cubic foot is the figure for steel. Concrete weighs roughly a third of that, about 150 lb per cubic foot.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: water unit weight applied to concrete
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: About 62.4 lb per cubic foot is the figure for fresh water. Concrete is more than twice as heavy, about 150 lb per cubic foot.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: timber unit weight applied to concrete
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: About 40 lb per cubic foot is in the range for dry timber. Concrete is far denser, about 150 lb per cubic foot.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: shipping paperwork assumed to be the named source
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: The rule does not name the trucking company. A shipping weight may be useful, but the rule's named example is the load's manufacturer.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: in-lift instrument reading treated as the named source
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: A load moment indicator reads the load once it is on the hook. The rule says the weight must be determined, and given to the operator on request, before the lift, and its named example is the manufacturer.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: rigging rating confused with load weight source
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: The rigging supplier rates the slings and hardware, not the load. The rule names the load's manufacturer.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: forgot to divide the cubic-foot weight by 12
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: About 490 lb is the weight of a full cubic foot of steel, which is 12 in. thick. A 1-in. plate is one-twelfth of that, about 40 lb.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: concrete figure applied to steel plate
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: About 150 lb is the weight of a cubic foot of concrete, not of 1 sq ft of 1-in. steel plate, which is about 40 lb.
This takes the correct 40.8 and slips the decimal point. The plate weighs about 40.8 lb per square foot per inch.
This multiplies the depth by the per-foot weight (12 × 50). The length sets the weight: 40 ft × 50 lb/ft = 2,000 lb.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: included nominal depth as a multiplier
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: This multiplies all three numbers (12 × 50 × 40). The 12 is a depth, not a factor in the weight. The answer is 40 × 50 = 2,000 lb.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: read depth as the per-foot weight
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: This multiplies the depth by the length (12 × 40) and ignores the 50 lb/ft. The weight is 40 ft × 50 lb/ft = 2,000 lb.
This uses only two dimensions (4 × 5 = 20, × 150). Volume needs all three: 4 × 5 × 2 = 40 cu ft, which gives 6,000 lb.
This adds the dimensions (4 + 5 + 2 = 11, × 150) instead of multiplying them. The volume is 40 cu ft, so the block weighs 6,000 lb.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: steel unit weight used for concrete
