loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: This multiplies 40 cu ft by steel's 490 lb per cu ft. The block is concrete: 40 × 150 = 6,000 lb.

loadchart.load-weight.misconception: relying on the LMI instead of determining weight
loadchart.load-weight.why_wrong: An LMI does not replace determining the weight. When the operator asks, the weight must be provided before the lift.

loadchart.max-radius.why_wrong: The operating limit is the applicable rated capacity. Applying another 75% factor confuses the published rating with a factor used in establishing some ratings.

loadchart.max-radius.misconception: Confusing rating development with chart use
loadchart.max-radius.why_wrong: The listed rating is already the rated capacity. The rule does not require reducing that rating to 85% merely because stability governs.

loadchart.max-radius.misconception: Treating the stability margin as usable capacity
loadchart.max-radius.why_wrong: The rule prohibits exceeding rated capacity. A margin between rated capacity and tipping load is not available as extra lifting capacity.
The hook block is suspended load, but the installed counterweight is part of the charted crane configuration. Net payload capacity equals gross capacity minus hook block and rigging weight.

loadchart.max-radius.misconception: Replacing the block deduction with boom weight
loadchart.max-radius.why_wrong: The chart accounts for the configured boom's weight. The suspended hook block must be deducted along with the rigging.

loadchart.max-radius.misconception: Confusing crane configuration with suspended load
loadchart.max-radius.why_wrong: Counterweight belongs to the charted crane configuration, not the suspended payload allowance. The required pair is hook block and rigging weight.
The boom foot pin is not the radius reference. The load's horizontal distance from the rotation axis determines its load moment about that axis.
The tipping edge is used in stability analysis, but it is not the chart's radius origin. Chart radius starts at the rotation axis.
Sloping distance includes height and does not give the horizontal lever arm. Use the horizontal distance to the load line.
The required gross capacity is 11,000 lb. The 25-ft rating of 12,000 lb also supports that load, so 20 ft is not the maximum.
The 30-ft rating is 10,000 lb, but the complete suspended load is 11,000 lb. Omitting either 1,000-lb deduction produces this incorrect radius.
The 35-ft rating is only 8,000 lb. Subtracting the block and rigging from the machine weight reverses the calculation; they must be added to find required gross capacity.
Required gross capacity is 10,000 lb. The partial-extension chart permits that amount at 25 ft, so stopping at 20 ft is unnecessary.
At partial extension, 30 ft permits only 8,000 lb. A full-extension capacity cannot be used for the actual partial-extension setup.
The 35-ft rating of 10,000 lb belongs to full extension. At partial extension, that radius permits only 6,000 lb.

loadchart.max-radius.misconception: Counting only half the suspended equipment
loadchart.max-radius.why_wrong: The 10-ft rating is 11,000 lb, which is 1,000 lb below the required 12,000 lb. The entire 2,000-lb assembly must be counted.

loadchart.net-capacity.misconception: Hook block excluded from suspended weight
loadchart.net-capacity.why_wrong: This omits the hook block. Net payload capacity equals the chart rating minus the block, slings, and beam.
This omits the slings. Their weight also consumes part of the chart capacity.

loadchart.net-capacity.misconception: Lifting beam treated as weightless support
loadchart.net-capacity.why_wrong: This omits the lifting beam. A beam remains part of the suspended weight even though it distributes the payload.
The listed capacity already accounts for the block. Deducting it again understates the capacity available for payload.

loadchart.net-capacity.misconception: Included block substituted for excluded hardware
loadchart.net-capacity.why_wrong: This deducts the block twice and omits the shackles. The additional deduction is the combined sling and shackle weight.

loadchart.net-capacity.misconception: Included block substituted for excluded slings
loadchart.net-capacity.why_wrong: This deducts the block twice and omits the slings. Both slings and shackles require deductions under the stated chart note.

loadchart.net-capacity.misconception: Assembly weight mistaken for per-leg weight
loadchart.net-capacity.why_wrong: The stated total already includes all four legs. Multiplying by four counts the same assembly weight four times.

loadchart.net-capacity.misconception: Load sharing reduces suspended device weight
loadchart.net-capacity.why_wrong: Load sharing among sling legs does not reduce the assembly's weight. Deduct its full documented total once.

loadchart.net-capacity.misconception: Per-leg share used as total deduction
loadchart.net-capacity.why_wrong: Dividing by four would estimate one leg's share, not the weight suspended from the crane. The whole assembly must be counted.
This results from deducting the 2,000 lb beam twice. The total device weight is 4,000 lb, leaving 12,000 lb.
This omits a 1,000 lb deduction. The block, beam, and rigging together require a 4,000 lb deduction.
This deducts only 2,000 lb. All three device groups total 4,000 lb and must be subtracted.
This counts the 1,000 lb rigging assembly twice. Each listed device weight is deducted once, leaving 13,000 lb.
This counts the 2,000 lb block twice. The combined deduction is 3,000 lb, not 5,000 lb.
This doubles the entire 3,000 lb handling-weight deduction. The chart requires one deduction for each suspended device.
This omits a 1,000 lb device group. The full deduction is 4,000 lb, leaving 10,000 lb.

loadchart.on-rubber.misconception: Assigns the travel duty to the rigger
loadchart.on-rubber.why_wrong: A qualified rigger handles rigging. The rule gives supervision and the travel determinations, including speed, to a competent person.
A signal person passes signals to the operator. Deciding the travel route is one of the competent person's determinations.
The rule says competent person, not qualified person, and ground support is one of that competent person's determinations. People often mix up these two roles across the crane rules.

loadchart.on-rubber.misconception: Field myth: soft tires spread the load
loadchart.on-rubber.why_wrong: Underinflation lets the tires deflect more. That shifts the radius and the stability the chart assumes. The rule requires the manufacturer's specified pressure.
Going above spec is not what the rule requires. The rule requires the manufacturer's specified pressure, not more.

loadchart.on-rubber.misconception: Tire maker's limit vs crane manufacturer's spec
loadchart.on-rubber.why_wrong: The sidewall maximum is the tire maker's limit. The crane manufacturer's on-rubber pressure is what the rule requires, and it can differ.
Fully extended outriggers alone do not make the front area permitted. The deciding factor is whether the manufacturer permits lifting there.
No percentage of the chart makes an over-front lift legal. Only the manufacturer's permission does.
The competent person's approval governs traveling with a load. Over-front lifting on wheel-mounted equipment depends on the manufacturer's permission.

loadchart.on-rubber.misconception: Overgeneralizes the ban to all cranes
loadchart.on-rubber.why_wrong: Traveling with a load is allowed in general when the manufacturer permits it and the competent-person controls are in place. Here it is barred only because this manufacturer prohibits it.
The competent person's duties apply only where traveling with a load is allowed in the first place. They cannot override a manufacturer prohibition.
Stationary ratings do not authorize travel. The manufacturer has prohibited traveling with a load on this model, whatever the capacity margin.
The 18,000 lb value applies only while the crane is stationary. Travel adds dynamic and ground effects, which is why the pick-and-carry column is lower.
The 360° column applies when the boom swings off the front. With the boom kept over the front, the 14,000 lb pick-and-carry value governs.

loadchart.on-rubber.misconception: Treats test-load percentage as allowable overload
loadchart.on-rubber.why_wrong: 110% is a typical load-test figure, not an operating allowance. Rated capacity is the limit for working lifts.
This leaves out the 400 lb block and 200 lb of rigging, which the chart counts as part of the load.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: The rule does not use 85 percent or the shortest radius. The shortest radius has the highest rating, so using it would make the check less strict than the rule requires.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Uses pick radius instead of longest radius
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: The percentage is right but the radius is wrong. If the load is carried out to a longer radius, the pick-radius rating overstates what the crane can hold where it sets the load.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Confuses LMI warning setting with the rule
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: 90 percent is a common LMI warning setting, not this rule. The rule sets the check at 75 percent at the longest radius.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Assumes qualified-person approval overrides the manufacturer limit
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: A qualified person cannot approve counterweight beyond the manufacturer's maximum. The limit is fixed by the manufacturer's specification.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Believes a one-time or limited-area exception exists
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: Extra counterweight is not allowed for one lift or in any working area. It also raises the risk of tipping backward when the hook is unloaded or the boom is high.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Field myth of a small-overage tolerance
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: No percentage tolerance exists. Any counterweight beyond the manufacturer's maximum is prohibited.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Majority of beams decides the chart
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: Capacity is limited by the least-extended beam. Most of the beams being fully extended does not raise the rating over the short side.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Invents zone ratings without a manufacturer chart
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: Splitting the swing into zones requires a manufacturer chart for that setup. Without one, the operator cannot make up ratings by zone.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Wrong chart family for the support condition
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: The crane is still on outriggers, so the on-rubber chart does not apply. The mid-extension chart covers this setup.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Believes a small overload is acceptable
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: 11,000 lb is more than 10,500 lb, so the lift would exceed rated capacity. There is no 'close enough' allowance.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Adds margin the chart does not require
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: 30 ft works but is not the farthest position that works. The chart does not require a 2-to-1 margin.
The chart note bans interpolation. At 45 ft, the next longer radius (50 ft, 10,500 lb) applies, and that does not cover 11,000 lb.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Longer boom chosen for clearance at the cost of capacity
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: The 120 ft boom clears the parapet, but its rating of 11,000 lb is less than the 12,000 lb load. Extra boom costs capacity.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Uses main-boom chart for a jib configuration
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: With a jib, the jib chart governs and the main-boom row does not apply. Jib capacities are lower, and the jib adds its own deductions.

loadchart.optimize-configuration.misconception: Chases the highest number without checking reach
loadchart.optimize-configuration.why_wrong: 80 ft is the highest rating, but the boom is too short to clear the parapet. The configuration must fit the site before capacity matters.
3 parts carry only 3 × 9,000 = 27,000 lb, which is less than 30,000 lb. Always round parts of line up.

loadchart.parts-of-line.misconception: Thinks more rope on the drum means more pull
loadchart.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The outer layer has the largest effective drum radius. The same drum torque therefore produces the lowest line pull and the highest line speed there.
How evenly the rope spools does not set line pull. Pull drops steadily as each added layer increases the effective radius.

loadchart.parts-of-line.misconception: Treats line pull as a fixed hoist rating
loadchart.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The hoist's torque may be fixed, but line pull is torque divided by radius, so it changes with every layer.

loadchart.parts-of-line.misconception: Equates line speed with hook speed
loadchart.parts-of-line.why_wrong: Drum speed sets line speed, not hook speed. The rope coming off the drum is shared among all the parts, so the hook moves more slowly.

loadchart.parts-of-line.misconception: Thinks less tension means faster travel
loadchart.parts-of-line.why_wrong: A lower load on each part does not speed up the hook. Adding parts trades speed for pulling capacity.
Hook speed is line speed divided by the number of parts. Going from 4 to 5 parts slows the hook to 4/5 of its old speed, not to half.
This paragraph sets no 2:1 strength ratio. Its requirement is that the rope be compatible with the safe functioning of the equipment.

loadchart.parts-of-line.misconception: Mistakes a spooling practice for this rule
loadchart.parts-of-line.why_wrong: Matching lay to the drum is a good spooling practice, but this paragraph does not state it. The paragraph sets the broader compatibility requirement.
Rope is replaced based on its condition, not on a calendar. This paragraph sets no replacement interval.

loadchart.parts-of-line.misconception: Uses hoist capability instead of rope limit
loadchart.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The hoist can pull 12,000 lb, but the rope is limited to 8,000 lb. The lower of the two values governs.
34,000 ÷ 8,000 = 4.25. With 4 parts each part would carry 8,500 lb, which is over the limit, so always round up.
The charted permissible line pull already includes the rope design factor. Applying another factor to it counts the safety margin twice.
The chart value applies only if the reeving can carry it. One part of line cannot carry 18,000 lb.

loadchart.parts-of-line.misconception: Uses hoist capability instead of rope rating
loadchart.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The hoist's capability does not raise the rope's limit. The lower of hoist pull and rope rating governs.
The load hangs from the auxiliary head on one part, so the main boom head rating does not apply to this lift.
This uses the old reeving, and it would still be capped at the 30,000 lb chart value. The block now has 4 parts.

loadchart.percent-capacity.misconception: chart capacity confused with line pull
loadchart.percent-capacity.why_wrong: The percentage is right but the base is wrong. Chart capacity covers stability and structure, while the brake test is about what the hoist line pulls.
75% is a common planning flag in the field, but it is not the trigger. The brake test applies at 90% or more of maximum line pull.
Both the number and the base are wrong. The test applies at 90% or more of maximum line pull.
Holding a load at full height puts it at the highest point before the brakes have been proven. The test is done a few inches off the ground.
An empty hook does not prove the brakes can hold the actual load. The test is done with the load, a few inches up.
A few feet is too high, and returning the lever to neutral does not deliberately test the brakes. The rule calls for a few inches and applying the brakes.
The signal person directs crane motions but does not run the hoist or its brakes. The operator performs the test.
A supervisor may plan the lift, but the rule puts the brake test on the operator.
The rigger attaches the load but does not control the hoist. The operator tests the brakes.
This uses only the piece weight. The rigging and hook block are part of the load, so the total is 9,000 lb.
This adds only one of the two 500 lb items. Both the rigging and the block count, for 9,000 lb total.
The division is upside down. Percent of capacity is load divided by capacity: 9,000 ÷ 10,000 = 90%.
The threshold is 90% or more, not 100%. At 92%, the test is required.
The test applies to any load at 90% or more of line pull. Duty-cycle work only changes how often it is repeated.
Testing every lift is the general case, but repetitive duty-cycle work has an exception: only the first lift needs the test.
The rule sets no time interval. The requirement applies to the first lift of the series.

loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: A qualified person's approval does not replace manufacturer permission for an over-front lift.
Supporting the crane on outriggers does not itself authorize a front-area lift. Manufacturer permission is required.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: Side ratings transfer to the front
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: A side-area capacity does not establish permission to lift over the front, even at the same radius.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: Lift supervision includes authority to permit front lifting
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: The lift director is not the authority named in this exception. The rule specifies the manufacturer.
Site engineering approval does not substitute for the manufacturer permission specified by this rule.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: Operator judgment authorizes an otherwise prohibited quadrant
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: The operator cannot create the exception by judging the lift manageable. The exception depends on manufacturer permission.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: Crawler and wheel-mounted restrictions are interchangeable
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: This provision identifies wheel-mounted equipment. It does not establish a front-area prohibition for crawler-mounted cranes.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: The front-area prohibition applies to every mounting type
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: Pedestal-mounted cranes are not the equipment category named in this provision.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: All mobile mounting systems share this restriction
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: Rail-mounted cranes are not the category identified by this front-area provision.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: An informal derating authorizes a prohibited area
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: Reducing the load to half the side capacity does not create manufacturer permission to lift over the front.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: Rear capacity can be reassigned to the front
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: A rear-area rating cannot substitute for permission to lift over the front.
A judgment about tipping does not override the prohibition. Front-area lifting requires manufacturer permission.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: The boom's forward direction defines the front quadrant
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: The boom points toward the carrier's rear, so the front-area value does not apply.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: The side rating is the default operating capacity
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: The load is directly over the rear, not over a side. Select the rear entry for the stated configuration.

loadchart.quadrants.misconception: Correct quadrant but wrong support configuration
loadchart.quadrants.why_wrong: That value belongs to the on-rubber chart. The crane is supported on fully extended outriggers.
This is the side capacity at the shorter 20-ft radius. At 30 ft, the lower adjoining capacity is 8,000 lb.

loadchart.radius-between-rows.why_wrong: If the nearest row is the shorter one, its rating is higher than what the crane is rated for at the actual radius. Distance to the row doesn't matter; the next longer row always governs.
Charts are not built for straight-line interpolation unless a note allows it, and the value it produces can be higher than the true rating. Use the next longer radius row.
The shorter radius has the higher rating, so using it overrates the crane at the actual radius. The longer radius row governs.
Being closer to 70 ft doesn't make that column valid. A 72 ft boom has more boom weight out than the 70 ft rating assumes, so use the next longer column.
Interpolating between boom columns isn't allowed unless the chart says so. The next longer boom column governs.
Rounding down overstates capacity because the longer boom carries more of its own weight. Boom length rounds up to the next listed column.
A higher angle means a shorter radius and a higher rating, so this overrates the crane. Drop to the next lower listed angle.
If the nearest row is the higher angle, the rating is too high. Being close to a row doesn't qualify it; the next lower angle governs.
This averages the 30 ft and 35 ft ratings. That has no basis on the chart and is higher than the governing 35 ft rating.
This subtracts only the 600 lb hook block (12,000 − 600). Rigging is part of the load the crane lifts, so the 400 lb must come off too.
This is the correct row but it's gross capacity. The block and rigging weights still have to be subtracted to get net.
The answer is no, but for the wrong reason. No 75 percent threshold applies here; the load fails because it exceeds the 8,500 lb rating at 55 ft.
This rounds the pick radius correctly, but the load travels out to 47 ft. The longest radius in the move governs, not the pick point.
This uses the pick radius and also rounds it down. Both mistakes overstate capacity; the set radius rounded up to 50 ft governs.
This is the 60° rating. The boom is below 60°, so it is at a longer radius than that row assumes. Use the next lower angle.
This rounds the radius up correctly but uses the 50 ft boom column, rounding 56 ft down. Boom length also goes to the next longer column.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Confusing a common working angle with maximum geometric height
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: At 75 degrees, part of the boom's length still extends horizontally. A vertical boom places its entire length above the pivot.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Treating a steep working angle as maximum height
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: A 60-degree boom has less vertical rise than a vertical boom of the same length. Its horizontal reach uses part of that length.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Substituting a possible operating limit for a geometric limit
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: An 85-degree boom remains slightly short of its greatest geometric height. Maximum geometric rise occurs at 90 degrees.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Using the boom pivot as the radius origin
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: The boom heel pin may be offset from the crane's axis of rotation. Measuring from it can omit part of the operating radius.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Confusing a tipping boundary with the radius origin
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: An outrigger can relate to the crane's tipping boundary, but it is not the origin for operating radius. Radius is measured from the axis of rotation.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Using a carrier landmark as the radius origin
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: The front axle's position does not define operating radius. The horizontal measurement starts at the crane's axis of rotation.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Treating tip height and hook height as one measurement
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: The hook moves relative to the boom tip as rope pays out. The fixed boom tip does not follow the hook downward.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Treating hook and boom tip as counter-moving ends
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: Lowering the hook does not raise the boom tip. With boom geometry fixed, only the hook's position changes.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Applying parts-of-line effects to boom-tip movement
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: Reeving affects rope travel needed for a given hook movement. It does not change boom-tip height when boom geometry stays fixed.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Assigning document access to the signal person
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: Keeping procedures with the signal person does not meet the cab requirement. They must be readily available in the cab for the operator.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Treating site availability as cab availability
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: Availability at the site office is insufficient. Applicable operating procedures must be readily available in the cab at all times.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Treating storage on the crane as storage in the cab
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: An exterior storage compartment does not satisfy the specified location. The procedures must be readily available in the cab.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Choosing greater reach without checking height
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: The 37° point gives a 40-ft radius and only 40 ft of tip height. It meets neither specified coordinate.
The 66° point has enough height but only a 20-ft radius. Extra height cannot compensate for insufficient horizontal reach.

loadchart.range-diagram.misconception: Selecting maximum height as the safest universal choice
loadchart.range-diagram.why_wrong: The 90° point has the greatest listed height but a zero radius. It cannot place the hoist line at the required 30-ft radius.
Both distances extend toward the load, so they add. Subtraction would apply if the pivot were 5 ft behind the axis relative to the load.

loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.why_wrong: Tipping does not require every far-side wheel to lift. The rule sets the point at half of the wheels farthest from the load.

loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.misconception: Confuses first wheel lift with defined tipping
loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.why_wrong: One wheel lifting is a warning sign, but the rule defines tipping as half of the far wheels leaving the rail.

loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.misconception: Weight-transfer definition instead of wheel lift
loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.why_wrong: The definition is based on wheels leaving the rail on the side away from the load, not on full weight transfer to the near wheels.
2.5% is looser than the rule allows. Track must be level within 1 percent grade.
The rule does not demand 0.5%. It sets the limit at 1 percent grade.
1.5% is a near miss. The stated limit is level within 1 percent grade.

loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.misconception: Applies locomotive rule to other mountings
loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.why_wrong: The rail-wheel and track-grade stipulations apply only to locomotive cranes. Crawler, truck and wheel-mounted cranes follow SAE J765.
The rule names a specific consensus test code, SAE J765, not each manufacturer's own procedure.

loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.misconception: Wrong standard in the B30 family
loadchart.rated-capacity-rules.why_wrong: B30.10 covers hooks, not stability testing. The stability stipulations come from SAE J765.
Tipping loads for ratings are not applied at line speed. They are applied under static conditions only.
No allowance for swing stops is added. Tipping loads are applied statically, without the dynamic effect of hoisting, lowering or swinging.
The test is not a worst-case dynamic stop. Tipping loads are applied without any dynamic effect.
Ratings are not based on the most common working position. They are based on the least stable direction.
A short front may be weak, but the rule ties ratings to the least stable direction, wherever that falls on the mounting.
Using the most stable direction would overstate capacity elsewhere. The rule uses the least stable direction.
The unloaded setting is only a starting point. Radius is measured to the hoist line center with the load applied.

loadchart.read-gross.why_wrong: The 35-ft value is higher than the true capacity at 38 ft. Using it overstates what the crane can lift.
Load charts are not meant to be interpolated. Capacity does not change in a straight line between radii, so you read the next longer listed radius instead.
Rounding to the nearer radius gives the 40-ft value here, but when the nearer radius is the shorter one it gives too much capacity. The rule is always the next longer radius.
On most cranes the foot pin sits ahead of or behind the center of rotation. Measuring from it gives a radius that does not match the chart.

loadchart.read-gross.misconception: Confuses radius with load overhang past the fulcrum
loadchart.read-gross.why_wrong: The tipping fulcrum is used in stability calculations, but chart radius is always measured from the axis of rotation.
That distance is boom length, which is a separate entry on the chart. Radius is a horizontal distance to the load line.

loadchart.read-gross.misconception: Reverses the structural and stability zones
loadchart.read-gross.why_wrong: Stability governs the values below the bold line, usually at longer radii. Above the line, structural strength governs.

loadchart.read-gross.misconception: Confuses the bold line with the reeving limit
loadchart.read-gross.why_wrong: Parts-of-line limits are a separate restriction listed in the chart notes. They are not what the bold line marks.

loadchart.read-gross.misconception: Confuses chart zones with ground conditions
loadchart.read-gross.why_wrong: Chart values assume firm, level support. Ground bearing is checked separately and is not shown by the bold line.

loadchart.read-gross.misconception: Reads the wrong boom length column
loadchart.read-gross.why_wrong: 21,000 lb is in the 70-ft boom column. The crane has 90 ft of boom out.
26,000 lb is the 90-ft value at 30 ft. The radius is 40 ft.
15,500 lb is the 90-ft value at 50 ft, one row too far out.
This value comes from interpolating: 19,000 − (2/5 × 2,500) = 18,000. The note forbids that and requires the 40-ft value.
The radius row is right, but 17,000 lb is in the 60-ft boom column. The crane has 80 ft of boom.
14,200 lb is the 80-ft value. That is the shorter boom, and the note requires the next longer one.
This value splits the difference between the 80-ft and 90-ft columns. Chart values are not interpolated.

loadchart.structural-vs-stability.why_wrong: The rule does not wait for every wheel on the far side to lift. Tipping is defined when half of the wheels farthest from the load leave the rail.
A single wheel lifting is not the defined tipping point. The rule sets it at half of the wheels farthest from the load.

loadchart.structural-vs-stability.misconception: confuses boom angle limit with tipping
loadchart.structural-vs-stability.why_wrong: Boom angle limits are a separate chart limit. Tipping is defined by wheels leaving the rail, not by boom angle.
The rule uses percent grade, not degrees. One degree is steeper than 1 percent grade, so this would allow more tilt than the ratings assume.
The stipulation is 1 percent grade, not half a percent. This number is tighter than the rule states.
Two percent is twice the stipulated limit. The ratings assume track level within 1 percent grade.
Over the rear is often the most stable direction on a carrier. The margin is set in the least stable direction, not the strongest one.

loadchart.structural-vs-stability.misconception: assumes side is always the test direction
loadchart.structural-vs-stability.why_wrong: The side is often weak, but the rule does not name it. The margin is set in whatever direction is least stable for that mounting.

loadchart.structural-vs-stability.misconception: typical use instead of worst case
loadchart.structural-vs-stability.why_wrong: How the crane is usually used plays no part. The margin is set in the least stable direction so it covers the worst case.
The rating covers everything hanging from the boom tip, including auxiliary handling devices. It is not for the load alone.
Slings and shackles count too, not just the block. Taking only 400 lb off misses the 100 lb of rigging.
There is no fixed percentage allowance. You deduct the actual weights of the block and rigging, 500 lb here.

loadchart.structural-vs-stability.misconception: relies on tipping feel in the structural zone
loadchart.structural-vs-stability.why_wrong: That warning only comes where stability governs. In the structural zone, components reach their limit before the crane gets close to tipping.

loadchart.structural-vs-stability.misconception: ground support confused with structural limit
loadchart.structural-vs-stability.why_wrong: Short-radius ratings above the bold line come from structural strength, not ground support. Mats help with bearing but do not create any warning of structural overload.

loadchart.structural-vs-stability.misconception: wrong reason for a correct conclusion
loadchart.structural-vs-stability.why_wrong: He is wrong, but not for this reason. Rated capacity limiters use the full chart, including the structural ratings. The real problem is that structural failure gives no tipping warning.

loadchart.structural-vs-stability.misconception: bearing improvement treated as capacity gain
loadchart.structural-vs-stability.why_wrong: Spreading the load lowers ground bearing pressure but does nothing for boom or component strength. The structural rating is unchanged.

loadchart.terminology.why_wrong: The foot pin is usually offset from the centerline of rotation. Measuring from it gives the wrong radius. Charts measure from the axis of rotation.
The tipping axis (the outrigger or track edge) matters in stability calculations, but chart radius is measured from the axis of rotation.
That is boom length, which is a separate entry on the chart. Radius is a horizontal distance, and it changes with boom angle even when boom length stays the same.
The rule counts the rigging as part of the load. The chart's design margin is not an allowance for rigging weight.
The load block is listed by name as part of the load. Leaving it out understates the weight on the hook.
Slings and shackles are named in the definition. Every item hanging from the hoist line counts.
A qualified person can plan a lift within the chart, but cannot create or raise the rated capacity. Only the manufacturer sets it.
Inspections and load tests check the crane against its existing ratings. They do not set new ones.

loadchart.terminology.misconception: operational aid treated as source of rating
loadchart.terminology.why_wrong: The LMI compares the lift to the rated capacity that is already programmed into it. Its reading does not define the rating.
The unloaded measurement comes before deflection, so it understates the real radius and overstates the capacity.
Chart radius is measured from the axis of rotation, not from an outrigger. Measuring from the float makes the radius look shorter than it is.
Averaging hides the worst case. Capacity must cover the longest radius the load reaches during the lift.
The maximum capacity on the nameplate applies only at the shortest radius. The LMI compares the lift with the rating for the current radius and configuration.
Rated capacity is already below the tipping load. 100% on the LMI means the rated limit has been reached, not the point of tipping.

loadchart.terminology.misconception: confuses LMI with boom length indicator
loadchart.terminology.why_wrong: Boom length is shown by a boom length indicator. The LMI percentage is a load-moment comparison.
Radius depends on both boom length and angle. At the same angle, a longer boom always increases the radius.

loadchart.work-area-diagram.misconception: Duty assigned to the wrong person
loadchart.work-area-diagram.why_wrong: The lift director cannot override the front-area prohibition. Only the manufacturer can permit lifting over the front.

loadchart.work-area-diagram.misconception: Assumes outriggers alone create a front rating
loadchart.work-area-diagram.why_wrong: Full outrigger extension alone does not open the front area. The manufacturer's chart and notes decide whether the front is a rated area.
The 75% figure belongs to the load-weight verification rule, not the front-area rule. A light load still cannot go over the front unless the manufacturer permits it.
The pickup radius is often the shortest radius in the lift, where capacity is highest. The rule uses the longest radius that will be used.
The radius is right but the percentage is not. The rule sets the trigger at 75 percent, not 50 percent.
85 percent is a common field figure, but the rule's verification trigger is 75 percent at the longest radius.

loadchart.work-area-diagram.misconception: On-rubber reference applied to an outrigger chart
loadchart.work-area-diagram.why_wrong: On outriggers the axles are off the ground and do not set the tipping lines. The floats do, so the boundary runs through the floats.
Work areas are not fixed 45-degree sectors. The angle depends on where the floats sit relative to the center of rotation.

loadchart.work-area-diagram.misconception: Uses the carrier body instead of the support point
loadchart.work-area-diagram.why_wrong: The carrier frame corner is not a support point. The extended float is what supports the crane, so it defines the boundary.
The rating at the pick point does not cover the rest of the swing. Over the side, the crane is held to 15,000 lb.
Ratings for different areas are never averaged. Each area's own rating applies whenever the load is in that area.
Verifying the weight does not raise the capacity. The load is known to exceed the 15,000 lb over-side rating, so the lift cannot be made as planned.
The over-side rating covers the side area only. Without the front jack, the front area has no rating at all.

loadchart.work-area-diagram.misconception: Assumes outriggers make the chart 360 degrees
loadchart.work-area-diagram.why_wrong: A chart with a front jack note is not a full 360-degree rating. The front area stays unrated until the jack is set.

loadchart.work-area-diagram.misconception: Invented a derate in place of the manufacturer's condition
loadchart.work-area-diagram.why_wrong: No reduced front rating exists in this case. The manufacturer's condition is to set the jack, not to lower the load weight.
The over-side rating governs only if the load enters the side area. Using it here is more conservative than the chart requires.

ops.attachments.misconception: Operator documentation substitutes for written approval
ops.attachments.why_wrong: An operator's record of a conversation does not replace the manufacturer's written approval. The manufacturer must approve the addition in writing.
Witnesses do not change the required form of approval. Manufacturer approval must be written.

ops.attachments.misconception: Owner approval substitutes for manufacturer approval
ops.attachments.why_wrong: The owner's written statement is not the manufacturer's written approval. This route requires written approval from the manufacturer itself.
The nonresponse interval is 30 days, not 15 days. Reaching it permits an alternative approval process, not immediate operation.
The specified nonresponse interval is 30 days. Waiting 60 days is not required for this condition.
The 120-day provision concerns a manufacturer that agrees to review but does not complete the review. This nonresponse condition uses 30 days.
The interval starts when the detailed description is provided, not when the manufacturer agrees to review it.

ops.attachments.misconception: Nonresponse interval applied to incomplete review
ops.attachments.why_wrong: Thirty days applies to failure to acknowledge or initiate review. A manufacturer that agrees to review has a separate 120-day incomplete-review condition.
This uses both the wrong interval and the wrong starting event. The applicable interval is 120 days from receipt of the detailed description.
An operator briefing does not replace necessary changes to charts, procedures, manuals, and instructional markings.

ops.attachments.misconception: Approval letter substitutes for corrected operating information
ops.attachments.why_wrong: Filing the approval establishes that approval exists, but it does not correct operating information that conflicts with the addition.

ops.attachments.misconception: Document corrections may wait for annual inspection
ops.attachments.why_wrong: The rule does not provide an annual-inspection delay for necessary document changes. Those changes are part of meeting the approval route.

ops.attachments.misconception: Manufacturer disclosure permits reduced safety factor
ops.attachments.why_wrong: Written disclosure does not waive the requirement. The original safety factor must not be reduced.

ops.attachments.misconception: Load test substitutes for design safety factor
ops.attachments.why_wrong: A successful test does not substitute for preserving the original safety factor.

ops.attachments.misconception: Operating below capacity cures an unacceptable modification
ops.attachments.why_wrong: Observing a revised chart does not cure a conversion that reduces the original safety factor. The conversion must satisfy that requirement itself.

ops.attachments.misconception: Operator experience confers engineering approval authority
ops.attachments.why_wrong: Operator certification and operating experience do not replace the required professional-engineer registration and equipment-specific qualification.

ops.attention.why_wrong: Lift assignments are planning communications. The express phone exception is for signal communications.
Weather information may be relevant to the job, but it is not the stated phone exception. The exception covers signal communications.
Service advice is not signal communication. A work-related purpose does not itself establish an exception.
The rule covers actual equipment operation, not just hoisting a load.
This provision states an operating condition, not a shift-long prohibition on unrelated activities.
Cab occupancy alone is not the condition stated here. The provision applies while actually operating the equipment.
The restriction is not limited to electronic devices. It covers any practice or activity that diverts operating attention.
An activity can divert attention even when the operator's hands remain on the controls.
A work-related activity can also divert attention. Relevance to the job is not the test.
Slower swing speed does not create an exception for a scheduling call during operation.
Hands-free use does not establish the exception. The call's scheduling purpose remains outside signal communications.

ops.attention.misconception: Another worker can supply operator attention
ops.attention.why_wrong: Another worker watching does not remove the operator's obligation to avoid the distracting activity.
This provision does not make the phone exception depend on lift supervisor authorization. It identifies signal communications as the exception.
The provision expressly excepts phone use for signal communications during operation. It does not impose a stop for each such message.
The stated exception is based on signal communications, not whether the hook carries a load.
An unloaded hook does not remove the attention restriction during boom operation.

ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: Crawler mounting does not create an exception. The exceptions are for derricks and hydraulic booms.
A truck carrier does not exempt its lattice boom. The boom type matters here, not the carrier.

ops.backward-stability.misconception: Jib attachment replaces the boom-stop requirement
ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: A fixed jib does not make a lattice boom exempt. Hydraulic booms and derricks are the listed exceptions.
Lattice-boom crawler cranes are not a listed exception. Derricks are expressly excepted.
Lattice-boom truck cranes are not excepted by this provision. The other named exception is derricks.
Pedestal mounting is not a listed exception. The provision expressly names derricks.

ops.backward-stability.misconception: Low boom angle always gives the least stability
ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: At a lower angle, the boom's center of gravity is farther forward. That increases its contribution to resisting backward overturning.

ops.backward-stability.misconception: Any suspended load reduces stability in every direction
ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: At the same steep angle, a suspended load ahead of the backward tipping edge adds forward balancing moment. It improves backward stability even though other capacity limits still apply.

ops.backward-stability.misconception: Forward tipping risk equals backward tipping risk
ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: Both the forward boom position and the suspended load contribute moment opposing backward overturning. This combination may challenge forward stability instead.
At the instant of release, the counterweight's weight and position have not changed. The loss is in the load's forward balancing moment.

ops.backward-stability.misconception: Unloading increases elastic stretch and forward moment
ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: Load release generally relieves elastic strain rather than increasing it. More forward boom moment would oppose backward overturning.

ops.backward-stability.misconception: Reduced total weight automatically reduces rearward moment
ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: Load release does not immediately change the counterweight's lever arm. A decrease in its rearward moment would help backward stability, not reduce it.

ops.backward-stability.misconception: A suspended load makes boom stops an overturning safeguard
ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: A forward load contributes balancing moment, but its presence does not turn boom stops into a guarantee against overturning. The entire crane's moment balance still controls.
The boom's center of gravity moves as its angle changes. Boom stops do not hold the combined center of gravity in a fixed location.

ops.backward-stability.misconception: Internal stop forces create external stability
ops.backward-stability.why_wrong: Stops transmit forces within the crane, but they do not create an external forward balancing moment. Track reactions still follow the crane's overall weight distribution.
The cylinder applies forces between crane components. It cannot replace the external balancing moment supplied by a suspended load.

ops.barge.misconception: Confuses external and internal inspection intervals
ops.barge.why_wrong: The annual requirement covers the external vessel inspection. The required internal survey interval is four years.
The internal vessel survey interval is four years, not three years.
The internal vessel survey interval is four years, not five years.
Modifying the barge load rating is a separate responsibility. The wind determination is assigned to a competent person.

ops.barge.misconception: Assigns every operating judgment solely to the operator
ops.barge.why_wrong: Being the operator alone does not establish the required designation. A competent person must make this determination.

ops.barge.misconception: Transfers the determination to the signal person
ops.barge.why_wrong: Signal-person duties do not automatically include this determination. It must be made by a competent person.
An empty shaft does not trigger this requirement. Hoisting over an occupied shaft does.

ops.barge.misconception: Treats all vessel-side hoisting as a trigger
ops.barge.why_wrong: Grapple work alongside a vessel does not by itself trigger this requirement. Personnel hoisting or hoisting over an occupied cofferdam or shaft does.

ops.barge.misconception: Treats the lifting attachment as the trigger
ops.barge.why_wrong: Magnet work above an open deck does not by itself trigger this requirement. The specified triggers concern personnel hoisting and occupied cofferdams or shafts.

ops.barge.misconception: Applies the onboard-manual rule to load charts
ops.barge.why_wrong: Being available aboard the barge is insufficient for load charts. For this movable station, they must be posted on the equipment.

ops.barge.misconception: Uses a common access point instead of the equipment
ops.barge.why_wrong: Posting charts ashore does not meet the location requirement. They must be posted on the equipment.

ops.barge.misconception: Substitutes supervisory access for required posting
ops.barge.why_wrong: Supervisor custody does not satisfy the posting requirement. The charts must be posted on the crane.
Competent-person status is sufficient for conducting the shift inspection, but the hazard determination requires a qualified person.

ops.barge.misconception: Defers a discovered deficiency to a scheduled inspection
ops.barge.why_wrong: The required qualification is correct, but the timing is not. The determination must be immediate.

ops.barge.misconception: Substitutes operating responsibility for required qualification
ops.barge.why_wrong: The operator's job title alone does not satisfy the qualification requirement. The determination must be made by a qualified person.

ops.barge.misconception: Substitutes rigging expertise for vessel stability expertise
ops.barge.why_wrong: Land-crane capacity expertise is necessary, but rigging expertise does not replace expertise in vessel stability.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Using the boom pivot as the radius origin
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: The boom foot pin is not the reference point for working radius. Radius begins at the crane's axis of rotation.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Confusing working radius with distance from the tipping boundary
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: An outrigger can be relevant to the tipping boundary, but it is not the origin used for working radius.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Measuring a sloping distance instead of horizontal radius
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: Working radius is a horizontal distance, not a diagonal distance to the load. Load height does not become part of that measurement.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Reversing the direction of loaded boom deflection
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: For the elevated boom described, downward bending normally moves the tip outward. The radius therefore increases.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Equating fixed boom length with fixed radius
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: The boom can bend without any change in telescope setting. That bending changes the horizontal position of the tip.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Equating fixed controls with fixed geometry
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: An unchanged control setting does not prevent elastic bending. The loaded tip can move outward even though the boom hoist has not operated.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Considering weight without its lever arm
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: Weight is only one factor in load moment. Increasing the horizontal radius increases the moment even when the weight stays constant.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Using height instead of horizontal radius
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: Tip height is not the horizontal lever arm used in this calculation. The increased radius increases the load moment.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Treating telescoping as the only source of additional moment
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: Any increase in horizontal radius increases load moment. Telescoping is not necessary; elastic deflection can produce that increase.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Rounding radius to the nearest chart entry
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: The chart directs use of the next longer radius, not the nearest radius. Since 26 ft exceeds 25 ft, the 30-ft entry applies.
Averaging is not permitted by the stated chart note. The applicable capacity is 10,000 lb at the next longer listed radius.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Locking in capacity from the unloaded radius
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: The original selection does not remain valid when the actual radius increases beyond that entry. The loaded 26-ft radius calls for the 30-ft entry.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Using hoisting to remove boom deflection
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: Shortening the hoist line raises the load but does not remove its weight from the boom. It does not reverse the deflection.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Confusing reduced diagonal distance with reduced radius
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: Raising the load vertically does not move it horizontally toward the pivot. Its settled radius remains about 32 ft.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Adding vertical travel to horizontal radius
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: Lifting height is not part of horizontal radius. With unchanged boom geometry and a settled vertical line, radius remains about 32 ft.

ops.boom-deflection.misconception: Applying the loading response during unloading
ops.boom-deflection.why_wrong: That is the direction associated with adding load in this scenario. Removing load reverses the elastic deflection.

ops.brake-test.why_wrong: The threshold for this brake test is 90% of maximum line pull, not 75%.
An 85% load is below this rule's 90% trigger.
Waiting until 95% misses loads from 90% up to that point that require the test.
The specified test height is a few inches, not a few feet.

ops.brake-test.misconception: Supported load treated as brake test
ops.brake-test.why_wrong: Applying the brakes while the load remains supported does not perform the required suspended-load test.
The brake test is made after lifting a few inches, rather than after reaching travel height.
The repetitive-lift exception removes this requirement for successive lifts after the first.

ops.brake-test.misconception: Test assigned to end of sequence
ops.brake-test.why_wrong: The required test belongs on the first lift, not the final lift.
The rule does not establish an alternate-lift testing interval.

ops.brake-test.misconception: Prelift check substituted for loaded test
ops.brake-test.why_wrong: A supported-load check does not meet the requirement to lift the load a few inches and apply the brakes.
The test must be performed at a few inches, not delayed until the load is a few feet high.
The trigger is 90% of maximum line pull, not 100%.

ops.brake-test.misconception: Chart capacity substituted for line pull
ops.brake-test.why_wrong: Chart-capacity utilization is not the percentage used to trigger this brake test.
The specified line-pull threshold is 90%, not 75%.

ops.brake-test.misconception: Full chart capacity treated as trigger
ops.brake-test.why_wrong: Although the test is not triggered here, this reasoning uses the wrong limit. The relevant comparison is with 90% of maximum line pull.
The threshold is met, but the successive-lift exception applies to this repetitive sequence.

ops.control-malfunction.why_wrong: A prompt verbal report does not meet the written-report requirement. The operator must promptly inform the employer's designated recipient in writing.
The report must be prompt. Waiting for a weekly reporting cycle does not satisfy that requirement.
Reporting before leaving does not remove the requirement for prompt written notice.

ops.control-malfunction.misconception: Equipment tag rule applied to one function
ops.control-malfunction.why_wrong: That is the tag arrangement for equipment taken out of service. Here, the employer has taken only the travel function out of service.

ops.control-malfunction.misconception: Restricted use replaces removal from service
ops.control-malfunction.why_wrong: The tag must state that the function is out of service and is not to be used. Case-by-case approval is not the required message.
A tag kept in a repair file does not meet the requirement for a conspicuous position.
Assignment as lift supervisor alone does not establish the required qualification. The determination must come from a qualified person.
Being designated to receive repair reports does not automatically qualify that person to determine that safety has been assured.
Being the next operator does not by itself establish the required qualification to resolve the safety concern.

ops.control-malfunction.misconception: Function tag substitutes for equipment tag
ops.control-malfunction.why_wrong: A function-specific tag does not communicate that the entire crane has been taken out of service. The required equipment tag belongs in the cab.
An office tag does not satisfy the specified cab location for equipment taken out of service.

ops.control-malfunction.misconception: Any visible location satisfies equipment tagging
ops.control-malfunction.why_wrong: An access-ladder tag may be noticeable, but it does not replace the required tag in the cab.

ops.control-malfunction.misconception: Unloaded testing bypasses a warning sign
ops.control-malfunction.why_wrong: An unloaded test still activates the tagged control. The release requirements apply before activation.
A spotter and reduced speed do not replace authorized sign removal or the required operator verification.
A supervisor's movement request does not itself satisfy either release condition for the tagged control.
The operator has a separate written reporting duty. Notification of all affected employees at each shift's beginning is the employer's duty.

ops.counterweight.why_wrong: Having the weight nearby does not satisfy the requirement. It must be in place as specified by the manufacturer.

ops.counterweight.misconception: Installation delayed until a heavy lift
ops.counterweight.why_wrong: The requirement applies to equipment operation, not only to lifts approaching capacity.
A load reduction does not substitute for having the specified counterweight or ballast in place.
Stationary operation does not create an exception to the manufacturer's maximum.
Reducing the suspended load does not authorize exceeding the maximum counterweight or ballast.
A successful test lift does not override the manufacturer's maximum.
A lattice-boom crawler crane is equipment other than a tower crane and falls under the non-tower provisions.
A telescopic truck crane falls under the requirements for equipment other than tower cranes.
Adding a fixed jib does not make a crawler crane a tower crane.
An improvised capacity reduction does not replace the specified counterweight.
A shorter radius does not satisfy the requirement to install the counterweight specified for this configuration.
A trial lift cannot establish permission to operate without the specified counterweight.
Reducing the lifted load does not permit counterweight above the manufacturer's maximum.
Restricting travel does not remove the maximum-counterweight requirement.
The crane must not first be operated with counterweight above the specified maximum.

ops.counterweight.misconception: Total weight is the only requirement
ops.counterweight.why_wrong: The correct total does not establish that the slabs are in place as specified.

ops.duty-cycle.why_wrong: The prohibition applies below 5, so a threshold of 3 would wrongly allow some prohibited rope uses.
The threshold is less than 5, not 5 or less. This particular prohibition does not include a factor exactly equal to 5.
The stated threshold is below 5, not below 6.
Designation as lift director alone does not satisfy this requirement. The inspection must be performed by a qualified person.
Being assigned to operate the crane does not alone establish the required qualification. An operator could perform this inspection if also qualified for it.
Supervisory responsibility alone does not meet the requirement for a qualified person to inspect the rope.
A daily entry does not replace the required annual entry. The specified documents are monthly and annual.
A daily log does not replace the required monthly inspection entry.
Those records do not substitute for recording each lift in the monthly and annual inspection documents.
A satisfactory inspection does not override the prohibition on this rope use.
Slower operation and additional inspections do not permit duty-cycle use below a design factor of 5.
Approval from the lift director cannot authorize a use the rule prohibits.
Separating cycles with pauses does not remove the repetitive nature of this assignment.
The restriction covers repetitive lifts as well as duty-cycle work; it is not limited to clamshell service.
The rule does not make uninterrupted operation a condition of the repetitive-lift prohibition.
The criterion counts broken wires in one rope lay, regardless of whether they occupy separate strands.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: Unused sling capacity permits shock loading
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: A low static load does not create an exception. Shock loading is prohibited.
Changing the sling material does not create an exception to the prohibition.
Compliance with crane capacity does not permit shock loading of the slings.
The rule does not require zero outward displacement. It requires keeping the load from swinging beyond a controllable radius.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: A fixed speed fraction satisfies the rule
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: The rule establishes no fixed fraction of available swing speed. The limit depends on maintaining load control at the resulting radius.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: Pickup radius is the mandatory swing boundary
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: The initial pickup radius is not the specified rotational-speed limit. The rule addresses the radius at which the load can be controlled.
Losing the suspended load does not remove counterweight. It removes the load's forward moment and can produce rearward rebound.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: Any reduction in weight improves stability
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: Less total weight does not guarantee greater stability. The location and sudden removal of the load's moment matter.
Fixed outrigger positions do not keep the crane's moments constant. Removing the load changes those moments immediately.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: Taking up slack is itself shock loading
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: Slowly removing slack does not produce the sudden force increase described here. The prohibited action is snatching the load with slack rigging.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: The initial lift always constitutes shock loading
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: A smooth lift and controlled hold do not inherently create shock loading. Abruptly taking up slack does.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: Any increase in hoist speed is shock loading
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: Smooth acceleration after gradual tensioning avoids the sudden engagement described in the shock-loading choice.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: A larger-radius capacity check replaces load control
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: Checking capacity at the larger radius does not correct the loss of control. Swing speed must meet the control requirement.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: An exclusion area permits uncontrolled swing
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: Clearing personnel does not make uncontrolled outward swing acceptable. Rotational speed must still keep the load within control.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: Weight reduction automatically corrects swing control
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: Capacity is already adequate in this scenario. Reducing weight to preserve capacity does not address the stated loss of control.

ops.dynamic-loading.misconception: The obstruction supplies the rebound force
ops.dynamic-loading.why_wrong: The obstruction stops exerting its restraining force when the snag releases. Boom rebound comes from released elastic energy, not an added lifting force from the obstruction.

ops.emergencies.why_wrong: Prompt verbal notice alone does not satisfy the requirement. The operator must provide written notice.
A scheduled maintenance review does not replace prompt reporting of a necessary repair.
The designated recipient must receive prompt written notice. A verbal shift handoff does not satisfy that obligation.
Appointment as lift director alone does not satisfy the requirement. The determination must come from a qualified person.
Operator assignment alone does not establish qualification to resolve the particular safety concern.
Supervisory authority alone is insufficient. The person making the safety determination must be qualified.
A weekly meeting does not satisfy the beginning-of-each-shift notification requirement.
The notice is tied to each shift, not to the maintenance inspection schedule.
Employees must be informed of necessary repairs and alternative measures at shift start, without waiting for completion.

ops.emergencies.misconception: Verbal handoff satisfies the written requirement
ops.emergencies.why_wrong: A verbal explanation can supplement the handoff, but the repair notice to the next operator must be in writing.
A maintenance copy does not replace written notification to the next operator on successive shifts.

ops.emergencies.misconception: Delegating a briefing completes the handoff
ops.emergencies.why_wrong: Requesting a future briefing does not itself provide the required written notice to the next operator.
The operator's authority does not depend on first identifying the failed component.
The operator need not reproduce the malfunction before exercising stop authority over a safety concern.

ops.emergencies.misconception: Stop authority depends on management approval
ops.emergencies.why_wrong: The operator must have stop authority whenever there is a safety concern; lift-director permission is not the trigger.

ops.emergencies.misconception: Confusing initial motion with return swing
ops.emergencies.why_wrong: The load initially retains its forward velocity. A backward swing can occur later in the oscillation, not as the initial response.

ops.fire-response.why_wrong: The rule requires an accessible extinguisher on the equipment; it does not restrict its location to the cab.
A nearby fire station does not satisfy the requirement for an extinguisher on the equipment.

ops.fire-response.misconception: Support equipment counts as crane equipment
ops.fire-response.why_wrong: An extinguisher on a separate service truck is not on the crane.
The rule names dry chemical, not pressurized water, alongside carbon dioxide.

ops.fire-response.misconception: Confusing wet and dry chemical agents
ops.fire-response.why_wrong: The rule expressly names carbon dioxide and dry chemical; wet chemical is not the other named type.

ops.fire-response.misconception: Treating dry powder and dry chemical as interchangeable
ops.fire-response.why_wrong: The rule says dry chemical. Dry powder is not the named alternative.
The second group identified by this requirement is maintenance personnel, not the assigned signal person.

ops.fire-response.misconception: Assigning operator preparation to the lift director
ops.fire-response.why_wrong: This omits operating personnel, whom the requirement expressly includes.
Emergency responders do not replace maintenance personnel in this crane-specific requirement.
The general-industry provision permits the cab or the crane's vicinity; it does not require the cab alone.
This imports the construction rule's on-equipment requirement into the stated general-industry setting.

ops.fire-response.misconception: Reading alternative locations as cumulative requirements
ops.fire-response.why_wrong: The provision offers alternative locations; it does not require an extinguisher in each.
This makes it reachable but removes it from the equipment.
A sign identifies the location but does not make the extinguisher accessible.
Preparing to remove the obstruction does not provide an accessible extinguisher.
Treat the base, not the flame tips.

ops.free-fall.why_wrong: The cutoff is October 31, 1984. July 31 would incorrectly exclude equipment manufactured during the following three months.
The cutoff is October 31, 1984, not the end of June. Equipment age alone also does not override the prohibited circumstances.
The exception requires manufacture before October 31, 1984. This later date would admit equipment outside the exception.
A clutch cannot count, but an internal static brake is a specified protective device for a hydraulic drum.
A ratchet-and-pawl device and a secondary friction brake are examples of acceptable secondary protection. They are not the excluded pair.
A hydraulic motor cannot count, but an internal static brake can provide the required protection for a hydraulic drum.
Automatic engagement is acceptable but is not the only permitted method. Manual engagement is also allowed.
Manual engagement is acceptable but is not mandatory. An automatically engaged secondary device is also permitted.

ops.free-fall.misconception: Backup device replaces the primary brake
ops.free-fall.why_wrong: The specified secondary device backs up the primary brake while the boom is held. It is not specified as a replacement for the primary brake during routine lowering.

ops.free-fall.misconception: Pressure testing substitutes for integral mounting
ops.free-fall.why_wrong: A successful hose pressure test does not satisfy the mounting requirement. The hydraulic boom cylinder must have an integrally mounted holding device.

ops.free-fall.misconception: Remote redundancy substitutes for integral mounting
ops.free-fall.why_wrong: Adding another remote valve does not meet the requirement for an integrally mounted holding device.

ops.free-fall.misconception: Successful holding test substitutes for required design
ops.free-fall.why_wrong: Holding the boom during a check does not establish compliance with the required device location. Integral mounting is required.

ops.free-fall.misconception: A second motor supplies braking redundancy
ops.free-fall.why_wrong: Hydraulic motors cannot be counted as brake or locking devices. Adding another motor does not provide the specified holding protection.

ops.free-fall.misconception: A clutch serves as a holding brake
ops.free-fall.why_wrong: A clutch cannot be counted as a brake or locking device. The hydraulic drum needs an integrally mounted holding device or internal static brake.

ops.free-fall.misconception: Remote hydraulic protection meets integral-mounting requirement
ops.free-fall.why_wrong: A remote valve connected through hoses does not satisfy the requirement for an integrally mounted holding device or internal static brake.

ops.free-fall.misconception: Applying the boom exception to the load line
ops.free-fall.why_wrong: The empty-shaft exception applies to the boom-free-fall prohibition. Load-line free fall is prohibited whenever the load is over a shaft.

ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: The specified accuracy is plus or minus 10 percent. A 5 percent determination would meet that requirement, but it is not the required threshold.
A 15 percent uncertainty exceeds the permitted plus or minus 10 percent.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Treating the total tolerance span as the one-sided allowance
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: The allowance is 10 percent in either direction, not 20 percent in either direction.
Three wraps exceed the stated minimum. The rule prohibits lowering below two full wraps on either respective drum.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Relying on the rope anchorage and one wrap
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: One full wrap is below the required minimum of two full wraps.
Four wraps exceed the stated minimum. The federal load-handling provision specifies two.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Confusing a per-lift test with a shift check
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: A shift-start test does not replace the test required each time a near-rated load is handled.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Making the test depend on configuration changes
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: An unchanged setup does not remove the requirement. Each near-rated load triggers the brake test.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Treating a previous heavier lift as continuing proof
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: The requirement also applies to repeated near-rated loads of the same or lower weight.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Treating tire condition as added capacity
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: Checking tire pressure does not increase the 6,000 lb without-outrigger rating. The 7,000 lb load exceeds it.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Applying a full-extension rating to partial extension
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: The stated 10,000 lb rating belongs to fully extended outriggers. It does not establish a rating for partial extension.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Using a brake test to justify an overload
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: A successful brake test does not authorize exceeding the without-outrigger rating. Outriggers are required for this load at this radius.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Confusing swing restraint with boom restraint
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: The swing brake controls rotation, not the boom-hoist locking requirement. Fixed-radius operation requires the boom-hoist pawl or another positive locking device.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Substituting brake testing for positive locking
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: Repeated brake testing does not replace engaging the required positive locking device.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Treating neutral control position as positive locking
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: Securing a control lever in neutral does not establish that the boom-hoist pawl or other positive locking device is engaged.

ops.general-industry-load.misconception: Substituting slow crane swing for load-rotation restraint
ops.general-industry-load.why_wrong: Controlled swing speed does not replace the required tag or restraint line when rotation of the load is hazardous.

ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: The trigger is more than 75%, not more than 50%, of maximum rated capacity at the longest planned radius.
Waiting for 80% misses readings above 75% that already require separate weight verification.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Confusing verification with a near-capacity warning
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: The verification trigger is above 75%, well before a reading reaches 90%.
Pickup radius governs this comparison only if it is the longest radius used during the operation.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Using the point of greatest resistance
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: Breaking the load free does not establish the comparison radius. The rule uses the longest planned radius.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Assuming the landing is always farthest
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: Landing radius governs only if no longer radius occurs elsewhere in the lift.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Treating hoisting as preliminary to the lift
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: Waiting until the first swing allows hoisting to begin without the requested information. It must be provided before the lift.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Moving the deadline to rigging attachment
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: The requirement sets the deadline before the lift, not before attaching rigging.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Moving the deadline to crane setup
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: The requirement does not make crane setup the deadline. Requested information must reach the operator before the lift.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Treating water pressure as an added downward load
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: Falling buoyant support makes the hoist carry more of the block's weight, not less.
The block's weight stays constant, but the upward force supplied by the water decreases. Hoist load therefore increases.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Assigning a peak load to the waterline
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: Drag is excluded from this scenario. With no retained water, the greatest hoist load occurs when buoyant support is gone.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Carrying underwater buoyancy into the emerged calculation
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: Subtracting submerged buoyancy understates the emerged load. Add retained water and do not credit buoyancy after the skip clears the surface.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Confusing displaced water with retained water
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: Displaced water determines buoyant force while submerged; it is not automatically carried with the skip. Add the water actually retained inside.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Assuming an open container drains completely
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: The plugged drains prevent water from leaving before emergence. Its weight must be included in the emerged load.

ops.lifting-from-water.misconception: Treating bottom support as relief from added hoist tension
ops.lifting-from-water.why_wrong: Taking additional strain increases rigging tension. Resistance from the clay can keep the plate seated despite that increase.

ops.manufacturer-procedures.misconception: Applies the operational-controls rule to capacity
ops.manufacturer-procedures.why_wrong: A qualified person develops procedures for the operational controls. Capacity procedures require a registered professional engineer.

ops.manufacturer-procedures.misconception: Wrong person: competent person or controlling entity
ops.manufacturer-procedures.why_wrong: No competent person or controlling entity has this role. Capacity procedures must come from a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment.
An inspection, however thorough, does not establish capacity. The rule calls for an engineer to develop the capacity procedures and sign them.
Operator certification shows the operator can run cranes. It does not make the operator the person who writes missing control procedures. The rule assigns that to a qualified person.

ops.manufacturer-procedures.misconception: Applies the capacity rule to controls
ops.manufacturer-procedures.why_wrong: A registered professional engineer is required for capacity procedures, not for the operational controls.
A competent person is not the person named here. Control procedures must be developed by a qualified person.

ops.manufacturer-procedures.misconception: Qualified-person approval treated as an override
ops.manufacturer-procedures.why_wrong: A qualified person's approval does not override available manufacturer procedures. A qualified person writes control procedures only when the manufacturer's are unavailable.
Extra caution does not replace the manual. Every applicable manufacturer procedure must still be followed.

ops.manufacturer-procedures.misconception: Engineer signature treated as an override
ops.manufacturer-procedures.why_wrong: An engineer's signature is required for capacity procedures when manufacturer procedures are unavailable. It does not allow replacing manufacturer procedures that exist.
Supervision by a qualified person does not replace the manufacturer procedure when that procedure is available.
The capacity chart is only part of the requirement. Erection and use steps for the attachment are manufacturer procedures too.
A qualified person writes procedures only when the manufacturer's are unavailable. Here they are in the manual.
