Operator experience is not a procedure. The employer must develop written procedures through a qualified person.
An engineer is required for capacity procedures. Control procedures need only a qualified person.
Another maker's manual is not this crane's procedure, and control layouts differ. A qualified person must develop procedures for this equipment.

ops.manufacturer-procedures.misconception: No federal number means no limit
ops.manufacturer-procedures.why_wrong: The federal rule makes the manufacturer's procedures mandatory, so the manual's 30 mph limit applies.

ops.multi-drum.why_wrong: The higher-speed characteristic is correct, but the whipline has lighter capacity than the main hoist.
The lighter-capacity characteristic is correct, but the whipline has higher speed.
This reverses both characteristics: the whipline has lighter capacity and higher speed.

ops.multi-drum.misconception: Emergency work creates an automatic exception
ops.multi-drum.why_wrong: This provision does not name emergency rescue as its exception; it names pile driving.

ops.multi-drum.misconception: Testing permission extends to occupied lifts
ops.multi-drum.why_wrong: Proof testing is not the stated exception to the prohibition during personnel hoisting.
Steel erection is not the exception identified in this provision.
The stated ceiling is 500 pounds, subject to the winch and platform ratings.
A 750-pound load exceeds the 500-pound ceiling for this occupied-platform operation.

ops.multi-drum.misconception: Equipment rating overrides the operating limit
ops.multi-drum.why_wrong: Equipment rated for 1,000 pounds does not eliminate the separate 500-pound ceiling.

ops.multi-drum.misconception: Additional supervision substitutes for the restriction
ops.multi-drum.why_wrong: A separate signal person does not create an exception to the prohibition on other-line lifts.
Available capacity does not authorize another-line lift while personnel are being hoisted.

ops.multi-drum.misconception: Occupancy and personnel hoisting are identical conditions
ops.multi-drum.why_wrong: This is more restrictive than the stated condition, which prohibits other-line lifts while personnel are being hoisted. It does not make dismounting the required endpoint.
This provision does not require halving the winch rating. The 400-pound winch rating is below the 500-pound ceiling and controls.
The 500-pound ceiling does not authorize exceeding this winch's 400-pound rating.
The limits apply together; they are not additive. The load cannot exceed the lower one.

ops.multi-drum.misconception: Splitting crane capacity equally between drums
ops.multi-drum.why_wrong: Dividing 12,000 by two ignores the actual 8,000-pound main-line load. Only 4,000 pounds of combined capacity remains.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Duty assigned to the person overseeing the lift
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: A lift director may oversee the work, but the rule names the operator's judgment as the one the devices must not replace.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Duty assigned to the signal person
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: The signal person passes on directions and what they can see. The rule about devices replacing judgment is about the operator.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Duty assigned to a qualified person
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: Qualified persons have their own duties elsewhere in the rules. This rule is about the operator's judgment during operation.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Confusing a chart limit with the LMI's validity condition
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: Boom angle is one of the inputs the LMI measures. Staying above a minimum angle does not fix a wrong setup entry.
Anti-two-block is a separate device that guards against two-blocking. It has nothing to do with whether the capacity percentage is right.
Warming up the hydraulics is good practice, but a warm crane still reads wrong if the setup entered does not match the crane.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Thinking a sensed input is unsensed
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: Boom angle is a basic LMI input, usually from an angle sensor on the boom.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Relying on the LMI as a tipping guard
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: The LMI cutout is based on its own inputs and does not account for footing giving way, so it may not cut out before the crane becomes unstable.
Moving slowly with a spotter still keeps the load on failing support. Watching the float does not stop it from sinking.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Treating a lower LMI percentage as the fix
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: Getting a lower LMI percentage does not fix the footing. The low number is the reading the operator must not rely on here.
A good function test shows the device works. It does not make the device a stand-in for the operator stopping the hoist.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Device purpose confused with normal operation
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: It is designed to stop hoisting if the operator fails to. A switch failure would leave no protection if the operator depends on it every time.
This reaches the right answer for the wrong reason. Which line the device covers is not the problem; using it as the routine stop is.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Treating the wind limit as permission
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: A reading under the limit does not prove the load can be controlled. The operator must judge the actual effect of the wind on this panel.
More tag lines put more workers near a load that is already out of control. The reading still does not replace judgment.

ops.not-a-substitute.misconception: Duty shifted away from the operator
ops.not-a-substitute.why_wrong: The operator cannot hand off this judgment. The rule says the operator's professional judgment is not replaced by the aids.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Only the upper and the load-handling parts count
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: No part is excluded. The carrier, outriggers and counterweight are parts of the equipment, so they must not strike anything either.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Limiting the rule to structural load members
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: The rule is not limited to load-carrying members. It covers the boom and the other parts of the equipment.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Thinking only the tip is regulated
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: The boom tip is the most common contact point, but the prohibition covers the whole boom and every other part of the equipment.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Thinking hydraulic pressure stiffens or raises the boom
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: Higher pressure in the lift cylinder holds the boom angle. It does not lift the tip or pull it inward. Deflection moves the tip down and out.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Ignoring the horizontal part of deflection
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: The tip does drop, but it also moves out, so the radius increases. Leaving out the outward movement makes clearance estimates too tight.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Ignoring the vertical part of deflection
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: Deflection moves the tip outward and also lowers it, which matters when the boom is working under an overhead structure.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Assigning the damage evaluation to the wrong person
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: The operator should report the strike and can look the boom over, but judging whether a struck boom is fit for service belongs to a qualified person.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Assigning the damage evaluation to the signal person
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: A signal person directs crane motions. A look from the ground cannot rule out a bent chord or cracked weld.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Deferring the check to a periodic inspection
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: Waiting for a scheduled inspection leaves a possibly damaged boom in service. The boom should be inspected before the crane is used again.

ops.obstructions.misconception: A spotter or slow speed makes a tight clearance acceptable
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: A slow swing with a spotter can still end in contact at 6 inches. The rule prohibits contact, so the clearance has to be fixed.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Thinking only the boom and load are covered
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: The rule covers the boom and other parts of the equipment, which includes the counterweight.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Confusing the swing-radius barricade rule with the no-contact rule
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: Barricades protect workers from being caught by the counterweight. They do not stop the counterweight from striking the pickup.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Thinking the signal person takes over responsibility for clearance
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: Signals direct crane motions, but they do not excuse a motion the operator can see will cause contact. The prohibition still applies.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Light or slow contact is acceptable
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: The rule prohibits any contact, including light contact. A slow strike can still damage the boom and knock the scaffold out of place.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Treating temporary works as something other than an obstruction
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: A scaffold is an obstruction. The rule covers contact with any obstruction, not just permanent structures.

ops.obstructions.misconception: Reversing the effect of boom angle on radius
ops.obstructions.why_wrong: Booming down increases the radius. It does not shorten it. The contact risk comes from the boom dropping onto the edge.

ops.over-front.misconception: Assigns the exception to the wrong person
ops.over-front.why_wrong: The exception belongs to the manufacturer. A qualified person's approval does not unlock the front area.

ops.over-front.misconception: Limits the rule to on-rubber work
ops.over-front.why_wrong: The rule does not depend on whether the crane is on rubber. It applies to wheel-mounted equipment in any setup, unless the manufacturer permits the lift.
Setting the outriggers does not create permission. Only the manufacturer can allow front-area lifts, and only on its terms.
Crawler cranes are not covered by this rule. Their working areas and capacities come from their own load charts.

ops.over-front.misconception: Narrows the scope to truck cranes
ops.over-front.why_wrong: Truck cranes are covered, but so are rough-terrain and other wheel-mounted cranes.

ops.over-front.misconception: Ties the rule to setup instead of carrier type
ops.over-front.why_wrong: The rule is tied to the type of equipment, not the setup. It still applies when a wheel-mounted crane is on outriggers.

ops.over-front.misconception: Borrows the engineer alternative from other rules
ops.over-front.why_wrong: Some crane rules accept an engineer when the manufacturer is not available, but this one does not. Its only exception is the manufacturer.

ops.over-front.misconception: Assigns the duty to the controlling entity
ops.over-front.why_wrong: The controlling entity has site-wide duties, but it cannot authorize front-area lifts.

ops.over-front.misconception: Treats a lift plan as a permission source
ops.over-front.why_wrong: A lift plan has to stay within what the manufacturer permits. It cannot add a front-area permission the manufacturer did not give.
The diagram for this exact outrigger setup excludes the front. Fully extended outriggers do not add permission the manufacturer did not give.

ops.over-front.misconception: Invents a derating to cover the prohibition
ops.over-front.why_wrong: There is no rule for turning a side rating into a front rating. With no listed front permission, no reduced value makes the lift allowed.
A supervisor cannot grant front-area permission. Only the manufacturer can.

ops.over-front.misconception: Ignores the conditions on the permission
ops.over-front.why_wrong: The manual permits front lifts only with the jack set. Leaving the jack up puts the lift outside the permission.
The ban has a manufacturer exception. With the jack set and the load within chart values, the lift is allowed.

ops.over-front.misconception: Applies one area's chart to another area
ops.over-front.why_wrong: Over-rear values apply only over the rear. The front has its own rating and conditions.
The permission here is for on-rubber work. Outriggers would put the crane under a different chart, and they are not needed for the on-rubber values.

ops.overload-response.why_wrong: The threshold for this verification method is above 75 percent, not above 50 percent.

ops.overload-response.misconception: Confusing an alert setting with the verification threshold
ops.overload-response.why_wrong: The verification requirement begins above 75 percent. Waiting until 85 percent misses the required threshold.
The verification threshold is above 75 percent, and operation above rated capacity is prohibited.
Pickup radius controls this check only if it is also the longest radius planned for the lift.
The rule specifies the longest planned radius, not the shortest radius with its potentially greater capacity.
An average can conceal the limiting portion of the lift. The check uses the longest planned radius.

ops.overload-response.misconception: Confusing lower height with lower moment
ops.overload-response.why_wrong: Height above ground is not a factor in weight times horizontal radius. Lowering alone does not reduce static load moment.

ops.overload-response.misconception: Treating rope length as load radius
ops.overload-response.why_wrong: Paying out rope does not increase the load's horizontal lever arm under these conditions. The stated load moment remains unchanged.
Once the load stops, the crane still supports its full weight. Lowering changes weight carried only when support takes some of that weight.
Increasing radius from 30 ft to 35 ft increases weight times radius for the same suspended load.

ops.overload-response.misconception: Confusing hook lowering with moment reduction
ops.overload-response.why_wrong: Lowering the hook without transferring weight to support leaves both load weight and horizontal radius unchanged.
Hoisting the load vertically does not shorten its horizontal radius. Its final static load moment remains unchanged.

ops.overload-response.misconception: Using the final radius as the denominator
ops.overload-response.why_wrong: Dividing the 5 ft change by the final 25 ft gives one-fifth, but percentage increase uses the initial 20 ft.

ops.overload-response.misconception: Treating boom angle as the only geometry factor
ops.overload-response.why_wrong: A fixed boom angle does not keep radius fixed during extension. The longer horizontal radius increases load moment.

ops.overload-response.misconception: Treating boom extension as load distribution
ops.overload-response.why_wrong: Extending does not spread the suspended weight over another support. It increases the horizontal lever arm and therefore load moment.
The support takes 2,000 lb, so the crane no longer carries the full 8,000 lb. Its supported share is 6,000 lb.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Treating engine idle as the verification deadline
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Checking after the engine reaches idle is too late. The verification must occur before starting the engine.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Substituting warm-up timing for startup timing
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: A check immediately before warm-up could occur after engine startup. The required deadline is before starting the engine.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Applying the check only before crane movement
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Waiting until hydraulic functions are engaged allows the engine to start before the required verification. The check must precede engine startup.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Assigning startup verification to the signal person
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: A signal person may assist with information about personnel, but the operator must verify the starting conditions.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Assigning the operator's check to lift supervision
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Oversight of the lift does not replace the operator's specific duty to verify the starting conditions.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Assigning startup verification to the rigger
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Rigging duties do not make the rigger responsible for this verification. The requirement applies to the operator.
Neutral may be the proper starting position for particular controls, but the rule does not prescribe neutral for every control. It requires each control's proper starting position.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Substituting control locks for proper positions
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Checking motion-control locks does not establish that all controls are in their proper starting positions. Locks alone are not the stated condition.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Equating shutdown settings with startup settings
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: A control's shutdown position is not necessarily its proper starting position. The operator must verify the starting condition rather than assume the prior settings are suitable.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Treating hydraulic isolation as personnel clearance
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Leaving hydraulic functions disengaged does not satisfy the requirement that all personnel be clear before engine startup. The mechanic's clearance must be established first.
A warning does not establish that the mechanic is in the clear. The operator must verify clearance before starting.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Limiting clearance to the lifting crew
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Confirming only the riggers' clearance leaves the mechanic unaccounted for. The requirement covers all personnel.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Treating cab attendance as a control check
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Remaining in the cab does not replace verification of proper control positions. Both conditions must be verified before restarting.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Carrying an earlier all-clear through a shutdown
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Workers have moved near the crane, and an earlier all-clear does not establish current clearance. Personnel clearance must also be verified before restarting.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Treating a warning as a restart exception
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: A horn warning does not replace either verification. The requirement applies before engine startup, including a restart during the same shift.

ops.pre-start.misconception: Correcting a starting condition after startup
ops.pre-start.why_wrong: Correcting the throttle after startup reverses the required order. All controls must be properly positioned before the engine starts.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Adds a boom length indication requirement
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: This combination includes an acceptable angle indicator, but it incorrectly makes a boom length indicator part of this requirement. The required alternatives are boom angle or radius indication.
Having both is acceptable, but requiring both overstates the rule. The provision permits a boom angle indicator or a radius indicator.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Substitutes boom length for boom angle
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: A boom length indicator alone does not satisfy this requirement. The permitted alternative to radius indication is boom angle indication.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Assigns indicator reading to the signal person
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: Visibility to the signal person does not satisfy this requirement. The indicator must be readable from the operator's station.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Confuses inspection access with operating visibility
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: A ground-level reading location is not the specified location. The indicator must be readable from the operator's station.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Treats nearby access as sufficient visibility
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: Readability from an access platform alone is insufficient. The required reading location is the operator's station.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Treats a visual scale comparison as measurement
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: Comparing the reach visually with carrier length is an estimate. The temporary alternative calls for measurement with a measuring device.
A previous lift's radius does not establish the current radius. The temporary alternative requires measuring radius or boom angle.
A person's qualification does not replace the specified measuring device. Radius or boom angle must be measured.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Reduces radius when swing direction changes
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: A quarter-turn changes direction, not the distance from the circle's center. The radius stays 30 ft.
Twice the radius is the circle's diameter. Load radius is measured from the axis to the load line, so it is 30 ft.
Swing angle does not add distance to the radius. The stated circular path maintains a 30-ft radius.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Uses the boom pivot as the radius origin
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: The boom foot pin can be offset from the axis of rotation. Radius uses the axis of rotation as its starting reference.
An outrigger is a support location, not the center from which load radius is measured. Use the axis of rotation.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Uses the carrier axle as the reference
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: The front axle does not define the crane's rotational center. Radius is measured from the axis of rotation to the load line.

ops.radius-verification.misconception: Confuses increased tip height with increased reach
ops.radius-verification.why_wrong: Raising the boom reduces its horizontal reach. With boom length fixed, the load radius decreases.

ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: The trigger is above 75 percent, not above 50 percent. A lower threshold may be conservative, but it is not this rule's threshold.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Confusing a warning setting with the verification threshold
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: The rule requires independent verification once the reading exceeds 75 percent. Waiting until 85 percent misses that requirement.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Confusing the verification threshold with the operating limit
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: Rated capacity is the operating limit. The additional weight verification requirement begins above 75 percent, before that limit is reached.
Pickup radius is controlling only if it is also the longest planned radius. The load may move to a longer radius later.
The rule does not average radii. It specifies the longest planned radius.
Placement radius controls only if no part of the route has a longer radius. The load's path must also be considered.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Treating initial hoisting as outside the lift
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: Requested weight information must be provided before the lift. Waiting until the load is suspended is too late.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Using swing as the verification deadline
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: The deadline is before the lift, not merely before swinging. Hoisting can already place the equipment under load.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Delaying verification until the limiting position
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: Providing the information during the lift does not satisfy the requirement to provide it beforehand.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Treating a similar load as an equivalent load
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: Similarity alone does not reliably establish this bundle's weight. Differences in beam sizes, lengths, or quantities can change the total.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Confusing carrying capacity with actual weight
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: Payload rating describes the truck's carrying limit, not the actual bundle weight. It is not a calculation of this load.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Substituting experience for reliable weight information
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: A visual estimate alone does not establish an industry-recognized calculation or equally reliable means of determining weight.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Treating supervisory acceptance as an overload waiver
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: Accepting responsibility does not create an exception to rated capacity or permit the supervisor to require an overloaded lift.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Trading operating speed for rated capacity
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: Reduced speed does not increase the applicable rated capacity. The verified load is above the limit.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Treating load balance as overload protection
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: A balanced load can still overload the crane. A rigger's check cannot authorize exceeding rated capacity.

ops.rated-capacity.misconception: Requiring paperwork for every unknown load
ops.rated-capacity.why_wrong: At 60 percent, this reading does not trigger separate verification through a recognized source. The device-based method is an allowed alternative.

ops.repairs-needed.why_wrong: A verbal report does not meet the rule, which requires writing. The report also goes to the employer's designated person, who may or may not be the lift supervisor.
The report has to be prompt and go to the designated person. A log entry that waits for the monthly inspection fails the timing requirement.
A radio relay is neither written nor addressed to the designated person. The signal person is not the employer's designated recipient.

ops.repairs-needed.misconception: operator duty confused with employer duty
ops.repairs-needed.why_wrong: The operator reports the problem in writing to the designee and the next operator. Briefing all affected employees each shift is the employer's job.
The rule does not give this notice to a lift director. The employer must notify affected employees, whoever it uses to deliver the message.
The owner of a rented crane may not employ the workers involved. The rule puts the notice duty on the employer of the affected employees.
The notice is not a one-time event. The rule requires it at the beginning of each shift.
End-of-shift notice reaches workers after they have already worked around the problem. The rule sets the beginning of each shift.
A weekly meeting leaves whole shifts uninformed. The notice must come at the beginning of each shift.
The night crew learns of the condition through the employer's shift-start notice. The operator's written report goes to the designee and the next operator.
The annual inspector is not a required recipient. The rule names the designated person and, with successive shifts, the next operator.
The employer may arrange repairs with a rental company, but the operator's written report is owed to the designee and the next operator.
Briefing all affected employees is the employer's duty at the start of each shift. The operator's failure here is not putting the report in writing.

ops.repairs-needed.misconception: writing tied only to periodic inspections
ops.repairs-needed.why_wrong: The writing requirement covers any necessary adjustment or repair the operator reports, whenever it is found.
A due date is not required, and leaving out the alternative measures leaves the crew without the workarounds they must follow.
Workers must be told the necessary adjustment or repair as well as the alternative measures. The rule requires both.

ops.shutdown.why_wrong: Assignment as the signal person does not confer this responsibility. The competent person must make the determination and implement the necessary restraints.
Site coordination does not make this the controlling entity representative's determination. This provision assigns it to the competent person.
Responsibility for rigging does not confer this authority. The required determination and restraint measures belong to the competent person.
Visibility alone does not meet the location condition. The operator must remain adjacent to the equipment without other duties.
Inspection paperwork is another duty. The exception requires the operator to remain adjacent without engaging in other duties.
Radio availability and a nearby location do not establish adjacency. The operator must remain adjacent to the equipment.
The comparison uses lifting capacity as the crane is positioned, not its maximum capacity in another configuration.
Being within capacity is insufficient. The gear's weight must be negligible relative to the crane's lifting capacity as positioned.
Barricades and notices do not satisfy this exception's location condition. The gear must be over an area other than an entrance or exit.
Function restraints satisfy a separate condition. The suspended hold must also exceed normal lifting operations.

ops.shutdown.misconception: Extended-hold exception limited to working gear
ops.shutdown.why_wrong: The extended-hold exception can apply to a load such as a beam. This pause fails because it is part of normal lifting operations.
Remaining adjacent without other duties is necessary but insufficient. A routine lifting pause does not satisfy the extended-hold condition.
Checking tickets is another duty even when the load stays visible. The operator must remain adjacent without other duties.
A load watcher does not replace the operator's duty restriction. The operator may not take on the ticket check under this exception.
Deferring other work is only part of the condition. A nearby signal station does not establish that the operator remains adjacent to the crane.
Necessary rigging work does not create an entry exception under this arrangement. No employees may enter the fall zone.

ops.side-loading.why_wrong: Supporting the weight on rollers does not permit using the crane to pull the machine sideways.

ops.side-loading.misconception: Pulling in the boom plane is permitted
ops.side-loading.why_wrong: Aligning the pull with the boom does not permit pulling a load sideways across the floor.
A level, strong surface does not change the prohibition on using the crane for a sideways pull.
A shorter boom does not create an exception to the prohibition on dragging loads sideways.
Pulling over the rear does not authorize sideways dragging.
Rollers do not create an exception. Pulling the load sideways remains prohibited.
The initial horizontal force acts toward the suspension point, not away from it.
The drum pulls along the inclined line. That force has a horizontal component as well as a vertical component.

ops.side-loading.misconception: Only crane swing can cause load swing
ops.side-loading.why_wrong: An inclined, tensioned line can start the load swinging even when the upperworks are stationary.
Skids may reduce friction, but the proposed operation still uses the crane to drag the pump sideways.
Using boom retraction instead of the hoist does not change the sideways pull into a permitted operation.

ops.side-loading.misconception: Slow swing within capacity permits dragging
ops.side-loading.why_wrong: Neither slow motion nor unused chart capacity permits dragging the pump sideways.
The tag line does not change the proposed crane motion: it would pull the supported end sideways.

ops.side-loading.misconception: Boom movement avoids the dragging prohibition
ops.side-loading.why_wrong: Changing the crane function does not eliminate the sideways pull on the beam.
Combining motions would still pull the beam sideways while it remains in contact with its support.

ops.side-loading.misconception: Lower tension permits a sideways pull
ops.side-loading.why_wrong: Reducing tension does not permit using swing to pull the restrained pipe sideways.

ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: This determination is assigned to the competent person. Assignment as the signal person does not itself establish that role.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Lift supervision substituted for competent person
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Supervising the lift does not by itself establish the designated role for this determination. The rule specifies the competent person.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Rigger qualification substituted for competent person
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Qualification as a rigger does not by itself establish the designated role for this determination. The rule specifies the competent person.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Trial lift used to complete prerequisite
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: A trial lift starts the lifting operation. The seating verification must occur before starting to lift.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Swing treated as the verification deadline
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Waiting until before swinging permits lifting before the required verification. The deadline is before starting to lift.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Landing sequence substituted for lifting prerequisite
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Verification before lowering would occur after the load has already been lifted. Seating must be verified before starting to lift.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Repeated drum check substituted for sheave check
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Another drum check does not establish sheave seating. A check after a trial lift also misses the before-lifting requirement.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Correct location checked at the wrong time
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Sheave seating must be verified before lifting begins. Waiting until the load clears its support is too late.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Static drum inspection substituted for complete verification
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Rechecking the drum does not address the unchecked sheaves. The required verification concerns seating as slack is removed.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Slack mistaken for a change in mechanical advantage
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Slack does not change the number of supporting rope parts. The tension increase comes from abruptly accelerating the load, not from a different reeving ratio.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Dynamic force mistaken for increased weight
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Slack does not change the load's weight. Motion can increase the force required while the load accelerates.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Radius effect confused with shock loading
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Taking up slack does not inherently increase load radius. The immediate tension increase results from acceleration when the rope becomes taut.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Repeated preliminary inspection treated as sufficient
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Repeating the inspection while slack remains does not verify seating as that slack is removed. That verification must precede lifting.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Low test lift treated as an exception
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: This sequence begins lifting before completing verification. A few inches of lift still crosses the rule's before-lifting deadline.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Required checks split across the lifting deadline
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Both locations must be verified before lifting begins. Splitting the checks across the start of the lift leaves sheave seating unverified at the required time.

ops.slack-rope.misconception: Continuous loading mistaken for greater peak loading
ops.slack-rope.why_wrong: Continuous stationary support requires force equal to the load's weight. Arresting a falling load requires additional upward force to reduce its downward speed.

ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: Load charts give capacities, not a legal swing rpm. The rule limits rotation by whether the load stays controllable, not by a listed speed.
No federal rule sets a percent-of-chart trigger for swing speed. The requirement applies to every lift: keep the load from swinging out beyond controllable radius.
The operator does judge the speed, but there is a federal requirement. The judgment has to keep the load from swinging out beyond the radius at which it can be controlled.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Assumes radius is fixed by the boom tip
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: The boom point marks the radius only when the line hangs plumb. An outswung load acts farther out than the sheaves.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Treats a temporary swing as harmless
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: A temporary outswing still loads the crane at the larger radius. Brief overloads from dynamic swing can tip a crane or damage the boom.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Relies on a static pre-swing reading
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: A reading taken before the swing does not show the extra radius the swing creates. The actual load position is what governs.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Assumes force is linear with speed
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: Outward force does not rise in step with speed. It rises with speed squared, so doubling the speed gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the force.
Cubing the speed ratio gives 8. Outward force depends on speed squared, not cubed, so the answer is 4 times.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Uses square root instead of square
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: 1.4 is roughly the square root of 2, which runs the relationship backward. Doubling the speed quadruples the force.
A full-speed start and a hard brake are the two actions that cause lag and overshoot. Less time in the air does not offset the shock loading.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Fixes the start but not the stop
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: The gentle start fixes only half the problem. Braking hard at the set point still lets the load keep going and swing past and out.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Uses taglines to absorb swing energy
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: Taglines guide and steady a load. They are not for stopping a heavy load moving at speed, and doing so puts the crew in danger.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Treats the static rating as dynamic capacity
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: The 9,500 lb rating assumes the load hangs at the chart radius. Normal swing speed can push it outward, and the 500 lb margin leaves no room for that.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Believes exposure time is the hazard
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: Faster rotation increases outswing, which is exactly what overloads the crane where capacity is lowest. Less time in the zone does not make it safe.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Compares zone ratings instead of load to rating
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: What matters is whether the load fits each zone's rating, not how the two ratings compare. 9,000 lb is within 9,500 lb, so the swing is allowed if it is controlled.

ops.swing-speed.misconception: Relies on brake instead of speed control
ops.swing-speed.why_wrong: Hard braking adds shock and makes the panel swing more. It does not stop wind and rotation from carrying the load outward.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Mixes up the response rule with the placement rule
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: The starting control comes up in the rule on how the operator must respond to a tag. For equipment taken out of service, the tag must go in the cab.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Thinks any visible spot on the crane is enough
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: A tag on the outside of the carrier doesn't meet the rule. The tag for out-of-service equipment must be in the cab, where the operator will see it.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Uses the single-function rule for the whole crane
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: Putting the tag on one function's control fits a single function taken out of service. When the whole crane is out of service, the tag must be in the cab.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Uses the whole-crane rule for one function
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: A cab tag saying the equipment is out of service is the rule for taking the whole crane out of service. Here only one function is out, and that needs its own tag in a conspicuous position.
The rule calls for a tag in a conspicuous position saying the function is out of service and not to be used. Saying the function is 'limited' doesn't meet that.
A log entry alone doesn't meet the rule. A physical tag must be placed in a conspicuous position.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Field myth that only the person who hung the tag can remove it
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: The rule doesn't limit removal to the person who hung the tag. Any person authorized to remove it may do so.
Being a qualified person doesn't give someone authority to remove tags. The person must be authorized to remove the tag.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Gives the duty to the wrong person
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: Being assigned to the crane doesn't make the operator authorized to remove the tag. Without that authority, he may only start the crane after verifying both required conditions.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Thinks supervisor authority overrides the tag
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: A written order from the foreman doesn't remove the tag or meet either verification condition. The rule's alternatives don't include a supervisor's order.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Thinks one of the two conditions is enough
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: A walk-around covers only the first condition. He must also verify the crane has been repaired and is working properly.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Applies an inspection requirement that isn't part of this rule
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: The tag-out response rule doesn't require an inspection. It requires removal by an authorized person, or the operator's verification of both conditions.
The rule calls for a tag saying the function is out of service and not to be used. It doesn't call for a note on the starting control about a limitation.
A verbal briefing doesn't replace the tag. When a function is taken out of service, a tag must be placed.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Thinks a no-lift startup is exempt
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: The rule bars starting the equipment until the tag is removed or both conditions are verified. Making no lifts doesn't create an exception.

ops.tag-out.misconception: Field myth that only the person who hung the tag can clear it
ops.tag-out.why_wrong: The reason is wrong. The rule lets the operator start after verifying both conditions, and any authorized person, not only the mechanic who hung it, may remove the tag.

ops.travel-preparation.why_wrong: Ten feet applies to voltages over 50 through 345 kV. A 34.5-kV line requires 6 feet during travel without a load.
Sixteen feet applies to voltages over 345 through 750 kV, not to 34.5 kV.
Twenty feet is the Table T clearance for voltages over 750 through 1,000 kV. It is also the separate threshold below which unloaded travel requires a dedicated spotter.

ops.travel-preparation.misconception: Using a clearance value as the spotter trigger
ops.travel-preparation.why_wrong: Six feet is a Table T clearance for one voltage band. The dedicated-spotter requirement begins below 20 feet.
Ten feet is a Table T clearance for another voltage band. The spotter trigger is closer than 20 feet.
Sixteen feet is a voltage-dependent minimum clearance. It does not replace the 20-foot spotter threshold.
Route clearance alone does not meet the hook requirement. The empty hook must be restrained against free swinging.

ops.travel-preparation.misconception: Using a low hook position as restraint
ops.travel-preparation.why_wrong: Hanging the block below the deck does not prevent free swinging. The hook must be lashed or otherwise restrained.

ops.travel-preparation.misconception: Confusing hoist braking with swing restraint
ops.travel-preparation.why_wrong: The hoist brake can hold hook elevation without preventing sideways swinging. The empty hook still requires restraint.
A diagonal position is not in line with the direction of motion. Clearing the aisle does not replace the alignment requirement.

ops.travel-preparation.misconception: Using available side clearance as permission
ops.travel-preparation.why_wrong: An open side does not permit transverse boom alignment during straight transit. The boom must follow the direction of motion.
Moving the boom away from the driver's view does not satisfy the transit rule. It must be in line with the direction of motion.
A spotter does not substitute for securing the superstructure. Neither stated exception applies to this move.

ops.travel-preparation.misconception: Treating low speed as an exception
ops.travel-preparation.why_wrong: Slow speed does not waive the requirement to secure the superstructure against rotation.

ops.travel-preparation.misconception: Using hook restraint as a swing lock
ops.travel-preparation.why_wrong: Hook restraint addresses free swinging of the hook. It does not satisfy the separate requirement to secure the superstructure.

ops.travel-preparation.misconception: Substituting a spotter for route assessment
ops.travel-preparation.why_wrong: Choosing the shortest branch and assigning a spotter does not establish a safe path. A safe path must be identified and used.

ops.travel-with-load.why_wrong: The determination belongs to a competent person. Assignment as the operator alone does not establish that role.
Attaching the load does not assign the rigger responsibility for travel-capacity determinations. That responsibility belongs to a competent person.
Directing movement does not itself make the signal person responsible for capacity reductions. A competent person makes that determination.
A suspended load is not itself the prohibition. The competent person must determine a safe load position.

ops.travel-with-load.misconception: Pick and carry is limited to crawlers
ops.travel-with-load.why_wrong: Travel on tires is not categorically prohibited. Manufacturer restrictions and the loaded-travel requirements apply.
A necessary capacity reduction does not automatically prohibit travel. The competent person's determination must be implemented.
Equal pressures do not necessarily match the manufacturer's specifications. The specified pressure, rather than uniformity alone, controls.
The competent person's travel responsibilities do not replace the manufacturer's tire-pressure specification.

ops.travel-with-load.misconception: Sidewall maximum is the operating specification
ops.travel-with-load.why_wrong: A tire-sidewall maximum is not necessarily the pressure specified by the crane manufacturer for the operation.
The loaded-travel rule assigns supervision to a competent person. Being a signal person alone does not satisfy that assignment.
A level route does not remove the competent-person requirement. The operator would need to qualify and serve in that role.

ops.travel-with-load.misconception: Crawler travel is a rigging responsibility
ops.travel-with-load.why_wrong: Tracks do not transfer travel supervision to the rigger. A competent person must supervise.
A clearance check by a signal person does not replace the competent person's determinations about the changed route and its conditions.
A capacity check alone does not address the changed route. The competent person must make the necessary travel determinations.
Checking rigging does not establish that the detour is suitable. The competent person must assess its travel conditions.

ops.travel-with-load.misconception: Signal person can revise load position
ops.travel-with-load.why_wrong: A signal person's approval does not revise the competent person's determination. The specified position must be used unless appropriately reassessed.

ops.unattended.why_wrong: Being the operator does not by itself assign this responsibility. The determination and restraint measures belong to the competent person.
Signal-person status does not authorize this determination. The rule assigns it to the competent person.

ops.unattended.misconception: Rigger qualification substitutes for the required role
ops.unattended.why_wrong: Rigger qualifications alone do not satisfy this responsibility. The person must serve as the competent person for this determination.
An ordinary signaling pause is part of normal lifting operations. The exception requires a planned hold exceeding normal lifting operations.
A routine adjustment within normal lifting operations does not meet the duration condition.
An ordinary placement pause remains part of normal lifting operations. A longer planned suspension is required.

ops.unattended.misconception: Carrier parking controls replace crane restraints
ops.unattended.why_wrong: This substitutes carrier functions for swing and outrigger or stabilizer functions, which the rule specifically includes.
This omits telescoping and substitutes carrier braking. Telescoping must be included in the necessary restraint measures.
This omits boom hoist and substitutes carrier steering. The rule explicitly includes the boom-hoist function.
Moving the paperwork closer does not fix the problem. The operator may not perform other duties while relying on this exception.
A signal person's presence does not permit the operator to take on other duties.

ops.unattended.misconception: Competent person can waive an exception condition
ops.unattended.why_wrong: The competent person cannot waive the prohibition on other duties. The operator must stop the paperwork.
Radio contact does not create an exception to the exclusion. All employees must remain outside the fall zone under this arrangement.
An escort does not authorize entry. Neither employee may enter the fall zone while this arrangement continues.

ops.unattended.misconception: Mechanical restraint substitutes for employee exclusion
ops.unattended.why_wrong: Checking a brake does not remove the fall-zone restriction. Restraints and employee exclusion are separate requirements.

ops.unattended.misconception: Extra clearance cures the entrance restriction
ops.unattended.why_wrong: Additional height does not change the fact that the bar is over an entrance. The exemption requires a different location.

other.articulating.misconception: Mixes up the overload device date with the two-block date
other.articulating.why_wrong: This is the date for the overload, load weighing or load moment device requirement on articulating cranes. The two-block date is December 31, 1999.

other.articulating.misconception: Uses a general effective date instead of the manufacture cutoff
other.articulating.why_wrong: This date is not tied to the articulating crane two-block requirement. That requirement covers cranes manufactured after December 31, 1999.
This date blends the two real cutoffs and appears in neither rule. The two-block cutoff is December 31, 1999.

other.articulating.misconception: Treats the two-block device as overload protection
other.articulating.why_wrong: Anti-two-block protection is a separate requirement. It is not one of the four overload-related devices that meet this rule.

other.articulating.misconception: Applies a telescopic or lattice boom aid to articulating cranes
other.articulating.why_wrong: A boom angle indicator is not on the list for articulating cranes. The list has only overload prevention, load weighing, load moment indicator and load moment limiter.

other.articulating.misconception: Confuses stability aids with capacity devices
other.articulating.why_wrong: Outrigger monitoring is not one of the four listed devices. The rule names only load-related devices: overload prevention, load weighing, load moment indicator or load moment limiter.

other.articulating.misconception: Applies the general device list to the exclusion
other.articulating.why_wrong: An indicator meets the general post-2011 device requirement, but the delivery exclusion names an automatic overload prevention device specifically.
Two-block protection is a separate requirement. The exclusion depends on an automatic overload prevention device.

other.articulating.misconception: Treats a weight readout as overload prevention
other.articulating.why_wrong: A load weighing device shows the weight but does not automatically prevent an overload. The exclusion requires the automatic prevention device.

other.articulating.misconception: Assumes every construction-site lift is covered
other.articulating.why_wrong: The standard specifically excludes certain delivery work on construction sites, including ground transfers without sequencing.

other.articulating.misconception: Applies the onto-structure condition to ground transfer
other.articulating.why_wrong: The overload device condition belongs to the fork/cradle delivery onto a structure. The ground-transfer exclusion has no device condition.

other.articulating.misconception: Confuses sheet goods with prefabricated components
other.articulating.why_wrong: Sheet rock is a building supply sheet good, not a prefabricated component, so ground delivery of it stays excluded.

other.articulating.misconception: Thinks the device alone creates the exclusion
other.articulating.why_wrong: The overload device matters only for building supply sheet goods or packaged materials placed with a fork or cradle. It cannot save a prefabricated component lift.
Roof trusses are listed as prefabricated components. Packaged materials are items like bags of cement or bundles of shingles.
Holding material in place is one reason for coverage, but prefabricated components are covered on their own whether or not they are held.

other.articulating.misconception: Thinks the material type alone decides coverage
other.articulating.why_wrong: Plywood is listed, but the exclusion ends once the crane holds the material for attachment, whatever the material is.

other.derricks.why_wrong: Four guys do not meet the default minimum. A different arrangement requires approval and a corresponding rated-capacity revision.

other.derricks.misconception: Higher guy count is the minimum
other.derricks.why_wrong: Eight equally spaced guys exceed the stated minimum. The default minimum is six.
Twelve equally spaced guys are not the required minimum. The rule specifies six unless an approved variation applies.
A weekly check does not satisfy the daily requirement for guy tension.
Guy tension is an additional daily inspection item, not merely a monthly item.
The additional annual items include the gudgeon pin and foundation supports. Guy tension requires daily inspection.
Seven days is not this requirement's threshold. The specified methods become mandatory at 30 days.
Fourteen days is not the stated threshold. The rule specifies 30 days or more.
Waiting for a 60-day shutdown misses the requirement that begins at 30 days.
Ready availability alone does not satisfy the posting requirement for this permanent installation.
A shift review does not replace posting the chart where responsible operating personnel can see it.
Office access does not meet the visible-posting requirement for this permanent installation.
The spotter observing the marks must communicate directly with the operator. An intermediary does not meet that condition.
A preliminary check does not provide observation of the marks during boom movement.
Estimating angle from the boom tip does not satisfy the cable-mark alternative, which requires the marks to be visible.
An operator's unloaded trial does not replace the required qualified-person evaluation.

other.floating.misconception: Confuses the freeboard stability wind with the load chart wind
other.floating.why_wrong: 60 mph is the wind speed in the freeboard stability table (Table M2). It is not the load chart wind minimum, which is 40 mph.

other.floating.misconception: Confuses the backward stability wind with the load chart wind
other.floating.why_wrong: 90 mph is the backward stability condition for a high boom with no load (Table M3). Load charts must consider at least 40 mph.

other.floating.misconception: Applies a typical land crane wind limit to marine charts
other.floating.why_wrong: 20 mph is a common land crane operating wind limit. Marine load charts must consider at least 40 mph.

other.floating.misconception: Uses the 25-tons-or-less row or the land crane cap
other.floating.why_wrong: 5 degrees applies to permanently attached marine equipment rated 25 tons or less, and it is the cap for land cranes on barges. A 40-ton unit gets 7 degrees.

other.floating.misconception: Applies the derrick row to a crane
other.floating.why_wrong: 10 degrees applies only to derricks designed for marine use. This crane is not a derrick, so the limit is 7 degrees.

other.floating.misconception: Assumes list and trim limits differ
other.floating.why_wrong: Table M1 gives the same value for list and trim in every row. For this crane both are 7 degrees.

other.floating.misconception: Assumes the land crane rule carries over unchanged
other.floating.why_wrong: The marine section limits the requirement to two situations: hoisting personnel and hoisting over an occupied cofferdam or shaft. It is not required on every lift.

other.floating.misconception: Borrows the Table M1 capacity threshold
other.floating.why_wrong: 25 tons is the capacity break in the list and trim table. It has nothing to do with when anti two-block is required.

other.floating.misconception: Invents a trigger based on nearby vessels
other.floating.why_wrong: A vessel alongside does not trigger the requirement. Only personnel hoisting or hoisting over an occupied cofferdam or shaft does.

other.floating.misconception: Thinks one diver's return releases the crane
other.floating.why_wrong: The rule covers every diver the crane serves. It stays dedicated until the last diver is out of the water.

other.floating.misconception: Treats the signal requirement as permission to multitask
other.floating.why_wrong: Line of sight (or electronic signals) between the operator and tender is a separate requirement. It does not allow other lifts while a diver is down.

other.floating.misconception: Assigns override authority to the wrong person
other.floating.why_wrong: No one can approve other lifts while a diver is in the water. The crane stays dedicated until all divers are back on board.

other.floating.misconception: Moves a monthly item to the shift inspection
other.floating.why_wrong: Watertightness based on chain lockers, fuel compartments and hatches is a monthly inspection item, not a shift item.

other.floating.misconception: Moves an annual item to the shift inspection
other.floating.why_wrong: Four-corner draft readings are part of the annual external vessel inspection by a qualified person.

other.floating.misconception: Requires only half of the dual expertise
other.floating.why_wrong: Knowing vessel stability alone is not enough. The person must also have expertise in land crane capacity.

other.floating.misconception: Assumes a PE license alone qualifies
other.floating.why_wrong: A PE license and land-side expertise do not meet the rule without expertise in vessel stability.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Using a more conservative number as the regulatory minimum
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: This section requires at least two full wraps on each respective drum. Three is not its stated minimum.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Confusing an extra rope reserve with the required minimum
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: Four wraps exceeds the minimum stated in this section. The required minimum is two full wraps.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Relying on the rope attachment with insufficient wraps
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: One full wrap is below the required minimum. Lowering must not leave fewer than two full wraps on either respective drum.
The stated track condition is level within 1 percent grade. A 2 percent grade exceeds that condition.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Substituting a travel-grade assumption for a rating condition
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: Five percent is not the track-level condition for these ratings. The section specifies 1 percent.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Treating a modest slope as sufficiently level
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: A 3 percent grade is outside the stated rating condition. The required value is 1 percent.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Treating the brake test as a shift inspection
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: A shift-start test does not replace the required test each time a load approaching rated load is handled.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Tying the test only to configuration changes
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: The requirement is triggered by each load approaching rated load, even when the crane setup does not change.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Testing a batch instead of each load
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: Identical loads do not create an exception. Each load approaching rated load requires its own brake test.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Using a brake test to justify exceeding the tire rating
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: A brake test does not increase the 7,000-lb rating without outriggers. The 8,000-lb load exceeds that rating at 20 ft.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Confusing resistance to rolling with lifting stability
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: Locking the travel brakes does not change the chart capacity. Outriggers are required because the load exceeds the rating without them.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Treating the rating without outriggers as an absolute crane limit
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: The stated outrigger capacity accommodates the load, and all other setup requirements are met. This rule does not require a larger crane.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Assigning the duty automatically to the operator
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: The rule assigns responsibility to a designated person. Being the operator does not automatically establish that designation.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Confusing signaling responsibility with travel planning
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: Serving as signal person does not automatically make someone responsible for these determinations. The responsibility belongs to a designated person.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Treating inspection approval as control of the travel operation
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: Completing an inspection does not automatically assign responsibility for loaded travel. A designated person must hold that responsibility.

other.mobile-general-industry.misconception: Confusing swing restraint with boom-hoist locking
other.mobile-general-industry.why_wrong: The swing brake controls rotation rather than positively locking the boom hoist. The fixed-radius requirement concerns the boom-hoist pawl or equivalent device.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Confuses the excluded paragraph with the pre-2001 provision
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: Paragraph (b)(2) is not excluded for permanently installed cranes. The date limit on (b)(2) applies only to cranes that are not permanently installed, under § 1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(C).

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Applies the definitions carve-out to the wrong configuration
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: The § 1910.179(a) definitions are not excluded for permanently installed cranes. The carve-out for the terms "hoist" and "load" applies only to equipment that is not permanently installed.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Picks a paragraph from the non-permanent list
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: Paragraph (e)(1) is not excluded. For permanently installed cranes, (b)(1) is the only paragraph removed.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Uses installation date instead of manufacture date
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: The test is the manufacture date, not the installation date. A crane built after the cutoff but installed earlier would not qualify.
This reverses the rule. Cranes made on or after September 19, 2001 fall under the listed ASME B30.2-2005 sections instead.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Mixes up the two date-based branches
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: The ASME B30.2-2005 sections are the alternative that applies to newer equipment. They are not a trigger for § 1910.179(b)(2).
"Crane" keeps its § 1910.179(a) definition. Only "hoist" and "load" switch to § 1926.1401.
"Bridge" is still defined by § 1910.179(a). The exception covers "hoist" and "load" only.
That is the rule for cranes permanently installed in a facility under § 1926.1438(a). This crane is temporary, so § 1926.1438(b) applies.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Assumes construction use triggers all of Subpart CC
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: § 1926.1438(b)(2)(i) applies only the listed Subpart CC sections, not the whole subpart.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Assigns the crane to the wrong section because it runs on rails
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: § 1926.1435 is not among the sections listed for this equipment. Coverage under (b)(1) does not depend on how the crane travels.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Applies the permanent-installation paragraph to a temporary crane
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: Paragraph (a) covers only cranes permanently installed in a facility. This crane is temporary.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Treats a wheeled gantry as a mobile crane under all of Subpart CC
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: For this equipment, § 1926.1438(b)(2)(i) applies only the listed Subpart CC sections, not the full subpart.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Field myth that only rail-mounted gantries are covered
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: Paragraph (b)(1) expressly covers this equipment however it travels, including on wheels.

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Applies the temporary-crane rule to a permanent crane
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: That combination is for cranes that are not permanently installed, under § 1926.1438(b).

other.overhead-construction.misconception: Assumes construction work always brings in Subpart CC
other.overhead-construction.why_wrong: Paragraph (a) expressly removes Subpart CC for permanently installed overhead and gantry cranes, even during construction.

other.overhead-general.why_wrong: This reverses the two minimum clearances. The overhead minimum is 3 inches, and the lateral minimum is 2 inches.
Three inches laterally exceeds the minimum. The required lateral minimum is 2 inches.
Two inches overhead is insufficient. The overhead minimum is 3 inches.
The 100-percent requirement applies with mechanical control braking. A single holding brake used with electrical control braking requires 125 percent.
The minimum for this arrangement is 125 percent, not 150 percent.
The rule does not require this single holding brake to provide twice the full-load hoisting torque. Its minimum is 125 percent.

other.overhead-general.misconception: Lower force mistaken for the limit
other.overhead-general.why_wrong: A brake may develop rated torque with 50 pounds, but that is not the maximum permitted requirement. The limit is 70 pounds.
A required force of 100 pounds exceeds the 70-pound limit.

other.overhead-general.misconception: Guard strength confused with pedal force
other.overhead-general.why_wrong: The 200-pound figure concerns certain guard strength requirements. Foot-operated brake force is limited to 70 pounds.

other.overhead-general.misconception: Bridge labels substitute for hoist labels
other.overhead-general.why_wrong: Bridge markings do not replace the required individual markings. Each hoist's rating must appear on that hoist or its load block and be legible from below.

other.overhead-general.misconception: Crane capacity assigned to every hoist
other.overhead-general.why_wrong: Each hoist needs its own rating, not the crane's total rating. These hoists must be identified as 15 tons and 5 tons.

other.overhead-general.misconception: Control labels substitute for equipment markings
other.overhead-general.why_wrong: Control labels alone do not meet the hoist-marking requirement. The ratings must be on the hoists or their blocks and legible from below.
The rule permits a visible or audible alarm. It does not require both forms of alarm.
A continuous display alone lacks the required alarm. The device must alert the operator at a predetermined wind velocity.

other.overhead-general.misconception: Alarm routed to the wrong recipient
other.overhead-general.why_wrong: The required visible or audible alarm must be given to the bridge operator. An office-only alarm does not meet that requirement.

other.overhead-general.misconception: Operating authority treated as engineering authority
other.overhead-general.why_wrong: Designation authorizes crane operation; it does not establish the engineering qualification required for this review.

other.overhead-inspection.why_wrong: Frequent inspections range from daily to monthly. A weekly lower limit misses components specifically requiring daily inspection.
Monthly to yearly describes the periodic-inspection range. It does not describe frequent inspections.
The frequent-inspection range extends through monthly intervals, although some checks must occur daily.
The periodic range begins at 1 month, not 3 months. Service conditions determine the appropriate interval within the range.
The periodic range extends to 12 months. Six months is not its general upper limit.
Periodic inspections may be needed more frequently than every 6 months. The classification spans 1 to 12 months.
Monthly is not the stated minimum frequency for standby-crane inspections. The standby requirement is at least semi-annually.
Quarterly inspections would be more frequent than the stated minimum. The standby provision requires at least semiannual inspection.
Annual inspection is too infrequent for the standby requirement. Standby cranes must be inspected at least semi-annually.
A monthly service interval does not satisfy this specific check. Air and hydraulic system leakage and deterioration require daily inspection.
This provision specifies daily inspection, not a separate inspection before every lift. Defects appearing during operation must also receive attention.
An overhaul schedule does not replace the daily hydraulic-system inspection. The required check addresses conditions that can develop between overhauls.
A bay number identifies a location, not necessarily the inspected hook. The record must identify the hook itself.
The required signature belongs to the person who performed the inspection. A supervisor's signature does not substitute unless that supervisor performed it.
A rated capacity does not uniquely identify the inspected hook. The record needs its serial number or another identifier.
Checking only the upper half leaves part of the indicator's range unchecked. The periodic inspection covers its full range.

other.overhead-operation.why_wrong: One full wrap is insufficient. Lowering must stop before fewer than two full wraps remain.
This rule requires two full wraps, not three. An extra wrap is not the specified minimum.
Four wraps exceed the minimum stated here. The rule prohibits lowering below two full wraps.
The interval is each operator's shift, not merely once per workday. The test is performed under no load.
The shift interval is correct, but a light load is still a load. The required test is under no load.
A weekly test does not meet the required interval. Each operator must have the switch tried out at the beginning of the shift.
Independent direction divides authority over one lift. The rule places the operation under one qualified responsible person.
Crane capacity does not automatically assign responsibility. The person in charge must be qualified and responsible for the operation.
Separate supervisors directing separate cranes do not provide the required single person in charge of the operation.

other.overhead-operation.misconception: Tag line substitutes for hook alignment
other.overhead-operation.why_wrong: A tag line does not replace positioning the hook over the load. The hook must be brought over it in a manner that prevents swinging.
Hook positioning belongs before hoisting. Lifting first can cause the load to swing toward the offset hook.
Simultaneous hoisting and alignment reverses the required order. Bring the hook over the load before starting to hoist.

other.overhead-operation.misconception: Empty-hook test substitutes for loaded test
other.overhead-operation.why_wrong: An empty-hook check does not perform the required loaded brake test. Raise the actual load a few inches and apply the brakes.

other.overhead-operation.misconception: Brake test delayed until travel height
other.overhead-operation.why_wrong: The specified test height is a few inches, not travel height. Test the brakes before lifting the load that far.

other.overhead-operation.misconception: Lighter test load substitutes for actual load
other.overhead-operation.why_wrong: A lighter trial load does not replace testing when the near-rated load is handled. The actual load is raised a few inches for the test.

other.overhead-operation.misconception: Fall protection permits riding the load
other.overhead-operation.why_wrong: Fall protection does not create an exception. No hoisting, lowering, or traveling is permitted while an employee is on the load or hook.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: An office copy does not meet the requirement unless the chart is also available at the control station.
Storage with maintenance materials is insufficient if the chart is unavailable at the operator's control station.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Supervisor access substitutes for operator access
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: The supervisor's access does not replace the operator's required access at the control station.
Operating experience alone does not satisfy the design requirement. The designer must be a qualified engineer.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Every engineering task requires professional registration
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: Registration is not expressly required by this design provision. A registered professional engineer is specifically required for certain other tasks, such as developing unavailable capacity procedures.
Inspection experience alone does not establish the engineering qualification required to design the equipment.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Sideboom live-boom cutoff applied to pile drivers
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: That date and direction resemble the sideboom live-boom exception. Dedicated pile drivers are subject to this provision when manufactured after November 8, 2011.
This advances the cutoff by one year. The dedicated pile-driver cutoff is after November 8, 2011.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Inclusive cutoff substituted for exclusive cutoff
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: The rule says after November 8, 2011. This choice incorrectly includes equipment manufactured on that date.
A project transfer alone does not trigger this incorporated requirement. Its applicability is limited to altered or modified equipment.
Changing operators is not the stated trigger. The incorporated rated-load-test requirement applies to altered or modified equipment.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Inspection and rated-load-test triggers are identical
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: An inspection event alone is not the stated trigger. Alteration or modification makes this requirement applicable.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Training automatically transfers between equipment types
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: The requirement concerns safe operation of the type the worker will use. Forklift experience alone does not meet that requirement.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Signal-person supervision substitutes for operator training
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: A trained signal person does not replace operator training. The operator must be trained before operating.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Operating demonstration may precede required training
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: This reverses the required order. Training must occur before the worker operates the equipment.

other.sideboom-small-piledriver.misconception: Load-weighing date controls anti two-blocking applicability
other.sideboom-small-piledriver.why_wrong: That manufacture-date condition concerns load weighing and similar devices on dedicated pile drivers. It does not remove their anti two-blocking exception.

other.tower.why_wrong: This is twice as tight as the rule requires. The default minimum is 1:500, about 1 inch in 40 feet.
This allows twice the lean the rule permits. The default is 1:500, about 1 inch in 40 feet.

other.tower.misconception: Confusing with a level or slope tolerance
other.tower.why_wrong: This is far looser than allowed. The tower must be plumb to at least 1:500 when the manufacturer is silent.
The rule sets the limit at the last 2 wraps, not 3.

other.tower.misconception: Field myth about keeping a full layer
other.tower.why_wrong: The rule protects the last 2 wraps, not a whole layer. A layer can hold many more wraps than that.
The device must protect the last 2 wraps. Five is a made-up margin, not the rule.
The A/D director confirms that foundations are installed according to the design but does not design them.
A qualified person has jobs elsewhere in the tower crane rules, such as verifying plumb. Design must come from the manufacturer or a registered professional engineer.
A competent person cannot design foundations. Only the manufacturer or a registered professional engineer can.
This is Option B for a failed trolley travel limiting device. It does nothing to prevent moment overload.
Marking the trolley rope is the measure for the trolley travel limiter. A moment overload needs both the radius and a known load weight.
The rule calls for no derating. It requires the radius from an indicator or a measurement, plus a reliable load weight given to the operator.
An airport report is not one of the listed alternatives. It also does not reflect the wind at jib height on this site.
The borrowed reading must come from a tower crane on the same site, not a neighboring site.

other.tower.misconception: Treating an operational aid like a safety device
other.tower.why_wrong: Stopping is not required. This is a Category II aid with listed temporary alternatives and a 30-day repair window.

other.tower.misconception: Operational-aid alternative applied to a safety device
other.tower.why_wrong: Spotters are temporary measures for some operational aids. Safety devices allow no alternative measures.

personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: The specified maximum deviation is one percent. A tighter setup may comply, but 0.5 percent is not the regulatory maximum.
A 1.5 percent deviation exceeds the one-percent limit for personnel hoisting.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Confusing firm footing with acceptable slope
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: A 2.5 percent deviation exceeds the one-percent limit, even if the footing is firm.
The limit is 50 percent, not 25 percent. Applying the personnel reduction twice unnecessarily halves the permitted load again.
The personnel-hoisting limit is 50 percent. A 75-percent threshold does not satisfy this requirement.
The full chart capacity is not available for an occupied suspended personnel lift. The total load is limited to half the applicable rated capacity.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Substituting load information for a travel limit
