personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: A load moment indicator does not replace the required boom hoist limiting device.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Treating capacity indication as boom protection
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: A capacity display does not satisfy the separate requirement for a boom hoist limiting device.
Boom length indication addresses a different equipment criterion. It does not replace the boom hoist limiting device.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Using a conservative chart to excuse unequal extension
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: Selecting the lower chart does not cure unequal outrigger extension. Personnel hoisting requires equal extension as well as the proper chart.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Assuming full extension is always mandatory
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: This provision requires equal, locked extension consistent with procedures and charts. It does not universally require full extension.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Confusing paired symmetry with equal extension
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: Matching opposite pairs is insufficient. The amount of extension must be the same for all outriggers.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Substituting human monitoring for automatic protection
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: An observer cannot replace the required automatic overload protection. The device must function before personnel hoisting begins.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Trading excess capacity for a required device
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: Reducing the load further does not remove the equipment requirement. Automatic overload protection must still function.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Applying the conventional variable angle boom device pair
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: Those devices do not substitute for an articulating crane's required automatic overload protection.

personnel.equipment-criteria.misconception: Confusing boom angle with boom length
personnel.equipment-criteria.why_wrong: Boom angle alone does not establish boom length. The rule permits a length-indicating device or measuring marks on the boom.

personnel.loading.why_wrong: The limit is 50 percent. Halving the crane rating twice applies a reduction the rule does not require.
The personnel-platform limit is 50 percent, not 75 percent of the applicable crane rating.
Ordinary personnel-platform lifts cannot use the crane's entire rated capacity. The total suspended load is limited to half that rating.

personnel.loading.misconception: Applying the crane reduction to the platform
personnel.loading.why_wrong: The 50-percent restriction applies to the applicable crane capacity. This paragraph does not halve the platform's marked rating.

personnel.loading.misconception: Transferring crane capacity to the platform
personnel.loading.why_wrong: Unused crane capacity does not increase the platform's rating. The platform must stay within its own rated capacity.
The platform loading limit is its rated capacity. A separate 75-percent platform limit is not established here.

personnel.loading.misconception: Confusing trial lifting with proof testing
personnel.loading.why_wrong: The stated exception is for proof testing. An unoccupied trial lift is not that exception.

personnel.loading.misconception: Treating a stationary load as exempt
personnel.loading.why_wrong: Holding the platform stationary does not remove the 50-percent capacity limit.

personnel.loading.misconception: Treating an initial lift as a capacity test
personnel.loading.why_wrong: The first occupied lift remains subject to the 50-percent limit. The exception concerns proof testing.
Half of 6,000 is 3,000 lb, and the existing total is 2,800 lb. The remaining allowance is 200 lb, not 100 lb.
Subtracting only the 2,500-lb loaded platform gives 500 lb. The 300 lb of hook, line and rigging must also be included, leaving 200 lb.
The applicable limit is 3,000 lb, and 2,500 + 300 = 2,800 lb is already imposed. Only 200 lb remains.
Removing 300 lb would bring the platform below its rating, but it is not the minimum. The load exceeds the rating by only 100 lb.
A 400-lb reduction is more than this capacity check requires. Removing 100 lb brings the platform load to its 1,000-lb rating.
This would reduce the load to 400 lb. The platform's stated load rating is 1,000 lb, so the required reduction is 100 lb.

personnel.loading.misconception: Confusing a possible payload with total loaded weight
personnel.loading.why_wrong: Half of the applicable 6,000-lb rating is 3,000 lb. A 1,000-lb total limit does not follow from the stated capacity.

personnel.platform-criteria.why_wrong: 5 degrees is tighter than the rule requires. The rule sets 10 degrees of level, regardless of boom angle.
15 degrees is too much tilt. The limit is 10 degrees of level.

personnel.platform-criteria.misconception: limit applied only at working angle
personnel.platform-criteria.why_wrong: The 10-degree limit applies regardless of boom angle, not just at the angle where the work is done.
Twice is too low. The platform must hold its own weight and at least five times the maximum intended load.
This puts the multiplier on the wrong term. The factor of five applies to the maximum intended load, and the platform weight is added once.
The platform's own weight is part of the requirement. It is added to five times the maximum intended load.
The minimum enclosure runs from the toeboard to the mid-rail, not up to the top rail.
1 inch is too large. Openings may be no greater than 1/2 inch.
The enclosure is required on the lower part of the side, from the toeboard to the mid-rail. That is where tools and feet could pass through.
The rule does not require a state-licensed engineer. It requires a qualified person familiar with structural design.

personnel.platform-criteria.misconception: welding duty confused with design duty
personnel.platform-criteria.why_wrong: The certified welder does the welding to the design. The welder is not the person the rule makes responsible for the structural design.
A rigger rigs the platform but does not design it. Design falls to a qualified person familiar with structural design.
Certification alone is not enough. The welder also must be familiar with the weld grades, types and material in the design, and a later inspection does not replace that.
Supervision does not meet the rule. The welder making the welds must be certified.
The rule requires a certified welder, not just a qualified one, and an engineer's check afterward does not change that.

personnel.platform-criteria.misconception: one requirement treated as exception to another
personnel.platform-criteria.why_wrong: The latch is a separate requirement that every gate must meet. Having one does not allow an outward swing.

personnel.pre-lift-meeting.why_wrong: The rule does not tie the meeting to shifts. It is triggered by a new work location, before the trial lift, or by newly assigned employees.

personnel.pre-lift-meeting.misconception: Wrong sequence relative to trial lift
personnel.pre-lift-meeting.why_wrong: This gets the order backward. The meeting must come before the trial lift, not after it.

personnel.pre-lift-meeting.misconception: One meeting covers the whole project
personnel.pre-lift-meeting.why_wrong: One meeting per project is not enough. A meeting is required before the trial lift at each new work location.

personnel.pre-lift-meeting.misconception: Assumes safety staff are mandatory attendees
personnel.pre-lift-meeting.why_wrong: A safety manager may choose to attend, but the rule does not list one. It lists the operator, signal person if used, hoisted employees, and the person responsible for the task.
The rule does not name the rigger. Riggers attend only when they are also hoisted employees or fill another listed role.

personnel.pre-lift-meeting.misconception: Duty assigned to the equipment owner
personnel.pre-lift-meeting.why_wrong: Equipment owners are not on the required list. Attendance is tied to people directly involved in the lift and the task.
The meeting rule does not mention re-rigging or moving the platform. It names new work locations and newly assigned employees.
The rule has no daily requirement. At an unchanged location with an unchanged crew, the meeting does not have to be repeated each day.
New employees are one trigger, but a new work location is a separate trigger that applies here.
A meeting at a new location must include all required attendees, not just the operator.
An unchanged crew does not carry the meeting to a new location. The rule requires one before each new location's trial lift.
An informal briefing from a coworker is not a pre-lift meeting. The meeting must be repeated for the newly assigned employee.
A new location is only one trigger. Newly assigned employees are a separate trigger that applies here.
Signing a sheet does not mean he attended. He must actually receive the repeated meeting.
A signal person is required only if one is used for the lift. No standby signal person is called for.
The equipment operator must always attend. Leaving the operator out does not meet the rule.

personnel.proof-test.misconception: Rated load mistaken for proof load
personnel.proof-test.why_wrong: Testing at rated capacity does not reach the required proof-test load of 125% of rated capacity.
A 10% overload is insufficient. The required proof-test load is 125% of the platform's rated capacity.
The prescribed proof-test load is 125%, not 150%, of the platform's rated capacity.
Two minutes is too short. The minimum suspended hold is five minutes.
Ten minutes exceeds the required minimum. The rule specifies five minutes.
Fifteen minutes is not the required minimum. The specified minimum is five minutes.
Operator certification alone does not establish the required role. The inspection and determination must be made by a competent person.
Overall authority for the lift does not replace the required competent-person inspection.

personnel.proof-test.misconception: Rigger qualification substituted for competent-person role
personnel.proof-test.why_wrong: Qualification to select rigging alone does not satisfy this requirement. The post-test inspection must be performed by a competent person.

personnel.proof-test.misconception: Inspection substitutes for new-jobsite proof test
personnel.proof-test.why_wrong: An inspection does not replace the proof test required at each jobsite.
The new-jobsite testing requirement applies even when no transport damage is visible.

personnel.proof-test.misconception: Configuration change is the only trigger
personnel.proof-test.why_wrong: A configuration change is not necessary to trigger this requirement. Moving to another jobsite requires a proof test there.
An unchanged rating does not waive proof testing after a repair.

personnel.proof-test.misconception: Component test substitutes for assembly test
personnel.proof-test.why_wrong: The required proof test covers the platform and rigging at 125% of the platform's rated capacity, not only the repaired attachment.

personnel.proof-test.misconception: Jobsite test remains valid after repair
personnel.proof-test.why_wrong: The repair independently triggers proof testing before further personnel hoisting.

personnel.proof-test.misconception: Proof test must be a separate first step
personnel.proof-test.why_wrong: A separate earlier proof test is not required. The two operations may be concurrent.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Ordinary safety latch equals locking closure
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: A spring-loaded latch alone does not establish that the hook can be locked. The required closure must close and lock, eliminating the throat opening.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Load tension substitutes for positive locking
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: Keeping a sling seated while tension is applied does not satisfy the closure requirement. The hook must be capable of closing and locking.
A closure that depends on carrying weight does not establish a locked connection. The hook must close and lock to eliminate the opening.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Abrasion protection substitutes for a thimble
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: Protective sleeves do not replace the required thimbles. The wire rope sling eyes must be fabricated with thimbles.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Additional fasteners substitute for eye protection
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: Adding clips does not satisfy the eye requirement. The specified feature is a thimble.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Connection hardware substitutes for a thimble
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: A master link provides a connection but does not replace a thimble within the eye.

personnel.rigging.misconception: General factor applied to rotation resistant rope
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: Five times is the general requirement for platform rigging hardware and hooks. Rotation resistant rope slings require ten times.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Ordinary lifting factor transferred to personnel slings
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: A four-times strength factor does not satisfy this requirement. Rotation resistant rope slings must support at least ten times their maximum intended load without failure.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Personnel factor doubled a second time
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: Twenty times exceeds the stated minimum. The required minimum for rotation resistant rope slings is ten times.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Screw-pin shackles are prohibited for personnel
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: The rule permits screw-type alloy anchor shackles when their pins are secured against accidental removal. Replacing every screw-pin shackle is not required.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Repeated tightening substitutes for pin security
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: Repeated tightening does not address the stated lack of protection against accidental removal. The screw pin must be secured against that removal.
Pin orientation does not satisfy the requirement to secure the pin against accidental removal.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Extra strength compensates for an unlocked closure
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: Extra strength does not replace the closing and locking requirement. The connection must satisfy both strength and closure requirements.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Only hooks and shackles are allowed
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: Other detachable devices are permitted if they provide equivalent closing and locking. A shackle is not the only allowed replacement.

personnel.rigging.misconception: Trial performance substitutes for required connector design
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: A successful trial lift does not establish compliance with the design requirement. The connector must be capable of closing and locking.

personnel.rigging.misconception: One bridle leg may serve only as a backup
personnel.rigging.why_wrong: The fourth leg cannot simply be treated as a backup. Each bridle leg must connect to a master link or shackle in an arrangement that evenly divides the load.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Stationing the signal person at the controls
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: The required station is at the shaft opening, not beside the operator.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Stationing the signal person at the destination
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: The rule requires the signal person at the opening, even though the employee is traveling toward the bottom.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Substituting equipment observation for the required station
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: Watching the winch does not satisfy the required station at the shaft opening.
Four times is insufficient. The chair must support its own weight plus at least five times the maximum intended load.
Six times exceeds the stated minimum. The required minimum is the chair's own weight plus five times the maximum intended load.
Ten times is not the stated requirement. The minimum multiplier for the maximum intended load is five.
Recreational approval alone does not meet the specified industrial-use approval requirement.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Substituting jobsite acceptance for required approval
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: Lift-director acceptance does not replace the required U.S. Coast Guard approval for industrial use.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Substituting vessel authority for required approval
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: The captain's selection alone does not establish the required approval. The device must have U.S. Coast Guard approval for industrial use.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Applying the pile-driving attachment rule to a drill shaft
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: That attachment is specified for the pile-driving chair case. For this drill-shaft lift, the fall-protection attachment must be independent of the crane.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Confusing a separate connector with an independent attachment
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: A separate connection to the chair suspension is still dependent on the crane's hoisting system. The required attachment is independent of the crane.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Treating a separate crane connection as independent
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: The boom tip remains part of the crane. Independence from the hoist line alone does not satisfy independence from the crane.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Applying the drill-shaft attachment rule to pile driving
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: This substitutes the drill-shaft arrangement. For a chair used in pile driving, the specified attachment is independently to the lower load block or overhaul ball.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Using the chair as its own fall-protection attachment
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: The chair frame is not the specified attachment location. The fall protection must attach independently to the lower load block or overhaul ball.
An independent connection at the boom point does not meet the specified lower-load-block or overhaul-ball attachment requirement.

personnel.special-cases.misconception: Treating spare weight capacity as spare occupancy
personnel.special-cases.why_wrong: Meeting weight limits does not allow exceeding the designed worker count. This device is limited to four workers.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Platform capacity substituted for anticipated liftweight
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: The trial-lift minimum is the anticipated liftweight. This requirement does not specify loading to the platform's maximum rated capacity.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Occupied preliminary check confused with trial lift
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: The trial lift must be unoccupied. The occupied check a few inches above the boarding location is a separate step.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Capacity percentage applied to trial load
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: The trial load must reach at least the anticipated liftweight. The 50-percent limit concerns equipment rated capacity, not a reduction in trial load.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Weekly interval substituted for each shift
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: A weekly trial does not satisfy the requirement. A trial is required immediately before each shift that includes personnel hoisting.
Keeping the same setup does not eliminate later shift trials. Each personnel-hoisting shift requires its own trial.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Daily interval substituted for each shift
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: A workday may contain multiple shifts. The required interval is each shift, not each day.
The applicable limit is 50 percent, not 75 percent, throughout the lift.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Ordinary capacity limit applied to personnel hoisting
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: Remaining within full rated capacity is insufficient for this personnel lift. The limit is 50 percent.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Extra capacity reduction treated as mandatory
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: This provision sets a 50-percent limit. It does not establish a 25-percent limit.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Separate trials substituted for sequential travel
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: Individual trials fit individual personnel trips. They do not match the planned sequential movement from the lower landing to the upper landing.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Highest destination assumed to cover all destinations
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: The trial must reach and position at each planned location. Merely passing the lower landing does not test that positioning.
This reverses the planned sequence. The trial method must match the method used to hoist the personnel.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Matching setup preserves an earlier trial
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: Matching the earlier setup does not waive the repeat trial. Returning to a previously used location expressly triggers another trial.
The no-new-safety-factors exception concerns a changed route. It does not waive a trial triggered by equipment relocation.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Balance check substitutes for repeat trial
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: The occupied balance check is a separate requirement. It cannot replace the trial required after returning the crane to this location.

personnel.trial-lift.misconception: Radius check substitutes for complete route determination
personnel.trial-lift.why_wrong: Maximum radius alone does not establish the exception. The competent person must determine that the new route presents no new factors affecting safety.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Assigning the employer's duty to the operator
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: The rule places this demonstration on the employer, not the operator.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Confusing equipment inspection with access justification
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: Inspecting the platform does not transfer the employer's responsibility for demonstrating why personnel hoisting is allowed.
Employee agreement or preference does not replace the demonstration required of the employer.
The exception extends through 8 feet, so 6 feet is not its largest included diameter.
A 10-foot drill shaft exceeds the exception's 8-foot maximum.
The drill-shaft exception ends at 8 feet, not 12 feet.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Treating any routine access as excluded
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: Repeating an elevated-access operation does not create an exclusion from the general prohibition.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Confusing a platform exception with an access exclusion
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: The drill-shaft platform exception does not itself exclude an operation from the general prohibition on personnel hoisting.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Extending the marine-device exception to permission
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: The marine-transfer provision is an exception to the platform requirement, not an express exclusion from paragraph (a).

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Treating cost savings as an allowed justification
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: Additional expense does not establish that conventional access is more hazardous or impossible for the specified reasons.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Treating schedule pressure as a worksite limitation
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: A schedule delay alone does not meet either condition for overcoming the general prohibition.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Requiring impossibility even when greater hazard is demonstrated
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: Impossibility is not the only route: an employer may instead demonstrate that conventional access would be more hazardous.
The rule expressly includes erection and dismantling in the comparison.
Conventional access need not be impossible when the employer demonstrates that it would be more hazardous.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Replacing comparative hazard with any hazard
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: The employer must demonstrate greater hazard; the mere presence of some exposure does not establish that comparison.

personnel.when-allowed.misconception: Limiting the tank exception to steel
personnel.when-allowed.why_wrong: The storage-tank exception explicitly includes both steel and concrete.

personnel.work-practices.why_wrong: 15 mph is not the trigger. The rule uses wind over 20 mph, sustained or gusts, at the platform.
30 mph is too high, and gusts count too. The rule uses over 20 mph, sustained or gusts.
Wind is measured at the personnel platform, not at the cab, and gusts count as well as sustained wind.
1,000 lb is double the limit. The fixed cap is 500 pounds, even if the winch is rated higher.

personnel.work-practices.misconception: Winch rating mistaken for the limit
personnel.work-practices.why_wrong: No 1,500 lb allowance exists. The winch line is capped at 500 pounds while the platform is occupied.

personnel.work-practices.misconception: Assumes only the winch rating applies
personnel.work-practices.why_wrong: 2,000 lb is far over the 500-pound cap that applies whenever employees occupy the platform.
The requirement applies at all times while the platform is occupied, not only while it is moving.

personnel.work-practices.misconception: Duty shifted to the platform occupant
personnel.work-practices.why_wrong: Radio contact is not enough. The operator must be at boom and swing controls and in view of the crane.
Hoist-only controls do not meet the rule. The operator's controls must include boom and swing functions.

personnel.work-practices.misconception: General rule applied without its exception
personnel.work-practices.why_wrong: This is the general rule, but it has stated exceptions for signal duties and for positioning the platform.

personnel.work-practices.misconception: Tie-off rule confused with signal exception
personnel.work-practices.why_wrong: Tying off is required before occupants exit or enter a platform that is not landed. It has nothing to do with the signal exception.
The rule specifically allows an occupant to reach out of the platform while performing signal-person duties.
Setting brakes holds the crane still, but the rule requires the platform itself to be secured to the structure.

personnel.work-practices.misconception: Personal tie-off confused with platform tie-off
personnel.work-practices.why_wrong: Moving fall protection over to the beam does not replace securing the platform to the structure before exiting.
Tag lines help control the platform when needed, but they do not satisfy the requirement to secure it to the structure.

personnel.work-practices.misconception: Trial lift confused with release check
personnel.work-practices.why_wrong: A trial lift is done before hoisting personnel, not each time the platform is untied. What is required here is confirmation that the platform hangs free.

powerlines.assembly.misconception: Confuses the screening distance with a Table A clearance
powerlines.assembly.why_wrong: Ten feet is a commonly remembered clearance for lower voltages, but it is not the screening distance. The assembly rule starts with a 20-foot check.
Fifteen feet is not the screening distance. The employer must check whether anything could get closer than 20 feet.

powerlines.assembly.misconception: Overly large distance from field myth
powerlines.assembly.why_wrong: Fifty feet is not the trigger for assembly. The rule's screening distance is 20 feet, measured in the direction or area of assembly.
Five working days is longer than the rule allows. The utility must respond within two working days.
The deadline is counted in working days, and it is two, not ten.
The numbers are reversed. The minimum is one in the cab and two on the outside.
Four outside warnings go beyond the minimum. The rule requires at least two on the outside.

powerlines.assembly.misconception: Applies the tower crane exception to a mobile crane
powerlines.assembly.why_wrong: Only overhead gantry and tower cranes are exempt from the outside warnings. A truck crane needs at least two.

powerlines.assembly.misconception: Leaves out the crew and others in the area
powerlines.assembly.why_wrong: The assembly crew and the other workers in the area are left out. The GC's foreman is not specifically required.

powerlines.assembly.misconception: Adds the utility in place of on-site workers
powerlines.assembly.why_wrong: The utility's crew is not a required attendee. Other workers who will be in the assembly area are required, and this option leaves them out.
The A/D director must attend, and a spotter is only one of several possible additional measures.

powerlines.assembly.misconception: Applies encroachment measures where they do not apply
powerlines.assembly.why_wrong: Spotters and alarms are encroachment measures for Options (2) and (3). They do not permit assembly below a line.

powerlines.assembly.misconception: Treats Table A clearance as enough under the line
powerlines.assembly.why_wrong: Assembly below a line is prohibited on its own terms, even if Table A clearance is kept. Only deenergizing and grounding allow it.
Insulating links and nonconductive tag lines do not lift the ban on assembly below a line. Deenergizing and visible grounding are required.
One dedicated spotter who meets the requirements is enough. What this spotter is missing is the visual aid.

powerlines.assembly.misconception: Confuses the spotter with the signal person role
powerlines.assembly.why_wrong: The spotter requirements here are continuous contact, a visual aid, good positioning, and timely information. Signal person papers are not one of them.

powerlines.below-lines.why_wrong: Notice that the line is deenergized is not enough. The rule also requires the line to be visibly grounded at the worksite.
Grounds at a remote substation do not meet the rule. The grounding must be visible at the worksite.
A test showing no voltage does not replace deenergizing and visible grounding by the utility owner/operator.
The fixed figure in the exception is more than 20 feet below the plane of the line, not 10 feet.
This exception measures vertical distance below the plane of the line, not horizontal distance from a conductor.
The rule states more than 20 feet below the plane of the line. It does not set 25 feet or refer to the sag point.
Measuring with the boom retracted understates how high the crane can reach. The rule requires the fully extended position.
The planned extension is not the test. The boom could be extended farther, so the rule uses full extension.
The working angle is not the test. The rule uses true vertical, where the boom reaches its maximum height.
That general rule does not apply when an exception is met. Here the crane's top at true vertical would be 30 ft below the line.
The answer is yes, but for the wrong reason. The test uses the boom at true vertical, not at the working radius.
The planned extension does not count. The test uses the fully extended position, where the boom would reach above the line.
Extensible and articulating booms have their own exception. It is evaluated at full extension, true vertical.

powerlines.below-lines.misconception: Extension limit substitutes for the test
powerlines.below-lines.why_wrong: The rule's test is the fully extended position. Limiting extension does not change the measurement the exception requires.
No written switching order is required. What is missing is the visible grounding at the worksite.
The rule places deenergizing and grounding with the utility owner/operator, not a voltage test by the crane operator.

powerlines.closer-than-table-a.why_wrong: Six feet is not the figure. The perimeter must be at least 10 feet from the equipment unless obstacles prevent it.

powerlines.closer-than-table-a.misconception: Table A number and wrong reference point
powerlines.closer-than-table-a.why_wrong: This mixes in a Table A distance and measures from the wrong point. The perimeter is measured from the equipment and must be at least 10 feet out.

powerlines.closer-than-table-a.misconception: swing-radius barricade confused with perimeter rule
powerlines.closer-than-table-a.why_wrong: The rule sets no 15-foot swing-radius figure for this barricade. The perimeter is at least 10 feet from the equipment.
The operator and spotter maintain the clearance. They do not set it. That determination belongs to the utility or a qualified registered PE.

powerlines.closer-than-table-a.misconception: Table A applied to closer-than-Table-A work
powerlines.closer-than-table-a.why_wrong: This work goes inside Table A by definition, so the Table A value cannot be the limit. A site-specific distance must be set by the utility or a qualified registered PE.
A competent person is not given this authority. Only the line owner/operator or a registered PE qualified in transmission and distribution may set it.

powerlines.closer-than-table-a.misconception: field myth that reclosing protects workers
powerlines.closer-than-table-a.why_wrong: Reclosing reenergizes the line after a trip, which can shock workers again. The rule requires disabling it where the design permits.
The requirement has no voltage threshold. It applies to any line with an automatic reclosing device.
A longer delay still reenergizes the circuit. The feature must be made inoperative, not just slowed.

powerlines.closer-than-table-a.misconception: insulating link treated as covering rigging
powerlines.closer-than-table-a.why_wrong: The link protects against current traveling down the load line. Conductive slings that contact or arc to the line below the link are still energized, so nonconductive rigging is required.

powerlines.closer-than-table-a.misconception: expired glove substitute applied to rigging
powerlines.closer-than-table-a.why_wrong: Voltage-rated gloves were part of an expired substitute for the insulating link. They never replaced the nonconductive rigging requirement.
Calling a stop does not make the spotter dedicated. The role requires continuous contact and positioning to gauge clearance, not part-time coverage.
The rule requires a dedicated spotter because the operator cannot reliably judge clearance from the cab. The operator cannot fill the role.

powerlines.closer-than-table-a.misconception: spotter confused with person directing implementation
powerlines.closer-than-table-a.why_wrong: The rule does not require the spotter and the person directing the procedures to be the same person. It requires that the spotter be dedicated.
Rated gloves appeared only in expired substitutes for the insulating link. The remote-operator rule calls for isolating wireless controls or insulating mats.
The equipment must be grounded, but the rule protects a remote operator with isolation: wireless controls or an insulating mat, not a bond to the crane.

powerlines.contact-emergency.why_wrong: Separation alone does not establish that leaving is safe. The operator should remain inside unless an emergency necessitates leaving.
The absence of visible arcing does not establish electrical safety or create an evacuation exception.
Stopping the engine does not remove electricity supplied by a contacted power line.
The crane operator's observations do not replace confirmation by the utility owner/operator.
Being the site's electrical subcontractor does not make that party the utility owner/operator required to confirm line status.
A dedicated spotter's observations do not establish deenergization and grounding.
The instruction also covers the load; it is not limited to equipment and exposed wire.

powerlines.contact-emergency.misconception: Danger stays at the contact point
powerlines.contact-emergency.why_wrong: The danger is not confined to the original contact point. Crew must avoid approaching or touching the equipment and load.
This omits the equipment, which crew must also avoid approaching or touching.

powerlines.contact-emergency.misconception: Routine evacuation applies to electrical contact
powerlines.contact-emergency.why_wrong: Normal dismounting can expose the operator to simultaneous contact with energized equipment and the ground. No emergency here requires leaving.

powerlines.contact-emergency.misconception: Any position on the crane is equivalent
powerlines.contact-emergency.why_wrong: Remaining off the ground is not a reason to leave the cab. The safe response described here is to remain inside.

powerlines.contact-emergency.misconception: Emergency exit technique makes any exit appropriate
powerlines.contact-emergency.why_wrong: An emergency escape method does not make unnecessary evacuation appropriate. The operator should remain inside under these conditions.
Avoiding the crane alone is insufficient; crew must also avoid the load. Ordinary work gloves do not change that instruction.

powerlines.contact-emergency.misconception: Grounded load is safe to handle
powerlines.contact-emergency.why_wrong: Landing the load does not establish that it is electrically safe to approach and unhook.
A tag line is not a substitute for staying away during electrical contact. The emergency instruction covers approaching or touching the load.

powerlines.contact-emergency.misconception: Any two crane contact points are the stated hazard
powerlines.contact-emergency.why_wrong: That does not identify the equipment-to-ground contact described. The critical action here is reaching the ground while still touching the crane.

powerlines.dedicated-spotter.why_wrong: Qualified rigger status covers rigging work. It does not qualify anyone as a dedicated spotter. The spotter rule points to the signal person qualifications.
A competent person identifies hazards and can correct them. That is not the standard for a spotter, who must meet the signal person qualifications.

powerlines.dedicated-spotter.misconception: Applies operator qualification to the spotter
powerlines.dedicated-spotter.why_wrong: Operator certification is for the person running the crane. The spotter needs the signal person qualifications, not operator credentials.
The boom and jib are only part of the job. The load line and the load with its rigging also have to stay clear.
The load itself is included, along with its rigging. Leaving it out ignores a load swinging or rotating toward the line.
The definition names rigging and lifting accessories. Slings and shackles are part of what the spotter must keep clear.
Contact only at the start of a motion leaves the operator without warnings while the boom or load is moving. Contact must be continuous.
No distance trigger exists. Contact must be continuous whenever the spotter measure is in use.
A supervisor cannot replace continuous contact with periodic check-ins. The rule requires continuous contact.
Being a qualified rigger does not change the sole-responsibility requirement. Any second task disqualifies him as the dedicated spotter.
The tag line material does not matter here. The problem is that the spotter is doing a second job.
No rule gives tag lines only to the signal person. The assignment fails because the spotter must do nothing but watch the separation.

powerlines.dedicated-spotter.misconception: Adds a requirement that does not exist
powerlines.dedicated-spotter.why_wrong: The rule calls for one dedicated spotter with a visual aid. It does not require a second spotter.

powerlines.dedicated-spotter.misconception: Positions for the operator, not the gap
powerlines.dedicated-spotter.why_wrong: She must stand where she can gauge the clearance, and she already does. Moving to the cab would make that worse and still leave her without a visual aid.

powerlines.dedicated-spotter.misconception: Paperwork in place of the visual aid
powerlines.dedicated-spotter.why_wrong: The spotter requirements do not call for a written lift plan. What is missing is a visual aid for the clearance distance.

powerlines.dedicated-spotter.misconception: Positions for visibility to the operator
powerlines.dedicated-spotter.why_wrong: Being visible to the operator does not help if the spotter cannot judge the gap. Positioning is about gauging clearance, and radios can handle communication.

powerlines.encroachment-measures.misconception: Confuses warning line with a minimum clearance figure
powerlines.encroachment-measures.why_wrong: 10 feet is a common minimum clearance figure for lower voltages, but the Option (2) warning line is set at 20 feet.
The warning line goes at the Table A distance only under Option (3). Under Option (2) it goes at 20 feet.

powerlines.encroachment-measures.misconception: Splits the difference between 10 and 20 feet
powerlines.encroachment-measures.why_wrong: No 15-foot figure applies here. Under Option (2) the warning line is set at 20 feet.
The 20-foot placement applies to Option (2). Option (3) uses the Table A distance.
No doubling is required. The warning line goes at the Table A distance itself.

powerlines.encroachment-measures.misconception: Invented buffer added to Table A
powerlines.encroachment-measures.why_wrong: No extra buffer is specified. The line goes at the Table A minimum approach distance.
Placed there, it would leave the hook block and rigging outside the protected part of the system. The link belongs at the end of the load line or below.

powerlines.encroachment-measures.misconception: Treats the link as a boom-tip device
powerlines.encroachment-measures.why_wrong: A link at the boom tip does not sit between the load line end and the load, which is where the link must be.

powerlines.encroachment-measures.misconception: Confuses insulating link with tag line requirement
powerlines.encroachment-measures.why_wrong: Tag lines must be non-conductive on their own. The insulating link is a separate device placed between the load line and the load.

powerlines.encroachment-measures.misconception: Grounding treated as an encroachment measure
powerlines.encroachment-measures.why_wrong: Grounding the crane is not on the list of (b)(4) measures. The choices are an alarm, a dedicated spotter, a range control warning device, a range limiter or an insulating link.

powerlines.encroachment-measures.misconception: Line covers confused with insulating link
powerlines.encroachment-measures.why_wrong: Covers on the conductors are not on the (b)(4) list. The insulating device on the list is a link installed at the load line.
Only one warning line is required. A second one does not count as the additional (b)(4) measure.

powerlines.encroachment-measures.misconception: Meeting limited to the crane team
powerlines.encroachment-measures.why_wrong: The ironworkers handling the load are in the area of the load, so they must attend.
The driver stays outside the equipment and load area, so the meeting requirement does not cover him.
The meeting must include the workers who will be in the area. A supervisor-and-operator briefing leaves them out.
Radios are fine. Where necessary, the spotter must use equipment that allows direct communication with the operator.

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Construction regulation substituted for general industry referral
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: This confuses the construction crane regulations with the referral in the general industry crane rule. Section 1910.180(j) points to 1910.333(c)(3).

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Industry operation standard substituted for federal referral
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: The operation chapter is not the provision named in this federal referral. The named provision is 1910.333(c)(3).

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Inspection standard substituted for electrical provision
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: The inspection chapter is not the destination of this referral. Section 1910.180(j) directs the reader to 1910.333(c)(3).

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Overhead and underground electrical hazards treated as identical scope
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: The referral expressly addresses overhead electric lines. It does not identify buried cables as its subject.

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Every overhead cable treated as an electric supply line
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: The referral specifies overhead electric lines, not telecommunications cables generally.

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Any nearby electrical equipment treated as the referral's subject
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: Electrical cabinets can present electrical hazards, but they are not the overhead electric lines identified by this referral.

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Referral remembered as a fixed-distance rule
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: Section 1910.180(j) does not state a clearance distance. It refers the reader to 1910.333(c)(3).

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Voltage table attributed to the referring paragraph
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: No voltage table appears in 1910.180(j). Its instruction is to consult 1910.333(c)(3).

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Travel requirement attributed to the referring paragraph
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: Section 1910.180(j) does not state a travel clearance. It sends overhead-line operations to another provision.

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Familiar construction requirements used for a general industry referral
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: The scenario establishes that 1910.180 governs the lift. Its overhead-line referral names 1910.333(c)(3), not the construction crane provisions.

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Industry operating guidance substituted for the named provision
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: An industry operation standard is not the destination named by paragraph (j). The paragraph expressly refers to 1910.333(c)(3).

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Inspection reference substituted for operating requirement
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: Inspection guidance does not answer where paragraph (j) directs the operator. The referral is to 1910.333(c)(3).

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Different voltage breakpoint imported into referral
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: Section 1910.180(j) states no 35 kV threshold for consulting the referenced provision. It addresses operations near overhead electric lines.

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Referral treated as an unknown-voltage precaution
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: The referral is not limited to lines of unknown voltage. Its stated condition is operation near overhead electric lines.
Section 1910.180(j) does not establish a 100 kV referral threshold. The voltage condition in this answer is an unsupported addition.

powerlines.general-industry.misconception: Remembered distance treated as wording of the cited paragraph
powerlines.general-industry.why_wrong: Paragraph (j) contains no numerical clearance. The claimed distance cannot be verified from that paragraph alone.

powerlines.options.misconception: Assigning utility confirmation to the controlling entity
powerlines.options.why_wrong: Option (1) requires confirmation from the utility owner/operator, not merely from the entity controlling the project.

powerlines.options.misconception: Substituting a qualified person for the utility
powerlines.options.why_wrong: A qualified person's assessment does not replace the required confirmation from the utility owner/operator.

powerlines.options.misconception: Assigning utility confirmation to lift supervision
powerlines.options.why_wrong: The lift supervisor is not the specified source of confirmation for Option (1). Confirmation must come from the utility owner/operator.
Option (2) specifies 20 feet. A different distance cannot be substituted while continuing to use this option.
The fixed clearance for Option (2) is 20 feet, not 15 feet.

powerlines.options.misconception: Treating an added buffer as the required minimum
powerlines.options.why_wrong: Twenty-five feet exceeds the required clearance, but it is not the minimum specified for Option (2).

powerlines.options.misconception: Substituting site geometry for voltage determination
powerlines.options.why_wrong: These dimensions may help describe the work area, but they do not establish the voltage and permitted approach distance required for Option (3).

powerlines.options.misconception: Combining electrical clearance with load capacity
powerlines.options.why_wrong: Voltage is required, but rated lifting capacity does not supply the Table A minimum approach distance.

powerlines.options.misconception: Using vertical dimensions to select electrical clearance
powerlines.options.why_wrong: Height information does not replace determining the line's voltage and the Table A minimum approach distance.
Another open disconnect does not replace visible grounding at the worksite under Option (1).

powerlines.options.misconception: Confusing crane grounding with line grounding
powerlines.options.why_wrong: Grounding the crane does not satisfy the requirement that the power line be visibly grounded at the worksite.

powerlines.options.misconception: Replacing grounding with continued outage monitoring
powerlines.options.why_wrong: Continued deenergization does not replace worksite grounding or the required confirmation from the utility owner/operator.

powerlines.options.misconception: Checking the boom while overlooking accessories
powerlines.options.why_wrong: The boom's 24-foot clearance exceeds 20 feet. The lifting accessory at 19 feet is the violation.

powerlines.options.misconception: Treating the load line as the only suspended component
powerlines.options.why_wrong: The load line is beyond the 20-foot minimum. The spreader beam is also covered and is too close.

powerlines.options.misconception: Measuring to the load while excluding its accessories
powerlines.options.why_wrong: The load's clearance satisfies the minimum, but that does not excuse a lifting accessory inside 20 feet.
Option (3) requires determining voltage and the permitted Table A distance. Apparent height does not supply those facts.

powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: At this voltage the 20-foot distance does not stay the same. Wherever 20 feet is specified, 50 feet must be used instead.
No 100-foot figure applies. At or below 1,000 kV, the substituted distance is 50 feet.
A distance set by the utility or an engineer applies only to lines over 1,000 kV. A line at exactly 1,000 kV is at or below the limit.
A PE license alone is not enough. The engineer must also be a qualified person in electrical power transmission and distribution.

powerlines.over-350kv.misconception: Assigns the duty to the controlling entity
powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: The controlling entity is not one of the parties allowed to set this distance. Only the utility owner/operator or a qualified registered PE may set it.

powerlines.over-350kv.misconception: Assigns the duty to the crane employer
powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: Being a qualified person for crane work does not authorize setting the clearance. Only the utility owner/operator or a registered PE qualified in transmission and distribution may do it.
500 kV is well inside the range that takes the 50-foot substitution. The upper limit is 1,000 kV.

powerlines.over-350kv.misconception: Treats the 1,000 kV boundary as exclusive
powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: A line at exactly 1,000 kV still takes the 50-foot distance. Only lines over 1,000 kV are excluded.

powerlines.over-350kv.misconception: Confuses an intermediate voltage band with the limit
powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: 750 kV is not where the substitution ends. It applies all the way up to and including 1,000 kV.

powerlines.over-350kv.misconception: Thinks assembly is exempt from the substitution
powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: Assembly is not exempt. The substitution applies wherever 20 feet is specified, whatever the activity.
No 35-foot figure is substituted. Lines at or below 1,000 kV get 50 feet.
A distance set by the utility or an engineer is required only for lines over 1,000 kV, not over 750 kV.

powerlines.over-350kv.misconception: Treats 50 feet as a universal maximum
powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: 50 feet applies only at or below 1,000 kV. Above that, no fixed figure applies, and the utility or a qualified PE sets the distance.
No doubling rule exists. Above 1,000 kV, the distance is whatever the utility or a qualified registered PE establishes.

powerlines.over-350kv.misconception: Spotter substitutes for an established clearance
powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: A spotter does not replace the required clearance. Above 1,000 kV, the distance must first be set by the utility or a qualified PE.

powerlines.over-350kv.misconception: Any PE qualifies when the utility is unavailable
powerlines.over-350kv.why_wrong: A slow utility does not lower the requirement. The engineer must still be qualified in transmission and distribution.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Insulation anywhere in the hoisting system qualifies
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: The listed location is between the end of the load line, or below, and the load. A boom-head installation does not match that location.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Boom isolation substitutes for the listed link
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: Insulating the boom mounting is not the listed link arrangement. The specified location is on the load side of the load-line end.
That position is upstream of the load-line end. The rule places the link between the load-line end, or below, and the load.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Two protective layers are always mandatory
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: The list requires at least one measure. Two may be selected, but two are not the stated minimum.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Warning and limiting devices must be paired
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: The list does not require pairing a warning device with a movement limiter. Its stated minimum is one listed measure.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Every device requires a dedicated spotter
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: A dedicated spotter is one listed selection, not a mandatory addition to every device selection.
An operator's preferred method does not replace the manufacturer's procedures and conditions for the device.
Site procedures do not replace the manufacturer's requirements for a device used for compliance.
An inspector's instructions cannot substitute for the manufacturer's procedures and conditions of use.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Alarm volume compensates for late activation
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: A louder warning at the same late point does not provide the needed stopping time. The warning must be sufficient to prevent encroachment.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Repeated warning compensates for late activation
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: Repeating a warning after it begins too late does not correct the setting. The alarm must give enough advance warning to prevent encroachment.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Avoiding contact is the alarm's only threshold
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: The required trigger must help prevent encroachment, not merely warn before contact with the conductor.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Every warning device must also limit motion
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: Automatic movement limiting is a separate listed measure. A qualifying warning device does not need that additional function.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: Warning devices always require a spotter
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: A dedicated spotter is a separate listed selection. This warning-device provision does not require pairing the device with a spotter.

powerlines.protective-limits.misconception: An instruction to stop equals automatic limiting
powerlines.protective-limits.why_wrong: Directing the operator to stop is a warning function. A limiter automatically limits the range of movement.
Stopping short of contact can still permit prohibited encroachment. The limiter must be set to prevent encroachment.

powerlines.table-a.misconception: Lower figure from another standard's distribution-line table
powerlines.table-a.why_wrong: 6 ft is not a Table A value. The smallest Table A distance is 10 ft, for lines up to 50 kV.
15 ft is the distance for over 50 to 200 kV. A 13.8 kV line is in the up-to-50 kV band, which is 10 ft.

powerlines.table-a.misconception: Option 2 distance confused with Table A
powerlines.table-a.why_wrong: 20 ft is the Option 2 distance and the Table A value for over 200 to 350 kV. Under Option 3, a 13.8 kV line needs 10 ft.
The controlling entity coordinates site work, but it does not set clearance for lines over 1,000 kV. The utility or a qualified registered PE does.
Manufacturers do not set power line clearances, and crane booms are not counted on as insulation. The utility or a qualified registered PE sets this distance.
No extrapolation formula is allowed. Above 1,000 kV, the distance comes from the utility owner/operator or a qualified registered PE.
The deadline is two working days, not one.
Five working days is longer than allowed. The utility must respond within two working days.
Ten days is not the deadline. The rule sets two working days so that planning is not held up.
115 kV is above 50 kV. It falls in the over 50 to 200 kV band, which is 15 ft.
The 20 ft placement applies only under Option 2. Under Option 3, the line goes at the Table A distance.
No buffer is added. The warning line goes at the Table A distance itself, which is 15 ft for 115 kV.

powerlines.table-a.misconception: Field myth: pole type indicates voltage
powerlines.table-a.why_wrong: Pole type does not establish voltage. Option 3 requires determining the voltage before a Table A distance can be used.
Deenergizing is one option, but it is not required. Option 2 lets work go ahead safely while the voltage is still unknown.
A Table A distance cannot be assumed before the voltage is known. Until then, the clearance must be 20 ft under Option 2.

powerlines.table-a.misconception: Spotter counted as the only measure
powerlines.table-a.why_wrong: A spotter alone normally counts as one measure. When the operator cannot see the warning line, the spotter must be added to one of the other listed measures.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Treats the two precautions as either/or
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: The precautions are not alternatives to each other. The only alternative is deenergizing the transmitter. Otherwise both the ground and the non-conductive tag line requirement apply.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Limits the rule to one crane configuration
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: The grounding requirement applies to the equipment no matter what boom type it has. Telescopic and lattice booms are both covered.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Believes grounding replaces the tag line rule
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: Grounding the crane does not make a conductive tag line acceptable. If tag lines are used, they must be non-conductive whether or not the crane is grounded.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Reads the conditional as a mandate to use tag lines
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: The tower rule does not require tag lines at all. The non-conductive requirement applies only when tag lines are used.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Confuses bonding a line with making it non-conductive
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: Tag lines are not required, and bonding one to the ground does not meet the rule. Any tag line used must be non-conductive.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Believes grounding the crane excuses conductive tag lines
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: Grounding the equipment and using non-conductive tag lines are separate requirements. A conductive tag line is never acceptable while the precautions are in use.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Forgets that the load is covered
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: The rule names the materials being handled along with the equipment. A charge in the load triggers the precautions even when the crane itself seems unaffected.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Adds a material-type condition the rule lacks
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: The equipment is part of the trigger too, and the rule sets no metallic-material condition. A charge in either one triggers the precautions.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Narrows the trigger to selected crane parts
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: The rule does not single out boom and load line. It covers the equipment and the materials being handled, including what is rigged below the hook.
Deenergizing is one of two choices, not a requirement. The rule says the transmitter must be deenergized "or" the precautions taken.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Substitutes a monitor for the required precautions
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: The tower rule has no monitoring requirement. With the transmitter on, it requires a ground on the equipment and non-conductive tag lines.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Applies a power-line clearance to a transmitter tower
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: A fixed clearance distance is a power-line idea. The tower rule is triggered by induced charge, and it is met by deenergizing or by the two precautions.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Thinks bonding a conductive line makes it acceptable
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: Wire rope conducts electricity, and bonding it to the ground does not change that. The rule requires the tag line itself to be non-conductive.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Judges conductivity by the outer cover
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: A steel core makes the line conductive even though the cover is synthetic. A tag line with any metal inside does not qualify.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Treats insulated grips as an insulated line
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: Grips protect only the spot where the line is held. The line is still conductive along its length, and the rule calls for a non-conductive tag line.

powerlines.towers.misconception: Ties the rule to a distance instead of induced charge
powerlines.towers.why_wrong: The rule is not tied to the fall zone or to any set distance. It applies wherever a charge can be induced in the equipment or materials.

powerlines.training.why_wrong: The controlling entity's competent person cannot make this confirmation. The second confirming party must be a registered engineer qualified in power transmission and distribution.

powerlines.training.misconception: Wrong person: site electrician or crane owner
powerlines.training.why_wrong: A site electrician or the crane owner's qualified person cannot confirm insulation. Only the utility owner/operator or a qualified registered engineer can.

powerlines.training.misconception: Leaves out the engineer and adds a survey requirement
powerlines.training.why_wrong: A qualified registered engineer may also confirm insulation, and the rule does not require a written survey.

powerlines.training.misconception: Remote lockout in place of visible grounding at the site
powerlines.training.why_wrong: A lockout at a remote substation is not what the rule requires. The line must be visibly grounded at the worksite, and the utility must confirm it stays deenergized.

powerlines.training.misconception: Paperwork mistaken for the physical condition
powerlines.training.why_wrong: Paperwork does not take the place of the confirmed condition. The line must be deenergized on a continuing basis and visibly grounded at the worksite.

powerlines.training.misconception: Wrong person confirms, and grounding is left out
powerlines.training.why_wrong: The operator's own test does not count. The confirmation must come from the utility owner/operator and must include visible grounding at the worksite.

powerlines.training.misconception: Scope too narrow: operator and signal person only
powerlines.training.why_wrong: The requirement covers every crew member assigned to the equipment, such as riggers and tag line handlers, not just the operator and signal person.
Crew members face electrocution and step potential hazards too, so they must also be trained.

powerlines.training.misconception: Scope too broad: everyone on site
powerlines.training.why_wrong: The rule covers operators and crew members assigned to work with the equipment. It does not cover every trade on the site.

powerlines.training.misconception: Emergency evacuation used when none is needed
powerlines.training.why_wrong: Jumping clear is the way out only when an emergency makes leaving necessary. With no fire or emergency, the operator stays in the cab.

powerlines.training.misconception: Thinks staying in contact with the frame is safe
powerlines.training.why_wrong: Climbing down while holding the frame puts the body in contact with the equipment and the ground at once, which is the electrocution path the training warns about.
Outrigger pads and mats do not reliably insulate, and stepping down still makes a path from the equipment to the ground. The operator should stay in the cab.
A tag line, even a dry synthetic one, cannot be counted on to insulate. The crew must not approach or touch the load.
Ordinary work boots do not protect against step potential or contact voltage. The rule is to stay back from the equipment and load.
Shuffling is a way to leave the zone, not a way to enter it and touch the load. Crew must not approach or touch the equipment or load.

powerlines.training.misconception: Treats the device as a full substitute
powerlines.training.why_wrong: Daily calibration does not turn the alarm into a substitute for other precautions. Training must stress the device's limitations.

powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 4 feet is the travel distance only for lines up to 0.75 kV. A 25 kV line falls in the over 0.75 to 50 kV class.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Applies the familiar 10-foot figure to every line
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 10 feet applies to lines over 50 kV up to 345 kV. Many people treat 10 feet as a single universal number, but travel distances depend on voltage.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Confuses the spotter trigger with the clearance distance
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 20 feet is the travel distance for lines over 750 kV up to 1,000 kV. It is also the distance that triggers a dedicated spotter. It is not the clearance for 25 kV.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Confuses a Table T clearance with the spotter trigger
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 10 feet is the travel clearance for lines over 50 kV up to 345 kV. It is not the spotter trigger. The spotter is required whenever equipment will be closer than 20 feet.
15 feet does not appear anywhere in the travel rule. The spotter trigger is fixed at 20 feet for every voltage.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Carries over a larger work-zone distance
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 50 feet is a larger zone that people carry over from other power line work. The travel rule sets the spotter trigger at 20 feet.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Assigns the duty to the controlling entity
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: The controlling entity coordinates site work but has no authority to set this distance. Only the utility owner/operator or a qualified registered PE can set it.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Confuses maintaining the distance with setting it
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: The operator and the spotter maintain the clearance during travel. They do not decide what the clearance is for lines over 1,000 kV.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Defers to the manufacturer when the rule names someone else
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: The manufacturer cannot know the characteristics of a particular line. The rule gives this decision to the utility or a qualified registered PE.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Wrong voltage class; treats the spotter as voltage-based
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 10 feet is the clearance for lines over 50 kV up to 345 kV. The spotter requirement depends on distance (closer than 20 feet), not on voltage.
The clearance is correct, but the spotter is required whenever equipment will be closer than 20 feet, not 10.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Treats the 20-foot trigger as a required clearance
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 20 feet is the spotter trigger, not the clearance for 13.8 kV. The pass is allowed at 15 feet as long as a spotter is used.
6 feet applies only to lines over 0.75 kV up to 50 kV. 230 kV is in a higher class.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Uses the next higher voltage class
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 16 feet applies to lines over 345 kV up to 750 kV. It is the next class up from 230 kV.

powerlines.travel.misconception: Confuses the spotter trigger with the clearance
powerlines.travel.why_wrong: 20 feet is the clearance for lines over 750 kV up to 1,000 kV, and it is also the spotter trigger. It is not the clearance for 230 kV.
The rule does not double the clearance at night. A radio is required only where it is needed for direct communication. The specific night requirements are identifying the lines and using a safe path.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Confuses the trigger with a smaller clearance figure
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: 10 feet is not the trigger for the assessment. The rule requires an option whenever any part could get closer than 20 feet.
15 feet sits between common clearance figures, but it is not the trigger. The assessment trigger is closer than 20 feet.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Site buffer mistaken for the rule trigger
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: Some sites use 50 feet as a planning buffer, but the federal trigger for choosing an option is closer than 20 feet.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Uses the planned lift instead of the crane's possible reach
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: The heaviest lift may not be the one with the longest reach, and planned picks don't limit where the crane can go. The rule uses the maximum working radius in the work zone.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Planned position treated as the limit
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: Planned set-down points don't stop the boom or load from swinging farther out. The rule evaluates the maximum working radius in the work zone.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Load chart extreme mistaken for the work-zone radius
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: The chart's largest radius for any boom length may not apply to the boom as rigged. The rule ties the check to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Wrong person and wrong protective step
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: A site electrician is not the source the rule names, and lockout at a switch point is not visible grounding at the worksite. Confirmation must come from the utility owner/operator.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Duty assigned to the controlling entity; grounds at the wrong location
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: The controlling contractor doesn't own or operate the line, and grounds at a substation are not at the worksite. The utility owner/operator must confirm visible grounding at the worksite.
The source is right, but the location is wrong. Option (1) requires the line to be visibly grounded at the worksite, not at a remote substation.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Planned radius used instead of maximum radius
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: The assessment doesn't depend on planned picks. It asks what could happen up to the maximum working radius in the work zone, and that reach comes within 15 ft.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: A single control treated as a substitute for choosing an option
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: A spotter can be one of the measures used under an option, but a spotter is not an exemption. If the crane could get within 20 ft, an option is required.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Applies the rule only to planned motion
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: The test is whether the crane could get within 20 ft while operating up to maximum radius in the work zone, wherever the lifts are planned.
The assessment covers the equipment, the load line, and the load, including rigging and lifting accessories, not just the crane structure.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Field myth that nonmetallic rigging doesn't count
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: The rule makes no exception based on material. Rigging and lifting accessories are counted as part of the load, whatever they are made of.

powerlines.twenty-foot-check.misconception: Counts the load but not the accessories
powerlines.twenty-foot-check.why_wrong: The spreader bar alone is enough to trigger the requirement. The panels don't have to reach the line, because rigging is counted with the load.
The utility is the right source, but being switched off is only half of Option (1). The line must also be visibly grounded at the worksite.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: The deadline uses working days, not calendar days.
The requirement allows two working days, rather than one.
The deadline is two working days, not three.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Electrical qualification substitutes for utility authority
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: An employer's electrician does not replace the utility owner/operator as the required confirming party.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Operator authority substitutes for utility authority
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: The crane operator's assessment does not replace confirmation from the utility owner/operator.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Site control substitutes for utility authority
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: The controlling entity is not the confirming party specified by this requirement; the utility owner/operator is.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Confirmation duty confused with presumption duty
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: The utility owner/operator supplies the required confirmation, but the energized-presumption duty is assigned to the employer.
This provision expressly assigns the duty to the employer, rather than naming the crane operator.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Employer duty assigned to signal person
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: The provision assigns this duty to the employer, not the signal person.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Voltage response treated as outage confirmation
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: Answering a voltage inquiry does not confirm continuing deenergization and visible grounding at the worksite.
The employer must presume the line energized; the rule does not leave its status unclassified pending an operator measurement.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Current assessment substitutes for required confirmation
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: An electrician's current assessment does not satisfy the required utility confirmation of deenergization and grounding.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Scheduled time treated as completed isolation
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: Passing the scheduled time does not establish that the outage occurred or that the grounding condition is satisfied.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Schedule verification substitutes for status confirmation
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: Checking the schedule does not provide the required confirmation of actual, continuing deenergization and worksite grounding.

powerlines.voltage-and-energized.misconception: Shift timing substitutes for required conditions
powerlines.voltage-and-energized.why_wrong: The exception depends on the required utility confirmation, not on a change of utility work shift.
Visible grounds do not eliminate the requirement for utility owner/operator confirmation.

powerlines.work-zone.why_wrong: The full-circle method includes 360 degrees, including the side opposite the planned lifts.
A planned lift sector does not replace the 360-degree area required by this method.
The full-circle method does not exclude a rear sector.
The day's planned lifts may use less than the equipment's maximum working radius. The rule uses the equipment's maximum.
The current radius describes one operating position. It does not establish the outer edge of the full-circle work zone.
An unloading point is a planned load location, not the equipment's maximum working radius.
The prohibition applies to equipment operation beyond the boundaries, not only operation with a load.
A signalperson does not replace the required prohibition against operating beyond the demarcated boundaries.
Reduced speed does not satisfy the requirement to prohibit operation past the boundaries.
Observation by a signalperson does not permit operation beyond the established boundary.
Hook height does not create an exception to the prohibition on operating the equipment beyond the boundary.
Restricting only suspended loads leaves unloaded equipment operation outside the boundary unrestricted.
Flags and the listed devices are alternative examples of boundary demarcation; flags are not required in addition.
The device can demarcate boundaries, but operation past those boundaries must also be prohibited.
The rule expressly includes a range control warning device. It does not require automatic stopping for this method.
The 360-degree method includes the western sector even though no lifts are planned there.

rigging.center-of-gravity.why_wrong: The rule sets no capacity percentage. What triggers it is whether the stability method depends on the CG.

rigging.center-of-gravity.misconception: Tied to the wrong condition (assist crane)
rigging.center-of-gravity.why_wrong: Which crane does the lift doesn't matter. The question is whether the stability method needs the CG location.
The number of sling legs doesn't trigger the rule. It turns on the method used to maintain stability.
The rule doesn't require stopping for manufacturer data. It requires measures that control movement if the CG estimate is wrong.
No engineer calculation is required here. The rule's answer to missing CG information is protective measures.

rigging.center-of-gravity.misconception: Capacity derate in place of movement control
rigging.center-of-gravity.why_wrong: Derating the crane doesn't fix the problem. A load whose CG is unknown can still shift or tip at any capacity.

rigging.center-of-gravity.misconception: Treats the attachment geometry as the CG
rigging.center-of-gravity.why_wrong: Where the attachment points are doesn't move the CG. The CG depends on how the weight is distributed, and the load hangs with the CG under the hook.
The CG falls at the geometric center only if the weight is evenly distributed. Many loads have heavy ends.

rigging.center-of-gravity.misconception: Confuses sling geometry with CG location
rigging.center-of-gravity.why_wrong: Sling length and angle change leg tension, not where the CG settles. The CG still ends up under the hook.
