Moving the hook toward the high end takes it farther from the CG and makes the tilt worse.
The load already hangs with its CG under the hook. Lifting higher won't change the tilt.
Booming moves the hook and load together. The rigging doesn't change, so the hook's position relative to the CG stays the same.
Legs share the load equally only when the CG is centered between the pick points. Here it is off-center.
A flatter angle does raise tension for a given share of the weight. But B's share is much smaller, and the steeper leg A still ends up with the higher tension.
This is backward. The farther a pick point is from the CG, the less of the load it carries.
A CG below the hook is what makes a lift stable. The problem here is that the CG is above the pick points.

rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: The rule ties the requirement to stability, not to a percentage of chart capacity. A light load can still need its CG located.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Ties the rule to the rigging configuration
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: The number of sling legs does not trigger the rule. What triggers it is whether the method for maintaining stability depends on knowing the CG.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Limits the rule to special lift categories
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: The CG rule is not limited to tandem lifts or lifts over people. It applies whenever the stability method depends on knowing the CG.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Assigns a calculation duty the rule does not state
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: The rule does not require a written calculation by a qualified person. It requires measures that guard against dangerous movement if the CG estimate is wrong.
No derating percentage is set for an uncertain CG. The required response is measures that prevent unintended dangerous movement.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Confuses load weight with CG location
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: A load cell gives the weight, not the location of the CG. Weighing alone does not meet the requirement.
This reverses the lever relationship. Each leg's share is proportional to the distance from the CG to the other leg, so the far leg carries less.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Assumes equal sharing regardless of CG
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: Vertical legs share equally only when the CG is centered between them. An off-center CG puts more load on the nearer leg.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Thinks rated capacity sets the load share
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: A sling's rating limits what it may carry. It does not decide what it actually carries, which depends on where the CG is.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Simple average of positions ignores weights
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: This comes from averaging 10 ft and 16 ft, or from dividing the shift by the skid weight alone. Moments must be divided by the total weight of 6,000 lb.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Shifts CG in the wrong direction
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: This moves the CG 2 ft away from the pump. Adding weight always pulls the combined CG toward that weight, so the answer must be past 10 ft.
This inverts the weight ratio, moving the CG 4 ft toward the lighter pump. The shift is 6 ft × 2,000/6,000 = 2 ft.
This assigns the larger share to the farther leg. The leg nearer the CG carries more.
An equal split applies only when the CG is centered. Here it is 4 ft from A and 8 ft from B.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Uses total span as the far-side distance
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: This uses 12 ft and 4 ft as the two distances, giving ratios out of 16. The correct distances from the CG are 4 ft and 8 ft, with a span of 12 ft.

rigging.cg-calc.misconception: Thinks a spreader beam equalizes an off-center load
rigging.cg-calc.why_wrong: A beam does not move the CG. With the hook at center, the load will tilt until its CG swings under the hook.

rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: A proof-test certificate must be retained, but the required fourth identification entry is reach.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Purchase history substituted for required identification
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: Purchase date is not one of the four required identification entries. The missing entry is reach.
A serial number does not replace the required reach entry. The rule specifies size, grade, rated capacity, and reach.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Shorter service-based interval treated as universal maximum
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: Service conditions may justify a three-month interval, but the rule's maximum interval is 12 months.
Six months may be appropriate for a particular sling's service, but it is not the longest permitted interval.
Even light use does not permit an interval longer than 12 months for a sling in use.
This reverses the two numbers. The throat-opening threshold is over 15%, and the twist threshold is over 10°.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Same numerical threshold applied to different measurements
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: The opening threshold is correct, but waiting until twist exceeds 15° allows a hook already beyond the 10° removal threshold.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Twist number applied to throat opening
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: The twist threshold is correct, but the specified opening threshold is greater than 15%, not greater than 10%.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Operating assignment automatically confers inspection authority
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: Assignment as the operator does not establish the required inspection role. The inspector must be a competent person designated by the employer.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Crew-selected qualified rigger substituted for designated inspector
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: Crew selection and a rigging qualification do not replace the requirement for an employer-designated competent person.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Proof-testing provider required for periodic inspection
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: The thorough inspection does not have to be performed by the original producer's technician. That confuses periodic inspection with proof-testing responsibilities.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Future schedule substituted for completed inspection record
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: A future schedule does not document the completed inspection. The required record identifies the most recent thorough-inspection month for each sling.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Proof-test record substituted for inspection record
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: Proof testing and thorough inspection have separate documentation requirements. A proof-test month does not replace the inspection-month record.

rigging.chain-slings.misconception: Storage-location record substituted for individual sling record
rigging.chain-slings.why_wrong: A rack-level entry does not establish when each sling was thoroughly inspected. The record must account for each individual sling.
Averaging component ratings does not establish assembly capacity. The 8,000 lb ring limits the assembly.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Reads the next row up on the efficiency table
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: About 65 percent is the efficiency at a 2:1 D/d. At 1:1 the bend is twice as tight and only about half the strength remains.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Mixes up the choker-hitch reduction with D/d efficiency
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: About 75 percent is the 4:1 value, and riggers also tie 75 percent to choker hitches. A 1:1 bend leaves only about 50 percent.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Believes bending barely affects wire rope strength
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: About 91 percent applies to a gentle 20:1 bend. A bend as tight as the rope itself cuts strength roughly in half.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Confuses the minimum clear-length multiple with D/d
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: The number 10 comes from the minimum clear length of 6 × 19 and 6 × 37 slings (10 rope diameters between fittings). It is not the D/d basis for basket ratings, which is 25:1.
The number 40 is the minimum clear-length multiple for braided slings. Basket-hitch ratings assume a D/d of 25:1.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Confuses the design factor with D/d
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: 5 to 1 is the usual design factor for wire rope slings, which is a ratio of strength to rated load. It is not a bend ratio. The basket rating assumes a D/d of 25:1.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Applies the 6 × 19/6 × 37 rule to braided slings
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: Ten diameters is the minimum for cable laid, 6 × 19 and 6 × 37 slings. Braided slings need 40.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Applies the grommet rule to braided slings
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: 96 times the body diameter is the minimum circumferential length for grommets and endless slings. It is not the braided-sling clear length.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Mixes up the D/d basis with the length rule
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: 25:1 is the D/d basis for basket ratings. It has nothing to do with clear length. Braided slings need 40 diameters.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Uses the radius of the bend object
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: This uses the pin's 2-in radius instead of its 4-in diameter. D/d is diameter over diameter, which gives 4:1 and 75 percent.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Uses the radius of the rope
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: This divides by the rope's 1/2-in radius. The ratio must use the full 1-in rope diameter, which gives 4:1.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Treats every pin bend as the worst case
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: Only a pin as thin as the rope is a 1:1 bend. A 4-in pin under a 1-in rope gives 4:1 and 75 percent.
This doubles the vertical rating but ignores the tight 4:1 bend over the pin. That bend cuts capacity to 75 percent, which gives 15,000 lb.
The efficiency is right, but this counts only one leg. A vertical basket has two legs, so the capacity is 15,000 lb.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Uses the pin radius and drops a row
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: 65 percent is the 2:1 row, which you get by dividing the 1.5-in pin radius by the rope. Using the 3-in diameter gives 4:1 and 75 percent.

rigging.d-over-d.misconception: Uses the load width as the bend diameter
rigging.d-over-d.why_wrong: The rope bends over each corner, not around the 6-in face. The corner's radius is what sets the bend, and here it is nearly zero.

rigging.hardware.misconception: Shouldered-eyebolt practice applied to a plain eyebolt
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: Eye alignment does not make a nonshouldered eyebolt suitable for angular loading.
This introduces bending across the eye as well as angular loading of the shank.

rigging.hardware.misconception: A retaining nut substitutes for a shoulder
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: Tightening the nut does not provide the support of a designed shoulder.

rigging.hardware.misconception: Frequent removal requires a bolt-type shackle
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: Frequent connection and disconnection are common uses for screw-pin shackles. Pin rotation under load is the concern.

rigging.hardware.misconception: The shackle pin cannot carry load
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: A properly seated pin is a load-bearing part of the shackle. Bearing on the pin is not itself disqualifying.

rigging.hardware.misconception: Bow loading requires a different pin type
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: Centered loading is desirable. It does not create the loosening hazard described by the correct choice.
That orientation loads across the eye and can bend it.

rigging.hardware.misconception: Splitting the angle reduces bending adequately
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: A halfway orientation still introduces cross-eye loading.
Shoulder seating does not eliminate the need for eye alignment.

rigging.hardware.misconception: A secured latch corrects improper seating
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: Securing the latch does not correct tip loading. The eye must not bear on the hook tip.

rigging.hardware.misconception: Higher capacity compensates for incompatible dimensions
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: Greater capacity does not solve the fit problem; a larger hook may fit worse.

rigging.hardware.misconception: An arbitrary derating permits tip loading
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: An assumed reduction does not authorize tip loading. Correct the connection geometry.

rigging.hardware.misconception: Reduced capacity permits a prohibited connection
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: Derating does not permit shortening a sling with a bolt. Use suitable rigging without the makeshift device.

rigging.hardware.misconception: Rated hardware makes any arrangement acceptable
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: A shackle used as an improvised chain shortener remains a makeshift arrangement. Hardware must be suited to its intended function.

rigging.hardware.misconception: A strength calculation overrides the prohibition
rigging.hardware.why_wrong: Bolt strength does not create an exception to the prohibition on shortening slings with bolts.
The upper slings pull Device 1's ends toward each other, not apart. Its principal axial force is compression.

rigging.hitches.why_wrong: Three degrees does qualify, but it is not the limit. The rule allows up to five degrees from vertical.
Ten degrees is twice the allowance. A leg 10 degrees off vertical must be rated with an angle factor.
Fifteen degrees is far beyond the allowance. A leg that far off vertical carries noticeably more tension than a vertical leg.

rigging.hitches.misconception: any wrap under the load is a choker
rigging.hitches.why_wrong: In a choker hitch, one end passes under the load and through the eye on the other end. Here neither eye passes through the other.

rigging.hitches.misconception: confusing a basket with a multi-leg bridle
rigging.hitches.why_wrong: A bridle is built from multiple separate legs gathered in a top fitting. One sling doubled under the load is not a bridle.

rigging.hitches.misconception: naming the hitch by leg angle
rigging.hitches.why_wrong: A vertical hitch supports the load with a single vertical part of the sling. Two parts under the load make a basket, even when both parts hang vertical.
Half is too low for a normal choke. Ratings drop toward this level only when the choke angle gets much sharper than 120 degrees.
A choker always reduces capacity because the sling bends sharply at the choke point. Tag ratings for the choker column are lower than the vertical column.
Doubling applies to a basket hitch with vertical legs, where two parts share the load. A choker has one part carrying the load through the choke.
The tag's vertical rating covers one part. A basket puts two parts under the load, so the capacity doubles when the legs are vertical.
No 50 percent rule exists. Vertical basket legs give twice the vertical rating, and angled legs reduce it from there.
The 25 percent reduction belongs to a choker hitch. A basket with vertical legs and an adequate bend diameter is rated at twice vertical.
A basket has more capacity but does not squeeze the load. Unbanded tubes can shift and slide out of a basket if the bundle tilts.
A single center pick on a long, loose bundle lets it seesaw, and nothing holds the tubes together. Pieces can slip out of either end.
A vertical hitch on one tube lifts only that tube. The rest of the bundle is not captured at all.
A tighter choke may grip better, but it lowers capacity. Rated capacity drops as the choke angle gets sharper.

rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: The threshold for this verification method is 75 percent, not 50 percent.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Confusing a warning setting with the verification threshold
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: The required weight verification begins above 75 percent; waiting until 85 percent misses that requirement.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Treating near-capacity operation as the only verification trigger
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: This method requires additional weight verification above 75 percent, even when the indicated load remains below rated capacity.
Pickup radius does not control this check when a longer radius will occur later in the lift.
The rule specifies the longest radius, not an average of the radii along the path.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Treating swing initiation as the controlling position
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: The start-of-swing radius is insufficient if the load will travel to a longer radius.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Assigning capacity verification to the rigger
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: The rigger may provide rigging weights, but the operator must verify that the load is within rated capacity.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Assigning capacity verification to the signal person
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: Directing crane movements does not make the signal person responsible for the operator's capacity verification.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Assigning capacity verification to the supervisor
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: Supervisory responsibility does not replace the operator's specific duty to verify the load against rated capacity.
This subtracts only the block. The 500 lb of rigging must also be deducted, leaving 10,500 lb.
This subtracts only the rigging. Subtracting the 1,000 lb block as well leaves 10,500 lb.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Treating gross capacity as net payload
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: The 12,000 lb rating includes the block and rigging. Treating it as payload capacity would exceed the gross rating by 1,500 lb.
The payload alone omits 1,000 lb of ball and rigging weight. The required total is 9,000 lb.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Treating the overhaul ball as weightless crane equipment
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: This includes the rigging but omits the 600 lb ball. The total is 9,000 lb.
This includes the ball but omits the 400 lb rigging assembly. The total is 9,000 lb.

rigging.hook-blocks.misconception: Reversing the effect of a lighter block
rigging.hook-blocks.why_wrong: A lighter block reduces the deduction. Available payload increases rather than decreases.

rigging.load-weight.why_wrong: 50 percent is a field rule of thumb, not the rule. The trigger is 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius.
85 percent comes from the tipping-load basis used for outrigger load charts. It is not the load-weight verification trigger, which is 75 percent.
90 percent is a common indicator pre-warning setting, not the verification threshold. The rule sets that threshold at 75 percent.
The pick radius is often shorter, so its capacity is higher and could hide an overload later in the lift. The rule uses the longest radius in the operation.
The set point is not always the farthest point. The rule specifies the longest radius anywhere in the lift operation.
The shortest radius has the highest capacity, so this would give the least protection. The rule requires the longest radius.
An approval signature does not establish the weight. The rule requires the weight itself to be verified.

rigging.load-weight.misconception: treats chart limit as only limit
rigging.load-weight.why_wrong: Being under 100 percent is not enough once the 75 percent trigger is crossed. The weight must be verified first.
The rule does not offer re-booming to get around the trigger. Once the reading is over 75 percent, the operator must not proceed until the weight is verified.
The 12 in the designation is nominal depth in inches, not length. Weight is length times weight per foot.
Changing 40 ft to 480 in. while keeping a per-foot weight mixes units. The answer comes out 12 times too high.

rigging.load-weight.misconception: used depth instead of weight per foot
rigging.load-weight.why_wrong: Depth times length does not give weight. Use the 50 lb/ft value with the 40 ft length.
Volume comes from multiplying the three dimensions, not adding them. Adding gives 11 instead of 40 cu ft.
This uses only the face area and drops the 2 ft thickness. Weight needs volume in cubic feet.
40 cu ft is about 1.5 cu yd (27 cu ft per yd), not 2. Rounding up to 2 cu yd overstates the weight.
This counts only the water and leaves out the 2,000 lb tank.

rigging.multi-leg.misconception: Confuses the table rating basis with the rigid-load assumption
rigging.multi-leg.why_wrong: Three legs is the basis many sling tables use for rating a four-leg bridle. On a rigid load the weight can still end up on just two diagonal legs, so the safe assumption is two.
Four legs share equally only in theory. Real leg lengths, lug heights and the location of the CG are never perfect, and a rigid load cannot bend to even out the tension.
A balanced load cannot hang on one corner leg. It settles until at least two legs, usually a diagonal pair, carry the weight.
Ten degrees is twice the allowance. Only five degrees or less from vertical may be treated as vertical.
Three degrees is tighter than the rule requires. The allowance is five degrees or less from vertical.
A leg near horizontal is the worst case for leg tension, not a vertical load. The five-degree allowance is measured from the vertical.

rigging.multi-leg.misconception: Confuses rigid-load field practice with the table rating
rigging.multi-leg.why_wrong: Two legs is the field assumption for rigid loads, which a rigger applies on top of the table. The published four-leg rating matches the three-leg rating.

rigging.multi-leg.misconception: Counts every leg as adding capacity
rigging.multi-leg.why_wrong: This assumes the fourth leg adds a full share. The tables give it no credit because it may carry little or nothing.
Doubling assumes all four legs share equally. That assumption is exactly what the tables avoid.

rigging.multi-leg.misconception: Counts three legs on a rigid load
rigging.multi-leg.why_wrong: When one leg of a rigid load goes slack, the weight shifts mainly to the diagonal pair. Counting three legs overstates the capacity.

rigging.multi-leg.misconception: Adds all leg ratings regardless of sharing
rigging.multi-leg.why_wrong: The slack leg shows that the four legs are not sharing. Total rated capacity means nothing when only two legs carry the load.

rigging.multi-leg.misconception: Believes leg adjustment guarantees four-way sharing
rigging.multi-leg.why_wrong: Shortening one leg changes which legs carry the load, but it does not guarantee that four legs share on a rigid load. Capacity still has to be based on two legs unless an equalizing device is used.
This is 4 × 5,000 and assumes all four legs share equally. A rigid load usually hangs on two of them.
This is 3 × 5,000, the table basis for a four-leg bridle. For a rigid load without an equalizer, the safe assumption is two legs.
This assumes a single leg carries everything. A centered rigid load settles onto at least a diagonal pair.

rigging.multi-leg.misconception: Confuses a gathering fitting with an equalizer
rigging.multi-leg.why_wrong: A master link gathers and supports all the legs, but it does not equalize them. Uneven legs still leave the load on a diagonal pair.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Assigns the rigging duty to the supervising role
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: The A/D director oversees the procedure. The rigging work itself must be done by a qualified rigger, and being director does not make someone one.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Confuses competent person with qualified rigger
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: For A/D rigging the rule calls for a qualified rigger. A competent person designation does not meet that requirement.
General rigging training is not enough. The rigging work must be done by someone who meets the qualified rigger standard.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Applies the operator certification rule to riggers
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: Accredited certification is required for crane operators. The federal rules do not require it for riggers, although a card can be evidence of qualification.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Thinks some card is always mandatory
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: No card of any kind is required. What counts is whether the person actually meets the qualified-person criteria.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Equates a single course with qualification
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: One sling class does not by itself make someone qualified. The person must show the ability to solve or resolve rigging problems through knowledge, training and experience.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Assigns the rigging duty to the signal person
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: The signal person directs crane motions. Signaling a lift does not satisfy the requirement that a qualified rigger rig the materials.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Assumes the person handling the load is automatically qualified
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: The worker hooking the load may rig it only if that worker is a qualified rigger. Doing the hooking does not meet the requirement by itself.
Supervision does not replace qualification. The person doing the rigging work must be a qualified rigger.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Thinks the rule covers production lifts only
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: The requirement applies specifically to rigging used for assembly and disassembly, before the crane is in service.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Assigns the duty to the operator by default
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: The rule does not give A/D rigging to the operator. It requires a qualified rigger, whatever that person's job title.
The connectors are still in the fall zone, so the condition still applies. Taglines do not replace the qualified rigger requirement.
Signal person qualification is a separate requirement. It does not meet the condition that a qualified rigger rig the materials.
A sling inspection checks the hardware, not who rigged the load. The rule requires the materials to be rigged by a qualified rigger.
Counterweight removal during disassembly is not exempt from the A/D rigging requirement because it happens often.

rigging.qualified-rigger.misconception: Assigns rigging duty to the A/D director
rigging.qualified-rigger.why_wrong: The A/D director oversees the work but does not have to rig personally. The rigging must be done by a qualified rigger.

rigging.safe-practices.misconception: Thinks the hazard starts only at liftoff
rigging.safe-practices.why_wrong: The rule also covers loads about to be lifted. The moment the slings tighten and the load breaks free is one of the riskiest points of the lift.
No height threshold applies. A load hanging at knee height can still swing, crush or drop on someone.

rigging.safe-practices.misconception: Ties the rule to percent of capacity
rigging.safe-practices.why_wrong: How heavily the sling is loaded does not matter. The keep-clear rule applies to every load about to be lifted and every suspended load.
Knots are specifically prohibited. A knot bends the rope sharply, damages the strands and greatly cuts its strength.

rigging.safe-practices.misconception: Clips make a doubled leg safe
rigging.safe-practices.why_wrong: Bolts and other makeshift devices are prohibited for shortening slings. Clipping a doubled leg crushes the rope, and the clips can slip.
Twisting is a makeshift shortening method. It can kink the leg or unlay the rope, and kinked sling legs are prohibited too.
Crane capacity limits the crane, not the rigging. A sling can be overloaded well within the crane's chart.
Design factors are part of how a manufacturer sets ratings. The user's limit is the safe working load marked on the sling, not a value worked out in the field.

rigging.safe-practices.misconception: Hardware rating applied to the sling
rigging.safe-practices.why_wrong: Every component has its own rating. A shackle's rating says nothing about the sling, and the weakest component governs.
Capacity is not the problem. The center of gravity sits at 10 ft, outside both baskets, so the bundle will tip and slide out.
A tag line controls rotation, not balance. It cannot hold an unbalanced load in a basket, and the load can still slip out.
A trial lift checks a correct rig. It does not make up for one that is plainly unbalanced, and this load is likely to slip as soon as it leaves the ground.
A sharp edge can cut two plies as easily as one. The rule requires padding or protection at the edges.
Derating does not stop the cutting. Edge damage can sever a sling far below its rating, so protection is still required.
A wider sling is still cut by a sharp edge. The edges must be padded or the sling otherwise protected.

rigging.safe-practices.misconception: Rule applies only to the crane
rigging.safe-practices.why_wrong: The prohibition applies however the sling is pulled. Hand-pulling a sling pinned under a load still damages it and can shift the load.

rigging.sling-angle.why_wrong: The factor 1.15 applies at approximately 60° above horizontal. At 30°, the factor is 2.00.
The factor 1.41 applies at approximately 45° above horizontal. The lower 30° angle requires a factor of 2.00.

rigging.sling-angle.misconception: Uses the component fraction as the tension factor
rigging.sling-angle.why_wrong: One-half is the vertical component fraction at 30°. Converting vertical share to tension requires dividing by 0.50, not multiplying by it.

rigging.sling-angle.misconception: Treats the angle as measured from horizontal
rigging.sling-angle.why_wrong: A factor of approximately 1.15 applies at 30° from vertical. A leg 60° from vertical requires a factor of 2.0.
The factor 1.41 corresponds to 45° from vertical. At 60° from vertical, the factor is 2.0.
A factor of 1.00 applies to a vertical leg. At 60° from vertical, tension is twice the vertical share.
A factor of 1.00 applies to a vertical leg. At 45°, the leg needs approximately 1.41 times its vertical share in tension.

rigging.sling-angle.misconception: Multiplies by sine instead of dividing
rigging.sling-angle.why_wrong: Approximately 0.71 is the vertical component fraction at 45°. The tension factor is its reciprocal, approximately 1.41.
A factor of 2.00 applies at 30° above horizontal. At 45°, the factor is approximately 1.41.
Dividing 8,000 by two gives the vertical share only. Multiplying 4,000 by 1.25 gives 5,000 lb of tension.
The result 3,200 comes from dividing 4,000 by 1.25. The angle factor multiplies the vertical share, giving 5,000 lb.

rigging.sling-angle.misconception: Applies the factor to the entire load
rigging.sling-angle.why_wrong: Multiplying the full load by 1.25 overlooks the two equal vertical shares. Each leg carries 4,000 × 1.25 = 5,000 lb.

rigging.sling-angle.misconception: Confuses vertical share with leg tension
rigging.sling-angle.why_wrong: This is each leg's vertical share. The 30° angle doubles that share to 6,000 lb of tension.
This applies the factor of 2 to the full load. Divide the load between the two equal legs first, giving 6,000 lb of tension per leg.
This multiplies the 3,000 lb vertical share by 0.5. Tension is found by dividing by sin 30°, so it is 6,000 lb.
This uses the approximate factor for 60° above horizontal. At 60° from vertical, use 2.0, giving 10,000 lb per leg.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Rigger qualification substitutes for inspection designation
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: Rigger qualifications alone do not satisfy this assignment. The inspector must be a competent person designated by the employer.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Operator assignment automatically includes inspector authority
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: Being the assigned operator does not automatically make someone the required inspector. The operator must also meet the competency and designation requirements.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Signal person automatically serves as sling inspector
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: Assignment as signal person does not establish the required inspection competency or employer designation.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Applies running-rope inspection counts to slings
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: Those are not the specified wire rope sling counts. The sling thresholds are ten randomly distributed or five in one strand within one rope lay.
Five broken wires in one strand within one rope lay already requires removal; waiting for six misses the threshold.
The specified counts are ten randomly distributed and five in one strand, each measured within one rope lay.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Treats a shorter service interval as the universal limit
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: Six months may be appropriate for particular service conditions, but it is not the universal maximum interval.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Extends the interval for light use
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: Infrequent use does not permit extending the interval beyond 12 months.
Mild conditions do not permit a two-year interval. The maximum is 12 months.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Defers event-driven inspection to a shift boundary
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: The pinching event warrants an additional inspection during the current use period. A shift change is too late if the sling will be reused sooner.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Uses a test lift as a damage inspection
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: A test lift does not replace inspecting for damage after a damaging event. The sling must be inspected before further use.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Treats the daily inspection as sufficient for all conditions
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: The daily inspection is a minimum, not permission to ignore potentially damaging service conditions during the day.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Applies only the total broken-wire threshold
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: The ten-wire criterion is an alternative threshold. Five breaks in one strand within one lay already requires removal.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Waits one break beyond the removal threshold
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: The single-strand threshold is five, not six, broken wires within one rope lay.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Requires the threshold in multiple strands
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: The criterion applies to one strand. A second damaged strand is not required.

rigging.sling-inspection.misconception: Treats internal deterioration as removable dirt
rigging.sling-inspection.why_wrong: Removing loose material does not resolve the removal condition. Powdered fiber between strands requires taking the sling out of service.

rigging.softeners.why_wrong: Protection is required where the chain bears on the sharp edge regardless of the hitch used.
The requirement does not have a load-percentage threshold. A lightly loaded sling still requires protection from sharp load edges.
Protection is required before damage occurs, not only after contact produces visible wear.

rigging.softeners.misconception: Padding is the only permitted method
rigging.softeners.why_wrong: The rule permits padding or protection. It does not require padding in addition to another method that protects the sling from the edge.
Unused rated capacity does not waive the requirement to protect the sling from sharp load edges.
The requirement applies to slings generally, not just those made from fiber.
More padding on the flat surfaces does not protect the sling at the exposed sharp edges.

rigging.softeners.misconception: Wire rope eliminates the need for softeners
rigging.softeners.why_wrong: Changing sling material does not remove the sharp-edge protection requirement. The wire-rope legs would also need protection.
Preventing sliding does not protect a loaded sling that still bears against a sharp edge.

rigging.softeners.misconception: Slow movement compensates for displaced protection
rigging.softeners.why_wrong: A slow hoist does not replace edge protection. Waiting until the load clears would expose the loaded sling to the sharp edge.

rigging.softeners.misconception: No visible damage means protection is adequate
rigging.softeners.why_wrong: Visible damage is not the trigger for protection. The exposed sharp edge must be addressed before hoisting continues.

rigging.softeners.misconception: Changing the hitch replaces edge protection
rigging.softeners.why_wrong: Changing the hitch does not satisfy the requirement if the sling still contacts the same unprotected sharp edge.
Inspection at the transition does not itself protect the slings. Protection must address the sharp edges they will encounter.

rigging.softeners.misconception: Capacity margin covers changing edge contact
rigging.softeners.why_wrong: Spare rated capacity does not authorize contact with unprotected sharp edges.

rigging.softeners.misconception: Gentle movement makes sharp edges acceptable
rigging.softeners.why_wrong: Reducing rotation speed does not satisfy the requirement to protect slings from sharp load edges.

rigging.softeners.misconception: Protect the rounded contact instead of the sharp contact
rigging.softeners.why_wrong: Leg 3 has an unprotected sharp-edge contact and must be addressed. The stated smooth, rounded contact at leg 2 does not create that requirement.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Strength alone makes an attachment acceptable
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Meeting a strength target does not make riveting acceptable. Stitching is the only permitted attachment method.
Clamping is not a permitted substitute for stitching, even if the connection could develop the webbing's strength.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: A full-strength adhesive joint is permitted
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Adhesive bonding is not an authorized attachment method. The rule specifically requires stitching.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Manila eye-splice minimum applied to synthetic rope
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Three full tucks is the minimum for a manila rope eye splice. Synthetic fiber rope requires at least four.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Manila short-splice total applied to a synthetic eye
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Six full tucks is the total minimum for a manila short splice. It is not the synthetic rope eye-splice minimum.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Short-splice total applied to an eye splice
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Eight full tucks is the total minimum for a synthetic fiber-rope short splice, with four on each side. An eye splice requires at least four.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Rigging qualification includes sling repair authority
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Being a qualified rigger does not by itself establish equivalence to a sling manufacturer for repairs.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Lift supervision includes sling repair authority
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: A supervisory role does not authorize sling repairs. The repairer must be a sling manufacturer or an equivalent entity.
Operating experience does not by itself qualify someone as an equivalent sling repair entity.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Diameter substitutes for required leg identification
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Nominal rope diameter is not one of the identification elements required by this provision. The missing required information is the number of legs.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Sling length is a mandatory identification field
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Overall length is not a required identification element under this provision. A sling with more than one leg must identify the number of legs.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Manufacturing date is required instead of leg count
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: A manufacturing date is not among the identification elements required here. The number of legs is required for this sling.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: A protective cover overrides chemical restrictions
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: The rule does not provide an exception for a covered nylon sling. Nylon web slings must not be used where acid mist is present.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Post-lift cleaning makes prohibited exposure acceptable
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Cleaning afterward does not authorize exposure during the lift. The prohibition applies while acid mist is present.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: Chemical exposure can be addressed by derating
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: Reducing the load does not resolve the restriction. Nylon web sling use is prohibited in acid mist, rather than permitted at a reduced capacity.

rigging.synthetic-slings.misconception: The aluminum restriction applies to forged steel
rigging.synthetic-slings.why_wrong: This chemical restriction expressly identifies aluminum fittings, not forged steel. Other suitability checks still apply.

rigging.tag-lines.why_wrong: Possible rotation alone does not establish the requirement. A line is required when necessary to prevent hazardous rotation.
Precise alignment may make a line useful, but it is not the stated trigger. The requirement addresses prevention of hazardous rotation.
Visibility alone is not this requirement's trigger. The deciding condition is whether a line is necessary to prevent hazardous rotation.
Electrical continuity provides a conductive path. A tag line must be non-conductive.
Grounding does not satisfy the tag-line requirement. The line must be non-conductive.
An insulated handhold does not establish that the tag line is non-conductive. The requirement applies to the line.
The requirement expressly allows a restraint line. It does not require a hand-held tag line instead.
The requirement expressly allows a tag line. It does not require a fixed restraint line instead.
The rule permits a tag or restraint line; it does not automatically require both.
Additional observation does not provide the rotational control found necessary. A tag or restraint line must be used.

rigging.tag-lines.misconception: Slow hoisting substitutes for rotation control
rigging.tag-lines.why_wrong: Slower hoisting does not replace the line needed to prevent hazardous rotation.

rigging.tag-lines.misconception: Trial lift delays a known requirement
rigging.tag-lines.why_wrong: The need for a line has already been established. A trial lift does not justify postponing the required control.

rigging.tag-lines.misconception: Every suspended load needs a line
rigging.tag-lines.why_wrong: The rule does not make every instance of rotation a trigger. The rotation must be hazardous and a line necessary to prevent it.
This requirement does not prescribe a trial lift or demand proof that all rotation is impossible.
The absence of a requirement does not create a prohibition. This rule does not prohibit optional line use.
Using a tag line for alignment does not create an exception. If used, it must be non-conductive.

rigging.wire-rope-slings.misconception: Nonfiber core threshold applied to fiber core
rigging.wire-rope-slings.why_wrong: 400 °F is the point above which nonfiber core slings must be used per the sling manufacturer's recommendations. It does not apply to fiber core slings, which are removed above 200 °F.
250 °F is not the limit. A fiber core sling is permanently removed once it has been exposed to more than 200 °F.
By 300 °F a fiber core sling is already past the 200 °F limit and must be permanently removed.

rigging.wire-rope-slings.misconception: Braided sling rule applied to strand slings
rigging.wire-rope-slings.why_wrong: 40 diameters is the minimum clear length for braided slings, not for 6 × 19 or 6 × 37 slings, which need 10.

rigging.wire-rope-slings.misconception: Grommet rule applied to eye slings
rigging.wire-rope-slings.why_wrong: 96 times body diameter is the minimum circumferential length for grommets and endless slings. It is not the clear length between fittings.
No 20-diameter rule exists for these slings. The minimum is 10 component rope diameters.

rigging.wire-rope-slings.misconception: Crane load-test factor applied to sling hardware
rigging.wire-rope-slings.why_wrong: 1.25 times rating is a familiar crane load-test figure, but welded sling end attachments are proof tested at twice their rated capacity.
1.5 times rating falls short of the requirement. The proof test is at twice rated capacity.

rigging.wire-rope-slings.misconception: Design factor confused with proof load
rigging.wire-rope-slings.why_wrong: Five is a common design factor for wire rope slings, not the proof-test load. The proof test is at twice rated capacity.
No 30% allowance exists. Opening of more than 15% of the normal throat requires removal.
Twist beyond 10 degrees and opening beyond 15% are separate removal conditions. Either one alone requires removal.

rigging.wire-rope-slings.misconception: Field myth that bent hooks can be reshaped
rigging.wire-rope-slings.why_wrong: An opened hook has been overstressed. Bending it back does not undo that damage, and the condition calls for removing the sling from service.

rigging.wire-rope-slings.misconception: Fiber core removal rule applied to steel core
rigging.wire-rope-slings.why_wrong: Permanent removal on heat exposure applies to fiber core slings above 200 °F. A nonfiber core sling above 400 °F is used according to the manufacturer's recommendations.

rigging.wire-rope-slings.misconception: Assumes steel core has no temperature limit
rigging.wire-rope-slings.why_wrong: The 200 °F limit is for fiber cores, but steel core slings still have a 400 °F threshold. Above it, the manufacturer's recommendations govern.
No fixed 50% derate is set. The sling manufacturer's recommendations for that temperature decide how it may be used.
A capacity table does not replace the required permanent marking. Limiting the sling to one hitch type does not make an unmarked sling usable.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Roles reversed between director and assistant
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: The person directing must be a competent person. A qualified person who lacks competent-person authority cannot direct, even with competent persons helping.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Operator certification treated as A/D director status
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: Operator certification does not make someone a competent person. The director must have the hazard-recognition ability and corrective authority of a competent person.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Qualified rigger assumed to be enough to direct
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: A qualified rigger meets the qualified-person criteria, not the competent-person criteria. A certified operator does not supply the missing competent-person role.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Technical knowledge alone treated as sufficient
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: Being qualified alone is not enough. A person working solo must also be a competent person.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Assisted arrangement applied to a solo worker
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: A competent person can only direct alone when assisted by qualified persons. Someone working solo has no assistant, so he must meet both sets of criteria himself.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Operator certification confused with A/D qualification
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: Operator certification covers operating the crane. It is not the standard for who may perform or direct assembly/disassembly.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Assumes the director must be a manager
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: The definition says management status does not matter. A non-management crew member who meets the criteria can serve.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Job title treated as the qualification
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: The definition applies regardless of formal job title. What counts is meeting the requirements, not the name of the position.
No countersignature is required. A crew member who meets the criteria is an A/D director in his own right.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Boom shortening treated as routine reconfiguration
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: Shortening a boom is listed as an example of partial dismantling. That makes it disassembly, which must be directed by an A/D director.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Assist crane use treated as the trigger
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: Whether the work is disassembly depends on what is being done to the crane, not on whether an assist crane is used to handle the parts.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Only full teardown counted as disassembly
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: Partial dismantling during a job counts, including shortening a boom or swapping a component. It does not matter whether the crane is demobilizing.
Spotting hazards is only half of the definition. A competent person must also be authorized to take prompt corrective measures, not just report.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Qualified-person criteria confused with competent-person criteria
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: A degree is one way to become a qualified person. Without authority to correct hazards, the engineer is not a competent person.
Experience and certification do not supply the authority to take prompt corrective measures that the competent-person definition requires.

roles.ad-director.misconception: Experience assumed to create competent-person status
roles.ad-director.why_wrong: His experience can make him a qualified person. Being a competent person also requires authorization to take prompt corrective measures, which he does not have.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Confuses competent person with qualified person
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: A competent person is a different designation. The authority-to-stop rule names a qualified person as the one who clears the concern.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Assigns the duty to the controlling entity
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: The controlling entity has other duties on site, but it is not the party named to determine that safety has been assured after an operator stops.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Assumes job authority equals the right to clear a safety stop
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: Rank on the site does not count here. The determination has to come from a qualified person, and a superintendent may not be one.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Applies the one-signal-person rule to stop signals
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: Normal directional signals come from the designated signal person, but stop signals are an exception: they are obeyed from anyone.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Limits stop authority to lift supervisors
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: The rule does not limit stop signals to the people running the lift. A stop from anyone at all must be obeyed.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Requires signal qualification to give a stop
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: No qualification is needed to give a stop. The rule says the stop is obeyed irrespective of who gives it.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Narrows the authority to overload cases
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: An overload is one valid reason to stop, but the authority covers any safety concern, not just capacity.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Puts the qualified person before the stop instead of after
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: This turns the rule backward. The operator can stop first, and the qualified person comes in afterward to determine that safety has been assured.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Ties the authority to a single named hazard
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: High wind is a common reason to stop, but the rule is not tied to one weather condition. Any safety concern is enough.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Treats a supervisor's sign-off as clearing the concern
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: Accepting responsibility on paper does not fix the ground. The rule requires a qualified person to determine that safety is assured.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Believes a slower lift offsets the hazard
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: Going slowly does not remove a support problem. The operator has the authority to refuse the pick until the concern is resolved.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Gives the restart decision to the controlling entity
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: The restart depends on a qualified person's determination that safety is assured, not on the controlling entity's approval.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Believes the operator must defer entirely to the signal person
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: The signal person directs movements, but that does not remove the operator's authority to stop when the operator sees a hazard.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Treats a warning as a substitute for stopping
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: A warning does not resolve the concern while the load is still moving over a worker. The operator may stop until safety is assured.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Requires another person's agreement before stopping
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: The operator does not need anyone's agreement to stop. The authority applies whenever there is a safety concern.

roles.authority-to-stop.misconception: Uses the LMI as a weighing tool
roles.authority-to-stop.why_wrong: Using the LMI to find out an unknown weight treats a safety device as a scale. The operator may refuse until the concern is resolved.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Confuses competent person with qualified person
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: This describes the qualified person, who is defined by credentials or experience plus demonstrated problem-solving. Authority to correct hazards is not part of that definition.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Believes paperwork or training creates the role
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: The definition does not mention a training course or a designation letter. It depends on the ability to identify hazards and the authority to correct them.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Treats reporting as equal to authority to correct
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: Reporting hazards up the chain is not enough. The competent person must have the authority to take prompt corrective measures personally, and the definition covers predictable hazards too.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Thinks credentials are the only route
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: Credentials are only one route. The definition also accepts extensive knowledge, training and experience when problem-solving ability has been demonstrated.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Applies the competent person element to qualified person
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: Authority to take corrective measures is part of the competent person definition. It does not make someone a qualified person.
The qualified person definition does not require a third-party assessment. Third-party accreditation and evaluation apply in other parts of the standard, such as signal person evaluation.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Links rigger to the wrong defined role
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: The definition is tied to the qualified person criteria, not the competent person criteria. Hazard recognition plus authority to correct is a different role.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Thinks a rigging card is mandatory
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: The definition does not require a certification card. A rigger can qualify through extensive knowledge, training and experience with demonstrated ability.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Applies the signal person evaluation scheme to riggers
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: Qualified evaluators assess signal persons, not riggers. The qualified rigger definition rests on the qualified person criteria.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Assigns the duty to the A/D director
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: The A/D director supervises the operation, but the rule does not require the director to rig. It requires the rigger to be qualified.
Supervision does not replace qualification. The rigging work itself must be done by a qualified rigger.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Confuses competent person with qualified rigger
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: Authority to stop work makes someone a competent person, not a qualified rigger. The rule requires a qualified rigger.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Thinks hazard recognition alone is enough
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: Hazard recognition is only half of the definition. Without authority to correct the hazard promptly, he is not a competent person.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Applies qualified person criteria to competent person
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: Credentials belong to the qualified person definition. A competent person needs no degree, only the ability to identify hazards and the authority to correct them.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Treats reporting as equal to authority
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: Reporting is not the same as having authorization to take prompt corrective measures. The definition requires the authority to act.

roles.competent-vs-qualified.misconception: Assigns a designation duty to the A/D director
roles.competent-vs-qualified.why_wrong: The definition requires no A/D director sign-off. Qualification comes from meeting the qualified person criteria.

roles.language-literacy.misconception: Oral vocabulary substitutes for written literacy
roles.language-literacy.why_wrong: An oral vocabulary examination does not satisfy the required written demonstration of literacy.

roles.language-literacy.misconception: Operating skill substitutes for written literacy
roles.language-literacy.why_wrong: A practical operating demonstration does not replace the written literacy demonstration required for verbal testing.
An employer's statement does not replace the candidate passing a written demonstration of work-related literacy.
The employer's working language is not the language this provision requires on certification documentation. The documentation must identify the test language.
The documentation records the test language. Equipment materials must then meet the certification-language restriction.
A candidate may test in any language the candidate understands, which need not be the first language learned.
Previous operating experience does not determine the required procedures. They must apply to the class or type for which certification is sought.

roles.language-literacy.misconception: Entire employer fleet must be covered
roles.language-literacy.why_wrong: This provision ties the demonstration to the requested certification, not the employer's entire fleet.
Similar controls alone do not establish that the procedures apply to the class or type being sought.
The jobsite's normal language does not establish that the candidate understands English. The test may be in Spanish, which the candidate understands.

roles.language-literacy.misconception: Working language replaces test language in records
roles.language-literacy.why_wrong: Spanish testing is permitted, but certification documentation must record the actual test language, not the jobsite language.
The documentation must note the language in which the test was given; the entry is not optional.
English reading proficiency does not replace the requirement for materials written in the certification language.

roles.language-literacy.misconception: Bilingual supervision substitutes for written materials
roles.language-literacy.why_wrong: A supervisor's review does not furnish the equipment with written materials in the certification language.
Employer approval does not create an exception to the certification-language requirement.
Oral explanations do not replace furnishing the crane with the required written manual in English.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Maintenance expertise substitutes for operator qualification
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Maintenance expertise alone does not establish eligibility to supervise this operation. The supervisor must be an operator meeting § 1926.1427.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Inspection expertise substitutes for operator qualification
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Inspection experience alone does not satisfy the direct-supervision provision. The supervising person must meet the operator requirements of § 1926.1427.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Site authority substitutes for operator qualification
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Responsibility for site operations does not establish the required operator qualification. The provision specifies a qualifying operator.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Inspection paperwork knowledge substitutes for equipment familiarity
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Knowing inspection administration does not establish the required equipment familiarity. The alternative addresses operation, limitations, characteristics and hazards of the equipment type.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Site orientation substitutes for equipment familiarity
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Site knowledge does not establish familiarity with the crane type. The alternative requires knowledge of the equipment's operation, limitations, characteristics and hazards.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Control knowledge and service history are sufficient
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Control identification and service history leave out required areas such as limitations and hazards. All four specified areas concern the equipment type.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Operating knowledge substitutes for repair qualification
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: This requirement concerns equipment and maintenance or repair tasks. Production-lift knowledge does not replace qualification for the actual repair work.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Service administration substitutes for task qualification
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Knowing records and service intervals does not establish qualification for the equipment and tasks performed. The requirement addresses the work itself.
Familiarity with a maintenance program or crew assignments is not the stated qualification. The person must be qualified with respect to the equipment and maintenance or repair tasks.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Supervision and familiarity are cumulative requirements
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Direct supervision is one route, but the stated equipment familiarity is an alternative. Both routes are not required together.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Site approval is a required substitute for operator presence
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Site-supervisor authorization is not the stated condition for this alternative. The inspector's equipment familiarity supports the limited inspection operation.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Every inspection control movement requires personal operator certification
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: This limited inspection provision provides an equipment-familiarity alternative. It does not require the inspector to obtain personal operator certification as an additional condition.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Direct supervision authorizes any crane operation
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Direct supervision satisfies one personnel condition; it does not authorize production work under this provision. Setting roofing material is not part of the stated repair verification.
Acceptance of the repair does not extend the maintenance operating permission. The permitted functions remain tied to maintenance, inspection or performance verification.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: A lower load makes production work part of testing
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: A lighter load does not change the purpose of the operation. This provision restricts functions, not merely the amount of load handled.

roles.maintenance-operators.misconception: Operating supervision substitutes for repair qualification
roles.maintenance-operators.why_wrong: Direct operator supervision is an alternative condition for operating equipment. It does not replace the mechanic's required qualification for repair work.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Confuses certification term with annual inspection interval
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: One year is the interval for the annual crane inspection, not for operator certification. An accredited certification is valid for 5 years.
Three years is how often the testing organization's accreditation must be reviewed, and how often an audited employer program is re-audited. The operator's certification is valid for 5 years.
No 10-year term exists for operator certification. The accredited certification runs for 5 years.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Mixes the deficiency re-audit window with the certificate term
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: The 180-day window is for the re-audit after a deficiency has been corrected, and 5 years is the certificate's term. Routine audits come within 3 months of start, then at least every 3 years.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Applies an annual interval to the program audit
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: The first-audit timing is right, but follow-up audits are required at least every 3 years, not every year.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Wrong trigger for the first audit and wrong recurring interval
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: The rule ties the first audit to the program's start (within 3 months), and later audits come at least every 3 years, not every 5.
The limit is 15 minutes per break and only one break per hour. Two breaks per hour are not allowed.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Treats it like a meal break
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: A 30-minute break is twice the allowed length. The limit is 15 minutes, once per hour.
The frequency is right, but a break may not exceed 15 minutes.
The 5-year term and the matching type don't matter. The certificate is not portable, so it does not count at a different employer.
No auditor review can transfer an audited-program certificate. Portability belongs only to certifications from accredited testing organizations.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Equates equal validity terms with portability
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: Both options do run 5 years, but having the same term does not make a certificate portable. Only the accredited-organization certificate is portable.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Applies the up-to-350 kV distance to a higher voltage
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: The 20-foot trigger applies only to lines up to 350 kV. This line is 500 kV, so the trigger is 50 feet.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Uses planned position instead of maximum working radius
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: The test is whether the equipment could get that close when operated out to its maximum working radius, not where the trainer plans to keep the load.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Field myth of a total ban near lines
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: The answer is no, but the reason is wrong. There is no line-of-sight ban. The limits are 20 feet for lines up to 350 kV and 50 feet for lines over 350 kV, measured at maximum working radius.

roles.operator-certification.misconception: Keys the rule to mounting instead of capacity
roles.operator-certification.why_wrong: How the crane is mounted does not matter. The exception depends on maximum rated capacity, and 2,000 pounds or less is exempt.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Earlier deadline confused with the evaluation cutoff
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: This date comes from an earlier stage of the crane rule's phase-in. The cutoff in the evaluation provision is December 10, 2018.
This is an older date from the crane rule's history. The cutoff for relying on previous assessments is December 10, 2018.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Rule's starting date mistaken for the cutoff
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: This date is tied to the original crane rule. The previous-assessment cutoff is December 10, 2018.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Mixing up certification records with evaluation records
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: The certification number is not one of the required items. A certificate alone cannot make someone qualified under the evaluation requirement.
The evaluator signs the document. The operator's signature is not required, only the operator's name.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Inspection documentation confused with evaluation documentation
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: Inspection records are kept separately. The evaluation document needs the make, model and configuration of the equipment used, not its inspection history.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Office record-retention habit applied to a worksite requirement
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: The rule requires availability at the worksite, and it sets no three-year period. The period runs as long as the operator is employed.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Tying the evaluation to the certification cycle
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: The evaluation is separate from certification. The document stays available for the length of employment, not until a certificate expires.
There is no one-year limit. The document must stay available while the operator remains employed by the employer.
Certification is a separate requirement. Holding a certificate does not, by itself, make an operator qualified for the employer's evaluation.
The certificate's age does not matter. Every operator needs the employer's evaluation, however recent the certificate.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Self-attestation in place of a demonstration
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: Saying he is familiar is not a demonstration. The employer must see him demonstrate the required skills and knowledge through an evaluation.
The firm acted as the employer's agent. Signing the record does not move the employer's duty to the firm.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Duty assigned to the individual evaluator
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: The evaluator must sign, but the employer stays responsible for making sure the evaluation covered what was required.
The evaluation duty is the employer's. The operator does not take it on by accepting an assignment.

roles.operator-evaluation.misconception: Thinking the evaluation covers only the equipment
roles.operator-evaluation.why_wrong: The evaluation covers the work as well as the crane. If multi-crane lifts are part of the assigned work, he must be evaluated on them.

roles.operator-in-training.why_wrong: Certification alone is not enough, and carrying the card has nothing to do with trainee status. The employee must also be evaluated on the assigned equipment.
An evaluation on paper is still only half of the requirement. Without certification or licensing, the employee remains an operator-in-training.

roles.operator-in-training.misconception: Substitutes a medical requirement for the evaluation
roles.operator-in-training.why_wrong: A physical does not replace the evaluation. The rule ties full operator status to certification/licensing plus an evaluation on the assigned equipment.
Clearing the swing area does not create a separate category for unsupervised practice. The only allowed status is operator-in-training under supervision.
No load percentage allows an uncertified, unevaluated person to operate. What decides it is trainee status with supervision, not how light the lift is.
A signal person tells the operator what moves to make. That is not the same as supervising a trainee, and it does not replace operator-in-training supervision.
A certification that matches the crane type still leaves out the evaluation on the assigned equipment. Without that evaluation he is still a trainee.
Having a signal person does not take the place of trainee supervision. He still needs the evaluation before he can operate on his own.

roles.operator-in-training.misconception: Overcautious: trainee status forbids all operation
roles.operator-in-training.why_wrong: This is stricter than the rule. It specifically allows operation as a supervised operator-in-training before the evaluation.
The evaluation is only one of the two requirements. Without certification or licensing, he may operate only as an operator-in-training.
The rule has no exception based on a percentage of chart capacity. Supervision as a trainee is required no matter how heavy the load is.

roles.operator-in-training.misconception: Overcautious: no seat time before certification
roles.operator-in-training.why_wrong: This is stricter than the rule. Operating as a supervised operator-in-training is allowed while he waits for certification.
How heavy the load is does not change what the rule requires. A trainee operates only under supervision, whatever the load.
An approved lift plan covers how the lift is done. It does not replace the supervision a trainee must have while operating.

roles.operator-in-training.misconception: Overreaction: treats lack of supervision as an equipment problem
roles.operator-in-training.why_wrong: Nothing about the crane is defective, so no tag-out or inspection is needed. The trainee only has to stop operating until supervision is back.

roles.operator-in-training.misconception: Mixes up certification type with evaluation
roles.operator-in-training.why_wrong: The certification card covers a type of crane. The evaluation is a separate check on the equipment the employee is actually assigned to.

roles.signal-person-qualification.misconception: Two knowledge tests replace practical testing
roles.signal-person-qualification.why_wrong: Two knowledge tests do not replace the required practical test. An oral or written test must be combined with a practical test.
Work history does not replace the practical test. The individual must demonstrate the required abilities through testing.

roles.signal-person-qualification.misconception: Training attendance substitutes for knowledge testing
roles.signal-person-qualification.why_wrong: Course completion does not replace the oral or written test. Both knowledge testing and practical testing are required.
The operator is not assigned this employer duty. The signal person's employer must ensure qualification before signaling.

roles.signal-person-qualification.misconception: Controlling entity owns every personnel duty
roles.signal-person-qualification.why_wrong: Site coordination does not transfer this duty. It belongs to the employer of the signal person.
The evaluator assesses qualifications, but the signal person's employer must ensure that the qualification requirement is met.
Knowing an operator's preferred signals does not replace knowing and understanding the Standard Method.
Familiarity with a crew's customary signals does not satisfy the specific requirement to know and understand the Standard Method.
Knowing posted site signals alone does not establish knowledge and understanding of the Standard Method.
Verbal confirmation does not make the qualification documentation available at the site.
An evaluator's telephone assurance does not replace making the documentation available at the site.
Office availability alone does not meet the requirement for availability at the site.
A channel assignment is an operating detail, not documentation that the individual meets radio-signaling qualification requirements.
Operator approval does not replace qualification documentation specifying radio signaling.
A successful communications check does not establish all the required signal person qualifications.
The requirement is basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including boom deflection, not detailed structural calculations.

roles.training.misconception: Assumes a fixed annual retraining interval
roles.training.why_wrong: Subpart CC sets no annual retraining cycle. Refresher training depends on what the employee's conduct or a knowledge evaluation shows.

roles.training.misconception: Confuses certification renewal with refresher training
roles.training.why_wrong: The 5-year cycle belongs to operator certification, not to refresher training. Refresher training depends on conduct or evaluation, not on a date.

roles.training.misconception: Treats an equipment change as the refresher trigger
roles.training.why_wrong: A new model calls for training on that equipment's safe operation, but that is not the refresher trigger. The refresher rule turns on conduct or knowledge evaluation.

roles.training.misconception: Excludes maintenance staff by applying the general lockout program
roles.training.why_wrong: Maintenance and repair employees who are authorized to start or run the controls are named in the crane tag-out training rule. They are not left to a separate program.

roles.training.misconception: Mixes up the crush/pinch audience with the tag-out audience
roles.training.why_wrong: Everyone who works with the equipment gets crush/pinch and work-area training. Tag-out training is limited to people authorized to start or operate the equipment.

roles.training.misconception: Assigns the duty to the wrong people
roles.training.why_wrong: The lift director is not named. Any other employee authorized to start or operate the controls, including mechanics, must be trained.
A repayment clause tied to quitting still makes the employee pay for required training, and the rule does not allow that.

roles.training.misconception: Believes off-hours scheduling shifts the cost
roles.training.why_wrong: Holding the class off-shift does not change the rule. Required training must still cost the employee nothing.

roles.training.misconception: Treats retraining as the employee's expense
roles.training.why_wrong: Refresher training after a weak evaluation is still required training, so it must also be free to the employee.

roles.training.misconception: Puts the adjustment ahead of the check
roles.training.why_wrong: The practice is to take the boom's weight first and then decide whether the brake needs adjusting. Adjusting before the check is guesswork.

roles.training.misconception: Substitutes a load test for the boom-weight brake check
roles.training.why_wrong: This is not the required practice. The check uses the boom's own weight, taken just off the support, not a rated test load.
A continuous boom-up skips the short-distance check, so a brake that will not hold is found only when the boom is high and loaded.

roles.training.misconception: Applies the friction-crane rule to a hydraulic boom hoist
roles.training.why_wrong: Adjusting the brake is the friction-equipment response. This boom hoist has no means of adjustment, so repair is required.

roles.training.misconception: Works around a failed brake instead of repairing it
