roles.training.why_wrong: A pawl and lighter loads do not fix a brake that fails to hold. Under the rule, a repair is necessary.

roles.training.misconception: Believes the brake will seat itself with use
roles.training.why_wrong: Raising a boom whose brake will not hold increases the hazard. The rule requires a repair, not more operation.

roles.training.misconception: Applies the tag-out audience to a ground worker
roles.training.why_wrong: Tag-out and start-up training is for operators and others authorized to start or run the controls. The laborer is neither.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: B30.9 covers slings. It does not cover the hook on the crane's block.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Lumping hooks in with rigging hardware
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: B30.26 covers rigging hardware such as shackles, eyebolts and links. Hooks have their own volume, B30.10.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Confusing below-the-hook devices with the hook
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: B30.20 covers below-the-hook lifting devices such as spreader beams and lifters. It does not cover the hook itself.
B30 deliberately separates the two words. Only 'shall' is mandatory; 'should' is advisory.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Reading the word as a role assignment
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: The word does not assign a duty to any party. The responsibility sections name the parties, and 'should' only signals that a provision is advisory.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Confusing advisory language with deferral to the manufacturer
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: 'Should' means the provision is a recommendation. It does not hand the decision to the manufacturer, although many provisions do refer to manufacturer instructions.
The operator controls the crane, but the rule gives this determination to a qualified person. The operator can make it only if they actually meet that definition.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Confusing competent person with qualified person
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: This determination calls for a qualified person, who has a recognized degree, certificate or extensive knowledge and experience. A competent person is a different role elsewhere in the construction rules.
The signal person directs the crane's movements. The rule does not let the signal person decide whether a latch may be removed.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Applying the pre-2010 rule to a newer crane
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: The 1968 edition is one of the options for cranes manufactured before November 8, 2010. A 2015 crane does not qualify for it.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Assuming the whole volume is incorporated
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: The rule picks out particular sections and paragraphs and leaves some out, for example 5-1.5.3(d) and 5-1.6.1(c). It does not adopt the whole volume.
The rule names a fixed edition, B30.5-2004. It does not follow whichever edition was current when the crane was bought.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Believing the lift director overrides operator stop authority
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: The lift director oversees the lift. The operator still keeps the authority to stop when safety is in doubt.

rules.b30-roles-and-language.misconception: Thinking stop authority needs a higher approval
rules.b30-roles-and-language.why_wrong: The operator does not need anyone's permission to stop. Waiting for a site supervisor ruling leaves the load at risk in the meantime.
The owner provides a crane in proper condition but is not the gatekeeper for a stop. The operator can stop on their own authority.
The user arranges for the crane on the site and directs how it is used. Supplying the charts and manuals that belong with the crane is the owner's duty.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Assigning employer duties to the controlling entity
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: This work-rule duty belongs to the employer. The controlling entity has other specified duties under Subpart CC.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Confusing individual actions with employer obligations
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: The operator must perform required actions, but the employer carries the duty to establish, communicate, and enforce the supporting work rules.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Treating equipment ownership as employer responsibility
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: Equipment ownership alone does not assign this duty. The rule places it on the employer.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Treating all mechanic's-truck work as excluded
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: Installing a new pump as part of construction is not equipment maintenance or repair. The truck's name does not establish the exclusion.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Classifying the lift by the building's future use
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: Placing a building's structural beam is construction work, even when the building will be used for equipment service.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Confusing construction location with work activity
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: Handling components for new construction does not become equipment repair because the project is a repair shop.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Treating every industrial crane as an overhead crane
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: A crawler crane does not fall within 1910.179 merely because it handles industrial materials. That section covers overhead, gantry, and related crane types.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Selecting the crane standard solely by workplace
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: Working in a fabrication yard does not make a truck-mounted crane one of the crane types covered by 1910.179.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Ignoring crane type in general industry
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: A rough-terrain crane is not brought under 1910.179 by operating at a plant. Equipment characteristics matter as well as the work activity.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Treating the forklift exclusion as unconditional
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: The forklift exclusion has an exception for the suspended-load configuration described. Original equipment classification does not preserve the exclusion.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Requiring a winch for forklift coverage
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: A winch or a hook can satisfy the configuration requirement. A winch is not mandatory.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Applying Subpart CC to all construction forklifts
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: Construction-site use alone does not bring every forklift under Subpart CC. The specified suspended-load configuration is the deciding condition here.

rules.construction-vs-general.misconception: Letting general coverage override a specific exclusion
rules.construction-vs-general.why_wrong: The specific excavator exclusion includes lifting with chains. The general coverage of multipurpose machines does not erase that exclusion.
The exclusion concerns the listed machinery, not the elevation of the load. A covered crane does not become excluded by placing pipe below grade.
Construction installation work does not eliminate expressly listed equipment exclusions. This excavator remains excluded from Subpart CC.
Subpart CC's scope requires construction use. Moving suspended loads during routine manufacturing does not establish that condition.

rules.controlling-entity.misconception: Lift director substituted for equipment user
rules.controlling-entity.why_wrong: The equipment user is a required recipient. Informing the lift director does not replace informing the user.

rules.controlling-entity.misconception: Site owner substituted for equipment user
rules.controlling-entity.why_wrong: The required recipients are the equipment user and operator. The site owner is not a substitute for the equipment user.
The operator must receive the hazard locations. Informing the rigger does not replace informing the operator.
Equipment ownership alone does not assign this training duty. The employees' employer has the duty.

rules.controlling-entity.misconception: All site safety duties belong to site management
rules.controlling-entity.why_wrong: Site management alone does not assign this training duty. The employer must ensure its assigned employees receive the training.
Directing the lift does not by itself make that person responsible for this employer duty.
The duty also covers hazards identified in records the controlling entity possesses off-site.
Off-site records count, but so do records held at the jobsite.
Delivery to the operator is not the trigger. Possession by the controlling entity is enough when the records identify a covered hazard.
Owning the crane does not replace the controlling entity's duty to ensure necessary ground preparations are provided.

rules.controlling-entity.misconception: Operator acceptance replaces site preparation duty
rules.controlling-entity.why_wrong: The operator's involvement in setup does not transfer this duty from the controlling entity.
Identifying a preparation need does not assign the inspector the controlling entity's duty to provide for it.
Known hazards must be disclosed even without a drawing entry. Drawing correction is not a prerequisite to notification.
Inspector confirmation is not a prerequisite when the controlling entity already knows the hazard exists.

rules.controlling-entity.misconception: Equipment user is the sole disclosure recipient
rules.controlling-entity.why_wrong: Informing only the equipment user leaves the operator uninformed. Both are required recipients.
A new field survey is not a prerequisite to disclosing the hazard identified in the controlling entity's records.

rules.definitions.why_wrong: That describes a load moment indicator. An indicator informs and warns the operator. A limiter actually cuts power to the functions that would increase loading.
A limiter does not lock out the whole crane. Lowering, telescoping in and luffing in typically stay available so the operator can reduce the load.

rules.definitions.misconception: Confuses with boom hoist limiting device
rules.definitions.why_wrong: Setting brakes to stop the boom from lowering describes a boom hoist limiting device at a set angle. A load moment limiter responds to overturning moment, not to boom angle alone.

rules.definitions.misconception: Equates fast lowering with free fall
rules.definitions.why_wrong: Driving the line down with the motor is powered lowering, not free fall. In free fall the drive mechanism is not used at all.

rules.definitions.misconception: Mixed control counted as free fall
rules.definitions.why_wrong: If the drive mechanism helps regulate descent, it is not free fall. Free fall uses the brake alone.
This is close to controlled load lowering, which uses the hoist drive motor to lower the load. It is the opposite of free fall.
The controlling entity has overall responsibility for the project, but this definition ties the evaluator to the signal person's own employer.
An independent entity with recognized expertise is a third-party qualified evaluator, which is the other definition.
A qualified rigger meets the qualified person criteria for rigging. That does not make someone an evaluator of signal person qualifications.
Rotation does not decide coverage. The definition uses a rotating machine as its example and still excludes the forks configuration.
Coverage depends on how the machine is configured at the time, not on its being multi-purpose. With forks it is outside the subpart.
The answer is right but the reason is wrong. Tires play no part. The same machine on tires is covered once it has a hooked jib.

rules.definitions.misconception: Swing radius treated as directly under
rules.definitions.why_wrong: Directly under the load requires part or all of the employee to be beneath the load. Being inside the swing radius does not meet that test.
The fall zone includes, but is not limited to, the area directly beneath the load. Foreseeable landing areas to the side count.

rules.definitions.misconception: Zone depends only on current overhead position
rules.definitions.why_wrong: The fall zone exists wherever a fall is reasonably foreseeable now, including from swinging or a failure. It does not wait for the load to pass overhead.

A qualified person must have successfully demonstrated the ability to solve or resolve problems with the subject matter, through credentials or extensive knowledge, training and experience. The foreman has not.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Extending the exclusion to every tower
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: The gin-pole exclusion names communication towers, not wind turbine towers.
Erecting a water tank tower is not the communication-tower use specified by the gin-pole exclusion.
The gin-pole exclusion specifies communication towers. The separate exclusion for certain digger-derrick operations does not extend this gin-pole exclusion.
Installing new equipment on a foundation does not establish an equipment maintenance or repair activity.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Extending the exclusion to material delivery
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: Ordinary material delivery does not qualify under the mechanic's-truck exclusion. That exclusion depends on maintenance or repair work.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Confusing the building's purpose with the lift's purpose
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: Building a maintenance shop is construction of a structure, not maintenance or repair of equipment.
The exclusion names a come-a-long or chainfall. A hydraulic winch does not establish this exclusion.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Confusing a drum hoist with a chainfall
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: A wire-rope drum is not one of the hoisting methods named in this exclusion.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Substituting a powered winch for a chainfall
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: An electric winch does not qualify machinery for the come-a-long or chainfall exclusion.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Assuming every suspended load triggers coverage
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: Excavators are expressly excluded even when they lift suspended loads using chains, slings, or other rigging.
The exclusion permits suspended loads. It does not require the load to remain in contact with the bucket.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Applying the forklift exception to an excavator
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: The excavator exclusion does not impose a no-swing condition. The forklift configuration exception is a different provision.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Treating powered lifting as the trigger
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: A powered boom alone does not trigger the exception. The stated exception concerns a winch-or-hook configuration for hoisting, lowering, and horizontally moving a suspended load.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Treating all elevated transport as crane work
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: Travel with an elevated load alone does not identify the exception. Ordinary fork-supported transport is different from the specified suspended-load configuration.

rules.exclusions.misconception: Using the load's destination to decide coverage
rules.exclusions.why_wrong: The destination does not decide the forklift exception. The hoisting and horizontal movement configuration does.
An original crane classification does not defeat this exclusion while the machine is converted for non-hoisting use.

rules.scope.why_wrong: The listing does not require hoisting to be the truck's primary function. It identifies service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device.
The listing does not restrict these trucks to telescoping booms. A hoisting device is the feature named in the scope.
The listing does not limit these trucks to structural-steel lifts. The scope concerns equipment and its use in construction.
The scope expressly includes a crane on a monorail. Two supporting rails are not a requirement of that listing.
The scope names a crane on a monorail without limiting the rail to ground level.
The monorail listing does not require temporary rails. Rail permanence is not the condition stated.
The provision expressly includes suspended attachments as well as crane-attached attachments.
The provision expressly includes crane-attached attachments. Suspension from a load line is not required.
Paragraph (b) applies Subpart CC to covered equipment when used with attachments. It does not remove attachments into a separate equipment scope.
Industrial cranes, including carry-deck cranes, are expressly listed. The word industrial does not override the crane's use in construction.
The scope does not impose an outdoor-use condition on carry-deck cranes. This crane is performing construction work.
The scope identifies equipment capabilities and construction use, not ownership or rental status.
Multipurpose machines are expressly included when configured as described. Lifting need not be their sole intended function.
The scope turns on the machine's configuration, without requiring the lifting equipment to be permanent.
The multipurpose-machine listing specifies a lifting configuration. Power operation alone does not establish coverage for every multipurpose machine.
The attachment provision applies to covered equipment used with attachments and expressly lists augers or drills. Drilling does not itself remove this crane from scope.

rules.standards.misconception: Edition year mistaken for coverage date
rules.standards.why_wrong: 2004 is the year of the adopted ASME edition. It is not the coverage date. Coverage starts with cranes manufactured on or after November 8, 2010.

rules.standards.misconception: Assumes coverage starts once the edition took effect
rules.standards.why_wrong: No 2004 or 2005 cutoff exists in this paragraph. It applies to cranes manufactured on or after November 8, 2010.
This turns the rule backward. The B30.5-2004 portions apply to cranes built on or after November 8, 2010, not to older ones.

rules.standards.misconception: Cutoff year mistaken for edition year
rules.standards.why_wrong: 2010 is the year in the manufacture-date cutoff. The edition adopted is still B30.5-2004.

rules.standards.misconception: Assumes the rule tracks the current edition
rules.standards.why_wrong: Incorporation by reference fixes one named edition, here 2004. A newer ASME edition does not automatically become the federal requirement.
The edition named in the rule is 2004, not an earlier one.

rules.standards.misconception: Stability section's extent applied to structural section
rules.standards.why_wrong: Paragraphs (a)-(d) is the extent adopted from 5-1.1.1, where stability governs. From 5-1.1.2, only paragraph (b) is adopted.
Paragraph (a) of 5-1.1.2 is not listed. Paragraph (b) is.
The section is not adopted in full. The rule lists only paragraph (b).
These are the adopted boom hoist paragraphs, but the rule carves out rotation resistant rope and sends it to § 1926.1414(c)(4)(ii)(A).

rules.standards.misconception: Load hoist confused with boom hoist
rules.standards.why_wrong: Section 5-1.3.2 covers the load hoist mechanism, not the boom hoist. The rope exception attaches to the boom hoist item.
Only paragraphs (a), (b)(1) and (b)(2) of 5-1.3.1 are adopted, and rotation resistant rope still falls under the federal exception.

rules.standards.misconception: Use date treated as the trigger
rules.standards.why_wrong: The trigger is the manufacture date, not the year the crane is used. A 2008 crane is not brought in by this paragraph.
Truck cranes are named, but only those manufactured on or after November 8, 2010.
The paragraph expressly includes truck cranes. This 2008 crane is outside it because of its build date.

rules.standards.misconception: Misreads the parenthetical as the full list
rules.standards.why_wrong: Crawler and truck cranes are listed as types of mobile crane, and locomotive cranes are named separately in the same sentence.

signals.audible.misconception: Removable-horn rule applied to a built-in horn
signals.audible.why_wrong: Removal-only is the rule for a removable horn. A built-in horn may be tagged-out instead.
The rule does not set a repair deadline. It requires the faulty built-in horn to be tagged-out or removed.
Writing it down is not enough. The faulty built-in horn must be tagged-out or removed.

signals.audible.misconception: Built-in horn option applied to a removable horn
signals.audible.why_wrong: Tagging-out is the choice the rule gives for built-in horns. A faulty removable horn must be removed.

signals.audible.misconception: Radio treated as a horn substitute
signals.audible.why_wrong: A radio is a way of sending signals, not a horn. The faulty removable horn still must be removed.

signals.audible.misconception: Means of transmission confused with signal type
signals.audible.why_wrong: Radio and video are ways of transmitting signals, not signal types. The types are hand, voice, audible, and new.

signals.audible.misconception: Field methods mistaken for listed types
signals.audible.why_wrong: Flags and lights are not listed types. They would count as new signals, which need a showing of equal effectiveness.
This list leaves out new signals, which the rule permits when the employer makes the required showing.

signals.audible.misconception: Nearby treated as on the equipment
signals.audible.why_wrong: Removable horns are allowed, but they must be on the equipment and immediately available to the operator, not near it.
The rule accepts either a built-in horn or one that is on the equipment and immediately available to the operator.

signals.audible.misconception: Duty assigned to the wrong person
signals.audible.why_wrong: The horn must be immediately available to the operator, not to the signal person.

signals.audible.misconception: Backup horn treated as cancelling the tag-out duty
signals.audible.why_wrong: A working backup does not remove the duty to tag-out or remove the faulty built-in horn.

signals.audible.misconception: Overcautious; believes only built-in horns count
signals.audible.why_wrong: The rule accepts a horn that is on the equipment and immediately available to the operator. A shutdown is not required.

signals.audible.misconception: Horn placed with the wrong person
signals.audible.why_wrong: Tagging-out is correct, but the working horn must stay immediately available to the operator.

signals.audible.misconception: Permitted type assumed to be suitable everywhere
signals.audible.why_wrong: Audible is a permitted type, but any signal must also be appropriate for site conditions.
Repeating a signal the operator can't make out does not make it suitable for the conditions.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Substituting the lead rigger for the lift director
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: The lead rigger does not replace the assigned lift director in this agreement. The required participants are the signal person, operator, and lift director.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Leaving the signal person out of the agreement
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: This group leaves out the signal person. The person giving the signals must participate in the agreement.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Substituting management agreement for operator agreement
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: This group leaves out the operator. Agreement among site supervisors and the signal person does not replace the operator's participation.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Using a test movement to establish signal meanings
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: Agreement must precede the operation. An initial test movement is not a substitute for advance agreement.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Treating load clearance as the agreement deadline
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: Waiting until the crane takes tension places agreement after the operation has begun. The participants must agree beforehand.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Agreeing on signals individually during the lift
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: Clarifying signals as they arise is too late. Agreement on the non-standard signals must occur before the operation.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Turning alternative posting locations into a dual requirement
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: The rule permits either equipment posting or conspicuous posting nearby. It does not require both locations.
Office posting alone does not establish posting near the hoisting operation, and keeping a chart in records is not posting it. The chart must meet one of the two specified locations.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Treating general site access as compliant posting
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: An entrance location does not necessarily place the chart near the hoisting operation, and carrying a chart is not posting it. Neither arrangement as stated establishes compliance.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Treating unanimous agreement as an exception
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: Agreement does not independently authorize non-standard signals. Here, the Standard Method is feasible and covers the operation.
An unloaded demonstration does not create an exception to the Standard Method requirement. Familiarity and successful practice are not the stated qualifying conditions.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Treating lift director approval as a waiver
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: The lift director cannot substitute personal approval for the conditions allowing non-standard hand signals. The Standard Method applies to this operation.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Assuming an uncovered function requires voice signals
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: The uncovered attachment function qualifies for non-standard hand signals with advance agreement. This provision does not require switching exclusively to voice signals.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Applying the nearest standard signal to a different function
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: A signal for a different function does not communicate this uncovered function. The exception permits an agreed non-standard signal for the attachment operation.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Treating the Standard Method as having no attachment exception
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: The rule does not require waiting for the Standard Method to add a signal. It expressly permits non-standard signals for uncovered attachment use when the agreement requirement is met.

signals.hand-signals.misconception: Correcting the agreement while imposing duplicate chart posting
signals.hand-signals.why_wrong: The lift director must participate, but an additional equipment chart is not required. Conspicuous posting near the hoisting operation already satisfies the chart requirement.

signals.horn.misconception: Horn may be located off the equipment
signals.horn.why_wrong: The horn has to be built into the equipment or kept on it. A horn at a separate station is neither.
A removable horn also complies if it is on the equipment and immediately available to the operator.

signals.horn.misconception: Site availability instead of on-equipment availability
signals.horn.why_wrong: Being on the site is not enough. The horn must be on the equipment, and the 50-foot distance is made up.
The rule has no 30-day grace period. A built-in horn that is not working properly must be tagged out or removed.
Logging the defect and waiting for the annual inspection leaves a bad horn in service without a tag. It must be tagged out or removed.

signals.horn.misconception: Removable-horn rule applied to built-in horn
signals.horn.why_wrong: Removal only is the rule for a removable horn. A built-in horn may be tagged out instead.

signals.horn.misconception: Built-in-horn rule applied to removable horn
signals.horn.why_wrong: Tag out or remove is the rule for a built-in horn. A removable horn that is not working properly must be removed.
A removable horn cannot be tagged out and left on the crane. It must be removed.

signals.horn.misconception: Nearby counts as on the equipment
signals.horn.why_wrong: Tagging out the built-in horn is correct. But a horn in the pickup is not on the equipment or immediately available to the operator.

signals.horn.misconception: Horn assigned to the wrong person
signals.horn.why_wrong: The bad built-in horn must be tagged out or removed. A horn carried by the signal person is not on the equipment for the operator.
Removing the bad horn is allowed. But a horn in the trailer is not on the equipment, so the crane has no compliant horn.

signals.horn.misconception: On the equipment alone is enough
signals.horn.why_wrong: Being on the equipment is only half of the requirement. A removable horn must also be immediately available to the operator.
The rule does not allow site storage. A removable horn must be on the equipment and immediately available.
Writing the defect in the log does not replace the requirement to remove a removable horn that is not working properly.
Radio contact with a signal person does not replace the horn requirement. A built-in horn that is not working properly must be tagged out or removed.
One good test does not make an intermittent horn work properly. It still must be tagged out or removed.

signals.interruption.why_wrong: The requirement applies even when only one crane function is operating. Simultaneous movements are not the trigger.
Personnel approaching is not a condition for this requirement. An interruption during any operation requiring signals triggers a safe stop.
Maintaining communication is a continuing requirement. An interruption during movement also requires a safe stop.
A clear-area report does not replace the required proper operating signal. That signal must be given and understood after communication is restored.
Repeating an earlier instruction does not satisfy the requirement for a proper signal to be given and understood after communication is restored.
Confirming an equipment repair establishes neither a proper operating signal nor the operator's understanding of it.
A supervisor's agreement does not replace the signal person's agreement. The required pair is the operator and signal person.
The operator must be part of the agreement. Agreement between the signal person and supervisor does not satisfy this requirement.

signals.interruption.misconception: Qualified person substitutes for required agreement
signals.interruption.why_wrong: A qualified person's judgment does not substitute for the required agreement between the operator and signal person.
Partial visibility does not remove the stated need for signals at the landing point. Continuing slowly does not satisfy the stopping requirement.
The interruption does not authorize an unsignaled repositioning movement. The required response is to safely stop the operation requiring signals.
The operator must safely stop when transmission is interrupted, rather than complete the previous movement instruction.
Reducing speed is not the required response to losing necessary signals. The operator must safely stop the operation.

signals.interruption.misconception: Last signal carries through a gap
signals.interruption.why_wrong: An earlier signal does not permit continued movement through an interruption. The stopping requirement applies when the signals become unavailable.
The rule provides no grace period for a short interruption. A safe stop is required when necessary signals are interrupted.

signals.interruption.misconception: Radio check renews the earlier signal
signals.interruption.why_wrong: A radio check restores communication but does not supply a proper signal for the movement. The earlier instruction is not enough to restart.

signals.multiple-cranes.why_wrong: Naming the crane once doesn't meet the rule. Under the naming method, every signal needs its own crane identification.

signals.multiple-cranes.misconception: Identify only on a change of crane
signals.multiple-cranes.why_wrong: The rule doesn't make an exception for back-to-back signals to the same crane. Each signal is identified.

signals.multiple-cranes.misconception: Wrong order: identify after the command
signals.multiple-cranes.why_wrong: The identification has to come before the function/direction. By the time the crane is named afterward, an operator may already be moving.
An operator repeating the call back is good practice. The rule, though, requires the signal person to identify the crane before giving the signal.

signals.multiple-cranes.misconception: Duty assigned to the lift director
signals.multiple-cranes.why_wrong: A lift director may plan the communication system. The identification itself is done by the signal person, signal by signal.

signals.multiple-cranes.misconception: Duty assigned to a qualified person
signals.multiple-cranes.why_wrong: No qualified person is named in this rule. The signal person who gives the signal identifies the crane.

signals.multiple-cranes.misconception: Naming is the only allowed method
signals.multiple-cranes.why_wrong: Naming the crane is one option, not the only one. The rule also accepts an equally effective method.
The rule doesn't require a written plan or controlling-entity approval. What matters is that the method identifies the crane as effectively as naming it.
The rule doesn't name flags or limit alternatives to hand signals. Any method works if it is equally effective.
The crane is named only after the function and direction. Both operators have already heard a motion command before they know whose it is.
“Same crane” depends on everyone remembering the last signal. It doesn't identify a crane, so neither operator can be sure.

signals.multiple-cranes.misconception: Command first, then identify and release
signals.multiple-cranes.why_wrong: The motion comes before the crane is named. An operator may start the swing before hearing it's meant for the other crane.
Pointing after the signal reverses the required order. The crane must be identified before the function/direction.
The rule requires a system for identifying the crane. Leaving each operator to guess from context is not a system.
The rule isn't limited to tandem lifts. What triggers it is one signal person communicating with more than one crane/derrick.
The rule's wording is “crane/derrick,” so a derrick counts toward “more than one.”

signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: Separating hoist and swing instructions does not permit simultaneous signalers. Only one person may give routine signals at a time.
Agreement between signalers does not create an exception. The one-person limit also applies when their routine instructions match.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: A lead signaler can supervise concurrent signalers
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: A lead signaler does not authorize others to signal simultaneously. Routine signals must come from only one person at a time.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Supervisor notification substitutes for the stop signal
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: The rule names the operator or signal person. Notifying a supervisor alone is not the specified signaling action.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Lift director replaces the operator as recipient
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: The signal person is a named recipient, but the alternative named by this rule is the operator, not the lift director.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Safety alerts must follow the management chain
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: Reporting through management does not replace alerting the operator or signal person with a stop or emergency stop signal.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Only the assigned signaler can stop
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: The assigned signal person is not the only person whose stop signal must be obeyed. The operator must obey anyone's stop signal.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Stop authority is limited to the lift crew
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: Being part of the lift crew is not a condition for giving a stop signal that the operator must obey.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Stop authority depends on supervisory responsibility
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: Supervisors can give stop signals, but the requirement is not limited to supervisors. It applies to signals from any person.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Assigned signaler must validate an outsider's stop
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: The stop signal does not need confirmation from the assigned signaler. The operator must obey it regardless of its source.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Reduced speed substitutes for obeying a stop
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: Slowing while seeking an explanation does not obey a clear stop signal. The operator must stop.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Finish the current movement before stopping
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: The operator cannot defer the stop until the current movement is complete. The signal must be obeyed.
Assigning each person a different function does not satisfy the one-person-at-a-time requirement.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Communication priority replaces the one-person limit
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: A priority between communication methods does not authorize two people to give routine signals simultaneously.
Compatible instructions do not create an exception. Routine signaling remains limited to one person at a time.

signals.one-signaler.misconception: Slowing the motion satisfies the safety-alert duty
signals.one-signaler.why_wrong: A slower movement signal is not the required safety alert. The laborer must give a stop or emergency stop signal.

signals.radio.why_wrong: A yard test does not show how the radios perform around the site's structures, distances and interference. The test has to be done on site.
The location is right but the timing is wrong. The test has to come before operations begin, not after the first lift.
The requirement is tied to the start of operations on site, not to crew changes. Waiting for a new signal person could mean the radios are never tested.
Keeping a handheld within reach still means the operator has to pick it up to listen. Reception must be hands-free.
The operator does not get to choose. The rule requires hands-free reception.
Having to key or hold a radio takes a hand off the controls. The operator's reception must be by a hands-free system.
The shared-channel exception covers cranes, derricks and signal persons, not other equipment such as telehandlers.
General site and delivery traffic is not an exception. Crane signals stay on a dedicated channel.
A concrete pump is not a crane or derrick, so the coordination exception does not cover it.
The multiple-crane exception is one of two. The second covers coordination with trains on the same or adjacent tracks.
The exception exists because the crane has to be coordinated with moving trains. Stopping the trains is not a condition of the exception.
This would be the default rule without the exception, but the railroad exception specifically allows shared signal traffic in this situation.
This reverses the rule. Hands-free is required for the operator's reception, not for the signal person.
Stopping motion first sounds careful, but the rule has no such workaround. Reception must be hands-free.

signals.radio.misconception: Radio not allowed for blind picks
signals.radio.why_wrong: On a blind pick the operator cannot see hand signals. Radio is a proper method as long as the operator receives it hands-free.
Naming the crane is good radio practice, but it does not make a shared channel dedicated. Laborer traffic can still step on a stop signal.

signals.types.misconception: Confuses a transmission means (radio) with a signal type
signals.types.why_wrong: Radio is a way of transmitting signals, not a type of signal. This list also leaves out audible and new signals, which the rule allows.

signals.types.misconception: Treats hand signals as the only permitted type
signals.types.why_wrong: Standard Method hand signals are the benchmark for new signals, but they are not the only kind allowed. Voice, audible and new signals are permitted too, and radio is a transmission means.

signals.types.misconception: Treats light and flag signals as standard types instead of new signals
signals.types.why_wrong: Horn signals are audible signals, but flags and lights are not on the list of standard types. They would count as new signals, which need the employer's demonstration first.

signals.types.misconception: Assigns the employer's duty to the operator
signals.types.why_wrong: The operator must understand and respond to the signals, but the rule puts the duty to justify new signals on the employer.

signals.types.misconception: Assigns the employer's duty to the signal person
signals.types.why_wrong: The signal person uses the signals, but the employer has to show they are at least as effective as the standard types.

signals.types.misconception: Assumes the manufacturer approves signaling methods
signals.types.why_wrong: The rule says nothing about manufacturer approval of signal systems. The employer makes the demonstration.

signals.types.misconception: Raises the bar from equal to superior
signals.types.why_wrong: The rule requires communication that is at least equal. A new system does not have to beat the standard methods.
The rule calls for no agency review or pre-approval. The employer makes the demonstration.

signals.types.misconception: Substitutes crew sign-off for the effectiveness test
signals.types.why_wrong: The rule does not require written acceptance from the crew. The employer must show the system is at least as effective as the standard methods.

signals.types.misconception: Treats hand signals as mandatory in all conditions
signals.types.why_wrong: Hand signals are one permitted type, not a required default. A signal the operator cannot see does not suit the site.

signals.types.misconception: Treats the planned method as fixed despite site conditions
signals.types.why_wrong: Suitability depends on actual site conditions. A plan made before the signal person's position was known does not override that.

signals.types.misconception: Invents a horn-only rule for blind lifts
signals.types.why_wrong: No rule makes horns the only option for blind lifts. Radio voice signals or video can also suit the site.

signals.types.misconception: Believes any permitted type is acceptable regardless of conditions
signals.types.why_wrong: Being a permitted type is not enough. The signal must also suit site conditions, and the operator cannot hear it.

signals.types.misconception: Assumes audible signals work best in noise
signals.types.why_wrong: Horn signals are audible and compete with the same hammer noise. No rule says audible signals suit loud sites.
Voice is not required. Hand, audible or new signals are also allowed, and hand signals work here.
The rule does not involve the manufacturer. The employer has to demonstrate equal effectiveness.

signals.voice.why_wrong: The function comes first, with the direction, so the operator knows which motion to move. Each signal also has to end by naming the function before the stop.
The direction goes with the function in the first element. Distance and speed go together in the second element.

signals.voice.misconception: Stop command placed in the middle
signals.voice.why_wrong: The stop command is the last element. Distance and/or speed comes second, before the stop.
The superintendent is not named in the voice-signal rule. The required parties are the operator, the signal person and the lift director, if there is one.
When there is a lift director, the lift director takes part in the agreement directly. A briefing after the fact doesn't meet the rule.

signals.voice.misconception: Adds riggers to the required group
signals.voice.why_wrong: Riggers are not among the workers the voice-signal rule requires to agree. The lift director is, when there is one.
A new shift alone doesn't trigger a new meeting. Once agreed, the signals stand unless a worker is added or substituted, there is confusion, or a signal changes.
Moving the crane is not a trigger for re-agreeing voice signals. The triggers are a worker added or substituted, confusion, or a changed signal.
A change in rigging doesn't require a new voice-signal meeting unless it leads to confusion or a changed signal.
Distance and speed are given before the function and direction. The function and direction have to come first.

signals.voice.misconception: Generic stop instead of function, stop
signals.voice.why_wrong: The last element has to name the function and then stop ("hoist, stop"). A generic "all stop" doesn't complete the required structure.
The stop is placed before the distance and speed. The stop command has to be the last element.
Adding hand signals doesn't satisfy the voice-signal rule. The workers must be able to communicate effectively in the language used.
The rule doesn't provide for relaying through a translator. The operator and signal person themselves must be able to communicate in the language used.
The voice-signal rule doesn't require a read-back. The requirement is effective communication in the language used.
The rule calls for all three to contact each other and agree, not for one person to set the signals and announce them.

signals.when-required.misconception: Boom visibility substituted for point-of-operation visibility
signals.when-required.why_wrong: This trigger concerns the load travel and placement area. An obscured boom tip alone is not the stated condition.

signals.when-required.misconception: Support visibility substituted for point-of-operation visibility
signals.when-required.why_wrong: Outrigger visibility is not the stated trigger. The required view concerns load travel and the placement area.

signals.when-required.misconception: Counterweight visibility treated as the automatic trigger
signals.when-required.why_wrong: Counterweight visibility alone does not establish this trigger. A site-specific safety concern could independently require a signal person.

signals.when-required.misconception: Agreement required between operator and load handler
signals.when-required.why_wrong: Joint agreement is not required. A determination by either named person is sufficient.
The requirement does not depend on a supervisor approving the operator's determination.
The load handler's determination does not require confirmation by a safety manager.

signals.when-required.misconception: Every pick-and-carry move automatically triggers signals
signals.when-required.why_wrong: A suspended load alone is not this trigger. Obstructed travel-direction visibility or another listed condition establishes the requirement.
Reverse travel alone is not the stated condition. The trigger is an obstructed view in the actual direction of travel.

signals.when-required.misconception: Boom position substituted for travel visibility
signals.when-required.why_wrong: Boom position alone does not establish this requirement. The travel provision addresses the operator's view in the direction of movement.
Seeing the tank does not replace seeing the area near or at its placement.

signals.when-required.misconception: Physical barrier treated as an unconditional trigger
signals.when-required.why_wrong: A wall is not itself the trigger. Here, the requirement arises because the wall hides the placement area.

signals.when-required.misconception: Final support area excluded from required view
signals.when-required.why_wrong: There is no exception for the final support area. An incomplete view at placement triggers the requirement.

signals.when-required.misconception: Travel signals limited to loaded moves
signals.when-required.why_wrong: The travel provision contains no suspended-load condition. It applies to the obstructed travel-direction view.
This provision does not impose an unconditional requirement on crawler travel. The obstructed view establishes the requirement here.

signals.when-required.misconception: Cleared route substitutes for travel visibility
signals.when-required.why_wrong: Clearing the route does not restore the operator's view. The obstruction still triggers the requirement.
Operator agreement is not required when the load handler makes the determination for a site-specific safety concern.

site.access-hazards.misconception: Duty assigned to the signal person
site.access-hazards.why_wrong: A signal person can relay the message if the employee asks, but the rule puts the duty on the employee entering the area, not on the signal person.
The operator's duty starts once the operator knows someone went in: no swinging until the agreed all-clear. Getting word to the operator before entry is the employee's job.
The swing-radius rule has no supervisor-approval step for entering the area. The duty to inform the operator belongs to the employee going in.
The exception does not list a spotter. The required substitute is signs plus high-visibility markings on the equipment, along with training.

site.access-hazards.misconception: Alarm devices mistaken for the required markings
site.access-hazards.why_wrong: Alarms and beacons may help, but the exception specifically calls for warning signs and high-visibility markings that identify the hazard areas.

site.access-hazards.misconception: General site signage in place of equipment markings
site.access-hazards.why_wrong: Signs at the site entrance do not mark the hazard area itself. The rule requires high-visibility markings on the equipment that identify the hazard areas.
The rule also covers temporarily mounted superstructures. A pinch hazard exists no matter how the superstructure is attached.
The rule is not limited to temporary set-ups. It covers permanently mounted superstructures too.
The rule depends on whether a rotating superstructure creates a foreseeable struck-by or pinch hazard, not on the type of carrier.

site.access-hazards.misconception: Person posted inside the hazard area
site.access-hazards.why_wrong: Putting a person in the gap places them in the pinch zone. The rule requires barriers that keep people out.
A horn warning can be good practice, but it does not mark the hazard area. The rule requires physical barriers when they are feasible.

site.access-hazards.misconception: Exception applied when barriers are feasible
site.access-hazards.why_wrong: Signs plus equipment markings are allowed only when barriers are infeasible both on the ground and on the equipment. That is not the case here.

site.access-hazards.misconception: Signal-person training confused with hazard training
site.access-hazards.why_wrong: Hand signals are a separate signal-person qualification. The swing-radius training requirement is about recognizing hazard areas.

site.access-hazards.misconception: Operator control duties assigned to laborer
site.access-hazards.why_wrong: The crane's swing controls belong to the operator. The laborer's required training is recognizing struck-by and pinch/crush areas.

site.access-hazards.misconception: Barrier duty confused with training content
site.access-hazards.why_wrong: The employer must put up and maintain barriers, but the rule's training requirement for authorized personnel is recognizing the hazard areas.
A swing signal does not confirm the rigger is safe. The operator's hold stays in place until the pre-arranged all-clear is received.

site.boom-position-loading.misconception: over-side sharing applied to over-corner position
site.boom-position-loading.why_wrong: The right-side pair shares the load evenly only when the boom points straight out over the side, between them. Over a corner, the load concentrates on that one outrigger.

site.boom-position-loading.misconception: confuses counterweight side with boom side
site.boom-position-loading.why_wrong: The outrigger diagonally opposite the boom carries the least load, and it is the first to go light as the crane nears tipping.
Leveling gets the crane level. It does not spread the reactions evenly. Once the boom and load swing off center, the reactions shift toward the boom.

site.boom-position-loading.misconception: equipment feature substituted for manufacturer permission
site.boom-position-loading.why_wrong: A front jack lets you work over the front only if the manufacturer provides for it. Setting the jack does not grant permission by itself.
No percentage of capacity allows front-area lifts. The only exception is what the manufacturer permits.

site.boom-position-loading.misconception: full extension assumed to permit 360 degrees
site.boom-position-loading.why_wrong: Fully extended outriggers are needed for many chart ratings, but they do not make the front area usable unless the manufacturer allows it.
The crane's owner usually has no access to the site's as-built drawings. The rule puts this duty on the controlling entity.
The A/D director supervises assembly and disassembly. The rule does not make that person responsible for passing on subsurface hazards found in site documents.

site.boom-position-loading.misconception: informed party confused with informing party
site.boom-position-loading.why_wrong: The operator's employer, the crane user, is the party the controlling entity must inform. It is not the party with the duty to inform.
That is the pattern with the boom over the front. When the boom swings to the side, the load moves to the boom-side track.

site.boom-position-loading.misconception: counterweight side assumed heaviest under load
site.boom-position-loading.why_wrong: With a heavy load on the hook, the boom side carries the most. The track under the counterweight gets lighter.

site.boom-position-loading.misconception: long track contact assumed to equalize pressure
site.boom-position-loading.why_wrong: The ground under the tracks is loaded evenly only when the combined center of gravity sits at the center of the track footprint. A suspended load moves it toward the boom.
At the pick, the right pair shares the reaction between two outriggers. At the set, the left-rear outrigger carries it nearly alone.

site.boom-position-loading.misconception: two-outrigger sharing treated as the peak
site.boom-position-loading.why_wrong: Over the rear, two outriggers share the load. The highest single reaction happens when the boom is over one corner.
The corner diagonally across from the boom gets lighter. It is the corner that lifts first if the crane tips.
The moment depends on radius as well as weight. Doubling the radius doubles the moment even though the load weighs the same.

site.controlling-entity-ground.misconception: Assigns site duty to the operator
site.controlling-entity-ground.why_wrong: The operator assesses the ground and may find it inadequate, but the rule does not require the operator to provide ground preparations. The controlling entity must ensure they are provided.

site.controlling-entity-ground.misconception: Equipment owner confused with site controller
site.controlling-entity-ground.why_wrong: Owning the equipment does not create the duty. The rule assigns ground preparation to the controlling entity, which controls the site.

site.controlling-entity-ground.misconception: Assigns site duty to the A/D director
site.controlling-entity-ground.why_wrong: The A/D director may find that ground conditions are inadequate, which leads to a discussion, but the A/D director does not provide ground preparations. The controlling entity does.
The signal person is not named. The disclosure goes to the equipment user and the operator, the two parties who decide where and how the crane sets up.
The owner and the riggers are not the named recipients. The rule names the user of the equipment and the operator.
These roles may be involved in the lift, but the disclosure duty runs to the equipment user and the operator.
Employing the operator does not create the duty. What decides it is authority at the site to make or arrange ground preparations.
The rule does not name the property owner. It names the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange ground preparations.
Owning or leasing the crane is not the test. The duty goes to the employer with site authority over ground preparations.
The rule explicitly covers documents held at the site or off-site. Keeping the report at the home office does not excuse disclosure.
Disclosure is an affirmative duty of the controlling entity. It does not depend on the operator asking.

site.controlling-entity-ground.misconception: Duty placed on the crane user
site.controlling-entity-ground.why_wrong: This shifts the duty to the wrong party. The controlling entity must inform the user and the operator.
The operator makes the determination, but the rule assigns the discussion to the operator's employer.

site.controlling-entity-ground.misconception: Assumes a safety role owns it
site.controlling-entity-ground.why_wrong: No safety officer is named. The employer of the person who found the problem must discuss it with the controlling entity.
The rigger did not make the determination. The discussion falls to the employer of the operator or A/D director who found the ground inadequate.
Documents are one trigger, not the only one. Hazards otherwise known to the controlling entity must also be disclosed.

site.fall-zone.why_wrong: Designation as a signal person does not establish qualification to rig the materials. These materials must be rigged by a qualified rigger.
Assignment as the operator does not establish rigging qualification. The person rigging these materials must be a qualified rigger.
Supervisory authority does not replace the required rigging qualification. A supervisor could perform this work only if qualified as a rigger.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Roof framing shares one hook exception
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: The exception names wooden trusses, not steel roof joists. Initial connection work within the fall zone otherwise requires self-closing latches or their equivalent.
Wood construction alone does not qualify a load for the exception. The exception specifically covers setting wooden trusses.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Exception follows the load's roof location
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: The exception does not cover precast roof panels. Self-closing latches or their equivalent are required for this connection work.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Concrete work grants general fall-zone access
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: Inspecting forms is not one of the stationary-load exceptions. The bucket-operating exception does not extend to everyone working on the concrete placement.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Quality-control work shares the bucket exception
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: Sampling concrete is not operating the bucket and is not a listed stationary-load exception.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Work related to the load permits entry
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: Checking a delivery ticket does not qualify an employee to enter the stationary bucket's fall zone.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Only fully suspended loads create a fall zone
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: Partial support does not remove the hazard. The fall-zone definition includes partially suspended materials.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Fall zone equals the load's vertical footprint
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: The fall zone extends beyond the area directly beneath a load when falling material could foreseeably reach farther.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Fall-zone controls begin only after lift-off
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: The hazard already exists with one end suspended. Full suspension is not the trigger for establishing the fall zone.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Supervisors may observe from the fall zone
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: The foreman's title does not authorize entry. The foreman is not needed to receive this load.
Recording the serial number is not needed to receive the pump. The inspector must remain outside the fall zone during landing.

site.fall-zone.misconception: Fall-zone access is limited to one receiver
site.fall-zone.why_wrong: The rule does not impose a one-person limit. Both installers may enter because both are needed to receive the pump.
A warning person does not replace the requirement to use an available route that minimizes employee exposure.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Assumes soft ground is excused along with wet ground
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: Firmness is not exempted. Soft wetland ground still has to be made firm enough, with supporting materials if needed, to meet the manufacturer's support specifications.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Applies the wetland exception to grading
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: Grading still applies in a marsh. The equipment has to meet the manufacturer's degree-of-level specification, and grading is part of how you get there.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Thinks level tolerance is relaxed on wetlands
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: The manufacturer's degree-of-level specification must be met on any ground. Only drainage is exempted.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Treats a change in side length as a change in area
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: Doubling one side halves the pressure. Doubling both sides multiplies the area by 2 x 2 = 4, so the pressure falls to one quarter.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Confuses total load with bearing pressure
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: Pressure is force divided by area. With the same force spread over more area, the pressure has to drop.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Double-counts the side and area changes
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: The 4x increase in area is the result of both sides doubling. It is not a separate effect to multiply in again, so the pressure falls to one quarter.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Uses the linear conversion for an area
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: 12 is the number of inches in one foot, a length. Area converts by 12 x 12 = 144.
1,728 = 12 x 12 x 12, the number of cubic inches in a cubic foot. Pressure is per unit area, not per unit volume.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Mixes up square yards with square inches
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: 9 is the number of square feet in a square yard. Square inches to square feet is 144.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Divides by a side length instead of the area
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: This divides by one side length (2 ft) instead of the area. The area is 2 x 2 = 4 sq ft, so the pressure is 10,000 psf.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Uses the perimeter as the area
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: This divides by the 8 ft perimeter. Bearing pressure uses the contact area, 4 sq ft, which gives 10,000 psf.
This multiplies the load by the area. Pressure is load divided by area: 40,000 / 4 = 10,000 psf.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Accepts an area just short of the required one
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: 4 x 4.5 = 18 sq ft. 60,000 / 18 is about 3,333 psf, which is over the limit.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Misjudges area when one side is a half foot
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: 3.5 x 5 = 17.5 sq ft. That is less than the 20 sq ft needed, so the pressure would be over 3,400 psf.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Picks a larger mat than the question asks for
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: 4.5 x 6 = 27 sq ft is adequate, but it is not the smallest. The 4 x 5 mat meets the 20 sq ft requirement.

site.ground-bearing.misconception: Confuses total load with individual outrigger load
site.ground-bearing.why_wrong: The total weight stays the same, but how it divides among the outriggers changes with swing. Each float's reaction rises and falls as the boom moves.

site.ground-conditions.why_wrong: Grading still applies in a wetland. Only the drainage requirement is lifted there.
The manufacturer's specs for support and degree of level apply everywhere. The wetland exception covers drainage only.
Drainage appears in the operating requirement, not in the definition. The definition lists slope, compaction and firmness.

site.ground-conditions.misconception: Plausible soil factors not in definition
site.ground-conditions.why_wrong: Moisture and soil type affect support, but the definition lists slope, compaction and firmness.
A soils report helps judge the ground, but the rule's benchmark is the manufacturer's specs for support and level.
The controlling entity has site duties, but the support and level benchmark here is the equipment manufacturer's specs.
A qualified person may assess conditions, but the standard to meet is the manufacturer's specs for support and level.
The rule says the equipment must not be assembled or used until the ground meets the requirement. Assembly is covered.
Watching does not satisfy the rule. The ground has to be firm, drained and graded before assembly starts.
Mats can add support, but they do not drain standing water. The ground must also be drained before assembly.
The rule says the drainage requirement does not apply to marshes and wetlands.
Only drainage is exempt. Support and level must still meet the manufacturer's specs.
Drainage is exempt, but level must still meet the manufacturer's spec, not the operator's own judgment.
Recent backfill can settle or give way under a concentrated float load even when the surface looks firm. It can also damage the pipe.
Stacking pads does not increase the area pressing on the soil. Only a larger footprint on sound soil lowers bearing pressure.
A spotter can only report a failure as it happens. The hazard has to be dealt with before the crane is set up.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Duty assigned to the individual and the wrong site role
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: The duty is placed on the operator's employer, not the operator personally, and the other party is the controlling entity, not a competent person.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Manufacturer confused with the party responsible for site ground
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: The manufacturer has no role in this discussion. The rule pairs the determining person's employer with the controlling entity.
The discussion is between the operator's employer and the controlling entity. The A/D director's employer is involved only when the A/D director makes the finding.
Electric power lines, cables and conduit are marked in red, not yellow.
Sewer and storm drain lines are marked in green.
Communication, alarm, signal and cable lines are marked in orange.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Derating treated as a fix for poor ground
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: The rule does not offer derating as a substitute for adequate ground. The discussion is about preparing the ground so it meets the requirements.
The rule does not require soil testing. It requires a discussion of the ground preparations needed, with supporting materials if necessary.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Belief that inadequate ground can be accepted by waiver
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: No waiver process exists. The ground has to be prepared until it meets the requirements.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Mats can bridge a buried void
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: A mat spreads load over only a few feet and cannot span a tank. The tank top would still carry the concentrated outrigger load.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Surface check treated as proof of subsurface support
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: A sound slab says nothing about the tank or void underneath. Probing the surface does not find buried structures.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Traffic rating confused with outrigger capacity
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: Being rated for traffic covers spread-out wheel loads, not a concentrated outrigger reaction that can be many times a wheel load.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Documentation treated as a substitute for the required discussion
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: Logging the condition does not satisfy the rule. The operator's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity.
The rule calls for a discussion of the preparations needed. It does not create a competent-person approval step for ground that has already been found inadequate.
The rule does not require an engineering report. It requires a discussion of the ground preparations needed.

site.hazards-below-surface.misconception: Time and drying assumed to compact fill
site.hazards-below-surface.why_wrong: Drying does not compact fill. Backfill that was not compacted in lifts stays weaker than the undisturbed soil next to it.

site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Hoist-rope inspection is not an exception permitting entry beneath a stationary suspended load.
Checking outrigger pads is not one of the activities that permits an employee to occupy this fall zone.
Preparing for a later lift does not qualify an employee to enter the current suspended load's fall zone.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: Operator certification substitutes for rigger qualification
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Operator certification alone does not establish the required rigger qualification.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: Signaling and rigging qualifications are interchangeable
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Designation to give signals does not establish qualification to rig the materials.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: Any designated lift worker may rig
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Designation as a spotter does not satisfy the requirement for a qualified rigger.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: The exception covers every truss material
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: The exception names wooden trusses, not steel trusses.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: The exception covers all roof components
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Precast roof panels do not fall within the wooden-truss exception.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: The exception covers every wooden load
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: The exception applies to wooden trusses, not every wooden structural component.
The foreman's supervisory role does not make observation necessary to receive the beam.
Preparing the next location is not receiving the load being landed.
Supervision alone does not establish a need to be in the fall zone to receive the beam.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: Observation substitutes for securing the load
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Watching for movement does not replace rigging that prevents unintentional displacement.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: Slow operation compensates for insecure rigging
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Reducing speed does not satisfy the requirement to rig the materials against unintentional displacement.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: Guiders can physically compensate for loose materials
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Workers holding a member do not replace the required secure rigging.

site.keeping-clear.misconception: All suspended-load fall-zone entry is prohibited
site.keeping-clear.why_wrong: Initial attachment is an express exception while the suspended load is motionless; release of the hoist is not a prerequisite to this entry.

site.leveling.misconception: Applies the built-in tag-out option to a removable unit
site.leveling.why_wrong: Tagging out is allowed only for a built-in indicator. A faulty removable indicator must come off the crane.
Writing up a defect does not make a faulty indicator usable. It must be removed so nobody relies on a false reading.

site.leveling.misconception: Defers a known defect to a later inspection
site.leveling.why_wrong: No inspection grace period applies. The faulty removable indicator must be removed as soon as the problem is found.

site.leveling.misconception: Confuses mats with a flotation exemption
site.leveling.why_wrong: Mats are ground support, not flotation. A crawler on mats on land must have a level indicator.

site.leveling.misconception: Thinks poor ground makes the indicator pointless
site.leveling.why_wrong: Ground conditions do not create an exemption. A rough-terrain crane on land must have a level indicator.

site.leveling.misconception: Assumes mobile road cranes are exempt
site.leveling.why_wrong: A truck crane on land is covered by the rule. A slope makes leveling and the indicator more important, not less.

site.leveling.misconception: Assigns the equipment requirement to a person
site.leveling.why_wrong: The indicator has to be on the equipment. A level that leaves with the lift director is not available on the crane.

site.leveling.misconception: Substitutes a survey for an indicator
site.leveling.why_wrong: A one-time survey is not a level indicator on the crane. Level can change during the shift as the ground settles.

site.leveling.misconception: Confuses an inspection with required equipment
site.leveling.why_wrong: Inspections do not replace the indicator. The crane itself must have one built in or available on it.
A known malfunction is not held for a later inspection. The built-in indicator must be tagged out or removed now.

site.leveling.misconception: Field workaround for a faulty device
site.leveling.why_wrong: A mental correction is not allowed in place of a working indicator, and the error may not stay constant.

site.leveling.misconception: Uses the planned radius instead of the actual radius
site.leveling.why_wrong: The planned radius no longer applies once the hook is at 45 ft. The rating must be read at the radius the load is actually at.
45 ft is listed on the chart, so its own rating of 16,000 lb applies. Averaging 20,000 and 16,000 does not apply here.

site.leveling.misconception: Gets the direction of tilt wrong
site.leveling.why_wrong: Leaning toward the load moves the boom tip outward, which increases the radius. The hook drifted out, not in.
Touching tires take some load off the floats and can shift as they flex. The chart assumes the crane rests fully on the outriggers.

site.leveling.misconception: Belief that sharing load is safer
site.leveling.why_wrong: Load carried on the tires is not part of an on-outrigger rating. Rubber compresses and can let the crane go out of level.

site.multiple-cranes-area.why_wrong: Crane size does not assign this duty. When a controlling entity is present, it must institute the coordination system.
Lift order does not assign this duty to an operator. The controlling entity must institute the system.
Providing a signalperson does not transfer the controlling entity's duty to that employer.

site.multiple-cranes-area.misconception: Coordination applies only to tandem lifts
site.multiple-cranes-area.why_wrong: Sharing a load is not the stated trigger. The requirement applies when any part of one crane is within the other's working radius.
The trigger does not require two suspended loads or simultaneous load travel.
Boom crossing is too narrow a test. Any crane part within another crane's working radius triggers coordination.
Operator seniority does not determine responsibility. The duty falls on the employer operating both cranes.
Ownership alone does not establish this duty. The rule identifies the employer operating the equipment.
Conducting inspections does not assign the duty to institute the coordination system. The operating employer has that duty.
Separate boom paths do not eliminate the trigger. An outrigger is part of the crane.
Handling separate loads does not remove the coordination requirement when a crane part is within the other's working radius.
Independently prepared schedules do not establish a system coordinating the two operations. The controlling entity must institute that system.
Approving separate plans does not by itself coordinate the operations. The controlling entity must institute a system addressing their interaction.
Arrival order does not assign the duty. The controlling entity is responsible for instituting the system.
Operator cooperation does not replace the controlling entity's responsibility to institute the system.
The stated trigger does not require both booms to be moving. A crane part within the other crane's working radius is enough.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Confusing jack extension with beam extension
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: The specified position is horizontal beam extension, not vertical jack-cylinder extension.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Confusing swing position with support position
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: Upper-structure rotation is a different position measurement. This requirement concerns horizontal extension of the outriggers or stabilizers.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Confusing level indication with beam position
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: Carrier inclination indicates level, not horizontal beam extension. A level indication does not provide the position measurement specified here.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Assigning operational verification to the inspector
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: An inspector's examination does not replace the verification assigned to the operator under this temporary alternative.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Assigning setup verification to the signal person
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: The temporary alternative assigns position verification to the operator, not the signal person.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Confusing site responsibility with operator responsibility
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: This verification is the operator's duty. Assigning site responsibilities to a controlling entity does not transfer this particular duty.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Treating symmetry as proof of correct setup
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: Equal extension alone does not establish the correct positions. The positions must comply with manufacturer procedures.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Assuming full extension is always required
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: This provision does not prescribe maximum extension as the temporary alternative. It requires verification of the correct positions under manufacturer procedures.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Applying the requirement only to outriggers
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: The requirement expressly includes equipment with stabilizers. Calling the supports stabilizers does not create an exemption.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Using a trial lift as the initial verification
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: A trial lift is already an operation requiring the deployed outriggers in this setup. Verification must occur before that operation begins.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Treating swing as the start of crane operations
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: Waiting until the first swing allows lifting to begin before verification. The deadline is before operations requiring outrigger deployment begin.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Deferring verification until after a successful lift
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: Completing a lift before checking the positions reverses the required sequence. Verification must precede the operations requiring deployment.
Equal extension is not the stated test, and the manufacturer permits some unequal configurations. The operator must verify the actual positions under manufacturer procedures.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Transferring verification after a configuration change
