site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: An inspector's approval does not replace the operator's verification under the temporary alternative. The operator must verify the revised positions.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Testing stability before verifying support positions
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: A test lift cannot precede the required position verification. Correct positions must be verified before operations requiring deployment begin.

site.outrigger-sensors.misconception: Using redundant level checks as position verification
site.outrigger-sensors.why_wrong: A second level reading checks inclination, not correct horizontal beam positions. The operator must verify the positions under manufacturer procedures.

site.outriggers.misconception: Pressure relief confused with load holding
site.outriggers.why_wrong: A main-circuit pressure relief valve does not satisfy the requirement for an integral holding device/check valve on the jack.

site.outriggers.misconception: Remote shutoff substituted for integral holding
site.outriggers.why_wrong: A pump-outlet shutoff valve does not satisfy the requirement for an integral holding device/check valve on the jack.

site.outriggers.misconception: Pressure indication confused with load holding
site.outriggers.why_wrong: A pressure gauge indicates pressure; it does not satisfy the required holding-device/check-valve provision.
Centering a loose float beneath a jack does not meet the attachment requirement.
Attachment is required when the floats are used, not only while a load is suspended.
The attachment requirement is not limited to sloping ground.

site.outriggers.misconception: Proportional capacity reduction authorizes partial extension
site.outriggers.why_wrong: Reducing capacity by an extension percentage does not establish an authorized setup. Partial extension must be permitted by manufacturer procedures and specified in the load chart.
A qualified person's approval does not replace manufacturer permission and the required load-chart configuration.
A tire-supported capacity does not authorize an otherwise unapproved outrigger position. The deployment requirement applies whenever outriggers are used.

site.outriggers.misconception: Equal jack pressure establishes proper support
site.outriggers.why_wrong: Equalizing pressure does not satisfy the requirement if the wheels still support equipment weight.
A capacity reduction does not replace the requirement to remove equipment weight from the wheels.

site.outriggers.misconception: Only drive wheels must be unloaded
site.outriggers.why_wrong: The requirement applies to the equipment's wheels, not just the drive wheels.
This applies the outrigger wheel-unloading requirement to stabilizers despite the explicit exception.
The provision does not prescribe selective wheel unloading for stabilizers; it excludes stabilizers from this requirement.
The stabilizer exception is not restricted to unloaded setup.
Inspection afterward does not provide visibility during extension and setting.

site.slopes-excavations.why_wrong: A qualified person may help evaluate support, but this requirement assigns the discussion to the operator's employer.
The excavation supervisor may have useful information, but the operator's employer has the stated duty to discuss preparations.

site.slopes-excavations.misconception: Person detecting the problem owns every corrective duty
site.slopes-excavations.why_wrong: The operator's determination triggers the requirement; the operator's employer is assigned the discussion.
Freshly compacted backfill has no stated drainage exception. Adequate support and level must also be established.
Using mats does not create a drainage exception. Supporting materials work together with the ground to provide adequate support.

site.slopes-excavations.misconception: Excavation drainage substitutes for setup drainage
site.slopes-excavations.why_wrong: Being beside an excavation does not create a drainage exception. The stated exception concerns marshes and wetlands.

site.slopes-excavations.misconception: Crane supplier automatically owns site preparation
site.slopes-excavations.why_wrong: Supplying the crane does not by itself assign this duty. The duty follows site authority to make or arrange ground preparations.
Having performed the excavation does not by itself assign this duty. Authority over necessary ground preparations is the deciding condition.

site.slopes-excavations.misconception: Largest contractor automatically controls ground preparation
site.slopes-excavations.why_wrong: Crew size does not determine this responsibility. The rule assigns it according to authority over ground preparations.

site.slopes-excavations.misconception: Ground support matters only during lifting
site.slopes-excavations.why_wrong: The restriction applies to assembly as well as use. Waiting until the first load does not satisfy it.

site.slopes-excavations.misconception: Favorable boom direction waives setup requirements
site.slopes-excavations.why_wrong: Choosing a different assembly direction does not excuse known inadequate support. Ground conditions must meet the requirement before assembly.
Reducing counterweight does not establish adequate support for the proposed assembly. The ground requirement must be met before proceeding.
Notifying only the excavation foreman does not meet the requirement to inform the equipment user and operator.
Visible settlement is not the trigger. The tank is already identified in a drawing possessed by the controlling entity.
The requirement includes documents held off-site and requires informing both the equipment user and the operator.

site.slopes-excavations.misconception: Lower contact pressure eliminates slope failure
site.slopes-excavations.why_wrong: Reducing contact pressure does not eliminate a potential soil failure zone. A larger mass of soil can move toward the excavation.

site.supporting-materials.misconception: Confuses ground preparation with supporting materials
site.supporting-materials.why_wrong: Compacted gravel is ground preparation. It falls under ground conditions (compaction, firmness), not the list of supporting materials.

site.supporting-materials.misconception: Treats crane components as supporting materials
site.supporting-materials.why_wrong: Outrigger beams are part of the crane's own support system. Supporting materials are what go between the crane and the ground.
Counterweight affects stability and capacity. It does not spread load into the ground and is not a supporting material.
Mats are supporting materials used in addition to ground that is firm, drained and graded. They do not waive drainage for any crane type.
The ground rule has no exception based on load percentage. The ground must support the equipment whatever the load.

site.supporting-materials.misconception: Thinks engineering review waives the rule
site.supporting-materials.why_wrong: An engineered mat plan helps meet the support requirement, but the rule names marshes/wetlands as the only drainage exception.
Moisture and soil type affect firmness, but the definition names slope, compaction and firmness.

site.supporting-materials.misconception: Mixes the definition with the set-up requirement
site.supporting-materials.why_wrong: Drainage is required in 1926.1402(b), not listed in the definition. Bearing load is not one of the three named factors either.
Frost can affect firmness, but it is not named. The third factor is compaction.

site.supporting-materials.misconception: Divides by one dimension instead of area
site.supporting-materials.why_wrong: This divides 40,000 lb by 8, one side length, instead of by the 40 sq ft area.

site.supporting-materials.misconception: Uses float area instead of mat area
site.supporting-materials.why_wrong: This uses the 4 sq ft float area. With the mat in place, the load spreads over 40 sq ft.
This uses only half the mat (20 sq ft). The stem says the load spreads over the full 40 sq ft.
The rule sets no fixed mat rating multiplier. The test is meeting the manufacturer's support and level specifications.

site.supporting-materials.misconception: Assigns the decision to the wrong person
site.supporting-materials.why_wrong: The A/D director supervises assembly. The ground test is the manufacturer's support and level specifications, not anyone's approval.

site.supporting-materials.misconception: Relies on a visual walk-on check
site.supporting-materials.why_wrong: A lack of visible rutting at walk-on does not show the ground will carry lift loads. The manufacturer's specifications are the measure.
Mats are supporting materials, but the rule still requires drained ground except in marshes/wetlands.

site.swing-radius.why_wrong: Operators and signal persons are not the only employees covered. Employees assigned to other work on or near the crane also need this training.
Planned entry into the marked area is not the training threshold. Assignment to work on or near the equipment is enough.
Riggers are covered, but the requirement also covers other employees assigned to work on or near the equipment.
Difficulty placing ground barriers does not establish the exception. The employer must also demonstrate that barriers on the equipment are infeasible.
Interference with equipment-mounted barriers alone does not establish the exception. Ground barriers must also be infeasible.
A short lift duration does not establish infeasibility. The exception depends on whether barriers can feasibly be erected in either location.

site.swing-radius.misconception: Entry notification assigned to lift director
site.swing-radius.why_wrong: The entry-notification duty is placed on the entering employee or someone that employee instructs. A lift director's title does not automatically satisfy it.
The entering employee must ensure that the operator is informed, either personally or through an instructed person.

site.swing-radius.misconception: Entry notification assigned by supervisory title
site.swing-radius.why_wrong: A supervisor or crew leader can relay the notification if instructed by the entering employee, but the title alone does not assign this duty.
The outrigger footprint does not necessarily contain the rotating-superstructure hazard. Here, the counterweight sweeps beyond it.
The carrier footprint does not define the hazard boundary. The barriers must account for the counterweight's hazardous sweep.

site.swing-radius.misconception: Load-path boundary substitutes for swing boundary
site.swing-radius.why_wrong: The load's travel path does not identify the rotating-superstructure hazard. This requirement addresses the area where the superstructure can strike or crush employees.
Pinch/crush hazards are one trigger, but struck-by hazards independently trigger the requirement.

site.swing-radius.misconception: Protection required only during loaded operation
site.swing-radius.why_wrong: The rotating superstructure can strike an employee with or without a suspended load. Hook loading is not the trigger.

site.swing-radius.misconception: Visible employees need no hazard boundary
site.swing-radius.why_wrong: Operator visibility does not eliminate a foreseeable struck-by hazard. Visibility affects the separate entry-notification procedure.
The requirement expressly covers temporarily mounted rotating superstructures. Permanent installation is not a prerequisite.

site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Four feet applies to lines rated up to 0.75 kV. A 50 kV line requires 6 feet during unloaded travel.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Moving a boundary voltage into the next band
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Ten feet applies above 50 kV through 345 kV. Exactly 50 kV requires 6 feet.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Confusing the spotter trigger with minimum clearance
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Twenty feet is the clearance for lines over 750 through 1,000 kV. It also appears as the dedicated-spotter trigger, which is a separate requirement.
Six feet applies above 0.75 through 50 kV. A 345 kV line requires 10 feet.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Assigning the boundary to the higher band
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Sixteen feet applies above 345 through 750 kV. Exactly 345 kV remains in the 10-foot band.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Applying the highest listed fixed clearance
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Twenty feet applies above 750 through 1,000 kV. The minimum at exactly 345 kV is 10 feet.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Using a clearance band as the spotter trigger
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Ten feet is a Table T clearance for one voltage band. The dedicated-spotter trigger is closer than 20 feet.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Using the high-voltage clearance as the trigger
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Sixteen feet is the clearance for lines over 345 through 750 kV. The spotter trigger is closer than 20 feet regardless of that band.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Adding an assumed buffer to the regulatory trigger
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: The trigger is closer than 20 feet. This rule does not establish a 25-foot trigger.
Additional spotters do not authorize a 15-foot clearance. This voltage requires at least 16 feet.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Treating the spotter threshold as the clearance minimum
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Twenty feet would provide extra clearance, but the required minimum at 500 kV is 16 feet. A dedicated spotter is required for travel closer than 20 feet.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Trading travel speed for minimum clearance
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Reducing speed does not lower the voltage-based minimum. Even with movement accounted for, 15 feet is insufficient.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Assigning electrical clearance authority to lift supervision
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Experience planning crane routes does not confer authority to establish this clearance. It must come from the utility owner/operator or the specified qualified registered professional engineer.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Treating crane expertise as electrical qualification
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: Crane operating expertise alone does not meet this requirement. The clearance must be established by one of the electrical authorities specified in Table T.

site.travel-without-load.misconception: Treating any engineering specialty as sufficient
site.travel-without-load.why_wrong: The controlling entity is not assigned this determination, and engineering registration alone is insufficient. The engineer must be qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution.
Being beside the cab is not the required criterion. The spotter must be positioned to effectively gauge the equipment-to-line clearance.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Applying the lattice-boom requirement to a hydraulic boom
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: Hydraulic booms are expressly excepted from this boom-stop requirement.
Derricks are expressly excepted, even when their booms have lattice construction.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Treating carrier type as the deciding factor
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: The hydraulic-boom exception applies regardless of whether the carrier is a truck or a rough-terrain chassis.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Using vertical height as the weight's moment arm
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: For vertical weight, moment depends on horizontal distance from the tipping edge, not height. Raising the boom shortens that horizontal distance.
Constant weight does not mean constant moment. The horizontal lever arm decreases as the boom rises.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Confusing forward lifting capacity with backward stability
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: A smaller radius can improve forward lifting capacity, but it reduces the boom weight's forward balancing leverage against rearward tipping.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Confusing loss of load moment with movement of crane mass
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: The forward balancing effect disappears, but the crane's own center of gravity does not move when all its component masses remain in place.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Including the payload in the crane's own center of gravity
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: The payload was excluded from the crane's own mass distribution. Its removal therefore does not lower the crane's own center of gravity.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Treating reduced component force as a mass shift
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: Changing force in the boom does not move its mass in this stated rigid configuration. The crane's own center of gravity stays fixed.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Imagining that boom movement changes counterweight position
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: Raising the boom does not move the fixed counterweight. The change is in the horizontal location of the boom's mass.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Equating greater height with greater forward leverage
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: The boom rises vertically while its center of gravity moves rearward. Its horizontal forward balancing lever arm decreases.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Confusing weight transfer with an increase in total weight
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: Boom angle does not change total weight. It changes the distribution of that weight relative to the tipping edges.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Treating the dropped load as a continuing downward force
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: The forward moment from the payload disappears rather than increases. Components can recover from their loaded deflection, producing a dynamic response.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Assuming counterweight force adjusts to the payload
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: The counterweight's mass and initial lever arm do not decrease when the load drops. The sudden loss of the opposing load moment is the concern.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Confusing removal of load force with removal of boom weight
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: The boom's weight does not change. Released elastic energy and the disappearance of load moment can nevertheless cause violent motion.

tech.backward-stability.misconception: Assigning the A/D director's duty to the operator
tech.backward-stability.why_wrong: The operator has an operational role, but the stated duty to address assembly/disassembly hazards belongs to the A/D director.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Treating lifting chain as a pendant type
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: The definition recognizes wire and bar types, not chain as an alternative pendant construction.
Bar pendants are recognized, but the other recognized type is wire rope, not chain.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Confusing running suspension rope with pendants
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: A running rope moves over sheaves or drums. A wire pendant is a fixed-length member with end fittings.
A shift-based test does not satisfy the requirement for each occasion when the brake will be relied on during assembly or disassembly.
A daily test does not cover every later reliance on the brake during assembly or disassembly.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Making the test depend on operator changes
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: The trigger is reliance on the brake, regardless of whether the operator changes.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Assuming every indicator includes the jib
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: An installed jib does not establish that the indicator includes it. Some indicators measure only the permanent boom.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Confusing boom length with telescope stroke
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: The definition describes boom length, not only the amount of section extension beyond the base.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Confusing boom length with horizontal reach
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: Horizontal reach is a projection that changes with boom angle. It is not the boom length described by this definition.
Securing the boom foot does not stabilize the outer section after its connection is released. The affected section must remain stable upon pin removal.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Using the last pin as temporary support
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: Waiting for the section to settle allows movement before proper support is established. Stability must be provided upon pin removal.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Replacing component support with an exclusion area
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: Clearing the area does not satisfy the requirement to keep the section stable when the pins are removed.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Treating slow movement as snag prevention
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: Slow movement and observation do not prevent snagging. The pendant must be kept from catching on the keeper.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Removing retention hardware to obtain clearance
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: Removing connection retention is not the correction for a pendant snagging hazard. The pendant must be arranged to clear the connection hardware.

tech.boom-types.misconception: Using tension to pull a pendant past a snag
tech.boom-types.why_wrong: Pulling a pendant against the keeper permits the catching condition the rule prohibits. Clear its path before continuing.
Padding does not establish that thin diagonal members can withstand the lifting forces. The attachment points must prevent structural damage.

tech.gauges.misconception: Confuses the 7-day parts window with the repair deadline
tech.gauges.why_wrong: Seven calendar days is the window for ordering parts, and also the time allowed for the repair after delayed parts arrive. It is not the basic repair deadline, which is 30 calendar days.
The rule counts calendar days, not working days. Weekends and days off count toward the 30.

tech.gauges.misconception: Ties repairs to the annual inspection
tech.gauges.why_wrong: The repair deadline does not depend on the inspection schedule. It runs 30 calendar days from when the deficiency occurs.
The 30-day period does not start over when the parts arrive. After a documented delay, the employer has 7 calendar days from receipt.

tech.gauges.misconception: Wrong starting point for the extension
tech.gauges.why_wrong: The 7 days are counted from when the parts arrive, not from the end of the original 30 days.

tech.gauges.misconception: Verbal report to the wrong person
tech.gauges.why_wrong: The report must be in writing, and it goes to the person the employer designated. The lift director is not named for this.

tech.gauges.misconception: Assigns the operator's duty to the employer
tech.gauges.why_wrong: The employer does brief affected employees at each shift, but that does not replace the operator's own written notice to the next operator.

tech.gauges.misconception: Lockout/tag practice substituted for the reporting rule
tech.gauges.why_wrong: No tag or qualified person is required here. The operator must give written notice to the designated person and the next operator.

tech.gauges.misconception: Completes the task before acting on a warning
tech.gauges.why_wrong: Finishing the lift keeps an engine with no oil pressure running longer than needed, which risks seizure while the load is in the air. Land the load and shut down.

tech.gauges.misconception: Field myth that low readings are normal
tech.gauges.why_wrong: Oil pressure is lower at idle, but this crane is at working speed and reading zero. That is a real fault, not a normal reading.

tech.gauges.misconception: Treats a warning as a sticky gauge
tech.gauges.why_wrong: A red warning light plus a zero reading means you shut down and investigate. Tapping the gauge does not confirm the engine has oil pressure.
Running harder under load keeps adding heat. A red-zone reading means you stop working, not push through.

tech.gauges.misconception: Treats topping off as a cure for overheating
tech.gauges.why_wrong: Add oil only if the level is actually low, and use the correct fluid. Adding oil does not fix the cause, and resuming at once ignores the warning.

tech.gauges.misconception: Field myth that red is normal in summer
tech.gauges.why_wrong: Hot weather raises temperatures, but a reading in the red zone is above the safe limit in any weather.
Loading cold, thick oil at full speed risks pump cavitation and jerky load control. Warm the oil gently first.
A cold reading at startup is normal and is handled with a warm-up. Waiting for the weather is not required.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: Type I definition applied to Type II
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: This is the Type I construction: at least 15 outer strands and at least three layers. Type I is the class with little or no tendency to rotate.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: Type III definition applied to Type II
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: This is the Type III construction, which has only limited resistance to rotation. Type II needs at least 10 outer strands.
The rule does not use 12 strands as a cutoff. Type II starts at 10 outer strands, and Type I starts at 15.
This reverses the two numbers. The throat limit is 15 percent and the twist limit is 10°.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: consensus or manufacturer limit used in place of the rule
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: Some manufacturers and consensus standards use tighter numbers, but this rule states 15 percent and 10°.
The throat limit is correct, but the twist limit is 10° from the plane of the unbent hook, not 5°.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: Type I exception mistaken for the absolute floor
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: This is the normal minimum for Type I, and the written approval exception applies only to Type I. Even with that approval, the design factor cannot go below 3.5.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: invented limit with the wrong approving person
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: The rule does not use 4, and a qualified person cannot approve a design factor below 3.5.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: per-lift conditions treated as lowering the floor
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: Logging and inspecting each lift are conditions for using Types II and III between 3.5 and 5. They do not allow anything below 3.5.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: strand count confused with swivel binding
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: Type I rope develops little or no torque, so it gives a swivel little reason to turn. The outer-strand count does not bind the swivel.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: partially resistant rope ranked worse than standard rope
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: Type III has limited rotation resistance and its pairing with a swivel follows manufacturer guidance. Standard rope, with no counter-laid layer, is the case that unlays freely.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: counter-lay misread as a torque source
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: The opposite lay in Type II rope cancels torque rather than creating it. Rope with all strands laid one direction is what drives a swivel.
One part goes down to a sheave and one comes back up, so each sheave serves two parts. Six sheaves would allow up to 12 or 13 parts.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: dead end counted as needing a sheave
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: A dead end is anchored, not wrapped around a sheave. With the dead end at the boom head, it adds nothing to the block.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: boom-head sheaves credited with the block's parts
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: Two block sheaves support only 4 parts, or 5 with the dead end on the block. Six parts needs 3 block sheaves.

tech.hook-block-selection.misconception: twist mistaken for lack of overhaul
tech.hook-block-selection.why_wrong: A locked swivel can let the line twist, but it does not stop the ball from descending. Slack at the drum points to too little overhaul weight.

tech.stability-moments.misconception: Requires all far wheels to lift
tech.stability-moments.why_wrong: The definition does not wait for every far-side wheel to lift. Tipping occurs once half of the wheels farthest from the load leave the rail.
A single wheel lifting is not the defined tipping point. The condition is half of the wheels farthest from the load leaving the rail.

tech.stability-moments.misconception: Applies outrigger-float criterion to rail crane
tech.stability-moments.why_wrong: The definition is based on rail wheels and applies with or without outriggers. It is not based on outrigger floats lifting.
0.5 percent is tighter than the rule requires. The rating stipulation is track level within 1 percent grade.
1.5 percent is outside the stipulation. Ratings are based on track level within 1 percent grade.
2.5 percent is well beyond the stipulation of 1 percent grade. Out-of-level track shifts the center of gravity toward the load.
Over the front is not necessarily the least stable direction. Ratings are based on the least stable direction, so they stay safe wherever the boom points within the chart's area.
That describes structural limits, which govern other parts of the chart. Stability-based ratings come from the tipping load.

tech.stability-moments.misconception: Averages direction instead of worst case
tech.stability-moments.why_wrong: Averaging would rate the crane above what it can hold in its weakest direction. The rule uses the least stable direction, not an average.

tech.stability-moments.misconception: Uses radius instead of tipping-axis arm
tech.stability-moments.why_wrong: The crane tips about the outrigger line, not the center of rotation. Measured from the tipping axis, the arm is 30 ft, not 40 ft.
The tipping axis sits between the center of rotation and the load, so its distance is subtracted from the radius, not added: 40 − 10 = 30 ft.
The 10 ft is the distance on the crane's side of the axis, not the load's lever arm. The load's arm is 30 ft.

tech.stability-moments.misconception: Linear subtraction instead of inverse ratio
tech.stability-moments.why_wrong: Capacity is not reduced by a fixed fraction. Moment = weight × distance, so doubling the distance halves the load to 10,000 lb.
Load moment grows in direct proportion to distance, not with its square. 400,000 ÷ 40 = 10,000 lb.
The crane's resisting moment is fixed, but the load's moment depends on its distance, so a longer arm means a smaller tipping load.
The rating covers everything below the boom tip, including block and rigging, not just the item being lifted.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Confuses the radius reference point with the tipping line
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: The center of rotation is where radius is measured from, not a support. Tipping happens about the outer supports, which sit well outboard of that point.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Applies the on-rubber tipping line to an outrigger setup
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: The tire line is the tipping line only when the crane is working on rubber. On outriggers the tires are off the ground and carry nothing.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Puts the tipping line at the retracted beam position
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: The beam boxes are where the outriggers leave the frame. The load goes down through the jacks to the floats, so the tipping line is out at the floats.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Uses the shoe edge instead of the track centerline
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: The shoe edge is close by, but crawler ratings take the track centerline. The outer edge would overstate the tipping distance.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Uses the over-the-end tipping point for a side lift
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: The idler or tumbler at the end of the track is the tipping point for lifts over the end of the tracks, not over the side.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Confuses the radius reference with the tipping line
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: Radius is measured from the center of rotation, but nothing supports the crane there. The crane tips about the track.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Treats a setup step as the authorization
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: A front jack may be part of what the manufacturer requires, but setting it does not by itself permit the lift. Front lifting must be allowed by the manufacturer.
The rule gives no percentage exception. Without manufacturer permission, no load of any size goes over the front.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Assigns the exception to the wrong person
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: A lift plan or a qualified person's approval cannot override the ban. Only the manufacturer can permit front-area lifting.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Credits deflection for a geometry effect
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: Boom deflection depends on load and boom length, not on swing direction. It does not explain a difference between quadrants.
Over the side, the side floats carry more load, not less. Charts rate quadrants by stability or structure, not by low float pressure.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Treats a stability limit as structural
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: At a 40 ft radius, ratings are usually set by stability. The lower side rating comes from the shorter tipping distance, not from frame twist.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Field myth that a flatter tire is a steadier tire
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: A wider contact patch looks steadier, but a soft tire lets the crane lean and moves the support inward. Stability goes down.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Thinks pressure affects only tire capacity
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: Underinflation affects tire capacity and also stability, because the support point moves in as the tire deflects.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Thinks the chart covers any tire condition
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: On-rubber charts are based on a stated tire pressure. Running below it voids the conditions behind the ratings.

tech.tipping-axis.misconception: Averages the outriggers instead of using the load-side line
tech.tipping-axis.why_wrong: The fully extended right side does nothing for a lift over the left. Stability depends on the tipping line on the load side.

technical.components.misconception: Mobile crane term applied to a tower crane
technical.components.why_wrong: Carrying the trolley does not make it a boom. On a tower crane the term boom is used only when the horizontal structure moves up and down.
The mast is the vertical tower structure. The fixed horizontal member is the jib.
A luffing jib moves up and down, which makes it the opposite of a fixed jib. On tower cranes, a horizontal structure that moves up and down is called a boom.
The layer change happens at every flange the rope reaches, not just the flange on the anchor side.

technical.components.misconception: Confusing normal wraps with layer change
technical.components.why_wrong: In the middle of the barrel the rope just lays beside the previous wrap. The layer change happens at the flanges.
The lead-off point is where the rope leaves the drum. Crossover points are defined at the drum flanges.
The device does not move the boom. It stops boom hoist power and keeps the boom from lowering.

technical.components.misconception: Confusing limiting device with boom stop
technical.components.why_wrong: Physically stopping the boom from toppling backward is the job of a boom stop, which is a separate device.
The device acts on boom hoist power only. It is not defined to lock out the load hoist or swing.

technical.components.misconception: Confusing boom suspension with load reeving
technical.components.why_wrong: Pendants support the boom tip and control the boom angle. The hook load still hangs on the load line.
Keeping the boom from toppling backward is the job of boom stops. Pendants hold the boom up from the front.
Pendants are fixed in length. The boom angle is still changed by the boom hoist rope and drum.
Hoisting up increases loading on the crane, so the limiter shuts it off.
Telescoping out increases the radius and the overturning moment. It is one of the functions the limiter shuts off.

technical.components.misconception: Confusing lower hook with lower moment
technical.components.why_wrong: Booming down (luffing out) increases the radius, so it increases loading and is shut off.
By definition, the load includes the load-attaching equipment, so the 600 lb of block and rigging must be added.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Assuming all cranes have rotating upperworks
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: Full slewing is associated with rotating crane upperworks. A sideboom crane's boom or hook moves vertically only.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Confusing sideboom movement with restricted slewing
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: A limited swing arc is not the defining movement of a sideboom crane. Its boom or hook lifts and lowers vertically only.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Applying trolley movement to a sideboom
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: Cross travel resembles trolley movement on other crane designs. A sideboom crane does not provide that movement through its boom or hook.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Treating every truck-carried boom as the same defined type
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: Folding, pin-connected members characterize an articulating crane. The mobile-crane definition specifically names cable-suspended lattice and hydraulic telescopic booms.
A fixed principal horizontal structure is a tower-crane jib. It is not the alternative boom construction named in the mobile-crane definition.
A tractor with a side-mounted lifting boom describes a sideboom crane. The alternative named here is a cable-suspended lattice boom.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Treating long-term securement as marine design
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: Securing a land crane for a project does not establish that it was designed for marine use by permanent attachment. Project duration is not the defining condition.
Location over water describes the worksite, not the crane's original design. A land crane can work at a marine worksite.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Classifying equipment solely by available charts
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: Capacity information for barge operations does not by itself establish floating-crane classification. The definition depends on marine design and permanent attachment.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Treating machine capability as coverage in every configuration
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: The multi-purpose-machine definition excludes the forks/tongs configuration. Coverage applies to the described jib-and-hook configuration.
This reverses the configuration distinction. The forks configuration is excluded, while the described jib-and-hook configuration is covered.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Exempting equipment sold primarily as a forklift
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: A machine need not be dedicated exclusively to crane work to be covered. This multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with the hook jib.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Equating hydraulic power with telescopic construction
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: Hydraulic cylinders alone do not make a boom telescopic. The folding, pin-connected members identify this as an articulating boom.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Treating structural pins as proof of lattice construction
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: The described members form a hydraulically operated folding boom. They do not describe a cable-supported lattice boom.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Confusing a folding truck boom with a sideboom
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: A sideboom crane has its boom mounted on the side of a tractor. This truck-mounted crane has folding articulated members.

technical.crane-types.misconception: Classifying by the task being performed
technical.crane-types.why_wrong: The current task does not establish dedicated-pile-driver status. The definition turns on exclusive design purpose.

technical.design-testing.why_wrong: The required load is 250 pounds. A 200-pound capability does not meet that requirement.
The specified load is 250 pounds, not 300 pounds.
The specified load is 250 pounds. Doubling it imposes a requirement this provision does not state.
The required markings are rated capacity and weight. Rope size does not replace the assembly's weight.
A test date does not replace the required weight marking.
Hook size does not replace the required weight marking.
The required directions are outward for swinging doors adjacent to the operator and rearward for sliding operator doors.

technical.design-testing.misconception: Boom direction substituted for outward opening
technical.design-testing.why_wrong: The swinging-door requirement is outward, not toward the boom. Rearward is correct for sliding operator doors.
Sliding operator doors must open rearward. Outward is correct for swinging doors adjacent to the operator.

technical.design-testing.misconception: Payload used to satisfy overhaul requirement
technical.design-testing.why_wrong: A suspended load does not substitute for sufficient hook-block weight. The block must overhaul the line from the highest hook position.
The requirement concerns the boom or boom-and-jib lengths and parts of line in use, not every arrangement available for the crane.

technical.design-testing.misconception: Planned working range replaces design condition
technical.design-testing.why_wrong: The required starting point is the highest hook position, even if the planned work uses lower positions.

technical.design-testing.misconception: Counterweight treated as a simple capacity deduction
technical.design-testing.why_wrong: The requirement is for alternate equipment ratings. Subtracting counterweight weight from a capacity is not a substitute for those ratings.
A proportional reduction does not establish the required alternate ratings for operation without the optional counterweight.

technical.design-testing.misconception: Current lift limits required cab information
technical.design-testing.why_wrong: Selecting one configuration for the current lift does not eliminate the requirement for alternate ratings covering use and nonuse of capacity-affecting optional equipment.

technical.design-testing.misconception: Latch treated as a load-bearing component
technical.design-testing.why_wrong: This requirement assigns the latch a slack-rigging retention function, not the function of supporting the sling's rated load.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Pressure relief substitutes for load holding
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: A pressure relief valve limits pressure. The required jack protection is an integral holding device/check valve.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Neutral control valve substitutes for integral protection
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: A control valve at the operator's station is not the integral jack holding device/check valve required by this rule.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Upstream check valve satisfies jack requirement
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: A pump outlet check valve is upstream circuit protection. The rule requires the holding device/check valve to be integral to the jack.
The relief setting limits available pressure and therefore force. Cylinder speed follows incoming flow divided by effective piston area.
Inlet pressure contributes to cylinder force. With area fixed, speed depends on the volume entering each second.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Stored oil volume determines operating speed
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: Reservoir volume is not the rate of oil delivery. Cylinder speed equals incoming volume per second divided by piston area.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Check valve acts as a pressure relief valve
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: For this valve arrangement, blocked-side load pressure acts to keep the check seated. The valve needs sufficient pilot opening force.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Loss of pump flow releases a holding valve
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: Removing pump flow does not supply an opening force. Without sufficient pilot pressure, the seated check continues blocking reverse flow.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Open return path automatically opens the check
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: An open return passage provides a destination for oil but does not itself unseat the check. Sufficient pilot pressure must open it.
Pressure is force per square inch, not total force. Multiplying 2,000 psi by 10 square inches gives 20,000 lb.
Force equals pressure multiplied by area, not divided by area. The cylinder produces 2,000 × 10 = 20,000 lb.
Double-acting construction does not automatically halve force. With negligible rod-end pressure, extension force is 2,000 × 10 = 20,000 lb.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Lower viscosity means lower trapped pressure
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: Lower viscosity affects resistance when oil flows. In this trapped chamber, thermal expansion instead tends to increase pressure.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: Only the pump can increase hydraulic pressure
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: A pump is not the only source of pressure change. Heating trapped oil can raise pressure without adding oil.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: A stationary piston means constant pressure
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: Restraining the piston prevents expansion through cylinder movement. That restraint contributes to pressure rise as the oil heats.

technical.hydraulics.misconception: A hose pressure drop pulls a check valve open
technical.hydraulics.why_wrong: The seated check blocks reverse flow toward the hose. A pressure drop outside that closed boundary does not create an open discharge path.

technical.instruments.misconception: Parts-order deadline used as repair deadline
technical.instruments.why_wrong: Seven calendar days is the parts-ordering deadline for the repair exception. The normal repair deadline is 30 calendar days.
The normal Category II repair deadline is 30 calendar days, not 14.
The normal Category II repair deadline is 30 calendar days, not 21.
The necessary parts must be ordered within 7 calendar days, with the order documented.

technical.instruments.misconception: Ordering allowed late in repair period
technical.instruments.why_wrong: Ordering within 21 days misses the exception's 7-calendar-day ordering requirement.

technical.instruments.misconception: Repair deadline used as order deadline
technical.instruments.why_wrong: Thirty calendar days is the normal repair deadline. The exception requires ordering the parts within 7 calendar days.

technical.instruments.misconception: Vertical jack travel confused with beam extension
technical.instruments.why_wrong: This requirement concerns horizontal beam extension, not the vertical travel of the outrigger jacks.

technical.instruments.misconception: Position sensing confused with pressure sensing
technical.instruments.why_wrong: The required position monitor detects horizontal beam extension. Hydraulic pressure is a different quantity.

technical.instruments.misconception: Position sensing confused with support-load sensing
technical.instruments.why_wrong: The specified monitor concerns horizontal beam extension, not the supporting force at each foot.

technical.instruments.misconception: Boom length treated as sufficient radius information
technical.instruments.why_wrong: Known boom length alone does not establish the working radius. The temporary alternative requires measuring radius or boom angle.

technical.instruments.misconception: Last valid reading substitutes for measurement
technical.instruments.why_wrong: A stored reading does not satisfy the prescribed measurement alternative. Radius or boom angle must be determined with a measuring device.
A visual judgment by a signal person is not the required measurement with a measuring device.
Measuring jib angle alone omits the required first step of ascertaining the main boom angle.

technical.instruments.misconception: Drum rotation estimate replaces jib measurement
technical.instruments.why_wrong: After ascertaining main boom angle, radius or jib angle must be measured with a measuring device. A drum-rotation estimate does not meet that procedure.

technical.instruments.misconception: Radius measurement eliminates main boom angle step
technical.instruments.why_wrong: Measuring radius is an allowed second step, but it does not eliminate the first step of ascertaining main boom angle.

technical.instruments.misconception: Telescope time treated as a length measurement
technical.instruments.why_wrong: Timing telescope movement is not a listed alternative. Listed methods include measured marks, calculation from angle and radius measurements, and direct measurement.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Reverses the direction a backstop protects against
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: A stop guards against going too high and tipping backward. Low-angle limits are a load chart and operating issue, not what a backstop does.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Confuses a backstop with lateral restraint
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: Side loading and wind are handled by the jib's mounting and its wind limits. A backstop resists backward movement past the maximum angle.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Confuses jib stop with anti-two-block protection
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: Block-to-sheave contact is two-blocking, which anti-two-block devices prevent. A jib stop limits the jib's angle.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Thinks only powered jibs need a backstop
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: A fixed jib can also be pulled backward, so the definition covers fixed jibs as well as luffing jibs.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Thinks the luffing jib limiting device replaces the stop
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: A luffing jib also has a limiting device, but the jib stop definition still names luffing jibs.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Limits the device to one crane type
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: The definition is based on how the jib works, fixed or luffing, not on the type of crane carrying it.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Right kind of device, wrong component
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: A kick-out is one kind of boom hoist limiting device. It cuts boom hoist power for the main boom, not the luffing jib.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Confuses an operator-set work limit with the jib angle limiter
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: The operator sets a range control device to keep the boom or jib tip inside chosen planes. It is not the built-in limit on the jib's angle.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Mixes up the stop with the limiting device
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: A jib stop is the jib's version of a boom stop, a physical stop against tipping backward. It is not the version of the boom hoist limiting device.
160 ft is the boom plus jib, but ruled markings cannot measure a jib pinned to the tip. Only some computerized systems show boom length with extensions.
Height depends on boom angle and jib offset. A length indicator shows length, not height.
Radius changes with boom angle and offset. You find it from the chart or a radius indicator, not from boom length markings.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Classifies by machine type, not configuration
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: Coverage depends on how the machine is set up. With forks it is excluded, but with a hook-end jib it is covered.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Thinks a winch is needed for coverage
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: A jib with a winch is one covered setup, but a jib with a hook at the end is named separately and is also covered without a winch.

technical.jibs-extensions.misconception: Mixes up signaling rules with coverage
technical.jibs-extensions.why_wrong: Coverage is set by the configuration that lets the machine hoist and move a suspended load horizontally, not by sight lines. Sight lines affect signaling, not coverage.
This swaps the terms. The fixed hammerhead structure is the jib, and the luffer's moving member is the boom.

technical.modifications.misconception: Derating permits a lower safety factor
technical.modifications.why_wrong: A lower rated capacity does not create an exception to the requirement to preserve the original safety factor.
Written approval and preservation of the original safety factor are separate requirements. Approval does not waive the safety-factor requirement.

technical.modifications.misconception: Every capacity increase requires a higher safety factor
technical.modifications.why_wrong: The rule prohibits reducing the original safety factor; it does not require an increase whenever rated capacity increases.

technical.modifications.misconception: Applying the incomplete-review deadline to silence
technical.modifications.why_wrong: The 120-day provision concerns a manufacturer that agrees to review but does not finish. The unanswered-request period is 30 days.
The unanswered-request period is 30 days, not 60 days.
The unanswered-request period is 30 days, not 90 days.
Operator certification and experience do not satisfy the specified engineering qualifications for this approval route.

technical.modifications.misconception: Any professional engineer can approve crane modifications
technical.modifications.why_wrong: Professional-engineer registration alone is insufficient. The engineer must also be qualified with respect to the equipment involved.
Inspection qualifications alone do not satisfy the requirement for a registered professional engineer qualified for the equipment.

technical.modifications.misconception: Inspection acceptance substitutes for manufacturer approval
technical.modifications.why_wrong: An inspector's acceptance does not replace the manufacturer's written approval of the modification.

technical.modifications.misconception: Recording oral approval makes it written manufacturer approval
technical.modifications.why_wrong: The employer's record of a call is not written approval issued by the manufacturer.
The operator cannot substitute an authorization for the manufacturer's written approval.

technical.modifications.misconception: Approval letter substitutes for affected instructions
technical.modifications.why_wrong: The affected manual instructions and decal also need revision. An approval letter does not replace those necessary changes.

technical.modifications.misconception: Operator briefing substitutes for document revision
technical.modifications.why_wrong: An operator briefing does not replace necessary revisions to the setup procedures and manual instructions.

technical.modifications.misconception: Document changes can wait for annual inspection
technical.modifications.why_wrong: The rule provides no annual-inspection delay for necessary procedure or decal changes.

technical.modifications.misconception: Unavailability requires the unanswered-request waiting period
technical.modifications.why_wrong: The 30-day provision addresses an unanswered request to a manufacturer. It is not a required delay when the manufacturer is unavailable.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Confuses qualified person with competent person
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: A qualified person handles engineering-type tasks such as reviewing designs. The weather rule names the competent person, who is on site and can spot changing conditions and correct them.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Assigns duty to the controlling entity
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: The controlling entity has site-wide duties, but this rule puts the weather adjustment on the competent person and not on the site's prime contractor.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Assigns duty to the signal person
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: A signal person passes the operator's movement signals. Deciding how wind, ice or snow affect stability and capacity belongs to the competent person.
Visibility matters in bad weather, but the rule ties wind, ice and snow to stability and rated capacity.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Names a related setup item instead of the stated effect
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: Snowmelt can affect support, but the rule's stated concern is equipment stability and rated capacity, not mat sizing as such.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Confuses operating rule with maintenance concern
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: Cold and moisture do affect maintenance, but the weather rule is about stability and rated capacity, not wear items.
Force does not rise in a straight line with speed. Wind pressure goes with speed squared, so twice the speed gives about four times the force.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Uses the cube instead of the square
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: Eight times would be speed cubed, which applies to wind power, not force. Force goes with speed squared, so the answer is about four times.
No simple rule gives three times. Squaring the speed ratio of 2 gives 4.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Assumes limits refer to ground wind
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: Manufacturers' wind limits usually refer to wind at or near the boom tip, where the wind acts on the boom and load. A ground reading isn't the governing value.
Buildings can cause local swirls, but wind speed generally increases with height above ground friction. A ground reading tends to understate the wind at the tip.
Averaging hides gusts and still measures the wrong height. Averaging doesn't fix a reading taken at the wrong elevation.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Judges wind risk by weight alone
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: Wind load depends on surface area, not weight. A light panel with a large face can swing, side-load the boom and exceed limits that the weight alone would never reach.
Tag lines help control rotation, but workers can't hold back the wind force on a 400 sq ft panel. They don't change the wind limit.
No such universal rule exists. The allowable wind for a large-area load comes from the manufacturer's information, applied by the competent person.

weather.competent-person.misconception: Thinks ice on the machine is ignored
weather.competent-person.why_wrong: Ice on the boom and block adds weight that the chart doesn't include. That weight uses up capacity and affects stability.

weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: The rigger is responsible for the rigging, not for the weather's effect on crane stability. The weather duty belongs to the competent person.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Duty assigned to the signal person
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: The signal person passes signals to the operator. Deciding how weather changes the crane's setup and operation is the competent person's job.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Duty assigned to the equipment owner
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: Owning the crane does not make someone responsible for adjusting for site weather. The rule names the competent person.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Shorter interval timed from the visible flash
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: Flashes are often hidden by daylight or cloud, and 15 minutes is too short. The guidance counts 30 minutes from the last thunder.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Timing the wait from the rain
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: Lightning often strikes before rain arrives and after it stops, so rain is not the measure. The recommended minimum is 30 minutes after the last thunder.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Treating wind as the lightning signal
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: Wind is not a measure of lightning risk. The wait is 30 minutes counted from the last thunder heard.
Fog limits visibility, but this paragraph does not name it. The paragraph names wind, ice and snow.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Assuming lightning is named in the paragraph
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: Lightning is a serious hazard, but this paragraph does not name rain or lightning. It names wind, ice and snow.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Confusing temperature practice with the rule text
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: Temperature and lightning are handled through the manual and accepted practice. This paragraph names wind, ice and snow.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Believing charts include an ice allowance
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: Load charts assume a clean boom. No allowance for ice is built in, so ice uses up part of the capacity margin.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Treating ice as only a controls problem
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: A function test can show stiff controls, but it cannot show the added structural weight and wind area. Those affect stability and capacity.
Lightning can strike miles ahead of a storm. Hearing thunder is the signal to stop, not seeing flashes close by.
The cab is attached to a tall steel structure that attracts strikes, and the current can pass through the crane. Lightning guidance says to leave the crane.
A field ground rod does not protect the operator from a direct strike or the current spreading through the ground. The crew must stop and take shelter.
Loading the system while the oil is cold risks pump damage and jerky, uncontrolled motion. The oil should be warmed first, without a load.

weather.lightning-temperature.misconception: Engine warm-up mistaken for hydraulic warm-up
weather.lightning-temperature.why_wrong: Hydraulic response depends heavily on oil temperature. Warming the engine does not mean the hydraulic oil is warm.

weather.severe-service.why_wrong: Confirmed damage is not required. A reasonable probability of damage or excessive wear triggers the requirements.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Treating every possibility as the trigger
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: The rule specifies a reasonable probability, not any conceivable possibility. The severity of the actual use or conditions matters.
Visible evidence is not required. Conditions can establish a reasonable probability of damage before damage is visible.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Assigning inspection by operating experience alone
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: Having operated the crane does not establish qualification for this inspection. The inspection must be performed by a qualified person.
Scheduling authority does not establish qualification for this inspection. The rule requires a qualified person.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Assuming every service mechanic is qualified
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: A service assignment alone does not satisfy the requirement. A mechanic may perform the inspection if qualified for it.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Substituting operating feel for inspection judgment
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: The operator's observations may be useful, but they do not replace the qualified person's determination based on the severe use or conditions.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Using the inspection calendar to set scope
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: Time until a scheduled inspection does not determine the additional scope. The qualified person must assess the severe use or conditions.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Substituting maintenance scheduling for inspection scope
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: A maintenance schedule does not replace the required assessment of the severe use or conditions by a qualified person.
Calmer wind does not resolve possible damage from the shock. The employer must stop use and a qualified person must perform the required inspection.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Using a trial lift to clear suspected damage
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: A reduced-load trial lift is not a substitute for the required severe-service inspection by a qualified person.
The employer must not wait for confirmation of an overload. The stated reasonable probability of damage already triggers the requirements.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Treating corrosion exposure as maintenance only
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: Cleaning and lubrication do not replace the required inspection after the severe-service trigger is met.

weather.severe-service.misconception: Substituting a visual check and derating
weather.severe-service.why_wrong: An operator's visual check and reduced loads do not substitute for the severe-service inspection by a qualified person.
The rule does not require visible corrosion before acting. The reasonable probability of excessive wear already triggers inspection.
A surface-only inspection does not satisfy the requirement to inspect the equipment for structural damage and determine whether safe use can continue.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Confuses qualified person with competent person
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: A qualified person (someone with a degree, certificate or extensive experience) handles engineering-type tasks. The storm-warning decision belongs to the competent person.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Assigns the decision to the operator
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: The operator carries out the securing steps, but the rule does not make the operator the one who decides. The competent person makes that call.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Assigns the duty to the site controlling entity
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: The controlling entity coordinates the site, but the storm-warning rule names the competent person, not the controlling entity.
Wind speed limits come from the manufacturer's information for each configuration. The storm-warning rule is triggered by a warning, not by a set wind speed.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Mixes lightning practice into the storm rule
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: Lightning distance is a separate safety practice. The storm-warning rule is triggered only when a local storm warning is issued.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Confuses a broad watch with a local warning
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: The rule refers to a local storm warning. A broad, statewide watch is not the trigger the rule names.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Treats one possible step as the rule itself
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: Lowering the boom may be one of the manufacturer's securing steps, but the rule requires a decision about the manufacturer's recommendations, not an automatic boom-down.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Confuses equipment securing with emergency evacuation
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: The rule is about securing the equipment. It does not require the competent person to decide on a site evacuation.
Wind derating comes from the manufacturer's data for the configuration. The storm-warning rule is about the manufacturer's securing recommendations.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Field myth that a steep boom is safest
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: A high boom angle with the boom extended keeps a long boom exposed to the wind and can risk a backward tip-over. It is not what this manual calls for.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Thinks setting the brakes is enough
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: Brakes alone don't reduce the boom's exposure to wind. The manufacturer's procedure in this manual calls for retracting and lowering the boom.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Improvised tie-off instead of the manual's procedure
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: Tying the boom to a structure is not a manufacturer's securing method. It can side-load the boom and damage both the crane and the structure.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Relies on tag lines in high wind
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: Tag lines can't hold back a wind-loaded panel, and they keep workers next to a swinging load. Land the panel instead.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Thinks a shorter radius solves wind load
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: A shorter radius doesn't stop the wind from pushing the panel or side-loading the boom. The load is still in the air as the weather gets worse.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Thinks a low suspended load is safe
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: A panel hanging low is still a sail. It can swing into the crew and still puts wind load on the crane.

weather.storm-warning.misconception: Assigns the duty to the controlling entity
weather.storm-warning.why_wrong: The controlling entity runs the site, but the storm-warning rule names the competent person as the one who decides.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Operator role substituted for competent person
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: Being the assigned operator does not by itself establish this responsibility; the rule assigns it to the competent person.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Rigging qualification substituted for competent person
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: The rule assigns the adjustment responsibility to the competent person, not to someone solely because that person is the qualified rigger.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Signal duties confused with weather responsibility
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: Directing crane movements as the signal person does not establish this responsibility; the competent person must make the adjustments.
Wind force varies with speed squared, so doubling speed produces four times the force, not twice the force.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Adding the speed increase to the original force
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: The relationship is squared rather than additive: twice the speed produces four times the force.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Wind force confused with a cubic relationship
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: Eight times would follow a cubic relationship; wind force follows a squared relationship under these assumptions.
More projected area increases wind force; doubling the area doubles the force.
Projected area enters the wind-force relationship directly, not squared.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Wind speed treated as the only variable
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: Constant wind speed does not mean constant force when the area facing the wind changes.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Boom position substituted for actual load position
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: The load's weight acts at its displaced position; unchanged boom position does not preserve the weight's moment arm.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Inclined line assumed to reduce supported weight
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: The line's vertical force must still support the weight, while the weight acts farther from the crane.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Weight treated as the only stability variable
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: Moment depends on both weight and its horizontal distance from the reference point.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Vertical capacity margin treated as side-load allowance
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: A vertical capacity margin cannot be converted pound for pound into a sideways force allowance.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Flexible rope assumed to isolate sideways force
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: The hoist line transmits tension to the boom tip, including the horizontal component created by its sideways angle.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: No movement mistaken for no horizontal force
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: A stationary panel can remain under wind force; a tilted line then transmits a steady horizontal component to the boom.

weather.wind-effects.misconception: Static balance mistaken for tension equal to weight
weather.wind-effects.why_wrong: Motionless means the forces balance; the line must balance both the downward weight and the horizontal wind force.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Assigning operating compliance to the controlling entity
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: This provision assigns compliance with manufacturer operating procedures to the employer, rather than to the controlling entity solely because it controls the site.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Transferring employer responsibility to the lift planner
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: A qualified person's planning role does not replace the employer's duty to comply with applicable manufacturer procedures.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Confusing the person operating with the party assigned the duty
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: The operator applies operating procedures, but this federal provision places the compliance duty on the employer.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Confusing west with the north reference
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: North is reported as 360 degrees. A direction of 270 degrees indicates wind from the west.
Wind traveling toward the west comes from the east and is reported as 90 degrees.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Confusing the compass bearing and direction convention
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: Wind traveling toward the north comes from the south and is reported as 180 degrees.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Treating wind force as proportional to speed
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: Twice the force assumes a linear relationship. The speed factor must be squared, giving four times the force.
There is no threefold multiplier for doubling speed under these conditions. The multiplier is 2 squared, or 4.
Eight times results from cubing the speed factor. Wind force uses the square, giving four times the force.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Substituting average wind for gust speed
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: An average can conceal a gust above the limit. These operating instructions specify gust speed.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Using a momentary reading to disregard a gust
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: A current reading below the limit does not cancel the measured peak during the check. The gust criterion governs.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Treating a lull as permission to lift
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: A lull is not the measurement specified by the operating instructions. Waiting for a low instantaneous reading does not satisfy a gust limit.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Treating a sheltered reading as site-wide wind
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: The building can shelter the handheld meter. That reading need not represent wind at the exposed boom.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Correcting away a real exposure difference
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: A valid local measurement is not corrected downward simply to match a sheltered meter. Height and exposure can produce a real difference.
Averaging two different exposures does not establish the wind acting at the boom. The locations measure different conditions.

weather.wind-indicator.misconception: Using load weight as a substitute for wind area
weather.wind-indicator.why_wrong: Equal weight does not establish equal aerodynamic force. With the other factors unchanged, force increases with exposed area.

wire-rope.clip-count.misconception: Clip belongs on the part that carries load
wire-rope.clip-count.why_wrong: A clip on the live line puts a crushing, load-bearing fitting on the part of the rope carrying the load. The rule allows clips on the unloaded dead end only.

wire-rope.clip-count.misconception: Field habit of clipping tail to live line
wire-rope.clip-count.why_wrong: Clipping the tail to the live line is the field habit this rule bans. It loads the clip and can damage the live line. Clips go on the unloaded dead end only.
Correct torque does not make a clip legal on the live line. Location is set by the rule: the unloaded dead end only.
This is the reversed installation. It puts the U-bolt's crushing bearing on the live rope and lowers termination efficiency. The saddle goes on the live end.
Alternating the clips leaves some U-bolts crushing the live rope. Every clip must have its saddle on the live end.
Saddle position depends on which part carries load, not on how the eye is oriented. The saddle always goes on the live end.

wire-rope.clip-count.misconception: Long free spans get most wear
wire-rope.clip-count.why_wrong: Straight runs are observed but are not a listed critical review item. The list includes terminal ends, reverse bends on boom hoists and drum crossover points.
The listed drum items are flange points, crossover points and repetitive pickup points, not rope in the middle of the drum.
The listed sheave item is rope on saddles, equalizer sheaves or other sheaves where rope travel is limited, not sheaves where the rope travels freely.
Three is the table value for small ropes only (1/2 and 5/8 in). The required count goes up with rope size. There is no single minimum for every size.
225 ft-lb is the 7/8 in value. Over-torquing does not replace a missing clip and can crush the rope. The 3/4 in termination needs 4 clips at 130 ft-lb.
18 in is the required turnback for 3/4 in rope anyway, so it is needed in addition to the fourth clip, not instead of it.
Category III covers items like a broken strand or power line contact. Improperly applied end connections are listed in Category I, which calls for a hazard determination.
A Category I deficiency cannot wait for the monthly inspection. The determination must be made immediately at the shift inspection.
At the shift inspection, the competent person makes the immediate determination. The qualified person and annual inspection are a different inspection level.
That is the thimble value. The chart note requires one more clip when the rope goes around a sheave, for 4 total.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Confuses strand lay with rope lay
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: This is the strand lay, meaning wires turning around the strand's center. The rope lay follows a strand around the whole rope, which is a longer distance.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Measures crest-to-crest instead of a full revolution
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: Going from one crest to the next adjacent crest covers only part of a lay. On a six-strand rope it is about one-sixth of a lay. One full lay ends where the same strand comes back around.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Borrows the rotation resistant counting length
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: Six rope diameters is the counting length for rotation resistant rope. It is not the definition of a rope lay, and a lay's length depends on how the rope is built.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Applies rotation resistant limits to standard rope
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: These counts apply to rotation resistant rope. A standard 6x19 running rope is counted per rope lay.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Applies standing rope limits to running rope
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: These limits are for pendants and standing ropes, not for running hoist rope.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Mixes counting lengths between rope types
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: This mixes up the counting lengths. For running rope, both counts are measured within one rope lay, not 30 diameters.
