wire-rope.construction.misconception: Applies the rotation resistant rule to standard rope
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: Core protrusion is Category III only in rotation resistant rope. In standard rope it falls under the Category I distortion list.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Assumes all wear findings are Category II
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: Category II covers broken-wire counts and diameter loss. Core protrusion is listed as a structural distortion in Category I.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Field myth that steel cores can show without concern
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: Core protrusion is not normal wear. The rule lists steel core protrusion between the outer strands as a significant distortion.
Six random breaks is one of two separate tests. Meeting the one-strand test of three breaks is enough by itself.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Treats broken wires as a broken strand
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: A broken strand means the whole strand has parted. Three broken wires in a strand is a Category II broken-wire count.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Assigns the running rope test to standing rope
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: The three-in-one-strand test is part of the running rope criterion. Pendants use a different count.
The next crest belongs to a different strand. That distance is only about one-sixth of a lay on a six-strand rope.
Six diameters is the counting length for rotation resistant rope, not the definition of a rope lay.

wire-rope.construction.misconception: Applies the standard running rope limit
wire-rope.construction.why_wrong: Six per lay is the limit for standard running rope. Rotation resistant rope has its own lower count based on rope diameters.
For rotation resistant rope, Category III covers core failure, not a single broken wire. Broken-wire counts are Category II.

wire-rope.designations.why_wrong: That treats a classification as an exact construction. The class includes several wire counts.
This reverses strands and wires. The first number identifies the six outer strands.
That wire-count range belongs to the 6 × 37 classification.

wire-rope.designations.misconception: Regular lay confused with Lang lay
wire-rope.designations.why_wrong: Matching right-hand directions describe right Lang lay.
Matching left-hand directions describe left Lang lay.
Opposite directions with left-hand strands describe left regular lay.
Ten is the minimum outer-strand count for Type II, not Type I.

wire-rope.designations.misconception: Total strands confused with outer strands
wire-rope.designations.why_wrong: The Type I minimum is 15. A rope's total strand count must not be mistaken for its outer-strand count.

wire-rope.designations.misconception: Familiar construction count treated as threshold
wire-rope.designations.why_wrong: Twelve outer strands do not meet the Type I minimum of 15.
That is a fiber core, designated FC, rather than IWRC.

wire-rope.designations.misconception: Wire strand core confused with IWRC
wire-rope.designations.why_wrong: A wire strand core is not an independent wire rope core.

wire-rope.designations.misconception: Steel core assumed to be solid
wire-rope.designations.why_wrong: IWRC is a rope made of strands, not a solid steel center.
IPS and EIPS identify grades. Core construction is identified separately, such as FC or IWRC.
Grade does not identify strand direction. Right or left lay identifies that feature.
The strength ranking is reversed: EIPS is higher than IPS.

wire-rope.designations.misconception: Below-five use treated as universally prohibited
wire-rope.designations.why_wrong: An isolated, non-duty-cycle lift is not prohibited solely because the Type III design factor is 4, provided the exception's requirements are met.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: The stated federal minimum is two full wraps. Three wraps may satisfy that minimum, but it is not the number required by this provision.
Four full wraps exceed the stated minimum. The provision requires at least two, not four.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Confusing wrap count with a design factor
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: Five is not the minimum wrap count in this provision. The required minimum is two full wraps.
The drum minimum for this exception is 18 times nominal rope diameter. Sixteen does not meet it.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Treating a larger acceptable ratio as the minimum
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: A ratio of 20:1 exceeds the minimum, but the required minimum is 18:1.
A ratio of 17:1 falls below the required 18:1 minimum.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Limiting the rule by mounting location
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: The requirement includes all sheaves in the system, including those mounted elsewhere.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Applying the minimum only at drum entry
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: The lead sheave is covered, but the same minimum also applies to every other sheave in the boom-hoist reeving system.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Limiting the rule to multiple-part reeving
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: The requirement covers all sheaves in the boom-hoist reeving system, not only those associated with multiple-part reeving.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Reversing the effect of a larger moment arm
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: At fixed torque, a larger radius reduces force. Line pull equals drum torque divided by the rope's effective drum radius.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Equating constant torque with constant force
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: Constant torque does not mean constant line pull when radius changes. Dividing the same torque by a larger radius gives less pull.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Using rope diameter instead of winding radius
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: Unchanged rope diameter does not keep the winding radius constant. Each added layer moves the rope farther from the drum axis.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Applying a 16:1 minimum to this exception
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: The calculated ratio is 16 ÷ 1 = 16:1, but the required minimum for this configuration is 18:1.
The calculation uses nominal rope diameter, not rope radius. Dividing 16 inches by 1 inch gives 16:1, which is below 18:1.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Reaching the right disposition with the wrong limit
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: The drum does fail, but the required minimum is 18:1, not 20:1.

wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.misconception: Treating wire rope like cable that can be pulled over-end
wire-rope.drum-and-sheaves.why_wrong: Pulling rope over the flange of a stationary reel can introduce twist. Pay the rope off a rotating reel while controlling its tension.

wire-rope.drum-wraps.misconception: Thinks one wrap anchors the rope
wire-rope.drum-wraps.why_wrong: One wrap is not enough. The rule sets the minimum at two full wraps on each drum.

wire-rope.drum-wraps.misconception: Confuses a common field habit with the rule
wire-rope.drum-wraps.why_wrong: Three wraps meets the rule, but it is not the federal minimum. The minimum is two full wraps.
Five wraps is far more than required. The minimum is two full wraps.
The rule names both the load and the boom, each on its own drum, so it is not limited to the main load drum.

wire-rope.drum-wraps.misconception: Applies only with load on hook
wire-rope.drum-wraps.why_wrong: The boom hoist drum is covered even when nothing hangs from the hook.
The rule makes no exception for drums with limit devices. The two-wrap minimum still applies.
Spooling quality depends on fleet angle and tension. The minimum wraps exist to protect the anchorage.
The design factor comes from rope strength compared with line pull. Wraps left on the drum do not add strength.
Reverse bending comes from the reeving path over sheaves. Wraps on the drum do not prevent it.

wire-rope.drum-wraps.misconception: No hook load means no rule
wire-rope.drum-wraps.why_wrong: A spotter does not change the minimum, and the boom's own weight still loads the boom hoist rope.

wire-rope.drum-wraps.misconception: Wrong person can waive the rule
wire-rope.drum-wraps.why_wrong: The rule has no exception for assembly or disassembly, and the A/D director cannot waive it.
The wraps are counted on each drum. A full main drum does nothing for the whip drum that is lowering the load.
The minimum is two full wraps on every drum. The whip line has no special three-wrap rule.
The rule does not depend on load weight. Two full wraps are required no matter what the load weighs.
With the hook raised, the drum holds the most rope. That check proves nothing about the lowest point.
Ground level at the setup is above the pit bottom. The hook will travel lower than that during the lift.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: More frequent interval mistaken for minimum
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: The required minimum is monthly. A weekly schedule exceeds this paragraph's minimum.
Quarterly inspection leaves too much time between thorough inspections; the minimum is monthly.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Annual crane inspection substituted for rope inspection
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: Annual inspection does not satisfy the monthly rope inspection requirement.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Operator certification automatically confers inspection authority
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: Operator certification alone does not establish appointment or authorization to perform these inspections.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Maintenance assignment automatically confers inspection authority
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: A maintenance assignment alone does not establish appointment or authorization for rope inspection.
This paragraph specifies an appointed or authorized person; it does not substitute a rigging credential for that status.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Operator signs in place of inspector
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: The required signature belongs to the person who performed the inspection, who may be someone other than the operator.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Rope specification substituted for rope identity
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: Rated breaking strength does not replace an identifier for the inspected ropes.
The record must include the inspector's signature; a name entry alone does not satisfy that requirement.
Heavy wear and broken wires may occur at limited-travel sheaves. Limited movement is not grounds for reduced attention.
Lubrication does not replace the particular care required when inspecting rope at these locations.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Special inspection location treated as automatic rejection
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: This provision requires particular inspection care, not automatic replacement merely because rope travel is limited.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Broken wires required before strength is questioned
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: Broken outside wires are not necessary for diameter reduction from core support loss to be a strength concern.
Greasing does not establish that lost core support or the resulting diameter reduction is safe for continued use.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Internal diameter loss treated as normal seating
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: An internal cause does not make diameter reduction acceptable; loss of core support is specifically listed.

wire-rope.general-industry.misconception: Sound wires prove a sound termination
wire-rope.general-industry.why_wrong: Sound adjacent wires do not establish that a cracked end connection is safe. The connection itself is a listed concern.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Thinks the criteria cover only running ropes
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: Paragraph (b) covers all wire rope except rotation resistant rope, so standing ropes such as pendants are included.
A standard running rope on the whip line is covered. Only rotation resistant rope is carved out, no matter which drum it is on.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Reverses the scope of the rule
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: Standard main hoist rope is the most typical rope these criteria cover.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Treats hoist line pull as the rope design basis
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: Maximum line pull is a hoist (drum) rating. It is a different thing from the rope's rated strength, and Option (2) measures the rope against the equipment's rated capacity, not the hoist pull.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Sizes rope to the job instead of the machine
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: Rope design is based on what the equipment is rated to lift, not on one job's planned loads.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Confuses hydraulic stall pull with rated capacity
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: Stall pull is a hydraulic system limit, not the reference in Option (2). Rope must be sufficient for the equipment's rated capacity.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Confuses higher line speed with higher pull
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: The outermost layer has the largest radius, so the same torque gives the least pull there, although line speed is highest.
Pull drops steadily as the radius grows. It does not peak in the middle of the drum.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Treats line pull as a single fixed number
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: Torque is fixed, but pull is torque divided by radius, so pull changes with every layer. That is why line pull charts list values by layer.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Treats max line pull as the rope's rating
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: The hoist can pull 12,000 lb, but the rope is only rated for 10,000 lb. The hoist rating does not raise the rope's limit.
Limits are not averaged. The lower one controls, and 11,000 lb is still 1,000 lb over the rope's allowable pull.

wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.misconception: Spends the design factor as capacity
wire-rope.line-pull-vs-swl.why_wrong: The design factor is already built into the 10,000-lb allowable pull. It covers wear, shock and inspection margin and is not extra capacity to use.
The first-layer rating applies only when rope is coming off the first layer. On the third layer the hoist can pull just 12,000 lb.
The rope could take 13,000 lb, but on the third layer the hoist can deliver only 12,000 lb, so the hoist is the lower limit.
The fourth-layer value applies only when rope is working on the fourth layer. Using it here underrates the crane for no reason.
The hook block hangs on the same lines. With it added, the total is 21,500 lb, which is more than 21,000 lb.

wire-rope.lubrication.misconception: Manual listing treated as the legal test
wire-rope.lubrication.why_wrong: The rule does not ban a lubricant for being left out of the manual. The test is whether it hinders inspection.

wire-rope.lubrication.misconception: Original-lubricant match treated as the rule
wire-rope.lubrication.why_wrong: Matching the rope maker's lubricant is good practice, but the rule's ban is on lubricants that hinder inspection, not on other brands.
The rule says nothing about where the lubricant goes on. Field lubrication is normal; the type of lubricant is what counts.
A straight, tensioned rope is closed up tight. Lubricant put on there mostly stays on the surface.
Lubricant does not wick along the full length of a rope from one end. Most of the rope would get none.
A slack rope does not open its strands the way bending over a sheave does, so penetration is poor.
A penetrating lubricant with a thin film is the kind that protects the rope and still lets you see the wires.

wire-rope.lubrication.misconception: Base stock treated as the test
wire-rope.lubrication.why_wrong: The base stock does not decide whether a lubricant hides the wires. What matters is the coating it leaves.
Needing frequent application is a maintenance cost. It does not block inspection.
How much protection the coating gives does not matter. A lubricant that hides the wires is prohibited.
No defect has been found yet. The first step is to clean the rope and inspect it, and the result decides whether it gets replaced.
Putting it off leaves a rope in service that can't be inspected. The shift inspection can't be done through that coating.
Weather protection does not override the ban. A thick opaque coat hides broken wires and corrosion.
Applying it right after an annual inspection does not help. Shift and monthly inspections still have to see the rope.
Lasting longer is a convenience, not a reason the rule accepts. Product X still hides the wires.
Straining takes out some solids but not the acids and moisture. Used oil is still not a suitable rope lubricant.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Confuses the extension limit with the regular interval
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: Six months is not the regular annual inspection interval. The regular maximum interval is 12 months.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Treats a conditional extension as the standard interval
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: An additional six months can apply to certain running-rope inspections when inspection is infeasible. It does not establish an ordinary 18-month interval.
The regular maximum interval is 12 months, not 24 months.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Equates operator certification with inspector qualification
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: Operator certification alone does not establish the required qualification. The annual inspection must be conducted by a qualified person.
Site authority alone does not satisfy the annual inspection requirement. A qualified person must conduct it.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Transfers assembly responsibilities to annual inspection
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: Designation as the assembly director alone does not establish qualification for this inspection. The annual wire rope inspector must be a qualified person.
The interval is each month, not every three months. Shift results do not lengthen it.
The requirement uses a monthly interval, not an operating-hour threshold.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Treats monthly inspection as a defect-triggered inspection
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: Monthly inspection is not triggered only by a reported deficiency. It must occur each month.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Leaves annual findings on an annual schedule
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: Waiting until the next annual inspection misses the required monthly checks.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Treats every deficiency as a removal condition
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: This finding requires monitoring, not automatic replacement. The qualified person determined that it is not presently a safety hazard.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Makes monitoring dependent on a new report
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: An operator's report does not control when the required monitoring occurs. The deficiency must be checked monthly.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Substitutes a function check for inspection clearance
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: An unloaded cycle does not establish the required monthly inspection result. The inspection must demonstrate that no corrective action is required.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Uses supervisory permission to bypass clearance
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: Restricted lifting authorized by a supervisor does not satisfy the inspection requirement. The unresolved condition must be addressed before use.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Defers clearance to a future inspection
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: Scheduling a later review does not authorize current use. The monthly inspection must first demonstrate that no corrective action is required.

wire-rope.monthly-annual.misconception: Applies routine visibility limits to annual inspection
wire-rope.monthly-annual.why_wrong: Normal operating exposure does not define the annual inspection's coverage. The surface of the entire rope length must be inspected.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Thinks a chart deduction removes weight from the rope
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: Block weight is a deduction from chart capacity, but it is also on the rope. The rope parts carry the block too, so it belongs in the parts-of-line total as well.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Leaves the hook block out of the suspended weight
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The hook block hangs on the rope parts like everything else. Leaving it out understates the tension on each part.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Uses chart capacity instead of actual suspended weight
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: Chart capacity is the most the crane may lift, not the weight actually on the rope. Parts of line are figured from the actual suspended weight.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Applies ordinary rounding to a minimum requirement
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: Normal rounding doesn't apply here. Rounding 4.3 down to 4 overloads every part by about 8 percent.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Treats the design factor as usable margin
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The design factor is already built into the allowable line pull. It is not extra capacity the rigger can spend.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Believes reeving must be an even number of parts
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: Odd reeving is normal: the dead end simply anchors at the block instead of the boom head. You round up to the next whole part, not the next even number.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Uses the hoist rating when the rope is weaker
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The drum can pull 12,000 lb, but this rope is only good for 10,000 lb. Using the drum rating overloads the rope.
Limits are never averaged. The lower of the two always governs.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Treats the design factor as spare capacity
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The design factor is already part of the rope's 10,000 lb allowable load. It does not let the rope run up to the drum rating.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Leaves out the block and rigging
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: This leaves out the 1,000 lb of block and rigging. With them included, 4 parts would carry 8,250 lb each.
The total is correct, but rounding down puts each part over its allowable pull. A minimum always rounds up.
Five parts already keep every part within the allowable pull. There is no rule to add a spare part on top of that.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Forgets to subtract the hook block
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: 45,000 lb is everything the parts can hold, block included. The block weight has to come out of that.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Thinks the dead-end part carries no load
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: Every part between the boom head and the block carries load, including the part that ends at the dead end. All six count.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Adds the block instead of subtracting it
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: The block uses up capacity, so its weight is subtracted, not added.

wire-rope.parts-of-line.misconception: Treats a successful test lift as proof of capacity
wire-rope.parts-of-line.why_wrong: A test lift that succeeds does not show the rope has its required design margin. It only shows the rope did not break that one time.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Exception applied to the wrong crane type
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: Crawler cranes get no exception. Their boom hoist reeving may not use fiber core rope.
Many hydraulic cranes use cylinders to raise the boom, but the ban on fiber core boom hoist rope still covers any boom hoist reeving. Only derricks are exempt.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Borrows the fiber core derrick exception
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: The derrick exception belongs to the fiber core rule in (d)(1). The rotation resistant rule points to (e)(4)(ii) instead.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Treats a conditional allowance as a ban
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: The rule does not ban it outright. It allows rotation resistant rope on a boom hoist when the (e)(4)(ii) conditions are met.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Diameter fit treated as the only test
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: Matching diameter is necessary, but it is not the condition the rule sets. Rotation resistant boom hoist rope must meet the (e)(4)(ii) requirements.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Thinks the fixed end carries no load
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: A dead end on the hook block becket runs up to a boom head sheave and holds up the block, so it counts as a part.
Every segment between the boom head and the block supports load, center ones included, so all of them count.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Confuses reeving order with load support
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: That segment runs between the two blocks and holds up the hook, so it is a counted part.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Diameter treated as the only requirement
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: Diameter alone does not decide it. Fiber core rope is barred from this boom hoist no matter what size it is.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Maintenance step treated as a workaround
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: Lubrication does not lift the ban. Only derricks are exempt.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Approval by a qualified person overrides the rule
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: No one's approval creates an exception. The rule allows fiber core boom hoist rope only on derricks.
This is 36,000 ÷ 5, which leaves out the block and rigging. The rope carries their weight too, so the total is 40,000 lb.
This is 40,000 ÷ 4, which counts one part too few. The reeving has 5 parts.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Divided by sheaves instead of parts
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: This divides by the 2 sheaves in a 5-part block instead of by the 5 parts holding the load.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Even-part rule applied to odd parts
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: A boom head dead end gives an even number of parts. That is right for 4 or 6 parts but not for 5.

wire-rope.reeving.misconception: Confuses lead end with dead end
wire-rope.reeving.why_wrong: The drum anchor holds the live (lead) end of the rope, not the dead end.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: Breaking strength does not decide this. Fiber core rope is barred from boom hoist reeving on cranes whatever its rated strength.
No parts-of-line limit unlocks fiber core rope. The prohibition covers all boom hoist reeving except on derricks.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Synthetic core treated as a steel core
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: The prohibition covers fiber core rope in general. A synthetic core is still a fiber core and still crushes under boom hoist loading.
The rule does not ban rotation-resistant rope from boom hoists. It allows that use once the stated added requirements are met.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Fiber core exception applied to the wrong rope
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: The derrick exception belongs to the fiber core rule. Rotation-resistant boom hoist rope has its own conditional allowance that is not limited to derricks.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Reeving geometry treated as the condition
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: Parts count is not the condition. Rotation-resistant rope on a boom hoist is allowed only when the specific added requirements are met.
This has the rule backward. Even parts end at the boom head and odd parts end at the hook block.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Part count size instead of odd/even
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: The size of the count does not matter, only whether it is odd or even. Five parts ends at the hook block.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Dead-end location seen as a free choice
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: The geometry fixes the location. Moving the dead end between head and block changes the part count by one.
This leaves out the 4,000 lb block and rigging. The rope carries everything below the boom head, which is 40,000 lb.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Counted the lead line as an extra part
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: The lead line to the drum is one of the 4 parts, not an extra fifth line. 40,000 / 4 = 10,000 lb.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Divided by sheaves instead of parts
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: Load is shared by the rope parts between head and block, not by the number of sheaves in the block. Four parts give 10,000 lb each.
Overhaul weight helps the line pay out but does not fix uneven rope pull. The block will still tilt under load.
Rope stretch does not move pull from one side of the block to the other. Cycling a mis-reeved block only adds wear.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Wrong cause; crane level confused with block balance
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: The crane is already level on its mats, and crane level would not tilt the block relative to its own ropes. The reeving is the cause.

wire-rope.reeving-patterns.misconception: Part count treated as the only requirement
wire-rope.reeving-patterns.why_wrong: Enough parts does not make a non-manufacturer pattern acceptable. Sheave position affects balance, side load and rope wear.

wire-rope.removal-criteria.why_wrong: Three wraps is more than the rule requires. The requirement is two wraps at the lowest position.
The number is right but the position is wrong. With the hook at its highest position the most rope is on the drum, so checking there proves nothing. The check is made at the lowest position.
Five wraps is a field habit, not the rule. The rule sets two wraps at the lowest position.
The operator may spot the condition, but the rule gives the hazard determination to the competent person.
The rule does not require an engineer here. The competent person makes the immediate determination.

wire-rope.removal-criteria.misconception: duty assigned to the A/D director
wire-rope.removal-criteria.why_wrong: The A/D director runs assembly and disassembly. That role does not decide whether a rope deficiency is a hazard.

wire-rope.removal-criteria.misconception: crane manufacturer instead of rope manufacturer
wire-rope.removal-criteria.why_wrong: The crane manufacturer is the wrong source. An alternate criterion must be approved in writing by the wire rope manufacturer for that specific rope.

wire-rope.removal-criteria.misconception: duty assigned to the competent person
wire-rope.removal-criteria.why_wrong: The competent person cannot approve an alternate criterion. Only the wire rope manufacturer can, in writing, for that specific rope.
An engineer's approval does not meet the rule. Written approval must come from the wire rope manufacturer.

wire-rope.removal-criteria.misconception: Category I rule applied to Category III
wire-rope.removal-criteria.why_wrong: The hazard determination applies to Category I only. A Category III deficiency stops use until the rope is replaced or the defect is severed out.
Severing is allowed, but joining lengths of wire rope by splicing is prohibited.

wire-rope.removal-criteria.misconception: deferring removal to a later inspection
wire-rope.removal-criteria.why_wrong: Category III stops use of the rope right away. The rule gives no grace period until the next inspection.
Tagging out the whole crane is one allowed choice, but it is not required. The rule also allows tagging out only the hoist with the removed rope.

wire-rope.removal-criteria.misconception: tagging the rope instead of the hoist
wire-rope.removal-criteria.why_wrong: A tag on the rope itself does not meet the rule. The hoist or the whole equipment must be tagged out.
Finishing the lift means using a rope that must already be out of service. The tag-out applies as soon as removal is required.

wire-rope.removal-criteria.misconception: treating replacement as the only option
wire-rope.removal-criteria.why_wrong: Replacement is not the only path for Category II. The manufacturer's criterion, an approved alternate criterion, or severing a localized defect may also apply.

wire-rope.rotation-resistant.misconception: Type II strand count applied to Type I
wire-rope.rotation-resistant.why_wrong: At least 10 outer strands is the Type II definition. Type I requires at least 15.

wire-rope.rotation-resistant.misconception: Type III strand count applied to Type I
wire-rope.rotation-resistant.why_wrong: No more than nine outer strands defines Type III, the type with the least resistance to rotation, not Type I.
Eight is not a threshold in any of the three definitions. Type I needs at least 15 outer strands.

wire-rope.rotation-resistant.misconception: normal minimum mistaken for the absolute floor
wire-rope.rotation-resistant.why_wrong: 5 is the normal minimum for each type, but exceptions allow lower values down to the 3.5 floor.
4.0 is not a threshold for rotation-resistant rope. The absolute floor is 3.5.
3.0 is below the 3.5 floor that applies to every type of rotation-resistant rope.
16 is the ASME value for sheaves in multiple rope reeving. For this use the federal rule raises it to 18.
20 is not the stated value. The minimum is 18 times the nominal rope diameter.

wire-rope.rotation-resistant.misconception: strand count confused with D/d ratio
wire-rope.rotation-resistant.why_wrong: 15 is the Type I outer strand count, not a pitch diameter ratio. The drum needs at least 18 times.

wire-rope.rotation-resistant.misconception: single-lift conditions applied to repetitive work
wire-rope.rotation-resistant.why_wrong: Inspection before each lift is a condition for non-repetitive lifts only. It cannot make repetitive work acceptable below a factor of 5.

wire-rope.rotation-resistant.misconception: 3.5 floor treated as the only limit
wire-rope.rotation-resistant.why_wrong: 3.5 is the absolute floor, but Types II and III below 5 are still barred from repetitive lifts.
Type II below 5 is allowed for non-duty cycle, non-repetitive lifts when the per-lift conditions are met. The problem here is that the work is repetitive.
A shift inspection by a competent person is the general wire rope requirement. Reduced-factor lifts also need a qualified person's inspection for each lift.
A monthly inspection does not cover these lifts. Each lifting operation needs its own qualified person inspection, and the lifts are then recorded in the monthly and annual documents.

wire-rope.rotation-resistant.misconception: duty assigned to the wrong person
wire-rope.rotation-resistant.why_wrong: The inspection must be done by a qualified person. Unless the operator is a qualified person, the operator's check does not meet the requirement.

wire-rope.rotation-resistant.misconception: Type II/III exception applied to Type I
wire-rope.rotation-resistant.why_wrong: Inspection by a qualified person before each lift is the exception path for Types II and III. It does not apply to Type I.

wire-rope.shift-inspection.misconception: Rotation resistant limit applied to standard rope
wire-rope.shift-inspection.why_wrong: This is the limit for rotation resistant rope. Standard running rope uses the six-per-lay / three-per-strand count.

wire-rope.shift-inspection.misconception: Standing rope limit applied to running rope
wire-rope.shift-inspection.why_wrong: This is the limit for pendants and standing ropes. Running ropes use six randomly distributed wires per lay or three in one strand.
These numbers are too low. The running-rope limit is six randomly distributed wires in one lay, or three in one strand in one lay.
10% is too high. The threshold is more than 5% from nominal.
The baseline is the nominal diameter, not a diameter measured when the rope was installed.
The shift-inspection criterion is a percentage of nominal diameter (more than 5%), not a fixed fraction of an inch.

wire-rope.shift-inspection.misconception: Wrong person and overly strict timing
wire-rope.shift-inspection.why_wrong: The rule calls for a competent person, not a qualified person, and it allows the inspection to be finished during the shift.

wire-rope.shift-inspection.misconception: Duty assigned only to the operator
wire-rope.shift-inspection.why_wrong: Any competent person may do it, not only the operator, and it may be completed during the shift.
The person is correct, but the rule only requires the inspection to begin before the shift. It may be completed during the shift.
The six-per-lay count is for standard running rope. Rotation resistant rope has its own, lower limit.

wire-rope.shift-inspection.misconception: Overclassifying broken wires as core failure
wire-rope.shift-inspection.why_wrong: Category III for rotation resistant rope is core protrusion or distortion that shows core failure. Broken wires fall under Category II.
Category I distortion means kinking, crushing, birdcaging and similar damage. Visible broken wires are listed under Category II.

wire-rope.shift-inspection.misconception: Category I treated like Category III
wire-rope.shift-inspection.why_wrong: Category I does not remove the rope automatically. Removal depends on the competent person's immediate hazard determination.

wire-rope.shift-inspection.misconception: Category II remedy applied to Category I
wire-rope.shift-inspection.why_wrong: A removal criterion approved by the manufacturer in writing is one of the Category II options. It is not the first step for Category I.
The rule requires an immediate determination now. The deficiency cannot be put off until the monthly inspection.
Severing is allowed for localized Category III damage other than power line contact. This exception rules it out.

wire-rope.standing-ropes.why_wrong: Ten days is too short. The thorough inspection for idle rope starts at a month or more.
Six months is a common guess, but the requirement starts at one month of idle time, not half a year.
A quarterly interval is not the trigger. Any idle period of a month or more requires the thorough inspection.
A routine operator check does not replace this inspection. It must be done by an appointed or authorized person, and that person's approval is required.

wire-rope.standing-ropes.misconception: Confused with written manufacturer approval rule
wire-rope.standing-ropes.why_wrong: Nothing requires the manufacturer to take part. An appointed or authorized person does the inspection and gives the approval.
No engineer's stamp is required. The inspector is an appointed or authorized person, and that person's approval releases the rope.

wire-rope.standing-ropes.misconception: Measurement data mistaken for required content
wire-rope.standing-ropes.why_wrong: Diameter and hour-meter readings are not required items. The record needs the date, the inspector's signature, and an identifier for the rope.
Rope length and load-test results are not listed. The required items are the date, the signature, and a rope identifier.
The operator's name and the crane serial number are not required. The inspection date and the inspector's signature are, and this list leaves both out.
Mid-span is not where heavy wear and broken wires tend to build up. The rule points to sections at equalizer sheaves, limited-travel sheaves, and saddles.

wire-rope.standing-ropes.misconception: Running-rope wear pattern applied to standing ropes
wire-rope.standing-ropes.why_wrong: Drum sections do need inspection, but the special-care locations named for these ropes are equalizer sheaves, limited-travel sheaves, and saddles.

wire-rope.standing-ropes.misconception: Weather exposure mistaken for wear point
wire-rope.standing-ropes.why_wrong: Wind exposure is not the concern. Concentrated wear happens where rope contacts equalizer sheaves, limited-travel sheaves, or saddles.
A load test is not what idle rope requires. The requirement is a thorough inspection for all types of deterioration, with approval and a record.
Being idle does not automatically condemn the rope. It may be used again once the thorough inspection is done and an appointed or authorized person approves it.

wire-rope.standing-ropes.misconception: Tension level mistaken for the named rope type
wire-rope.standing-ropes.why_wrong: Pendants need careful inspection at saddles and fittings, but the rope type singled out for particular care is nonrotating rope.

wire-rope.standing-ropes.misconception: Line speed mistaken for inspection trigger
wire-rope.standing-ropes.why_wrong: Line speed is not the basis for the requirement. Particular care is required for nonrotating rope.

wire-rope.terminations.why_wrong: The rule specifies the unloaded dead end, not the loaded live end.

wire-rope.terminations.misconception: Conventional clipped eye applied to a wedge socket
wire-rope.terminations.why_wrong: Clipping both portions together engages the loaded rope. Ordinary clips must attach only to the unloaded dead end.
The installer cannot choose either portion. The attachment restriction specifically identifies the unloaded dead end.
The requirement identifies the wire rope or fitting manufacturer. It does not assign this instruction to the crane or hoist drum manufacturer.
The boom and head sheave manufacturers are not the sources identified for socketing instructions. The rule names the wire rope or fitting manufacturer.
Hook or load-block instructions do not establish the required socketing method. The rule identifies the wire rope or fitting manufacturer.

wire-rope.terminations.misconception: Only the usable rope needs seizing
wire-rope.terminations.why_wrong: Seizing only the retained side omits the other side. Both sides must have seizings before the cut.

wire-rope.terminations.misconception: Seizing is an after-cut finishing step
wire-rope.terminations.why_wrong: Installing seizings after the cut reverses the required order. They must be installed before cutting.

wire-rope.terminations.misconception: Seizing may follow the progress of the cut
wire-rope.terminations.why_wrong: Seizings must already be in place before cutting starts. Installing them during the cut is too late.
Adding a clip does not correct attachment to the loaded live end. Ordinary clips must engage only the unloaded dead end.

wire-rope.terminations.misconception: Distance from the socket controls compliance
wire-rope.terminations.why_wrong: Moving the clip leaves it joining the live and dead ends. The violation concerns which rope portion it engages.
Reversing the clip still leaves it attached to the loaded rope. Orientation does not remove the dead-end-only restriction.
A familiar shop procedure is not controlling merely because the rope diameter matches. It must satisfy the applicable manufacturer's socketing instructions.
The operator's preference does not establish the required socketing method. The rule identifies the wire rope or fitting manufacturer's instructions.
A procedure selected for similar fittings does not replace the applicable manufacturer's specified method.
Equal total seizing length does not satisfy the specified number. The instructions require two 2-inch seizings on each side.
